INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. That is this Exhibit 806. You have one Georgia mill reported here.
Answer. I knew that.
Question. But I don't see any North Carolina mill. Well, are those Is that Georgia mill, for instance, the Hodgson Oil Refining Co., is it a member of the South Carolina Division?
Answer. It is not. It is a member of the Georgia division.
Question. Does it report prices to the South Carolina division?
Answer. It does not.
Question. It buys seed in South Carolina?
Answer. It hasn't this year or last.
Question. Did it report prices last season?
Answer. It did not.
Question. Well, this is just a matter of comity, would you say between the mills that come into the State, in the South Carolina division, of reporting their prices to you?
Answer. In this particular instance, the man referred to travels and is not located at any particular point. He picks up seed where he can find it for Hodgson mill, and that is the reason Mr. Hodgson reported it to this division, because he might buy some seed over here and the principal could be located, in case he did.
Question. Well, would that involve a report being made of the prices paid in South Carolina?
Answer. It might, if he reported, if someone reported, that this buyer was paying a higher or a lower price in the State than was published by the mills in this State someone would notify my office that this man was buying seed at a certain price and they would want to know whom he represented. I would then know, and I would be able to wire Mr. Hodgson: "What is your last paid price at such-and-such a point?" Question. Just while we are on that point-when mills from outside the State buy in South Carolina, do they report the prices paid to you?
Answer. They do. I had an instance of it this morning.
Question. Do you know whether when South Carolina mills buy in North Carolina or Georgia, as I assume they do sometimes, whether they report to the secretaries of the divisions in those States?
Answer. They do.
Question. Is there any provision or rule regarding that matter?
Is it just a matter of custom-or how? What is the foundation for it, in other words?
Answer. Why, section 2, I think it is, in Group I, of the Federal trade practice rules (I don't know what you call them-the Memphis trade practice rules) provides that you must publish the prices.
It doesn't say you must publish them in South Carolina and not in Georgia, but wherever you buy, you must publish.
Question. It would be possible for a Georgia mill to buy in South Carolina and publish the South Carolina price with the Georgia secretary?
Answer. Some do that way and then the Secretary transmits it to the other State, but I have been fortunate enough to have the mills who buy in this State report to me.

Answer. I will identify them as coming from my files.
Mr. WOODEN. I offer them for the record.

Answer. I therefore took it up with Mr. Marsh and asked him to have all of his mills list their 50-cent buyers in South Carolina, and if any of them had high commission agreements with them, to list those, but I never got any reply from Mr. Marsh.

Answer. The party that was supposed to be getting a dollar was Dr. Wade Stackhouse of Dillon.

Answer. I think it was under our code.

Answer. Any commission over and above the published price or the paid price of the mill would be something that was being concealed-anything above the paid price.

Examiner SHEPPARD. Mr. Taylor, right here, I want to ask you to get the matter straight in my mind. When the Memphis code was approved, did it supersede your working rules here in South Carolina?
The WITNESS. No, sir; I think that the Memphis code was largely based upon the trade practice that were in existence in this State, and others, and they were largely based upon the Federal Food Commission-what do you call it? The Federal Food Administration.
Examiner SHEPPARD. During the war?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY The WITNESS. During the war. And there were some practices that had grown up that were considered unethical, discussed at that meeting and were thrown out, or ruled against, and those that were good, I think, were adopted.
Examiner SHEPPARD. Then your old South Carolina rules are still in force?
The WITNESS. They are, yes; with some amendments.
By Mr. WOODEN: Question. Didn't you have some rules, trading rules, of the old South Carolina association prior to the war?
Answer. Not as specific as you have in the present rules.
Question. But you had some covering the same general topics and subjects?
Answer. Yes, we had our rules about how much commission to pay, and how much to pay for seedhouses and scales, such things as that, how much to allow for loss in weight and how to grade seed.
I think that was about all.
Question. Did you have a provision for reporting prices similar to that which was adopted under the Memphis rules?
Answer. I think I might explain it in this way. That for many years, and up to November, 1929, it was a common practice of the mills to publish and quote the current prices or whatever was being offered by mills for seed. The present practice, of course, only allows us to report paid prices. We did publish, as I say, up to November of last year, the current prices for seed. We no longer do so.
Question. Was there any difference in the method of reporting current prices in the old association and what existed, you might say, the first few months of the division operations?
Answer. Our old practice was to receive from a mill a telegram or telephone message, or a copy of a written quotation saying that I am bidding so much for seed and that would be passed to the bidding mills in various and sundry ways, but not made public, that is, to the general public, and the mills would then use their judgment as to whether they would meet this price or issue some other price and in that way the publication of prices was carried on. And about once a week a circular letter was sent out giving the prevailing price for seed. Consequently that was quite confusing in those days.
There would be probably a failure to notify a mill of a change in price and we were being constantly advised that so and so was paying such and such a price at such and such a place, and we would have to call them up and find out whether they were or not.
Question. When you speak of "in those days," what days do you refer to?
Answer. I mean previous to 1929.
Question. Now, what means of knowledge did you have of just what method was followed here prior to your becoming secretary; for several years prior to your becoming secretary?
Answer. I was superintendent of mills from 1905 to 1917, and from September, 1919, to May, 1926, I was in the oil-mill game with the Southern Cotton Oil Mill Co.
Question. In South Carolina?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. No; I had charge of the operations of the Southern throughout the South and, of course, I was pretty close to South Carolina. In other words, I was located in Savannah.
Question. Between 1926 and 1929 what knowledge did you have of it?
Answer. Between 1926 and 1929, I only had a casual knowledge of the way they were conducting the business, until I got into office and saw how Mr. Acree had been conducting it, through his correspondence.
Question. You reviewed his operations for some time past when you went in?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. You had the benefit of contact with and consultation with Mr. Lipscomb who served under Mr. Acree?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. In this exhibit 812 is a letter from Mr. Johnson about the status of J. P. Commander and Buckeye's connection with him, and in it you said that Buckeye had lent him money to build a gin and had received three cars of seed from him under the regular commission of $3 over the wagon seed price for buying. Was that just the regular arrangement or the regular differential you were speaking of there, or does that imply that they were paying above wagon-seed prices?
Answer. There is no regulation about it.
Question. What is the practice?
Answer. That is the only case that I know of in South Carolina that you have just mentioned.
Question. How is it looked upon-is it looked upon as bad practice?
Answer. I would consider it bad practice.
Question. You would not?
Answer. I would.
Question. How does your executive committee regard it?
Answer. Well, I have never taken the matter up with them, but I know from general interpretations that they would not look upon it as the right kind of arrangement to make.
Question. What would be the objection to it?
Answer. The objection to it-I will illustrate it in this way: The Buckeye Cotton Oil Co., just a short while ago sent out quotations of $25 for seed in carload lots when the published price of the Rock Hill mill was $23.
Question. And what would prevent Mr. Commander, who was the commission man for the Buckeye and authorized to pay $25 in carloads from taking seed that should have gone to Rock Hill and INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY shipping it to the Buckeye at $2 above the market price, or $2.50 more than he would have gotten?
Answer. His own seed?
Question. His own seed or anybody else's seed.
Answer. It wouldn't make any real difference as far as the mill was concerned?
You see, he is serving two masters. On man he is supposed to buy car-lot seed for 50 cents, which would make a cost of the seed of $23.50 on the Rock Hill quotation. Buckeye comes along and tells him "I will pay $25 for anybody's seed." Why couldn't he buy up car-lot seed for the Rock Hill mill and send it to Buckeye and make $2.50 more. Of course he did. I don't want a man like that working for me.
Question. The Rock Hill mill, did they ever make any objection to that arrangement?
Answer. They say they didn't.
Question. Was Mr. Kirkwood discontinued by the Maxton Oil Co.?
Answer. They offered to discontinue him, but nobody else was discontinued and I didn't feel called upon to make him do it. He was not discontinued.
Question. I notice he offered to, that is why I asked. You spoke a while ago of Mr. Culvern meeting that situation about Stackhouse by meeting a price, was that done through that Mr. Adams?
Answer. I think so.
Question. That had the effect of increasing the prices paid by both mills?
Answer. It did.
Question. And I suppose it had an effect upon other mills in the same locality?
Answer. I don't think it affected anyone else.
Question. The local situation?
Answer. Yes.
Question. There is always that possibility, isn't there, that it may affect a much wider territory?
Answer. Yes; there is that possibility.
Question. And in times it has done that?
Answer. And it might result in some mill coming and saying "You paid this man $1 more, why shouldn't I pay him $1.50 and get all of his seed "-an endless chain.
Question. Will you state, Mr. Taylor, what has been the history and the status of so-called hauling allowances here in the State?
Answer. There were some few hauling charges being paid previous to 1918. The Food Commission, under the regulations adopted, prohibited hauling charges. Since that timequestion. Do you know what is the ground on which the prohibition was based?
Answer. I do not. I know a good many reasons why it should not be done.
Examiner SHEPPARD. Had they used it before 1918?
The WITNESS. Yes, in a few cases. There are a few in existence in the State at the moment. For instance, at Bowman, S. C., about 20 miles from Orangeburg and about 16 miles from Branchville, there used to be a railroad connecting at Branchville. The town was built up after that railroad was built. Then the railroad was torn up and INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY left this considerable community without means of communication, and a transportation company was organized, known as the Bowman Transportation Co., regularly chartered and I think under the regulations of the Railroad Commission. The Southern Cotton Oil Co.
has a mill at Orangeburg and has been paying the transportation charges from Bowman to Orangeburg to that company. Buckeye, Swift of Columbia, and the Southern Cotton Oil Co. of Augusta had connections there and did not care to pay the freight to Orangeburg, load it on cars and then go down 25 or 30 miles to Branchville and pay to Augusta by rail. They preferred to haul seed by truck direct to Orangeburg and save that freight. That condition exists there to-day.
By Mr. WOODEN : Question. How long has it existed?
Answer. It has existed for, I suppose, 15 years.
Question. It went back prior to the Food Administration rules?
Answer. Yes. There is a hauling charge being paid at Union, S. C., from Jonesville and another little station just out of Jonesville. There is a hauling charge being paid at Rock Hill of 50 cents for about a 5-mile haul from a country gin. Hauling charges, or rather hauling is being done by an Elberton oil mill in Georgia from points in South Carolina. The Buckeye Cotton Oil Co. has one connection in South Carolina whose seed is hauled or hauling charges paid on it from that point to the Charlotte mill. Otherwise, I am not advised of any hauling charges.
Question. My understanding is that the mills in South Carolina have gone on record as being opposed to the making of hauling charges, or hauling allowances?
Answer. That is so.
Question. That is in line with the old Food Administration when it was prohibited?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What are the grounds on which the mills of the State have opposed the making of hauling allowances?
Answer. In the first place, it increases the cost of local seed that is bought at the mill without the price being reflected in the price paid the farmer. It causes the terminal mills, or those mills distant from the market to pay a higher price in the local market. It encourages the large mills to establish trading posts at mill towns.
Question. Concentration points?
Answer. Concentration points. It increases the cost of the seed to the larger mills in all instances without being of any benefit to the producer.
Question. Well, with all those objections and from the standpoint of both large and small mills, why is it that the practice has existed at all?
Answer. It usually starts with some small mill that thinks he has got an advantage by making a hauling charge from some gin five or ten miles away.
Question. Wouldn't he have gotten that seed anyway?
Answer. He would have gotten it anyway, or he might not have, but most likely he would have gotten it, and he makes a secret arinvestigation OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY rangement to haul the seed and handle the man's business, and the first thing you know some large mill finds out about it. The position of the large mill or any mill, when he competes in his local market, would be this: You are buying seed at your mill, from John Brown, say at 50 cents above the price that you say you are paying.
If you can pay 50 cents more for seed, delivered in your mill, I can pay 50 cents more for seed delivered in the warehouse, because I am meeting your prices and it is satisfactory to me. As soon as that is done, why the local mill immediately has an advance on his local seed price and still pays the hauling charges, until the thing gets to a point where it is obliged to stop on account of his losing money.
Question. Didn't it reach such a point as that during 1928 season?
Answer. I think it reached that point in this season in Georgia and North Carolina.
Question. How about 1928?
Answer. I have no knowledge of 1928.
Question. That payment of a hauling charge or allowance of hauling charge by a local mill on seed would have amounted in effect to them paying that much more for seed?
Answer. It amounted to paying that much more for seed.
Question. Why is it that in South Carolina the mills are on record as against any hauling allowance, while in North Carolina, as I understand it, the hauling allowances are permitted and standardized?
Answer. I think that is largely due to our people down here being more conservative-I was going to say "had better sense than that." Question. Your mills here in South Carolina are very largely in the class of small or independent mills?
Answer. As to the number of them. If you count the Southern's mills, I think they are about equally divided between what you might call the large interests and the small interests. Not in tonnage but in number.
Examiner SHEPPARD. Mr. Taylor, do you think that the paving of roads in this State is increasing your desire of the mills for hauling allowance?
The WITNESS. I am sure it will, Mr. Examiner.
Examiner SHEPPARD. I believe I got that impression from North Carolina?
The WITNESS. I am sure it will. You can not stop it. They are going to get paid for hauling, but we are trying to stave it off.
By Mr. WOODEN: Question. Do you think that the making of hauling allowances by all mills tends to increase the cost of the seed to the mills?
Answer. Unquestionably.
Question. By the amount of the hauling allowance or something else?
Answer. No; not to the amount of the hauling charge, but I will illustrate it in this way. From time immemorial we have bought seed in South Carolina on the basis of carload lots at stations. Now, when you start the hauling charge you are going to encourage the building of country gins away from the railroads, and you will pay INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY that man transportation of this seed into your mill, and you will pay him the carload price for those seed. In the meantime you have got a gin sitting alongside of your oil mill that you want to operate, and that man that you have encouraged to build a gin out in the country will be taking away ginning from you, taking away seed that you are buying at wagon-seed prices, and you will be paying him car-lot prices plus hauling into your mill.
Question. Do you think the measure and direction of a hauling allowance is an uneconomic measure?
Answer. I think it is uneconomic as far as the mill is concerned..
Those things work in two ways. What is one man's loss is another man's gain. There may be a farmer loss.
Question. I thought you said the making of a hauling allowance did not inure to the benefit of the farmer?
Answer. I don't think it does. I am speaking of the man who puts up a gin in the country. I don't think it inures to the benefit of the farmer.
Question. But the farmer who operates a gin would profit by it?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Wouldn't there be some possibility that a ginner who was not a farmer, if he profits by it, that he could pass part of his profit back to the farmer?
Answer. But they don't do it.
Question. Wouldn't that depend on competitive conditions whether they would bid against each other for the seed?
Answer. He would not have any competitor out there 5 miles in the country. He would put it there because there was no gin there.
Question. And the only buying point?
Answer. The only buying point, and he would depend on the mill to pay him $3 commission on top of the price of wagon seed, and he would pay the same price for wagon seed that the farmer would get at the mill town.
Question. The farmer would benefit, however, in not having to haul his seed so far to the gin?
Answer. Likely so; yes.

Question. The Memphis resolutions recite that in many instances where excessive commissions had been paid they had been split with the seller of the seed. I was just wondering how it was here in South Carolina.
Answer. I will tell you the reason why I don't think it has been split. The man that splits his commission usually is a street buyer who controls a very small tonnage of seed. The man that gets the big commissions is usually a party who controls a large tonnage of seed.
Question. You mean owns it, when you say "controls" it?
Answer. I mean he buys and handles a large quantity of seed that he can ship anywhere he pleases.
Question. Something in the nature of a broker?
Answer. No, I wouldn't say that; but here is a man that has been buying on a commission of $3 and has been shipping a couple thousand tons of seed a year. Some other mill slips in there and wants that man for a buyer. He is perfectly satisfied with his connection, and the one who wants him will pay him $4 to get him and the man signs up with him. Maybe next year somebody else comes in and offers him a half dollar more. That kind of buyer doesn't give away any of his commission. He is usually a pretty astute dealer.
Question. You spoke yesterday of a $3 commission being the cause of a lot of your troubles to-day, because of its being excessive, as I understood it, in proportion to the present price of seed. Answer. I think it was rather based on the cost of labor and service at that particular time because the prices had been estimated as increasing some 60 or 70 per cent on all articles, including labor; and they, in arranging the set-up for the buying of seed, decided that the commission buyer ought to get about double what he had been getting, including all expenses, and fixed it in that way.
Question. The hauling and storing and everything of that kind comes out of the $3?
Answer. Out of the $3.
Question. Then, you wouldn't claim that it ought to be fixed on a percentage relation to the price of seed?
Answer. Not entirely; it would be rather impractical because the price changes so often.
Question. You would have your commission changing all the time, too.
Answer. Yes.

(Thereupon, said documents were received in evidence marked as part of "Commission's Exhibit No. 814, Witness Taylor.") By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Mr. Taylor, another question regarding hauling allowances. Would you consider the making of hauling allowances equivalent to buying seed on a delivered basis?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Well, has that ever been tried in the industry-buying seed on a delivered basis? That is, including railroad freight?
Answer. It has been tried, I think, in Atlanta. I don't know that it has ever been tried in South Carolina.
Question. What is the objection to buying seed on a delivered basis?
Answer. Well, there are a good many objections. The first is that it has been the universal practice to buy seed from cars at a railroad station, and in that way all mills have equal opportunity to compete for material at some sort of price. As soon as you commence buying on a delivered basis each mill will have a different delivered price, according to the distance that the seed is hauled, and that makes it impossible to tell exactly what your competitors are doing.
That has been demonstrated very often, I think, in Atlanta territory by the mills that operate out of Atlanta, who do buy on delivered basis.
Question. What mills do buy that way?
Answer. Keenan's Mill; Marion Harper's Mill, particularly.
Question. It has never been a general practice in Atlanta?
Answer. Not in this territory.
Question. In Atlanta?
Answer. In Atlanta it has ever since those mills have been built there.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. You mean the other mills buy on a delivered basis, too?
Answer. No; I don't think they do, but it eliminates the commission buyer to a great extent, and it causes confusion by the fact that the man who is buying on a delivered price pays no regard to the fact that there are contractural relations between these commission men and the mills they represent, and they will often pay a higher price on account of the nearness of the seed to his mill than the mill who has contracted with the commission buyer is willing to pay.
Question. Well, wouldn't the near-by mill, buying near-by seed, really be warranted in paying a higher price for that near-by seed, from a standpoint of cost of operation?
Answer. In the end, if you start, it is going to spread, and everybody is going to have to get on the same basis. When you do that, it means the elimination practically of your local seed market and causes competitors to pay the same price you pay delivered at your mill for a lot of seed and have it delivered in their seed house, to be shipped by cars to their mill, to the other mill, you understand.
Question. Everybody would be on the same basis, but on a higher basis, I think.
Answer. On a higher basis.
Question. Products, as I understand, are largely sold on the basis of delivered prices. Is that correct?
Answer. That is so, particularly with reference to long hauls, distant points. Usually, the mills in this State will base their price on Augusta or Columbia, and add the freight.
Question. For what products?
Answer. Meal, for instance, or hulls. And add the freight from those points to the destination, and that would be the price they would quote. They would not quote f. o. b. the mill because they would have to meet competition from these two points.
Question. Well, where is the market for meal in South Carolina mills, chiefly?
Answer. The chief market is in the northern and western section of the State.
Question. In other words, not much of it is shipped out of the State?
Answer. Yes; considerable is shipped outside of the State.
Question. The market out of the State is where?
Answer. Boston freight points-New England, North Carolina, West Virginia, and Virginia, or occasionally when conditions are right, we export to Europe considerable quantities of cake.
Question. What is the idea in figuring freight on an Augusta basis for shipment up into New England territory?
Answer. They would not.
Question. I misunderstood you, then, that Augusta is used for what territory?
Answer. For delivery in South Carolina.
Question. I see. Well, I was just interested in getting your explanation of why products should be sold on a delivered basis and seed ordinarily bought on an f. o. b. station basis.
Answer. They are bought practically on the same basis-both of them; that is, delivered at the station either of the buyer or of the INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY S seller of the seed-buyer of the products or seller of the seed. I will illustrate it this way: Suppose, instead of making a sale, we made an exchange of meal for seed. We always base that on point of delivery. The seed is delivered in cars at the station. The meal is delivered freight paid at the station.
Question. Will you state, in a general way, Mr. Taylor, just what you have done as secretary on the subject of spread between seed prices and products prices?
Answer. I believe I issued several circulars last year indicating the average spread between the value of products, based upon the prices reported to my office and the prices paid for seed, and the yields of products, as indicated from analyses of seed received, and that spread varied considerably with different mills. The only thing I could do was to estimate an average working cost, in one instance, I think, and show the mills their approximate average spread in the State.
Question. Had you done work of similar kind in your old service as secretary of the South Carolina association?
Answer. I had not. We never heard of spread until the Food Administration based their prices, and so forth, upon spread.
Question. Were you merely continuing work on the same subject, that had been done by your predecessor, Mr. Acree?
Answer. I don't know.
Question. Mr. Lipscomb?
Answer. I don't know.
Question. Well, how did you come to initiate or take up the matter of spread?
Answer. I think the first time it came to my attention was soon after I came to be secretary, in December, 1929, that the mills were paying a higher price, I believe, than they had been paying at the first of the season, and I checked up to see what the difference in the spread was, and it indicated that there was a lessening of the spread as the season approached its end.
Question. Was there anything peculiar about that? Wasn't that a condition that existed for many years?
Answer. Yes; it had existed for years, but under the Trade Practice Rules we were supposed to be as fair as possible at all times to the producer and it seemed to me that if the mills were working on a reasonable spread at the first of the season, and then toward the end of the season, reduced that spread, that it was unfair to the producer because many of them had sold their seed at the comparatively lower price to speculators, and then the mills in that circumstance would have been paying the speculator a profit that should have been going to the producer, and I did not think it was fair to the producer for them to regulate their business in that way.
Question. Well, were you able to bring about any improvement in the condition thatanswer. I don't think it had any effect at all.
Question. Then, would you say that that unfairness to the producer persisted?
Answer. Well, I thought so.
Question. Did you ever see the statement analyzing the spread that was put out shortly before you became secretary, I think, by INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Mr. Asbury? I am showing it to you. Exhibit No. 27. [Hands witness paper.] Answer. I don't think I ever saw that statement.
Question. Isn't it a fact, Mr. Taylor, in that situation regarding spread, that at the close of the season, or toward the close of the season, a mill may have taken care of its overhead and be in a position to reduce its spread on the remainder of its crush?
Answer. That has been the practice for a good many years, but it is a fallacious one from a bookkeeping standpoint.
Question. How do you figure that?
Answer. Well; you have got a certain amount of overhead to take care of and you go ahead and buy seed on a profitable basis from month to month, figuring that overhead as you go along, and you find, say, on the 1st of February, that you have got a profit of $1 or $2 a ton. Well, now, you say, "Well, if I can just work now a couple of thousand tons more seed with no profit in it all, it will reduce my average overhead cost, by, say, 50 cents or $1, and that will result in my having the profit that I have secured so far, plus the reduction on the average overhead." And I go ahead and start trying to do that by raising the price of seed and taking it away from my competitors. It is a good theory, but competitors ain't going to let you do it, and the first thing you know, and it has almost invariably been the case, you have expended more than you expected to reduce your overhead and have consequently reduced the profit you have already secured.
Question. Well, other mills presumably would be in the same position of seeing the same advantage if they did the same thing, wouldn't they?
Answer. Well, they feel that way, and this is a foolish business.
Everything goes in cottonseed by the highest price quoted; everything goes in products by the lowest price quoted.
Question. Is that any different from what it is in business generally?
Answer. I don't think there are as big fools in other businesses as there are in cottonseed. They seem to be unable to sit down and say, "I am not going to take that seed because I am unable to see the profit in it." It is largely due to a lack of an adequate supply of raw material.
Question. There is a factor in there, too, isn't there, along this line, that a mill, toward the end of the season, unable to get sufficient crush to take care of its overhead, may figure that it can reduce its loss by the end of the season by reducing its spread?
Answer. That is the theory.
Question. Yes; hasn't it been the practice, too?
Answer. No; it hasn't been the practice. As I say, the practice has been for those fellows not only not to conserve any of their overhead, or reduce their overhead, but almost invariably to increase their working cost.
Question. I meant, didn't the mills proceed on that basis?
Answer. Yes; they have been doing it for almost, I don't know how long.
Question. Has that whole question been up for consideration or deliberation in the proceedings of your division?
Answer. No.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY S Question. At the outset of the season, has it been customary to discuss the matter of spread?
Answer. No; I don't remember the spread question ever having come up as it did last year, in my experience. Now, it may have in the interim between 1917 and 1929. I don't know anything about it, but I will say this, that as long as I was with the Southern Cotton Oil Co., the question of spread was constantly before the officials of the company, and each mill was required to figure spread, almost daily, so as to keep before it whether it was losing money or whether it was making money, but whether it was done with the other mills, I don't know.
Question. Has there not been discussion, particularly, at the opening of the season, as to the relation between the price of products.
and the margin in between that and the price of seed?
Answer. I haven't heard it.
Question. Have you had any cost surveys made of the cost of operation, crushing operation in mills?
Answer. Not to my knowledge since the food administration.
That was discussed, however, and we decided that it would serve no useful purpose at that time.
Question. What time was that?
Answer. That was last year, when the investigation started, and we thought it would be advisable to get at the actual cost of working yields and profit and loss sheets of the mills of the State, with the idea of having that information available for the commission, but it appeared that the commission was getting the information itself and we didn't think we would bother the mills with it.

Answer. Never.

Answer. I should say so.
Question. Would you say, that without that, operating on a uniform spread throughout the season, a mill would be operating on a speculative basis? That is, unless they operate on a uniform spread, they do operate on a speculative basis?
Answer. Yes, I wouldn't say uniform spread, Mr. Wooden, but a spread that would give them a profit.
Question. In other words, you might say a minimum spread that would give them a profit?
Answer. Yes; because there is no such thing as a uniform spread.
Each mill has its own.
Question. I don't mean that. I mean a given mill having the same spread throughout the season. As a matter of fact, with different mills having different costs of operation, you couldn't have a uniform spread for all mills, without having, you might say, a chaotic condition as to prices.
Answer. I don't know that that would have so much to do with price, because it has been pretty commonly observed by me that it does not make any difference who the mill is that makes the price, the other mills are going to meet it, if it is a high one, and in most instances, they are awfully glad to pay a lower price if they are able to, so the matter of the spread of a particular mill, I don't think, would enter into the question of the actions of the other mills with respect to the price of seed.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Mr. Pearsall, in his letter, referring to the proposed investigation in the legislature, said that if there was anything wrong in the oil-mill business it is in the price of oil. Has that matter of there being anything wrong with the price of oil come to your attention here in the State?
Answer. Not that I know of. Of course, we have been very much dissatisfied at the decline in the price of oil for several years, but we can not help it. Competitive conditions force it.
Question. Mr. Pearsall was of the opinion evidently by this letter and also by letters of his that went in up in Raleigh, and supplemented by his testimony, that the situation with reference to the refineries being such prominent factors in the purchase of seed and also the buyers of oil, was, in some way, the key to the situation, if I may use the expression. Í just wondered if you can tell me whether that similar question has arisen in South Carolina?
Answer. It may have, but I haven't discussed it with anybody.
The trouble with a great many men is they don't have the information about matters. For instance, on the price of crude oil, it is practically fixed by the price of other competing fats of a crude nature. When you get a manufactured product from oil, such as compounds and salad oils and things like that, they also are fixed by competitive conditions and are usually well advertised products that create a tremendous demand for them, and naturally they ask a profitable price for their products, but the average crude-oil man doesn't know anything about that.
Question. The advertised product is not subject, I suppose, to ordinary influences, such as a decrease in the cost of the raw material entering into it. It creates its own demand?
Answer. It creates its own demand from the advertisement.
Question. Even if the price of crude oil went down it wouldn't mean anything to them?
Answer. It wouldn't mean one cent change in the cost of one quart of Wesson's oil.

Will you identify them as authentic copies?
Answer. Yes.

Question. Has the matter of storage of seed been of considerable consequence here in South Carolina?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. I would not say it has been of considerable consequence, but it has been of considerable trouble. In other words, I don't believe that storage by the mills would amount to more than 1,000 or 1,500 tons.
Question. In the whole State?
Answer. In the whole State.
Question. Because the trouble is all out of proportion to the quantity?
Answer. Yes.
Question. In what way?
Answer. Well, the mills know that it is contrary to the general practice, and contrary to the code and ethics, contrary to the Memphis resolution, and yet will continue, in cases, to it. That is disconcerting to the competitors who are buying in their markets and has a tendency to create friction, because the seed is not free seed.
That is, the man who owns the seed has got it tied up so that competitors can not bid on it and get a shot at it.
Question. Does storage carry with it the obligation, or imply the obligation that the seller of the seed will sell it to the party with whom he stores it?
Answer. Yes; if he wants it.
Question. Was the practice quite a common one in the older days?
Answer. Yes; it was quite common and I know of several mills that failed on account of storing seed.
Question. How did the practice grow up? What was the advantage that a mill sought to acquire by storing seed?
Answer. Two advantages that they thought they had. One was that they were preventing seed from going to some other mill. The second one was that they worked up that seed and got the money for the products and consequently did not have to borrow from the banks and only had to pay for those seed months after they had realized on them: Question. So they didn't really keep them on storage?
Answer. They didn't keep them on storage. It is impossible to keep a man's seed in storage the same way as a bale of cotton. You can not identify it. It deteriorates in value and there is no way to keep a man's seed.
Question. Wasn't it used frequently so that the seller could call the price later on in the season and get the benefit of the usual raise in price that came later on in the season?
Question. It worked out that way, didn't it?
Answer. Yes; it worked out that way ordinarily.
Question. Will you state just generally and comprehensively what method of grading seed was followed in the State last year, 1929-30 season, and if you can, just how that method differed from the season preceding?
Answer. We used the modified Meloy plan last year. It took into consideration the amount of free fatty acid and the amount of moisture and trash. That system did not provide for any premium on cottonseed.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. It was a quantitive basis and did not take into consideration the quantity of oil or meal in a ton?
Answer. It did not. I am not familiar with the grading system of the previous year. I have, I think, a circular that was printed and distributed, describing that grading system, but I can not compare them because I don't remember what it was.
Question. Develop further how the system was operated last year with reference to how it was used by car seed and wagon seed and so on.
Answer. Car seed was sampled at mill destination and graded and in most instances the deductions applied where there were deductions. In the case of wagon seed the State was divided into zones, which corresponded at the first of the season with the agricultural reporting zones of the Agricultural Department.
Question. What were those agricultural reporting zones-what were they, how were they formed? Did they have reference particular to cotton or to all crops grown in the State?
Answer. I can not tell you why the Agricultural Department made those zones as they did, but I think it was more for convenience of reporting of other crops than cotton.
Question. You saw no connection between the zones as they existed and the cotton?
Answer. None whatever; because there was one zone where there was very little cotton produced and yet it was one of the zones provided. Well, we started off by using these zones as a basis for determining the character of the wagon seed being offered and had analyses made each week and determined the average grade of the seed in that particular zone. That average applied for the succeeding week.
Question. In case there was no average for a particular district for the succeeding week, did it continue until another average was reached?
Answer. That was the system adopted.
Question. Did the analysis of car seed figure on the average of the grade of the district?
Answer. Toward the latter part of the season it did when we found we were not getting sufficient number of wagon samples to make the average, then we used car seed also in obtaining the average.
Question. When did that begin-about along in January?
Answer. No; February, I think.
Question. What would you say was the degree to which the grading under the modified Meloy plan last year was observed by the mills in the State?
Answer. I think very good-between 90 and 100 per cent.
Question. Would you say that that applied also to the purchase of the wagon seed on this average of the grade plan?
Answer. I would say so as far as the mills were concerned.
Question. What do you imply there when you say mills were concerned "?
“ as far as the Answer. I imply that where a buyer was representing a mill and operating under instructions from the mill, or where the mill itself INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY was buying seed, that the grading system was observed very well, but, where independent buyers purchased seed, in very great numbers of instances they paid no attention to the grading and purchased wagon seed without regard to grading.
Question. Did that prevent, in some instances, your mills observing the grading system in that particular locality?
Answer. It necessarily did.
Question. Is the same method being followed this season with regard to the average of the grade?
Answer. Yes; it is.
Question. Have you changed your districts?
Answer. Yes.
Question. By rearrangement of the counties?
Answer. Yes; we have one in the instance of Lee County and Orangeburg. We have placed them in different districts, because of the similarity of conditions.
Question. Orangeburg was placed in another last season?
Answer. Yes.
Question. And it is in the same district this season?
Answer. The same district this season.
Question. Was Lee County changed last season?
Answer. Yes; Lee County was changed last season also.
Question. Have there not been some mills in the State that did not follow the grading system last year?
Answer. There have been some that did not follow the grading system 100 per cent.
Question. Were there some that didn't follow it at all?
Answer. I don't know of any that didn't follow it at all.
Question. Even that one mill at Clio-was it Clio?
Answer. I was talking about mills in the division. Clio never bothered about grading at all last year.
Question. Isn't it your information in a general way that they started out during the preceding season to operate under a similar plan and it broke down before the season got very far?
Answer. That was the information I got. They broke down at the end of the season, along in January.
Question. To what extent was the taking of samples from a seller's warehouse and the buying on those samples a factor in that breakdown?
Answer. It had a great deal to do with it.
Question. Do you know to what extent any effort was made during that preceding season to apply an average of the grade to the purchase of wagon seed?
Answer. I don't know; I don't think so.
Question. Do you think any?
Answer. I think not.
Question. How was this average of the grade for purchasing wagon seed arrived at-what process was used to get at it?
Answer. Each mill sent in samples of gin and wagon seed twice a week to the chemist for analyses and on occasions the commission men in the country were requested to get samples of seed and send them in. These samples were analyzed and the averages reported by the chemist and disseminated from my office.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. When you say the mills did send in samples twice a week, you mean they were supposed to, do you not?
Answer. I mean that they did.
Question. There was a good deal of difficulty in getting sufficient samples at the outset of the season, was there not?
Answer. Only from some districts. For instance, the district, I forget what number it is, I think it is No. 6, consists of Williamsburg and Georgetown Counties. That district has no mill, yet there are some seed sold there, and we had great difficulty in getting samples from that particular district. Then there was another distract that had very few mills in it-I don't remember the number, probably No. 3.
Question. When chemists made up their analyses by districts did they report the results to you?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Did you then circularize the result of the analyses to the members?
Answer. Yes, and published it in the newspapers.
Question. Do you know to what extent car seed figured as a part of this average of the grade later in the season?
Answer. I could not tell exactly to what extent, but the latter part of the season there was so little wagon seed being offered that we had to get the car-seed samples in order to make anything like a representative average, and the chemist did not report to me whether they were wagon seed or car seed toward the latter part of the season that were included in his average.
Question. When you say the latter part of the season, do you mean about the time that car seed was made a part of the average?
Answer. That is what I mean.
Question. Along in January or February?
Answer. I think it was February, March, and April. I don't think it was as early as January.
Question. It was in January, wasn't it, that the number of samples being inadequate was brought up?
Answer. I think so.
Question. How many samples would you consider necessary from each district to make a representative showing on wagon seed?
Answer. From 10 to 20.
Question. Were there some mills that didn't use the average of the grade in buying wagon seed?
Answer. Where competition forced them, there were some mills that had to abandon his known grade.
Question. To what extent. Was it at Leesville?
Answer. That was one of them.
Question. To what extent was the Leesville mill in that group?
Answer. Last year Leesville mill occupied a somewhat anomalous condition. They were in zone 5, I think, but they were located on the edge of a district that showed a very much higher average grade, and they refused to use the district average for this other district because of that and adopted the plan of just paying a flat price for seed there, because it was practically prime.
Question. Did they continue that throughout the season ?
Answer. They continued it throughout the season.
Answer. Well, that was a case of grading where he wanted to and partially grading in other cases and not grading at all in others.
Question. How about Clover?
Answer. I think Clover cotton mill bought most of its seed on the zone average. He bought a few carloads of seed last year that I don't think he graded.
Question. Did you have a check up made of the various mills to see to what extent they were following the grading plan?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Did you do it yourself or through Mr. Lipscomb?
Answer. I did it myself, the most of it, last year.
Question. Do you know whether or not any of the mills last season used an average of their own gin samples rather than your average reports from your office?
Answer. I think Leesville did that.
Question. Do you know whether the Southern Cotton Oil Co. did it to any extent?
Answer. I don't think the Southern did it to any extent except to indicate that one case that Orangeburg was all out of line and stated that they had reduced their price there on account of the known condition of the seed. That resulted in our taking Orangeburg out of the district and putting it in another one.
Question. Do you know of a man, a buyer, by the name of J. C.
Roper?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What is his line of business?
Question. That Rock Hill mill is the Highland Park?
Answer. Yes; the Highland Park.
Question. Do you know whether or not Mr. Roper, in buying for Highland Park last year made any representations concerning the extent to which grading would be applied by the Highland Park mill?
Answer. Yes; he is quite a disturber and made statements last year, representing himself as a representative of the Highland Park Manufacturing Co., that were intended to create trouble and discord that were not true.
Question. You mean he misrepresented the policy in the Highland Park mill?
Answer. He did.
Question. Did you check up the Highland Park Co. to ascertain whether his statements were true?
Answer. I did; yes.
Question. Did you go into the records to check on it?
Answer. I thought you were talking about his statements and some of his actions. I did check up his statements with Highland Park Manufacturing Co. and got them to make him say that he had not told the truth.
Question. Wasn't there some trouble caused last season by differences in the analyses made by different chemists on car seed?
Answer. Yes.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Some certain chemists' results being more favorable to the seller of the seed than others?

Answer. Yes.
Question. Did you ever go into the causes for such conditions?
Answer. Yes.
Question. What did you find?
Answer. I found sometimes it was due to not getting a proper sample; at other times it was due to conditions in the work of the chemist.
Question. Did some mills represent to the seller of the seed that their chemist would be more favorable to the seller if sold to another mill and analyzed by another chemist?
Answer. I don't know whether the mills made such representations or not, but the buyer very soon found it out in some way.
Question. It was a fact?
Answer. It was a fact.
Question. Would you say that independent buyers rather uniformly did not observe the average of the grade when they bought seed last year?
Answer. I think that is a fact.
Question. And where they didn't the mills could not either?
Answer. The mills were forced to do whatever they did.
Question. I understand that the grading system applied, in carlot seed only, to seed bought from independent shippers?
Answer. How is that?
Question. It applied only to seed bought from independent shippers?
Answer. The grading system applied only to them.
Question. Under the grading system of car-lot seed the chemical analysis was applied only to purchases made from independent shippers?
Answer. Of course, farmers shipped a lot of seed in that they purchased themselves, and merchants and different people.
Question. It was not applied, as I understand it, to the purchase of seed on commission?
Answer. Why, we didn't analyze and grade car-lot shipments received from the commission buyers, but we tried to grade those seed before they were put into the car by observing the zone differences.
Question. Of course, under any system of grading over a large district, or applying an average grade over a large district, where you purchase a number of lots of seed it is bound to occur that here and there there is a lot of seed that is better than that average of the grade and likewise, in the other direction, some of it may be below the average of the grade, but is it all bought in the district on the average of the grade?
Answer. Certainly, there would be differences.
Question. And those differences would manifest themselves as between counties in the same district and as between portions of the same counties, would they not?
Answer. It might.
Question. How many counties are there in these various districts?
Answer. I think 42.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. You mean the total in all districts?
Answer. Yes.
Question. I mean what is the number of counties in the various districts, for each district?
Answer. I don't remember. They run from two, which is the least. I don't know what the highest is. I have one of those chemical reports. I can show you from that. That shows the number of counties in each zone.
Question. I have before me a map of these districts counties is sufficiently representative?
Answer. I should think so, Mr. Wooden, because the seed coming in wagon lots is not sampled from one wagonload, but from the total receipts received during a week. The sample is taken out of the seed house where the wagon seed is dumped.
Question. You might have got the samples more largely from one mill than from another, might you not?
Answer. Yes; I think the larger the mill, or at least the bigger its wagon-seed receipts are, the more representative the analysis would be. Mr. Wooden, may I say this?
Question. Yes.
Answer. That there has been a remarkable check between the average of those zone analyses and the actual report of the production of oil in South Carolina.
Question. Last year the free fatty acid in oil, you might say, was the dominant factor in the grading of the seed?
Answer. Yes; but I should qualify my statement and say this year, because we have the total analysis of the seed this year.
Question. You take one of these districts with, say, 8 or 10 counties, there might be considerable differences between the quality of the seed in one end of the district and that from the opposite end?
Answer. It might be.
Question. And say one end had seed that ran above average and the other end had seed that ran below the average?
Answer. That might be the case.
Question. Independent buyers of seed in the end of the district, where the quality was running above the average, would make an extra profit there, wouldn't he?
Answer. Yes.
Question. And if the independent buyer at the other end of the district, where the seed ran below the average of the grade, he would be showing a loss?
Answer. That would be so, but so far we haven't encountered any wide variations. These shippers would kick like a steer if they found that they were being penalized for seed that they bought on the average-of-the-grade this year.
Question. Last year, however, there were quite wide differences?
Answer. There were quite wide differences in sections and the independent buyers, should be the ones who would have the seed graded under those circumstances, never paid any attention to grading at all last year, whether it was up or down.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Last year, however, even if the independents had followed the average-of-the-grade, some of them would have profited by it and some would have lost by it, would they not?
Answer. I imagine that might be the case.
Question. Due to the variations in quality that existed?
Answer. It might be.
Question. Wouldn't you say that a condition which results in some independents profiting by the creating of the grading system and others in losing by it results in discrimination?
Answer. No; there is no discrimination. They all know what we are doing, or what we are trying to do, and they have ample opportunity and experience in the seed business to know whether their seed is good or bad.
Question. Take last season?
Answer. They knew it last year and by reason of the fact that they had been buying seed for themselves as is, regardless of grade, and with foolish mills taking it off their hands as good seed at the same price as good seed they thought they would get away with it another year.
Question. If they had followed the average grade?
Answer. If they had followed the average grade they would not have lost a single cent.
Question. Some would have made some loss?
Answer. Well, you can not help it in the condition surrounding the cottonseed business. Wagon seed is obliged to be bought on an average just the same way cotton is to-day bought on an average in most of the small towns by merchants there. My cotton might be a quarter of a grade higher than yours but they will pay you the same price for it, over at North, as they will for mine. Then he will take it and grade it. The merchant will grade it in each case, ready to sell it and classify it into this grade or that grade. Naturally one cotton man will get a lower price than the other, grade being considered. It is the same way in cottonseed, only to a more accentuated degree.
Question. The fact remains that last season if independent buyers did have the average-of-the-grade in making their purchases that some would profit by it and others lose by both following the same systems?
Answer. I think some would have to; taken on the average, I don't think that would have been the case. There were wide variations in zones last year, particularly those located in the eastern section of the State. We are having the same kind of variation in one of the zones this year, but the average of the seed in that particular zone is going to come up all right. I mean between independent buyers. It might be buyers there, who if you step across the line over into another county, where it might be singularly affected by this particular zone. There might be a man there that would lose by buying on the grading system. It is something you can not help.
Question. In other words, those districts last year, as formed for more or less agricultural reporting districts, did not necessarily represent any distinct differences in the quality of the seed?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. At the first of the season that is a fact and we remedied it as soon as we could.
Question. Have there been only two counties changed?
Answer. Only two in this State.
Question. Were those two counties the only cases last year where the districts were not strictly on the basis of quality?
Answer. Yes.

Question. Instructions would be sent to the commission buyers in a particular district advising him to give $25 for wagon seed, $3 for a discount in that particular district. That was $3 below wagonseed prices?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. I should say in that instance it may have been, or it may have been $3 commission and then take off the discount for wagon seed. I could not tell without reading the letter.
Question. You say some of the mills did that. Which ones did and which did not?
Answer. Well, the smaller mills, not having any mailing list or any large number of buyers, did not bother about it. They simply reduced their prices if there was a discount in their zone and marked it up on the blackboard and probably telephoned some ginner out in the country a few miles and told him, "I am now paying so much for these seed," and didn't make any regular or printed quotations to the buyers and mills like the Southern Cotton Oil Co., and the Planters at Kershaw had their buyers listed as a district and would send each one of the buyers in that district a quotation with authorization to pay a certain price for cottonseed, which carried with it the discount. I will illustrate it by saying that if the price they were offering to pay were $20 for prime seed and there was a discount in that zone of $1 for grade, the buyer would be instructed to pay $19 for cottonseed.
Question. In some districts, I understand, that can not be carried out, because independent buyers did not make a corresponding deduction.
Answer. The matter of advising the buyer what to pay was carried out, but usually if there was a buyer in the market competing with him that would not allow him to buy at the lower figure, he would then call up his principal and say, "I can not buy seed at the quotation you gave, because my competitor is paying full price for the seed, $20. What must I do about it?" Then the mill manager would use his discretion as to whether to authorize that man to meet the competition or conform to what he instructed him.
Question. To what extent did that situation exist last season?
Answer. Well, I think it was pretty general in certain sections of the State, particularly between here and Barnwell.
Question. In that section, then, the deduction below the wagon price on account of grade can not be effective?
Answer. In those cases it can not be made effective.
Question. In the case of mills who posted a price making a deduction for grade below the regular wagon seed price, how would they be able to keep any record of the prices they were paying for prime seed-seed that they might have purchased for prime seed?
Answer. It would be easy enough to keep a record. Whether they did it or not I can not tell you. I will tell you one way they could do it. They could get my weekly circulars and look up to see what the discount was and see what they were offering for car seed and figure back to wagon seed prices.
Question. Do you know whether it was customary for the small mills to keep a record that would show their prime prices when they were not paying prime prices?
Answer. I would see no reason for them to do it.
Question. You don't know whether they actually had that record?
Answer. I don't know.

Question. Has there been any noticeable increase in the number of commission buyers this season compared with last?
Answer. I think there are probably about the same. I haven't heard of many conversions. The reason for it, of course, is that we are getting premiums on most of the seed this year and most of those independent boys are happy, they have no incentive to change.
Question. I thought possibly some of them will change before the season begins?
Answer. I don't think so. They just changed last year for the purpose of getting rid of a certain line of seed that they had on hand.

Answer. Yes.
Question. With what result?
Answer. I never had the result reported to me but that question of agreement of chemists on samples has been coming up from time to time and when one of them seems to be out of line, I get them to check with other chemists and they usually locate what the trouble is and straighten themselves out.
Question. Has there ever been some instances where a split sample was analyzed by different chemists with rather widely varying results?
Answer. Yes; I imagine so.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Haven't you followed it up enough to know that that has been the case?
Answer. Oh, yes.
Question. How do you account for a split showing such wide variations in results by different chemists?
Answer. Improper preparation of the sample, improper packing of the sample, errors in calculations of the results of the analyses, improper analyses. In fact, the usual errors due to human error.
Question. Some of those errors or some of those elements are in a broad way incapable of being removed; that is, a certain percentage of certain errors are to be expected?
Answer. Yes; I think so, but it is seldom that they are very long continued, or of sufficient importance to affect the general result.
Question. Hasn't there been a variation frequently by more than cent?
per Answer. Yes.
Question. Wouldn't that have quite a substantial bearing upon the price paid for the seed?
Answer. On $25 would be 25 cents.
Question. One per cent?
Answer. Yes.
Answer. All right, we will take oil, for instance, and say there is an average of 300 pounds of oil to a ton of seed and there is a change of a quarter of a cent in oil quotations. That would mean 75 cents, wouldn't it, practically a dollar, and it is awfully hard to figure seed in fractions of a dollar particularly so on wagon seed.
Question. Sometimes the oil price changes an eighth of a cent?
Answer. If it does, there isn't much change in the change in the price of it.
Question. But if a quarter makes a change of 75 cents?
Answer. You would be more than apt to find a change of a dollar in the quotation.
Question. The one-eighth presumably would be 372 cents?
Answer. About 3712 cents or 35 cents, and the mills would not care to bother with figuring seed on a fraction of a dollar.
Question. That would be enough to make quite a difference to the seller?
Answer. Yes.
Question. It would be enough to turn the seed if somebody wanted it?
Answer. Yes.
Question. And 50 cents would?
Answer. Yes; 10 cents would turn it.
Question. Has there ever been a time when seed was bought by less units than a dollar?
Answer. I have seen quotations with half dollars, but not with quarters.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. That is on the basis of seed-house prices?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. I wouldn't say so, for this reason, Mr. Wooden: The question of grading seed is a very difficult one to begin with. It is just being initiated. It is going to take years to perfect it. We all know that it has objectionable features. It is the best plan we have got, and if anybody will offer a better one we will be very glad to adopt it. It is impracticable to grade wagon seed at every point in the State. We are obliged, therefore, to work on averages in grading wagon seed. However, the general result would be fair.
While one individual might receive more for seed than he should get, another individual would receive less than he should get, and, on the average, the farmer's seed would result in dollars and cents to the community, to what the average of the seed should have brought.

By Mr. WOODEN : Question. When you first became secretary last December, Mr.
Taylor, were the members then reporting prices on car seed only, or wagon seed, as well as car seed?
Answer. They reported them both ways.
Question. Did you understand that they had been reporting them both ways for some time previous to your coming in?
Answer. That is my understanding.
Fishburne stated that "the matter of reporting through the secretary's office on past and closed transactions was fully discussed, and it was suggested that on market changes mills could report on closed transactions in the way of purchases of wagon seed at prices paid for prime cottonseed, wagon loads." Can you suggest any reason why the emphasis should be placed on the reporting of wagon seed prices on the market changes?
Answer. Yes; there are some very good reasons. We will take first, in case of a mill trying to buy seed at a rise from the previous price paid. Ordinarily seed shippers would not sell seed on a rise, a general rise, because they have pegged that price. They know INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY they can get it before the market declines, and the market showing a rise, the tendency, they feel it will go higher and they will not dispose of large lots of seed. On the contrary, should the market price decline they might or might not sell, but would be more inclined to sell in car lots. But the car-lot prices, we have found, occasionally would take 2 or 3 days, sometimes 10 days, before any transaction would be completed so as to be reported as a paid and closed transaction. Now, with wagon seed it is entirely different.
The farmer comes to the gin with a load of seed and he is going to sell it regardless of the market; whatever the market is he will take for his seed that day. The result is the wagon-seed market, or the effect of a transaction in wagon seed is almost immediate and can be reported immediately. In that way you quickly know when any mill has raised or lowered its previous paid price.
Question. It is more difficult, I take it, to sell car seed on a declining market than it is on an advancing one, isn't it? Isn't there more resistance to the decline?
Answer. It is easier to sell on a decline. That is the case with all commodities.
Question. Turning it around from the standpoint of the purchaser, it is easier for the mill to buy ordinarily on the rise than it is on the decline?
Answer. No; it is not.
Question. Isn't there more resistance on the part of the seller of the seed on the decline?
"" Answer. No; he gets panicky and thinks it is going lower and that he had better take that last price. When I said " pegged awhile ago, he has a $25 price, say, and some mill comes and says, "Look here, I am going lower on the price after to-morrow, to $24, maybe. If you sell to-day, you will get $25." All right; under those circumstances the seller is more inclined to sell than if you say to him, "I am going to raise my price to-morrow." Question. The result is, anyway, that wagon-seed purchases are made very frequently and continuously and any change in a mill's current bid price is almost immediately reflected in their purchase price?
Answer. That is so.
Question. A mill would report a car-seed purchase as having been made as soon as it had been confirmed rather than waiting for making payment for it, wouldn't it?
Answer. Why, certainly.
Question. I gather possibly that your other statement might have been open to another interpretation. Up to what point of the season does this frequent and continuous character of dealing in wagon seed continue?
Answer. It continues usually through May; but, of course, the volume of business is much heavier during the ginning season.
Question. Well, if mills were to report wagon-seed purchases today, say, at $25, just for illustration, that would mean that if there were any car-lot purchases available, it would be a $3 differential above that?
Answer. That is the usual differential.

Question. Did you say, in substance, as reported by Mr. Soter, that the difference between reporting the bid and paid prices was a distinction without a difference?

Question. From the practical business standpoint, there is no difference?
Answer. From the practical business standpoint, there is no difference.
Question. Have you already stated the grounds on which you would base that statement or can you enlarge on it?
Answer. Well, I consider the paid and closed transaction method of reporting as misleading to a large extent, because it simply represents something that has happened in the past. It does not represent what is current, what is actually going on at the moment.
Question. What is misleading about it if everybody understands it is just what happened in the past?
Answer. They understand what happened in the past, but that does not help you a bit about the minute. It might be peaceful here today or yesterday, and the newspapers will say everything is quiet in Columbia, and as a matter of fact this morning there might be a riot out there in which many people were killed, and that is the same way in the cottonseed game. That is all it really means, we know that bid price.
that INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. I think you are in accord, apparently, with Mr. Asbury when he made the statement at the Memphis conference?
Answer. I am in accord with him to this extent. That the paid and closed transaction reported does not give you an up-to-date idea of what is going on in the business. I don't agree with him with reference to saying that the whole plan would break down and so forth, if we have to confine ourselves to the paid and closed transaction reporting.

Answer. Yes.
Question. Why do you continue a practice that misleads the mills?

Question. Wouldn't it be better to have none at all than to have one that will mislead the mills?
Answer. No.

Question. But is it better to have misleading information than none at all?
Answer. The question you are talking about, the prices quoted, is not misleading, but as far as paid and closed transactions is concerned, the thing that is misleading is that you don't know, when it is perfectly feasible to know, what he is doing at this moment. In the old days, we used to report in this way. The mill would send out a quotation to its seed shippers saying, "Effective to-morrow morning, you will pay so much for wagon seed, and we will pay you so much in car lots." I would get a copy of that quotation before it was even given to the shippers out in the country and I would give that information to the other mills, so they would know what that man was going to quote to-morrow morning.
Question. Now, you don't know until he puts it up on his board?
Answer. Now, I don't know anything about it. I can not tell you to save my life what is being offered for seed in South Carolina.
Question. But with the frequent purchase of wagon seed, change would be quickly reflected in the paid price?
Answer. Yes; it would.

Question. Do you state what points?
Answer. I don't state what points except occasionally. I had that up this morning. There are two points in South Carolina, one where $23 is being paid and the point specified. Another where the man reported he was paying $24 for wagon seed, but didn't specify the point. I instructed Mr. Lipscomb to phone that man and find out where he was paying $24 for wagon seed and if it was general it would be stated in the newspaper to-day, but if it was a specific point, I instructed Mr. Lipscomb to name the two points where those particular prices were paid.
Question. Has that been your policy since you have been secretary?
Answer. That has been our policy; yes.
Question. Is this frequent and more or less continued in the purchase of wagon seed that the old paid prices continues in effect, as a matter of fact, up to within a couple of hours of the change?
Answer. Yes; I should say so.
Question. In practice isn't that nearly as useful to the mills in determining going, current prices as though they were put in the form of bid prices?
Answer. It is as good as we can get.
Question. Isn't it quite close to as good as the other arrangement?
Answer. I don't think it is as good as the other arrangement. I am speaking from the secretary's end of it now. I suppose when you put Mr. Culvern on the stand, or some of those other mill operators, they will be able to tell you better whether the present practice is as good as the old one.
Question. You say that some of your small-mill members last season who published their paid prices, only put out a new price that was higher than the old?
Answer. I don't think so.
Question. You say that some did not publish any new price when they lowered their prices from the former?
Answer. Very often, I would only get those reports off the daily report. Compartively few mills report by telegram. I mean by that that there are a number of mills in the State that do not bother to telegraph me when they have made a change, following the telegrams that I have sent indicating that other mills had changed their prices. I don't know whether you understand me, or not.
If the Southern Cotton Oil Co., Swift Co., Buckeye, Kershaw, or Hartsville publish a paid price, the smaller mills get telegrams from me, and they don't bother to wire me when they have changed, INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY if they follow, or if they don't. They simply send me a daily report saying what they have paid.
Question. As a matter of fact they do follow it?
Answer. Sometimes they do and sometimes they don't. We have mills in the State that don't pay any attention to what the other fellow is doing.
Question. Mr. Dawkins's report shows you as stating that where there was information to the effect that Southern, Kershaw, Hartsville had paid a certain price that would have the effect of making that price general?
Answer. I think it does.
Question. And that would be true on a decline, as well as on an advance in the market?
Answer. Usually it is. At the moment the condition is an exception to the rule.
Question. You sometimes sent out wires using the present price, generally, without giving names of the companies publishing the prices?
Answer. Not me.
Question. Was it done during last season before you became secretary?
Answer. I think so.
Question. Wouldn't you say that where that is done that amounts to substituting the judgment of the secretary for the individual mill operator?
Answer. No; I think it would really be giving information that was accurate and truly reflected the condition. I think I stated in one of my circulars that so-and-so had paid a certain price but I had not received enough reports to show whether this was general or not. I think you will find such a circular. I think I saw it yesterday.
Question. Exhibit marked "847" for identification, Mr. Taylor, is a tabular statement, which I understand Mr. Dawkins prepared from the price reporting telegrams in your office for the season 1929-30. It gives the f. o. b. basis prime price, with a column showing what the secretary's office did or reported and what each particular mill reported on particular dates. I am going to ask you if you will have that tabular statement checked, so that you could state whether or not it is correct. There are not so many figures on it as the size would indicate?
Answer. Yes, but that would involve a good deal of work. I would have to pick out all those telegrams to check it.
Question. I don't want to put any undue burden on you?
Answer. I have it arranged this year so that there would be no trouble, but last year they were stuck in the files indiscriminately and even Mr. Dawkins found trouble in picking out those telegrams, because some were stuck to the daily report files and some were in other files.

Answer. Usually, if there are differences.
Question. They are only occasional, as I understand it?
