Question. Mr. Dawkins' report shows you as stating to him that such conditions, when they occurred, existed along the State boundary line, because of the system of making a paid price according to the State divisions?
Answer. I said that was one of the contributing factors. I didn't say that was the only one.
Question. You agree that it is one?
Answer. I will; that is one.
Question. What others would you name?
Answer. Matters of freight rates.
Question. Do freights change at the State line?
Answer. Yes.
Question. On both sides?
Answer. Both sides; hauling charges in other States that do not exist in this State; to a material extent competition, the character of the men in the different States who are operating oil mills and sometimes difference in grades.
Question. You are accounting for a difference between two States as a whole and not why that condition should manifest itself right along the State boundary line, aren't you?
Answer. Well, I gave an illustration yesterday with the Sapona Mills showing two paid prices; one for North Carolina at $26 and one for South Carolina at $25.50. I don't know why he made that difference. The price in South Carolina that was being paid by border mills, such as Hartsville and Kershaw at the time, was $25 in South Carolina. Now, why he made a difference of 50 cents in South Carolina from what he was paying in North Carolina, I don't know, but I assume that it was a matter of hauling charges.
Question. If the price reporting boundaries were changed from State boundaries to some boundaries that are not, say, some distance from the State line, wouldn't those differences manifest themselves according to those boundaries?
Answer. Not always. For instance, I have known last year and this year of cases in Georgia that were reported through telegrams from Mr. Hutchinson's office of differences in prices in zones in Georgia alone, so it is not a question of State line entirely. There are other factors that enter into it, but I will say this, that where mills located in South Carolina are receiving from my office reports of prices paid in South Carolina and do not get prices from Texas, Georgia, and North Carolina, that the tendency would be to follow INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY whatever the larger interests, or those that were governing the whole State in this State.
Question. And when the company publishes a price in this State it is effective right up to the State line?
Answer. Supposed to be, because that is reporting prices paid in South Carolina. He doesn't say a thing about what he is paying in Georgia or North Carolina.
Question. And if he reported the price in North Carolina, the price there would be effective right up to the North Carolina State line?
Answer. Naturally so.
Question. Have you exchanged information as to the market price either paid or bid with secretaries of other divisions?
Answer. I send copies of my wires from my office to the list that you have there, to the North Carolina and Georgia secretaries and to Mr. Wilson of the Buckeye in Atlanta, and to Mr. Jordan of the Southern Cotton Oil Co. in Memphis and to Mr. Murphy of Swift Co. in Atlanta, and I get similar telegrams from the other secretaries in South Carolina and Georgia. We are not interested in the markets farther west and consequently do not exchange telegrams with the other secretaries.
Question. You said South Carolina and Georgia. I suppose you meant North Carolina and Georgia?
Answer. Georgia and North Carolina, I should have said. We do send copies of our circular letters to all secretaries, as well as to the executive secretary and also receive similar documents from them.
Question. Have you sent your telegrams to men like Mr. Wilson and Mr. Murphy at their request or just as a matter of course?
Answer. Because they all have interests in the State operating in the State, and so with Augusta and Charlotte, in the case of the Southern. They own mills here and Mr. Murphy owns a mill in this State.
Question. How much of your time would you say that you spend in the office, as distinguished from the time you spend in traveling among the mills?
Answer. Last year I spent about two days out of a week on the road and this year I have been in the office continuously and Mr.
Lipscomb has been on the road most of the time.
Question. How much time did he spend on the road last year?
Answer. Very little.
Question. Do you consider that traveling work of equal or greater importance than the office work, or how about it?
Answer. I would not say it is of greater importance, but it is of equal importance.

That contract enabled Mr. Kemp to buy up seed, or to have his customers hold seed until the prices rose, or until they were ready to sell, and then to dispose of them as car seed.
Question. You mean the storing was involved?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. The storing was involved. In addition to that, the same company had a contract with the Trenton Fertilizer Co. for the purchase of seed at Trenton.

F. E. CULVERN, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. What is your business, Mr. Culvern?
Answer. Cottonseed oil and fertilizer business, principally.
Question. What is the name under which the cottonseed oil business is carried on?
Answer. We have several corporations.
Question. Just name them, will you please?
Answer. Kershaw Oil Mill, Kershaw, S. C.; Marion Cotton Oil Co., Marion, S. C.; Lancaster Oil Co. Principally our business is in Alabama. Those are our operating mills.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. What is your connection with the various companies which you name?
Answer. I am vice president.
Question. Of each?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Was any one of those corporations-does any one of those corporations own the controlling interest, as such, in any of the others?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Which one?
Answer. Kershaw Oil Mill owns all of the stock of Marion Cotton Oil Co. and two-thirds of the stock-approximately two-thirds-of the stock of all the Alabama Cotton Oil Co., Huntsville, Ala.
Question. Is the remainder of that Huntsville, Ala., stock owned by Mr. E. T. Allen?
Answer. Yes; with the exception of a small amount. I think we started off with a fifth this year, and it has been increased to twothirds, owned by Mr. Stephens and myself, a small amount each.
Question. Who are the individuals in general that control these various corporations?
Answer. John T. Stephens, Kershaw, S. C.; Le Roy Springs, Lancaster, S. C.; C. J. Shannon, Camden, S. C., has a little stock in the Kershaw Mill, which, of course, owns Marion, as I explained, and myself; and a few other very small stockholders.
Question. Are there any other oil-mill men who own any stock in your companies?
Answer. None other than Mr. Allen, as I explained.
Question. Do any of the men you named, and including yourself, own any stock in any other oil mill than those you have named?
Answer. Mr. Stephens owns some stock in the Palmetto Oil Co., at Bishopville, S. C. I don't remember the exact amount.
Question. Have all these companies that you have operated as a unit under one management?
Answer. Yes; the head office is Kershaw; we have local managers at these points.
Question. But you undertake to direct the policy of each mill from your Kershaw office?
Answer. Yes. We leave the Alabama Cotton Oil Co. more to Mr.
Allen. As a matter of fact, I know practically nothing as to market conditions out there. Oh, we do talk to him sometimes about the sale of products, quantity of seed we want to buy, and things like that, but the general details we leave to him.
Question. How far back does your connection with the cotton-oil business go?
Answer. About 33 years.
Question. All that time in this State?
Answer. Yes; about 25 years at Kershaw; prior to that at 'Chester.

Answer. I can give it to you exactly if you would like to have it.

Question. Has it been your experience and observation that the farmers bringing seed cotton in to the ginner sell their seed at the time the cotton is ginned?
Answer. They do, to more or less of an extent, depending a good deal on the market price of seed, or the market price for cotton, you might say, and their financial condition.
Question. Well, isn't the financial condition of the average farmer such that he sells it ordinarily at the time the cotton is ginned?
Answer. We find the different proportions in different sections, I have noticed. Sometimes another point, but we always buy some seed at the gins.
Question. What becomes of the balance represented in those figures? What becomes of that?
Answer. It is taken home, usually, to hold for when they get ready to sell.
Question. Is there much of it that is sold at the time, hauled away from your gin and sold to someone else in your locality, in the same town?
Answer. Some. Of course, I don't know just what proportion.
Question. Who are the buyers that would be buying up seed of that kind?
Answer. Well, usually the other companies have buyers at these different points and they are always independent buyers.
Question. Doesn't that seed that gets away from your own gin ordinarily go to independent buyers?
Answer. Well, not always. They may go to a buyer representing some other company, but the independent buyers of course do buy some.
Question. Well, some inducement has to be offered to get that seed away from your gin?
Answer. Usually there must be some inducement of some kind.
Otherwise, to avoid hauling them, they leave them there.
Question. Are there some independent buyers who operate general stores and buy seed in connection with their trading with particular farmers?
Answer. Yes; there are.
Question. Partly as a means of checking what is due them?
Answer. Yes.
Question. You mean, on merchandise?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Well, buyers of that kind would be in a position, I suppose, to offer the farmer some extra inducement in the way of price?
Answer. They quite often do, and take them away from the ginner.
Question. Are there mills of other companies located at the same points where you own your mills?
Answer. Not at our South Carolina mill points, there are no other mills.

Question. What would you say is the result of that seasonal operation, with regard to your overhead costs?

By Mr. WOODEN : Question. What has been your experience generally with the degree of promptness with which gin loans have been paid?

Question. What is your opinion as to the results of making gin loans by mills? Does it have a good effect on the trade and industry, generally, or a bad effect?
Answer. Why, I don't know that it has had any bad effect. The only objection we have to it is that it ties up so much money, and, of course, there is some element of risk, though we try to see that we get good collateral when we make the loans.
Question. Wouldn't you consider that it represented a more serious problem from a standpoint of the smaller mills, because of their relative financial weakness? In other words, it takes a mill, or interest, of considerable financial strength to really engage in making gin loans on such a large extent.
Answer. Yes; they have to have surplus money or they couldn't do it.
Question. Your reaction toward it has not been influenced by the lack of ability to engage in the practice yourself?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. What has been your policy, Mr. Culvern, with reference to storage of seed on call, at your mills, and also by the ginners to whom you had loans?
Answer. We don't store seed at our mills. And the gins where we made loans, they may or may not store seed.
Question. You do not attempt to influence their policy with regard to storing?
Answer. We don't, although we let them know we don't feel responsible for stored seed. That is a matter that is up to them.
Question. Well, is that true with reference to your commission seed buyers also?
Answer. It is. That is, we don't store their seed. They may store their seed for their own account, but we don't know of it.
We don't think it is good business to store seed.
Question. Have you had any noticeable tendency on the part of ginners to whom you have made loans, with reference in connection with the storing of seed on call?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. Haven't had any trouble with it. Did you formerly store seed at your mills?
Answer. We have never stored seed.

I imagine from our three South Carolina mills they might at some time aggregate, oh, not so much, $10,000, or $15,000, or $20,000. We do as little as possible to meet competition, as it is forced on us.
Question. Advances of that kind-how are they secured?
Answer. On promises to give you the seed when they are ready to ship.
Question. How many such advances have you made?
Answer. Oh, altogether, probably 30 or 40 for the three mills.
Question. Have you noticed any effect on the erection of new gins resulting from the practice of making gin loans?
Answer. I think that possibly there have been a good many gins erected that would not have been, and could not have been, erected had not the oil mills helped finance them. I think the activity of the gin salesmen had a good deal to do with that. They go around trying to work up a sale, naturally, to try to sell the machinery; then they go to a mill to get them to finance it. Maybe one mill won't do it, and they go to their competitors.
Question. I suppose many of these ginners already established in business felt very much the need of obtaining financial assistance from the mills?
Answer. I think it is true; on account of financial conditions, and all, they were up against it themselves and could not finance it.
Possibly they borrowed money from the banks or gin people and had to pay it up.
Question. I was going to ask why they didn't finance themselves through the ordinary channels, banks.
Answer. Most of the banks in this section have not been in a position to do much lending in the last few years.
Question. Has the character of the risk, character of the loan itself, to the ginners, prevented the banks from making such loans?
Answer. I shouldn't say so; not in our case, because what papers we have taken we considered bankable. Didn't always turn out that way, but at the time we thought they were. I don't know about others.

By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Have there been times within your experience when mills who were short on seed were given a share of the seed of mills who were not short?

Answer. To a small extent; yes, sir.
Question. How long ago was it?
Answer. Three or four years ago, possibly, or more.
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What were the reasons which lead to that interpretation?
Answer. Our own reason for wanting exclusive buyers was that we wanted some one to represent us entirely, and not represent our competitors. We had no way of knowing if we we didn't know when one of these so-called brokers would call us up and ask us our price on seed and we might give it to him, thinking he was going to buy for us, and he might be more friendly to our competitor and give them the business. We felt, speaking for ourselves, that we would prefer to have him represent us entirely, and put the time on our business.
Question. You didn't, in those days, hesitate to inform your competitors directly what your prices were, did you?
Answer. If they would call us and ask us, I presume we would have told them.
Question. What was the objection to having a broker in on your prices?
Answer. There was no objection to his knowing our prices. We did not know whether we would get the business if he called us and asked our prices.
Question. You would have gotten it if your prices had been better.
Answer. I imagine we would have.
Question. Isn't that what the broker would do, try to get the best price from the mills?
Answer. Yes; I supopse so.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. And play one mill against the other to get the price up to the highest they could get?
Answer. Naturally, that is what they would do.

Answer. No; except one may have been more friendly than another. The compensation would have been the same, I imagine.

Answer. I think not. They would be getting commission on their own seed, and I don't think they were entitled to a commission on them.
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Of course, for a broker to get a commission on his own seed, that simply amounted to his getting a higher price for his seed?
Answer. Yes, sir; that is all.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Didn't the mills from North Carolina that made hauling allowances take seed away from you?

Question. What was the effect of that situation on the market conditions in this locality of South Carolina and North Carolina?
Answer. A continually advancing market. Our competitors would pay one price for seed at seed house and we would offer a dollar a ton more for the seed, loaded on cars. Then, if he would come back again and meet our price, loaded on cars, at the seed house, we would raise it again in some cases. I mean, anybody who wanted it naturally would have to do that.
Question. What interests were making these hauling allowances?

Question. Even when they came into South Carolina?
Answer. Not so many came into South Carolina. The smaller mills did not. Some of the larger companies would.
Question. Some North Carolina mills came into South Carolina and made hauling allowances on South Carolina seed, didn't they?
Answer. In a few cases, I think.
Question. Was that the cause of your trouble?
Answer. The cause of our trouble was our inability to buy seed in North Carolina on equal basis with them, because we were not prepared to do trucking in North Carolina.
Question. And the only offset you had to the hauling allowance was a higher price for the seed?
Answer. Yes; higher price for the seed, on cars.

By Mr. WOODEN: Question. Did this St. Paul cotton mill make a commission contract with you for the current season?
Answer. No, sir; they did not.
Question. How about Mr. Williams? Did he become a commission buyer that season?
Answer. No; I think not. I am quite sure not. They do a lot of talking and then decide to go independent when they can finance themselves.
Question. Were you interested in the matter of a Greer oil mill and feed company giving bonuses to its commission buyers, which Mr. Taylor had up last summer?
Answer. No; we were not interested, except in that it might affect us competitively. We were not interested otherwise.
Question. I notice Mr. Taylor sent a report on the matter to you and Mr. Lawton and Mr. Caldwell.
Answer. Possibly because I was on the executive committee and may have just passed it along as information.
Question. Of course, that amounted, I take it, in your opinion, to the payment of a commission, in excess of the $3 specified in the Memphis resolutions?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Has it ever been worked out, that particular matter?
Answer. Not to my knowledge. That was the last I ever heard of it. I don't know what they did later.
Question. I note in the trading rules for South Carolina, for the South Carolina division, Exhibit 807, provision for furnishing scales in seed houses, that fixes the rent on houses at $0.06 a square foot and scales not more than $10 for each set of scales. What was the reason for fixing the exact amount of allowances for those things?
Answer. To have some reasonable working basis, just like the $8 per ton commission, or anything of that kind. It varied considerably.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Had some mills made allowances for rental that were in effect nothing but a method of paying more for seed?
Answer. I think so.
Question. And was the same thing true in making allowances for scales, scale allowances?
Answer. Yes.
Question. There is a rule 9 in this Exhibit 807, 1930 trading rules, providing that loans and advances should not be made to f. o. b.
contract shippers, carrying agreement for the mill to furnish cash for the purchase of seed in consideration of the preference on such seed. Is that in line with what you have described as your own practice and policy on such loans?
Answer. That is. We would prefer not to make them, but we do make them.
Question. It is in line with your desire, but not in line with your practice?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. From your contact with other mills in the State, would you say that that represents the consensus of a great majority of the mills?
Answer. I believe it would, sir.
Question. Then I take it that the existence of the practice is the result of some competitor or competitors engaged in it whose power is sufficient to just force all the other mills to follow in line?
Answer. Yes.
Question. As far as you know, what mills in the State, or mill interests, really, believe that the practice of making gin loans or advances is a good and desirable thing?
Answer. Well, the cause for our making those open advances there was competition from the Buckeye Cotton Oil Co.
Question. Do you know any other mills who are operating in the same way in this State? In the same fashion as Buckeye?
Answer. Not from my own knowledge.
Question. Well, from your contact with the industry, you would have occasion to know?
Answer. Yes; I would.
Question. Are these allowances for scales and seed-house rental?
Have they been made frequently to independent shippers of seed, or ordinarily to them?
Answer. I wouldn't-that refers to where we have contracts with them, that those allowances are made, where we have contracts for the purchase of commission seed, $3 commission seed.
Answer. Yes.
space or scales in the case of independent shippers at all?
Answer. I don't know of any, of my own knowledge, that have been done as an inducement to have them sell them the seed.
Question. Has it been your experience that the average independent ginner sells his seed rather promptly or does the average independent ginner hold it to sell later in the season?
Answer. I think it depends entirely on his financial condition.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. That is what I had in mind when I used the word average." Taking the average run of ginners, how is it?
Question. Is he likely to get loans from the mills for the purpose of holding seed?
Answer. He gets the loan. He won't tell me he wants to hold the seed, but after he gets the loan, he does what he likes. That is one objection to it. He may take that loan and sell the seed to somebody else and make you wait on your money.
Question. Can't that be remedied by an understanding in advance, that he is not to hold the seed?
Answer. You can have the understanding all right. We have to comply with our end of it, but whether he does or not, is up to him.

By Mr. WOODEN: Question. You made some reference this morning in your testimony, Mr. Culvern, about your leasing certain mills; will you describe for us now in a comprehensive way just what your interests have done in regard to leasing other mill properties?
Answer. Yes. Would you like to know what we have under lease at present?
Question. Yes; and would you approach it from, you might say, a historical standpoint-go back to the beginning and bring it down to the present time, so that we may get it clearer?
Answer. About two years ago we leased, together with the Lawton interests, from the Carolina-Georgia Service Co. their three mills located at Seneca, S. C., Anderson, S. C., and Belton, S. C. The Kershaw oil mill handles the business entirely from this Anderson mill, Mr. Lawton's interest from the Seneca mill, and we have approximately divided the business at Belton.
Question. When you speak of dividing the business, you mean dividing the seed that comes in?
Answer. Dividing the seed, and let him furnish some of the products if he cares to.
Question. Have the mills at those points, so leased, been operated?
Answer. Not since we have leased them.
Question. That is what I mean.
Answer. No, sir. In addition to the leases above, last season, season 1929-30, we leased the West Union Oil Mill at West Union, S. C., jointly with Mr. Lawton's interest.
Question. You have those leased in both cases of the Carolina Service Co.-is that correct?
Answer. Carolina-Georgia Service Co.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. And the West Union?
Answer. Yes.
Question. How was the leasing financed as between you and Mr.
Lawton?
Answer. He paid half of the lease and I paid half the lease.
Question. In both cases?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Now, the West Union Mill, has that been operated since you took it under lease?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. Now, what others?
Answer. Cheraw Oil Mill, Cheraw, S. C., was leased jointly by Kershaw Oil Mill from Mr. Lawton. That is, speaking of 1929-30.
Kershaw Oil Mill had no lease 1929-30 season. Citizens Oil Mill at Easley, S. C. During this present season we still have jointly with the Lawtons, Seneca, Anderson, Belton, and West Union. We have for ourselves the Citizens Oil Mill at Easley.
Question. Last year you had it in conjunction with Lawton?
Answer. No, sir; in other words, I believe we have the same leases.
as in 1929-30, with the exception of Cheraw.
Question. Has the Cheraw oil mill been operated since it was taken under lease?
Answer. It is operating this season.
Question. How about last season?
Answer. No; I didn't operate it. In fact, I might state that when we leased these properties these people generally approached usin fact, I think almost always-and on account of financial conditions and so on they wanted to lease instead of operate themselves.
Question. Did they want to lease rather than sell?
Answer. No; I think they would have preferred to sell.
Question. The leasing suggestion was your side of it?
Answer. It may have been and it may not have been.
Question. The Citizens mill-has that been operated since you had it under lease?
Answer. No.
Question. That is the full extent of the leasing that you have engaged in; is it?
Answer. I think so.
Question. How did it happen that you and the Lawton interests shared in those various leases?
Answer. I don't know just how the matter came up, or who proposed it. Mr. Stephens and I were partners in business together.
Mr. Stephens is in partnership with Mr. Lawton-they were in the fertilizer business, and so on-and while competitors we have always been good friends. I had a thought in there, too, that while we wanted the business and wanted the connection for our mills, it might be good to have a partner so that in some cases where leases would give us bad business and bad crops in one section, we wouldn't have to be tied up in any one point.
Question. Have you and the Lawton interests been operating in much the same section of the State?
Answer. Pretty much, I guess. They buy pretty well all our offer and we buy pretty well all their offer from the different mills.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. So far as you know, have any other mill interests in the State engaged in the leasing of mills such as the Lawton interests have?
Answer. I don't know; I don't recall. Probably there have been.
I don't know, Mr. Wooden; I don't recall any leasing of mills. I do know that some of our competitors tried to lease these same ones, but they didn't lease them; we did.
Question. As I understand it, you have used these mills leased only as points from which or at which to collect and garner seed?
Answer. No; sell our products, handle fertilizer, in most cases coal, and doing a general trading business.
Question. How about as far as seed business?
Answer. We don't crush seed.
Question. But you do collect seed there?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Did you do any work here in the State during the year 1929 with reference to a survey of different mills for the purpose of ascertaining which ones might be acquired and which ones might be obtained under option?
Answer. I did do so.
Question. Will you state just how it came about that you did that?
Answer. I did it at the request of Mr. Stephens.
Question. Do you know what it was that led Mr. Stephens to make a request?
Answer. I do now.
Question. You did not then?
Answer. I did not directly know then. I know more about it today than I did-within the last few days.
Question. What have you learned since about it?
Answer. I heard Mr. Stephens tell Mr. Dawkins the other day that he had a little conference with Mr. Geoghegan and a few others whereby they decided to approach some of the mills to see if they would like to sell out, the idea being to form some large company, which I understand would probably be financed by some New York bank, and one reason I did so much work was that we wanted to sell our mills. I wanted to sell my interest in it.
Question. Did you ever get as far as to get an option on your mill?
Answer. No; we attempted to sell them, but never have gotten any options.
Question. Did you obtain options on some mills after Mr. Stephens suggested that you do that?
Answer. Yes; three of them.
Question. Which ones?
Answer. Ninety Six, S. C., Easley, S. C., and West Union.
Question. Was it before you obtained those options that you leased the West Union and Cheraw, or afterwards?
Answer. The option at West Union had happened at the time, or we took an option to release the mill with an option to buy West Union.
Question. What about Cheraw?
Answer. I don't think there was any option taken on Cheraw. At least if there was, I didn't take any.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. It is Easley I am thinking of.
Answer. That was at the same time. I leased it in our name or in my own name in the case of West Union. We wanted it at a certain price.
Question. Did you propose to exercise the option and then resell, or to turn the option over to whatever parties might be interested?
Answer. I really didn't have much to do with that. If something did materialize, probably we would let them come in on the same basis that we did. That was my information-they never did.
Question. Do you know if others in the State were engaged in a similar survey?
Answer. I heard a little-possibly that one or two others were.
Question. What others did you understand at that time to be engaged in that?
Answer. I don't remember any other except Mr. Lawton may have seen one or two, or some of his crew. That is all I know of in this State.
Question. Did you ever discuss the matter with parties other than Mr. Stephens during the time that you were doing this?
Answer. No; I don't think so; no, sir.
Question. Did you know at the time whether or not the Southern's representatives in this section were making a survey with reference to possible acquisition of various mills?
Answer. No, sir. I remember once on that line seeing Mr. Fishburne and saying something about it to him, but he didn't seem to know anything about it. At least, he said he had no instructions from his company. I remember speaking to him something about it.
Question. Did Mr. Stephens suggest to you which mill you should approach on the matter?" Answer. I don't think so. I am familiar with most of the mills.
A good many have taken up with us from time to time, saying they would like to sell or do something. He may have mentioned some.
Perhaps I was more familiar with that than he was.
Question. Had you ever approached, or had you ever discussed or negotiated with any representative of the Southern or of the Buckeye interests with reference to the sale of your mills?
Answer. Yes; I talked to Mr. Procter about it at one time myself with reference to selling him all of our mills.
Question. How long ago?
Answer. That was, I should say, about three years ago.
Question. Was it a year prior to this time that you took these options up?
Answer. I think so.
Question. That would be 1928?
Answer. I think that would be about right, 1927 or 1928. I know Mr. Stephens had some trouble with his health and was advised by his physician to let up on business and he was anxious to sell. I believe I know I have mentioned it in conversation. I let the Southern know we were willing to sell. We did sell two mills two or three years ago.
Question. To the Southern?
Answer. No; to Swift Co.
Question. Those were in South Carolina?
Question. Did you ever approach Swift Co. with reference to the sale of your mills?
Answer. I have spoken to some of their men and told them we would be interested in selling them.
Question. Did they ever ask you to put a price on your property?
Answer. I don't think so. They usually say they were either not interested or we wanted too much or something. We didn't get that far.
Question. Some of these mills that you arranged to take leases on had given considerable trouble in the State in a competitive way?
Answer. Not to us.
Question. Were you aware that they had given trouble to other interests in the State?
Answer. Not particularly. I have heard something said about it.
In fact, I have heard something right recently. Some of the things that have come out with reference to Citizens mill. That didn't bother us.
Question. The Citizens, is that one of the Carolina group?
Answer. No, sir, that nor the Easley mill. Our object in leasing them was to secure seed for our mills and a place for our products.
As competitors they didn't bother us.
Question. Weren't you buying in the same territory as those mills?
Answer. Yes, some of them were.
Question. Whatever their policy might have been it would have affected you to some extent?
Answer. They have taken a few seed from us, that is all.

That is the only discussion I have ever had with reference to it.

Question. I have before me one of your letters in which you speak of your experience in operating small mills. You make a general statement that you had found by experience that these small mills could not be made to pay in operation. What do you class as a small mill?
Answer. I refer there to the oil mill at Clinton which is a fourpress mill. I attempted to operate it three or four seasons unprofitably.
Question. Did you draw the line at some particular point on capacity between mill that is profitable and one that is not?
Answer. I would not say that, exactly. Unless you get a reasonably large crush, it is pretty hard to do anything. You have to have good men, competent men and it is pretty expensive to keep them all the year round with a small mill with a small crush. A larger mill with a larger crush, naturally, you can crush seed cheaper and should be more efficient.
Question. Is that because of a lessening in overhead, or lessening in the actual manufacturing cost?
Answer. Both. The capacity and tons has to do with both manufacturing cost and the overhead.
Question. The larger the crush of the mill, the more months you can operate, would you say?
Answer. Well, either the more months, or they do more business during that period whereby they can afford to have better men and better machinery and keep it up better.
Question. These mills that you have leased jointly with the Lawton interests have they been in the category of mills that you thought too small to operate profitably?
Answer. They were, as far as we were concerned. We would not attempt to operate them.
Question. Did Mr. Lawton agree with you on that?
Answer. I presume so. He never said anything about operating them. I never discussed it with him.
Question. As a matter of fact you understood at the time you leased them that you were not going to operate them?
Answer. Absolutely, I knew that.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Have you found that the use of those mill properties for purchasing seed only and not operating them, has paid you a return on your investment and lease?
Answer. During the season 1929-30 the leases we had showed a profit in themselves. That is, the business of those mills.
Question. Including, however, other business besides seed, such as fertilizer?
In 1929-30 they showed a loss. I think, however I know, howeverpart of the loss last season was due to the fact that we carried seed at those points like we were at the others. That is the seed stood on their own bottom. We carried some seed and seed declined and we had advanced on them. That helped to complete the loss.
Question. During 1928-29 season those three mills of the Carolinageorgia Service Co. were all that you had under lease?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Did you do anything during the year 1929 with reference to acquiring either by purchase or on lease any mills in North Carolina?
Answer. In 1929, I believe we purchased Mooresville.
Question. Did you negotiate for the purchase of Statesville mill in North Carolina?
Answer. They took it up with us. They wrote to me and said they would like to sell, but we were not interested.
Question. You didn't attempt to get any option on it?
Answer. I don't think there was any option. I may have asked for a price, but we were not interested in it.
Question. You had an option on the Ninety Six mill, did you not?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What did you understand to be the reason that nothing ever come of these options that you were obtaining?
Answer. I don't know. It simply died of its own accord.
Question. You didn't know very much about it at the time just what was going on or how broad the proposition was?
Answer. No; I wasn't so very familiar with it.
Question. Did you know anything was being done in North Carolina and Georgia?
Answer. I heard that there was; yes.
Question. Did you get any extensions on any of those options on those mills?
Answer. Yes; I think we got an extension on the Ninety Six mill, for I don't know how long, probably sixty and a half days, I believe. That is all that I remember.
Question. Did you get all the options originally, as to the same period of time covering the same period of time?
Answer. As to that I can not say. The option usually expired with the lease, whatever time we made them. I think they varied.
Question. Was a form of option agreement supplied to you?
Answer. I didn't see a form. I mean I don't see it now. It is there somewhere?
Question. Where did it come from?
Answer. I think Mr. Stephens gave it to me.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. You don't know where he got it?

Question. Do I understand that in all these leasing arrangements that you have made jointly with the Lawton interests, you divided the seed half and half between you?
Answer. Approximately, that was the idea.
Question. You made some effort, or at least expressed a willingness to sell the Charlotte Cotton Oil Co. sometime last winter-that is the one that the Southern was interested in 50-50?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Nothing ever came of those negotiations?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. You touched on as an element in your negotiations that you were willing to consider the requirement that the mill would not operate if it were sold?
Answer. No; that the mill would not be used for oil mill purposes.
That is the same thing probably, not to be used for mill purposes.
Question. Did your mills, Mr. Culvern, operate last season on the grading system adopted by the South Carolina division?
Answer. That was the modified Meloy plan of quality, I believe.
Question. Can you state just to what extent you did operate under it?
Answer. We operated under it entirely as far as the purchases of car seed was concerned, and do so now.
Question. As to the purchase of wagon seed, to what extent did you operate under it?
Answer. As far as possible, as far as competition would permit.
We followed it pretty closely.
Question. To what extent did competition make it impossible to follow the wagon-seed plan of grading?
Answer. I would say 10 or 15 per cent, possibly.
Question. That was only at certain points?
Answer. Yes; usually at certain points.
Question. What competition did you have in mind to prevent it at certain points?
Answer. Independents, usually. Some times the anxiety of our competitors to secure seed.
Question. What difference was there between the grading plan used last season and the plan used the season before, 1928-29 season?
Answer. I think the plans were similar, except that I believe last season we attempted, where possible, to buy seed in different zones based on what they were actually shown to be worth by analysis.
Question. So, in the 1928-29 season, you didn't have any system of applying the average of the grade to the purchase of wagon seed?
Answer. No; I believe not.
Question. Then the whole plan of grading according to the modified Meloy plan broke down before the season had progressed very far, didn't it, during 1928-29 ?
Answer. Pretty well broke down.
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. This season are you operating under what is known as the full Meloy plan?
Answer. Yes; the quality and quantity both.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. And under that, premiums are paid for seed that is better than prime?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Last year, however, there were no premiums allowed?
Answer. No premiums.
Question. What has been your observation and experience with reference to the closeness that the chemists will come in analyzing seed under the Meloy plan?
Answer. We find more or less difference, and again we will check samples, and find them identical, but some differences do exist, whether the average works out pretty close either way I am not able to tell. It may.
Question. Has the system of grading seed through chemical analysis proven more satisfactory to you than the old cut-and-count method?
Answer. I would say it is more accurate.
Question. And, therefore, more satisfactory to you-has it been?
Answer. Well, more satisfactory to us than to the sellers, I would say.
Question. Are you as well satisfied with the system as it is functioning this year, as you were with the system last year?
Answer. Not so well.
Question. Why not?
Answer. On account of the-I rather think it is harder for a chemist to determine exactly the cake-meal content, probably harder than it would just to get the quality.
Question. You think that the results differ more than they did last year on that account?
Answer. I rather think so. Of course, there were some differences last year.
Question. Is it possible or feasible for these premiums that are being paid this year to be passed back to the farmer?
Answer. Only in this way. I think that the farmer gets the advantage of the premium zone. He gets the advantage when he sells the wagon seed.
it?
Question. But the whole zone has to be premium for him to get Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. He would not get it if his own seed happened to be premium or prime seed provided the zone fell below that?
Answer. No. I will say he would not get it as wagon seed. If a farmer sold a carload of seed he would get it.
Question. Are there some entire zones this year that are paying premiums?
Answer. Yes; there have been some several times during the season?
Question. You say several times, you mean several weeks during the period?
Answer. Yes.
Qustion. Most of the weeks the premium has not shown?
Answer. I can not say as to that. Some weeks they are shown and some they are not.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Do you know whether or not the independent ginner pays a premium when he buys wagon seed?
Answer. If he buys them at a premium zone he would be more than apt to have to pay it, because the mills instruct our buyer to pay it.
Question. In figuring your deductions last year as the result of the average of the grade and the application of that average to the purchase of wagon seed, did you figure the deduction to the nearest dollar?

Answer. Yes.
Question. Are premiums figured the same way this year?
Answer. Yes; you mean premiums on wagon seed or car seed.
Car seed would be figured exact.
Question. Did you last season some time use an average for the purchase of wagonseed based on your own chemist's report instead of the average from the association?
Answer. Occasionally.
Question. Why did you in some cases and not others?
Answer. In one or two cases we found from our own results that the seed were not good as it appeared; in some other cases we made them, they were a little better than the chemist's average.
Question. Wasn't the actual situation last year that in different counties or in different localities within a given district, the actual quality might vary from a few cents to several dollars above or below the average for the district as a whole?
Answer. Well, I think that may be possible.
Question. Under such conditions independent buyers in individual cases, if he followed the average of the grade, same times he would profit and other times he would suffer a loss when he bought in competition with commission buyers who bought on the average of the grade?
Answer. He might.
Question. How many wears was it that your mills operated on the basis of purchasing seed on the cut-and-count method?
Answer. We always tried to buy seed on the basis of quality, for a good many years.
Question. Using the so-called cut-and-count method?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Up until 1928?
Answer. Yes.
Question. What was your own experience with reference to the shortcomings or advantages of that method of buying, or grading rather?
Answer. We found it fairly satisfactory.
Question. Did you have complaints from your sellers of seed?
Answer. Sometimes, for the reason that our competitors were probably not buying seed that way. They may have been buying them as is, while we tried to conduct our business on a businesslike basis.
Question. You bought wagonseed during all those years, I suppose on an as-is basis?
Answer. Yes.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. It was only the car seed that was graded according to the cut-and-count?
Answer. Yes.
Question. You did not find, did you, that during all those years the cut-and-count method was resulting in a loss to your mills?
Answer. That would be rather hard to say. We had no direct way of knowing just exactly what it amounted to. We would only know at the end of the season.
Question. You were, during that period, at any rate for a considerable time during that period having deductions made against your oil?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. For excess free fatty acid?
Answer. Yes, sir. We usually found the deductions on oil were more than we were able to deduct.
Question. The use of that method of testing and grading oil and the deductions based on it then, I take it, were a prominent factor in bringing about a grading of seed on the same basis of free fatty acid?
Answer. I imagine so.
Question. Exhibit marked "869" for identification, is that an authentic copy of your letter to a couple of your mill managers?
Answer. It is.

Examiner SHEPPARD. Admitted.
(Thereupon said document was received in evidence and marked "Commission's Exhibit No. 869, Witness Culvern.") By Mr. WOODEN : Question. It appears from this exhibit, does it not, Mr. Culvern, that up to that time during 1928 season deductions were being figured on the delivered prices of seed instead of f. o. b. prices?
Answer. Must have been.
Question. The practice was changed by instructions issued through Mr. Acree's office?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Why should a shipper or seller of seed have a deduction based upon the delivered price?
Answer. He should not. That is the reason we changed it. We didn't think about it at first, I imagine.
Question. Was the shipper aware that the deductions were so based for that time?
Answer. Yes; he probably was. He must have been.
Question. Wasn't there ever any complaint from shippers?
Answer. I don't remember any. There may have been. That may have been the cause for it.
Question. If they had been aware of it they would have complained?
Answer. I should think so.
Question. There seems to have been some. Because of unusually bad weather conditions during 1929-30 season, it was necessary to put this new system in operation; that is correct, is it not?
Answer. Yes.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. You usually had had equally bad weather conditions through a number of years going back over a particular period, had you not?
Answer. Not equally as bad. We have had bad weather conditions at times, however.
Question. You think the weather during 1929-30 season was absolutely worse than you had ever known?
Answer. It was pretty bad.
Question. Of course, it is easier to remember that than some of the older seasons. It is possible, isn't it, Mr. Culvern, to have extremely wide variations in testings and analyses averages depending on the way samples are taken of the same seed?
Answer. Yes.
Question. How wide a variation have you known to exist based on the difference in samples, the same lot of seed?
Answer. I have seen differences of two and three or four points and I can not say of my own knowledge how those samples were taken. In our own mills we try to take them as near as possible to represent the lot. I have seen some variations in our own samples of two or three points.
Question. When you say two or three points, you mean what?
Answer. Two or three per cent, is what it really means.
chemists blame that on the samples.

Question. That changed, Mr. Culvern, some time in November, didn't it?

Question. Have you found the reporting system based on paid prices as valuable to you as the system based on bid prices?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. What difference have you found?
Answer. Well, while we know what our competitor has paid for seed, we may not know what he is offering to pay now.
Question. Do you freely inform the competitor who inquires what your current price is?
Answer. If he inquires I would. I don't take the trouble to inform him, but if he inquires I inform him.
Question. Do you find that some do inquire occasionally?
Answer. Yes, they say I have heard a certain price has been offered.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Have you inquired of other mills their current price?
Answer. At times.
Question. Do you have difficulty in getting them?
Answer. Usually not.
Question. Doesn't that largely supplement the defect in the system that comes through the secretary's office?
Answer. Largely it does. To an extent we have to find it out ourselves. It may be several hours before we do find it out. I have to-day found out something several hours after it happened.
Question. Do your mills make very frequent purchases of wagon seed?
Answer. Yes, some of our mills do.
Question. They are buying wagon seed every day?
Answer. Practically, during the season.
Question. How long sometimes is it between your purchase of a load of wagon seed at a changed price before you make a car-lot purchase on the changed market?
Answer. That time varies.
Question. Give us some idea of how long it is?
Answer. Should it be an advance, we probably would buy car seed at a different price quicker than we would buy seed at a different price on a decline. That might vary from an hour or two to several days.
Question. Were you present at the Memphis conference where the matter of reporting prices was discussed?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. You maintain bulletin boards at your mills on which you post your prices?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How long have you been doing that?
Answer. For some time. I don't know, probably since last season, at most of them.
Question. If you post a different price of wagon seed at your mill ordinarily, you will make a purchase at that price the same day?
Answer. Ordinarily we would.
Question. Have you reported wagon seed prices to the division secretary as well as car-lot prices?
Answer. Yes, sir.

Answer. I would like to qualify that a little. Answer. Sections 3530, 3531, 3534, and 3535, of volume 3, of the Code of Laws of South Carolina will give you that.
Question. Have you ever compared your South Carolina statute with the Federal law?
Answer. No, sir; I have not.
Question. Was any complaint made to you, or statements made to you, concerning the operation of the grading system?
Answer. Yes, sir; they said that they had a way of-when a man was buying on commission, why, they just took his seed without analysis, but if a man was buying as an independent, or was shipping in any way, except through their commission buyers, why they analyzed his seed and that they requested him to take samples of those seed when they were at their owner's destination, but that they refused to take any samples unless they loaded them up and shipped them down to where they were going to sell them, and that, in some cases, then, where they couldn't agree on the prices, they would have to ship them all the way back, paying expenses both ways.
Question. Did you ever investigate any of those particular instances to see whether they were well founded in fact?
Answer. Why, I don't think there was any question about it. I think I discussed it with some of the-perhaps I discussed it with Mr. Taylor [indicating Mr. B. F. Taylor], or at least, called his attention to the information I had in that line. I am not sure it was Mr. Taylor, but I think it was.
Question. Did you have information concerning the operation of the zone system of purchasing?
Answer. I don't know much about that zone system.
Question. Of purchasing wagon seed?
Answer. I don't know much about that, sir.
Question. Did you get any information at all direct from any of the mills, or their representatives?
Answer. No, sir; I have never been able to get any information from them. The work at my office is such that I can't get out on these investigations with my usual helpers. I have one or two assistants and the work is just so heavy that I couldn't give this my undivided attention, and that is the reason I had to pick it up the best I could, and that summer I took advantage of being out to get as much information as I could, but I couldn't trace that down.
Question. Didn't the mills, or some one in their behalf, offer their assistance to you?
Answer. Mr. Taylor and his association, Mr. Benet over there [indicating Senator Benet] came down after this investigation was opened, and Mr. Lawton, they came over and said their files were open to me, and they would be glad to give me any help they could in that way. I said I would be glad to receive anything they could give me.
Question. Did you ever accept their offer by going into their files?
Answer. No, sir; I did not.
Question. Or anything like that?
Answer. No, sir; I am not an expert at it, and I couldn't go over there to their files and get any information from them. I don't doubt but that they keep it pretty nice, but I couldn't do it.

Answer. No, sir.
Question. Is it in your province as Attorney General to hold a grand-jury investigation on such matter?
Answer. In the last legislature they gave me authority to act in that way, to call witnesses in an investigation of this kind.
Question. Was the authority granted subsequently to and separately from the resolution itself?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Examiner SHEPPARD. Did that have particular reference to this inquiry?
The WITNESS. This particular reference is to give me authority to summon witnesses, under that section, in making inquiries with regard to that investigation.
By Mr. WOODEN: Question. You haven't, I take it, operated to carry on your investigation under that authority?
Answer. No, sir; I have one statement of a situation that occurred here in the spring of 1930. [Reading.] This informant says he sold a lot of cottonseed to the Hartsville Oil Co., delivered to their agent at Cartersville, S. C., unloaded the seed in box cars designated by the agent after being weighed by the agent. When the seed was settled for by the Hartsville Oil Co., they deducted, as I remember, exactly $1 per ton for offgrade and 100 pounds per ton in the weight after they were delivered to the oil company. The name of the oil company agent at Cartersville to whom he sold the seed is Mr.
Sellers.
Question. Well, you have no knowledge, of course, as to whether the deduction was properly made or not?
Answer. The party who made the statement had no explanations except the one he made here; nothing was given to him. That explanation is given by my assistant attorney general, Mr. Humphrey, of his own personal dealings.
Question. To what extent, if any, do the various county or district attorneys throughout the State come under your supervision?
Answer. They are solicitors, as we call them in this State. There are 14 judicial circuits and each circuit has a solicitor and a judge.
The solicitor handles the criminal business in his circuit and they are all under the direction of the attorney general.
Question. Have you used such officials in any way in connection with your inquiry under the resolution?
Answer. No, sir; don't know as I would have authority to use them.
Question. Is your South Carolina statute, antitrust statute, a criminal statute?
Answer. No, sir; I don't think it is.
Question. Doesn't it provide for any penalty?
Answer. It provides a penalty in regard for putting them out of business, or things of that kind.
Question. No provisions for fine?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. I don't recall whether there is any fine to it or not, sir.
There is a provision under which the party injured might, under certain circumstances, recover damages.

Answer. Sir?
Question. Triple damages?
Answer. Well, sir, I haven't gone into that phase of it. I have not looked over the statute carefully I have read it over since this investigation has begun to get a general idea of it.
Question. The reason I asked was because that is the provision of the Federal statute, and I thought possibly yours might follow it.

We don't have very much use in this State for that statute-we haven't heretofore. There are many others used much more often than the one dealing with monopolies or things of that kind. That is a sort of new version to us.

Question. How much difference would it make in price?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY By Mr. WOODEN: Question. Do you see any difference in making a hauling allowance on seed and buying seed on a delivered basis?

Question. Will you explain why not?
Answer. Yes, I think I can. I hope I can.
Question. All right.
Answer. It looks to me if seed were bought on a delivered price that all of the seed would have to be bought right around the mill.
Question. How do you figure that?
Answer. Well, suppose the price of seed was $25 delivered. A man that was 100 miles away from there could not deliver them for $25.
Question. Well, couldn't you vary the price according to the distance and the cost of delivery to the mill?
Answer. I just don't see how it would work. If you gave a delivered price that would be your published price.
Question. Well, you mean that you could not buy seed on a delivered basis and have a uniform published price?
Answer. Well, I just don't see how you would get any seed except right around your mill.
Question. Well, you can afford to pay more for seed that are close by your mill, can't you?
Answer. Well, if you could get them all close; yes.
Question. Well, for such as you do get close you could afford to pay more?
Answer. A little more; yes.
Question. Well, why can't you go out in wider territory and pay what you have to and the freight added even though you pay less away from your mill than you do close by?
Answer. You would not buy any away from your mill.
Question. Why not? Wouldn't other mills be in the same position?
Answer. They would go somewhere else.
Question. Well, wouldn't other mills be in the same position?
Answer. Yes; they would be. But there is one thing I want to say for the benefit of all concerned, and that is this, the high prices we are all having to pay for labor I don't see how a mill with a small tonnage can possibly live. I have got two shut down right now. That is the reason.

Do you accept that statement?

Question. Have you found that the publication of prices on past and closed transactions has resulted in business being conducted on a discriminatory basis?

(Reporter thereupon read the question, commencing, "Have you found," and concluding with "discriminatory basis?") I don't know how to answer that. I don't exactly get your meaning. Amplify yourself.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. We have here a resolution with which you agree, that the publication of prices is a necessary factor in the conduct of business on a nondiscriminatory basis. I want to know whether you have found the publication of past and closed transactions has caused business to be conducted on a discriminatory basis?
Answer. I wouldn't say that; no. My thought is just this about the bid and published price, that I may buy some seed to-day and give my published price. That is my price and I published it, but competition may make me give more than that 30 minutes afterwards, and that is my bid price. Now, I am bidding that price and not buying any seed, and yet I have published another price.
Question. As soon as you do buy at the new price, why then you have to report it?
Answer. That is my objection to it. Just as soon as I buy some seed at the new price, I report it, but there may be a change in there in 30 minutes, or it may extend over several days. I have published the price and I am bidding another price. It is just misleading. That is my point.
Question. As a matter of fact, ordinarily, your price doesn't change in 30 minutes, does it?
Answer. No; not ordinarily it doesn't, but I am just using that extreme situation to try to make clear the thought that is in my mind.
Question. Frequently your price actually paid runs on as your current price maybe for a week or two weeks, doesn't it?
Answer. Might do it for a week, or 10 days; might not do it for an hour. That is the reason that I think the bid price is fair because it lets everybody know what you are doing.
Question. I have before me, Mr. Lawton, minutes of the executive committee of last January, Exhibit 798, at which you were present, according to the minutes, and the executive committee expressed itself as considering it unethical for a mill to issue a quotation either raising or lowering the price on an article, and then continuing to buy at the old price. Further, it said that it is not considered fair to the sellers and such practice would mean having two prices.
Answer. Let me read that, please. [Reads paper.] Question. It is right in the middle of the page.
Answer. That is right.
Question. What is the relation of that action of the executive committee to the subject we have just been discussing, the difference between the bid prices and closed transactions?
Answer. There is a custom that has grown up in the trade that when you change your published price, they take seed at the old price, and I don't think it is ethical or fair.
Question. Well, that has reference to protecting the seller on a decline?
Answer. That's the idea.
Question. This action of the executive committee specifically refers to either raising or lowering the price.
Answer. That is what I think that had reference to there. That is my understanding of it. Of course, my opinion has nothing to do with it. I have never been able to make any impression on the industry, but I think that is unfair.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Do you consider it unfair or unethical for a mill to issue a quotation raising its price and then continuing to buy at the old price?
Answer. Why, of course, I do.
Question. Do you think that would amount to having two prices?
Answer. Why, yes; two prices.
Question. Has there been, in your experience, quite a good deal of the practice of mills going out and making a special price to obtain a special lot of seed at a price higher than the general price, and then, as soon as they got that special lot, to just continue on their old general price?
Answer. I have heard of that; yes.
Question. Have you experienced it?
Answer. I have never done that.
Question. I meant, have you had other mills do it to you?
Answer. Yes; I have had other mills do it to me.
Question. Don't you think that if a mill has to report every price it would have a tendency to prevent that sort of activities?
Answer. I think it would.
Question. Will you explain how?
Answer. Well, I will explain it this way: That the fellow that does that, doesn't ever report anything.
Question. But if he had to report it, it would mean that it would raise a question why he didn't make his general price that everywhere.
Answer. I think that would be the general effect. It isn't fair for him to give one man more for the same article than another.
Question. You didn't think it fair to pay a higher price for a thousand tons of seed than for a hundred tons?
Answer. I wouldn't say so; no. It is not worth any more to him if it is the same quality of seed.
Question. Wouldn't there be some saving in cost of getting one lot of seed in a thousand-ton lot instead of picking up 10 or 20 lots to make a thousand?
Answer. No, sir; because he is unloading. It comes in carloads; he doesn't save anything. If it costs him $5 a car to unload one car, it costs him $500 to unload a hundred cars.
Question. But it costs more to buy 10 or 20 lots of seed than to buy one lot, doesn't it?
Answer. Most of them are bought over the telephone; you know how much it costs to talk to a fellow over the telephone.
Question. Has it been your experience and belief that the system of reporting prices through the secretary's office has been made use of by the sellers of seed to ascertain what the prices of seed were?
Answer. I hardly know how to answer that question.
You see, we publish them. The secretary publishes them in five or six of the daily papers.
Question. That is rather recent, though, isn't it?
Answer. We have been doing that the whole season in South Carolina.
Question. I meant it was begun the middle of last season?
Answer. I don't remember, sometime like that, I think, and if a man takes a daily paper, why he ought to be able to post himself INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Just as to what is going on. It seems to me it may not be a perfect method. We may reach something that is more perfect later on, but that is the best thing we have been able to think up up to now.
Question. Hasn't it long been the fact that the sellers of seed have quickly obtained knowledge of prices being paid without regard to any method of reporting prices through the secretary's office?
Answer. The larger shippers, yes, but the smaller men in the country, I would say no. The larger dealers keep posted, but the smaller people would not be posted.
Question. Well, the smaller people have kept in touch with the mills in their immediate locality at any rate.
Answer. So far as they could, yes.
Question. You mean wagon-lot sellers when you say smaller people?
Answer. Yes, I mean wagon-lot sellers, maybe car-lot sellers, but here is a farmer that just makes 10 or 12 tons. We call 10 tons a carload. I would call him a small man, as compared to the man that handles 100 or 150 tons.
Question. Well, until you began publishing the prices in the papers, as a matter of fact, the system of price reporting did not carry through to the seller of the seed, did it?

Question. Do you know whether or not Mr. Black was a member of the executive committee in the Georgia division?
Answer. I don't know that. He may or may not be. I just don't know. I think I can explain what is worrying you in regard to that letter. If you want an explanation I will be very glad to give it to you.
Question. Go ahead and see if you can guess what is worrying me..
Answer. Of course, you are trying to bring out something about.
the mills being in collusion to keep from making so much lint.
Question. I want the facts.
Answer. I know what you are after. Here are the facts: Last year we simply could not sell our lint at all, and all of us were up in the air as to what to do, what to make this year. The buyers claimed that there was no demand for the lint; they couldn't sell it,.
so they wouldn't buy it from us. Black was in the same predicament that I was. He didn't know what to do. That letter was written in July, I think, along in the summer, and he just wanted to find out form me at least, this is the way I take it; he wanted to find out what I was going to do under those conditions-no use for him to go making a lot of lint if he could't sell it. "Mr. Lawton, what are you going to do?" He knew I was a pretty good operator.
Question. Why did he go and pick a mill in South Carolina to take it up with instead of one in his vicinity, in his own State?
Answer. I don't know who else he took it up with; I know I sold 1,300 pounds of linters for at least 1 cent less a pound than it cost.

Answer. Yes; we reduced it very much.

Answer. Well, about 45 pounds to the ton.

Answer. I remember the resolution. You know, these people are the greatest folks to "resolute " you ever saw, and then forget about it when they get home.
Question. Do you know whether other mills in the State are reducing their lint?
Answer. I rather think most of them are. They'd better. I don't know about that, though, of my own personal knowledge.
Question. When you say 45 pounds per ton, is that what you were cutting?
Answer. Yes; we reduced 45 pounds per ton. We are cutting about 80. Last year we cut 125. We reduced them about a third.
Question. Do you know to what extent the other mills reduce their cut, whether it is a third or what?
Answer. I couldn't answer that. I know they are all reducing, though.

Answer. What is that?

Question. It stays on the hulls, then?
Answer Do you know what linters are?

Answer. It is a little fiber that comes off the seed. If you don't cut it off the seed, you won't have any lint.
Question. It stays on the hull then?
Answer. It stays on the hull, but, as a matter of fact, we are forced to cut it off. If I could manufacture seed without taking getting for it when it is taken off.
Question. You get more weight on the hull.
Answer. It costs so much to take it off. If I could let it slip in on the seed without letting it go into the linter room, I'd make money.
Question. Their added weight on the hull, at the low price, would be negligible?
Answer. Very little. As a matter of fact, we have got to take them off because we can't crush the oil and get the meal if we don't take it off.
Question. What was the poundage of lint you are taking off this year?
Answer. We are making about 80 pounds of second-cut lint.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Will you state what the substance of it was?
Answer. Mr. Fraser got into some trouble with the association about some claim and one of the strongest things about the old interstate, and the new National Cottonseed Products Association is the fact that we all agree to arbitration if there is any difference between buyer and seller, and when we have a difference, which we frequently do, as to grade or something else, there is a board of arbitrators composed of five men that are located at different cities, for instance, our nearest one is in Atlanta; then, they have one at Montgomery, and one at Memphis, and one at Little Rock, and one at Dallas, and one at Houston, all about over the country, to the effect that they will be convenient to the arbitrators. Then when anybody wants to have their case arbitrated, it is presented in written documents and these five men get together and say who is right and who is wrong, and they agree to the arbitration.
Question. I think we understand.
Answer. You understand that? Because I wanted to explain what led up to what I told Fraser. Well, Fraser got into an arbitration and the arbitration went against him and he failed to abide by it, so he was expelled from the association. Well, he wanted to go on and do business with me and he came and asked me the question, "What would you do, Mr. Lawton, if you were me?" I said I'd go and straighten that arbitration out, I'd pay that award, and reinstate myself.
Question. Did you know, or did he inform you that he had compromised the claim with the other party?
Answer. Mr. Fraser sent me a document there, Mr. Wooden, that thick, for me to read. Well, I never read it, to tell you the truth, because I was too busy. It was that thick, and as I understand it, he never made good the arbitration award and consequently was expelled.
Question. Do you understand that to be necessary, even though the parties compromise the claim in connection with a lawsuit over it?
Answer. Well, here is the proposition: If two people agree, and they go back, he can be reinstated, you know. I can't explain his actions because I don't know all about them, but I know this, that whenever a man settles that arbitration, why, he is reinstated immediately into the association, because that is the only penalty they can inflict on him.
Question. You mean expulsion?
Answer. Expulsion. And I told him that. I said, "You want me to do business with you. I frankly tell you, I won't do any business with you. I have a right to pick the people I deal with, and if you and I differed in some matter in the trade, I've got to go to court to enforce my side of it, and there are so many people I can sell linters to who are members of the association, and if I had differences with them, it would cost me nothing to settle it. There is no reason for me to go and sell to you." Question. Yet you have sold to some dealers who are not members of the association?
Answer. Yes, I have a right to do that.

Caldwell?
Answer. I am president of the Caldwell Co.
Question. What is the business of that company?
Answer. Manufacturing cottonseed and ginning and fertilizer.
Question. Is the bulk of its business cottonseed and cottonseed products?
Answer. Yes, sir.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. How long have you been engaged in the cottonseed business?
Answer. About 30 years.
Question. Have you operated here in the State of South Carolina all of that time?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What is the approximate crush or what was the approximate crush last year of your mill?

Answer. Yes, sir.

Question. Well, how has this use and practice of gin loans of other companies affected your company, if at all?
Answer. Well, I don't see that it has so seriously affected us.
Of course, it gets some seed probably that we would get to make that loan.
Question. Well, when you make advances yourself do you take an f. o. b. refusal contract?
Answer. Well, we have in some cases, but we don't do very much of it. I sold a man, a concern, a gin a few years ago because they were talking about building one, and they gave me a contract.
That contract has not been adhered to by them, so I don't know.

Question. In your experiences have hauling allowances sometimes been used as a means or method of paying more for seed?
Answer. Well, it would be paying more for seed.
Question. They include it in the announced or published price for seed?
Answer. Yes; if you did that and didn't include it in your published price it would be.
Question. Well, wasn't that one objection raised against the practice, that it permitted the paying of more for seed without treating it as a proper or published price?

North Carolina, I have heard from it up there. And that is the remarks I made in one or two of those letters there. I heard it had crossed over from North Carolina in one or two cases there.

Question. What was the basis of your objection to it?
Answer. Well, it just increased the cost of your seed that much.
Question. Well, why should any mill want to make hauling allowances if it had that effect?
Answer. I saw no reason except competitive conditions. Some one concern might be doing it and force somebody else to do that.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. In other words, hauling allowances were made sometimes as a method of getting ahead of a competitor?
Answer. No; not getting ahead. Somebody probably did that first to try to get ahead, and that might result in that; but if we ever did it it was only just in a special case or some case where we did it to meet some condition. In one of those instances that you referred to there I said something to a man about giving him the storing on seed, but that was at the end of the season when we were trying to get enough seed to clear up, and I made that plain to him, that we were not making that as a precedent.
Question. Do you consider making hauling allowances equivalent to buying on a delivery basis?
Answer. Well, I hardly know what you mean by that question.
Our hauling allowances would come largely from people on the interior and we would have to deliver that seed f. o. b. cars somewhere if they didn't bring it to us.
Question. A hauling allowance made under such conditions, how would you characterize it, as equivalent to buying on a delivery basis?
Answer. You would naturally buy the interior seed adjacent to your mill on a delivery basis with your $3.
Question. You mean $3 commission?
Answer. Yes, sir; because that seller would have to deliver it somewhere and he would rather deliver it to a mill where he had 10 days to deliver his tonnage in than load it in a car in 2 days.
Question. These hauling allowances were sometimes allowed to a seller of that kind who had to deliver it somewhere?
Answer. Well, I expect they were if they were allowed. We had not been seriously disturbed by that practice in our section, not enough to be as intimate with it as you seem to think I might be. I don't know much about it up there. We haven't had it like North Carolina had it as I understand.
Question. Did you have any experience with it during the season of 1928-29 with reference to its bearing upon the general competitive market for seed?
Answer. I don't recall it now.
Question. Did you buy seed to some extent through brokers prior to 1928?
Anewer. Yes, sir.

Question. Those same brokers buy for other mills, too, didn't they?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. When you say you had them, you didn't have them exclusively?
Answer. No; not at that time.

Answer. Question. If you knew that the seller had shipped his seed to another mill and was dissatisfied with the grade of it and wanted to sell it to you would you feel perfectly free to buy it?
Answer. Well, I would not try to buy that seed very hard. I might if I thought there was some very good reason for it, that they could not agree, I might buy it, but I would want to treat my competitor mill just as I would want to be treated. I would not hesiate to buy the seed if they had failed to agree but I would buy it on weight and quality at destination.

Question. In other words, the sampling and grading of every lot of wagon seed is impracticable?
Answer. You just don't take the time to do that.
