Examiner SHEPPARD. Mr. Caldwell, if you wish to make a statement with further reference to this situation, I will be glad to give you the opportunity, sir, or, if not, I will excuse you.
The WITNESS. I'd like to say this, that in all we have done and tried to do, it was in the spirit of fairness to all sides, which, I think, is clearly shown by our letters, and I think we gave Mr. Dawkins every assistance we could, in giving him all the information when he came to our place. We have nothing to hide from him. As far as our own people up there are concerned, the people we deal with, I would be glad if they knew all about it. There is nothing up our sleeves at all, and I really feel that since the matter has gone on as it has with the trade commission, I believe the whole matter is one based on fairness, and I think we have room for still further improvement in our industry, and when it has passed the stage of being tipped around every way, I believe everybody will be better satisfied. I am confident of that. I think what we have had was a spoiled set of people, who have been running our business and we are just beginning to get our business lined up in a way that it is going to get somewhere in the line of legitimate business. Heretofore, the seed speculators ran it. We still have a bad practice, one that is right now in existence. I am doing it, and all other mills are doing it, that no other line of business is doing. We couldn't sell an oil buyer a tank of oil two minutes after the price has gone down; we couldn't sell a bale of cotton 10 minutes after the New York price has been set; at above what the price is. But we will go out and still pay the same price, take in seed at the same price from the seed speculators, that we haven't got a dollar invested in, and give him the price, when we know the market has declined two hours ago; and that thing is practiced. I had one large speculator to ask me one day, a friend of mine (and he is a financial success; president of a cotton mill), he asked me one day, he said: "You people do business the funniest of any folks I ever saw." He said: You know, I wouldn't buy cotton from you 10 minutes after the market had gone down, and pay you a higher price;" he said, "I don't understand it." I said, "We are wizards of trade." Mr. WOODEN. Who were these spoiled people you referred to?
The WITNESS. Yes; we have gone too far, no doubt about it, taking things like that, but now he asked me the question, "Why do you do it?" I said to him, "The only thing I could tell you is that I am in competition with a lot of mill managers who don't own any stock in the mills they work for and a lot of seed buyers who are buying seed on commission, getting their per-ton commission, and if I, as the owner of a mill myself, don't do what the other fellows are doing I will get no seed because there is more seed sold on a decline than any other time.' Mr. WOODEN. You also told us this afternoon that you were in competition with seed buyers for interests that are not concerned with whether they make a profit on the seed end of the business or not.
The WITNESS. Yes.
Mr. WOODEN. Who are the spoiled people you referred to?
The WITNESS. I refer to them as the speculator, largely, who has been buying the seed up and profiting by it largely and has been INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY selling the seed without grading, holding them maybe several months, letting them go through heat, and these people who take the seed that had been heated and not graded, those people I refer to as spoiled.
Examiner SHEPPARD. Mr. Caldwell, I was interested in your reference to the tariff on oils. You don't believe that to put a tariff on oil will keep the price of oil up, do you?
The WITNESS. I think it will keep out the competition on oriental oils or coconut oil, which they can produce for nothing in the Philippines. I believe that the coconut oil is responsible for the low price of seed.
Examiner SHEPPARD. You think to keep out those oils would improve the price of seed?
Examiner SHEPPARD. Isn't it against the law to put a tariff on Philippine products?
The WITNESS. Yes; as long as they belong to us it is. Give them their independence and you can do it. During the war there was a famine in the production of fats. There is one concern, the International Vegetable Oil Co., which was closely connected with it, and Davison Kennedy, the American Machine Co., formerly made a great deal of machinery and sent it to the Philippines and Manchuria, to press coconut oil, and we didn't know what we were up against. But we had no idea what we were doing at that time, and we have a real competitor there now, and we won't get any great relief until something is done. We may expect cheap seed, and while I was beginning to get on to it, two or three years ago, a little further study enlightened me that we are on lower levels and are liable to stay on lower levels awhile. We have another condition. We have people buying 8-pound buckets of compound lard for less than a dollar, with hogs scarce, they tell us, poorer hogs all over the country than we ever had, and the public wants to buy things as cheap as they can; we are in one corner of the United States producing cottonseed oil out of which compounds are made, and we have the whole country on an economical basis trying to buy everything up as cheap as you can; and so there it is, to produce your lard and get the stuff as cheap as you can. So we hold three-fourths of the products of the United States, while the rest of the country is getting the benefit of the low price of oil. Now, the consuming public is getting the benefit of it, and that is the thing that makes our cottonseed worth money. We get oil selling at 6% and 64 cents. You can't figure any high prices for seed, not at that rate.
Mr. WOODEN. Mr. Caldwell, will you check up those two points you were asked to?
The WITNESS. Yes, sir.

Question. A rather speculative proposition?
Answer. The biggest gamble I know of.
Question. Did you have anything in mind with reference to declining markets and losses from storage in your statements about Buckeye making it unprofitable to everybody?
Answer. I don't know-I don't know what I had in mind, excepting that all of the mills stored a good lot of seed. They were not the only ones.
Question. And the markets declined?
Answer. I don't know.
Question. Mills lost a lot of money?
Answer. I can't recall at this date.
Question. You said the hauling in North Carolina certainly made a mess of the seed business in that State.
Answer. It did.
Isn't there an explanation in one of those letters about how it applied?
Question. You give an explanation about Clayton, N. C., and, as I understand it, simply pointed out that the only result was that that cost the mills a certain additional amount for the seed.
Answer. That is right.
payquestion. Wasn't hauling frequently used, just as a device for ing more for seed, without including it in the published price?
Answer. I think it was used as a device more to buy seed, lost sight of the fact of cost or anything else, but just to buy tonnage.
Question. But it also had the effect that I mentioned, didn't it?
That is, it was in effect paying more for seed?
Answer. It was, in effect, paying more for seed.
Question. Without adding it to the price?
Answer. That is right.

Answer. Usually it is. At gins we keep it up. When somebody else is running the gin, they say, "I have bid on all this seed here, and can't change it until to-morrow." That is when they go down.
When it goes up, I think he makes it retroactive.

You couldn't do much of it.

and belief in the situation?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Now, will you explain just what your idea about that is?
Answer. Well, for one thing, that very few who now own the mills owned them back five or six years ago. The sheriff has sold some of them and some of them have been forced to sell out; banks have been operating some of them.
Question. Has any particular kind of competition destroyed the business?
Answer. No; just internal strife more than anything else. That is all, just competing.
Question. What is this reference to "so far as being a legitimate manufacturing industry is concerned?" What does that have to.
do with it?
Answer. A legitimate manufacturing industry would be one where you buy your raw material and on the day you buy your raw material you can add your manufacturing cost and a profit to it and sell the products.
Question. Well, then, I take it, your thought is that conditions had become such, that that could not be done?
Answer. It hasn't been done.
Question. And that means, does it not, that the business had become rather hazardous and speculative in character?
Answer. You want to try to borrow money from the banks to operate one of them and see.
Answer. Yes.
Question. What is it?
Answer. Yes.

Answer. None at all.

Answer. The single biggest element. It is not half or anything like that.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. I thought it was just about half, equal to about the rest of the products put together.
Answer. Wait a minute. Right now, it is more than half.
Question. Wouldn't you think it would be a more normal condition if the refined oil, or the price of refined oil did have a bearing on the price of seed?
Answer. It might. You see, you still have your value of your crude. You can most always sell crude. When you buy seed, you know what the value of the oil in that seed is going to be, the amount you are going to get out of the seed approximately.
Question. There is a certain differential between the refined and the crude, isn't there?

Answer. I think so.
Question. And refined oil certainly would have a bearing on the price of crude oil.
Answer. Supposed to have; yes.
Question. And yet has no bearing on the price of seed, according to Mr. Jasspon, and, as I understand it, you agree?
Answer. Well, that is so, probably. It has never been taken into account or figured in any way, but we figure the value of the oil in seed-what we can get for crude, regardless of what the refined market happens to be.
Question. Well, the refined market and the futures market in refined oil has a direct bearing, doesn't it, on the price of crude?
Answer. It makes the price of crude.
Question. Well, I must confess, I don't understand why the price of refined oil makes the price of crude and yet does not affect the price of seed.
Answer. Well, as a general thing, the price of refined oil fluctuates, goes up and down. I don't pay any attention to it because I am not interested in it, but the price of crude does not fluctuate with the price of refined oil.
Question. Yet I thought you said the refined made the price of crude?
Answer. It has to, finally. When they buy cotton, they buy_cotton so many points on or off a certain month, quoted in New York.
You don't sell crude that way. You sell crude at the price the refiner quotes.
Question. Do you consider the Memphis code of trade practice rules a valuable thing to the small mill?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Will you state just why?
Answer. I don't see any reason why it shouldn't be just as valuable to them as to the large mill.
Question. Well, do you think the small mill has more to gain through it and by it than the large mill?
Answer. My opinion is that he has.
Question. Now, will you explain that?
Answer. I can't. I have never operated a small mill. That is an opinion.
Question. Do you think the existence of the small mill, its days, are numbered, without the code?
Answer. That has been my thought.

Question. Answer. Our position has been to keep away from hauling or paying for hauling of cottonseed wherever it was possible to do so.
And competition has never forced us to do any great amount of hauling in South Carolina.

Answer. If competition would allow us to stay away from hauling in North Carolina we would do it.

Answer. No, sir.

Question. Is it your understanding that hauling allowance is something that has been championed by local mills as distinguished from terminal mills?
Answer. No, sir. The local mills, I imagine, consider that they have that natural advantage of being near-by the seed, and you see it can be trucked to them readily, more so than the terminal mill.
Question. Well, haven't hauling allowances been used in the past as a device for paying the seed seller more for his seed without including it in the published price?
Answer. Yes, sir. In years gone by they would pay a certain.
price if they were hauled to the mill, which generally was in excess of the price that they would pay where the seed were loaded and shipped.

Answer. It got them to a speculative basis.

The grade method for wagon seed for a district would establish a price for the wagon seed in that district based on their quality.
However, you find in practice that mill buyers through their gin connections and otherwise in competition with themselves even pay higher prices. Consequently, the independent must buy against them at higher prices.

Answer. The code trade practice states that $3 a ton commission can be paid to the mill buyers, which must include everything. However, we have local interpretations that mill buyers can be paid sums not exceeding certain amounts for seed house and scale rental.

Each cottonseed, Mr. Wooden, is a separate unit, a separate entity, you might say. You might have one cottonseed that is completely rotten and the free acid in the extracted oil from that seed may run a net per cent FFA. 121200 S. Doc. 209, 71-2, pt 6- -26 INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. That simply goes to the question of how thoroughly you mix your sample?
Answer. And also takes into consideration the number of seed that the chemist uses to make his determination. I figured it out some years ago. I am speaking from memory. I think that the chemist used a hundred cottonseed to make the determination. I figured that a hundred cottonseed on the basis of the number of seed that my mill crushed in one day was something like about to a billionth or some big number. I figured it at that time, worked on this basis, that if somebody would drop on this world from another planet and the first man he touched that represented the human race, it was in that percentage as to the amount of seed that would be crushed in one day. But I think it has been rearranged and the methods of making the chemical determination with considerably more seed are now employed in the laboratory to make this determination from.
Question. A while ago you said that the free fatty acid method was doomed to failure and that it was right. What do you mean by that?
Answer. Because it don't take into consideration the other valuable constituent parts of the seed. In addition to the quality of the oil in the cottonseed you have also got the quantity of a fixed amount of ammonia and meal that can be produced from this seed. You have also got to take into consideration the color that that meal is going to manufacture into. All of it is reflected into the final price for which that product can be sold.
Question. When you said it wasn't right, did you have in mindanswer. That it wasn't fair. It wasn't fair and accurate methods of making determination on the seed to both buyer and seller. I had in mind the part of the buyer. I knew it wasn't fair to us because it wasn't fair to us because-we had to meet competitive price, and the measure was established by the grade on the oil of the seed. And when we bought that seed and manufactured it we found that it made a smaller amount of meal of a dark quality that had to be discounted in price when sold.
Also I found that storm-damaged seed produced a lint of off quality that had to be sold at a discount in price from prime seed.
Ultimately, in order to get a fair and accurate method to both buyer and seller for grading cottonseed, the method of analysis must eventually take into consideration the quality and quantity of the oil, the quality and quantity of the meal, the quality and quantity of the lint, which in some sections in some seasons is a decided factor in establishing the price of cottonseed.
Question. Which of those factors have not yet been provided for?
Answer. Lint.
Question. How about meal?
Answer. The meal quantity on the ammonia basis is provided for.
Question. Now, those are all elements which I gather you said were not fair from the standpoint of the mill. In other words, the system was inadequate to take care of those factors?
Answer. Protect them.

Answer. Now?
Question. Now.
Answer. Well, the stock is owned by the Murray Co. in Atlanta, or tentatively it is owned by them; that is, a majority of the stock, and the other part of the stock is owned by a bank in Greenwood.
Question. Is this the Murray Gin Co. you are speaking of?
Answer. Yes, sir; the Murray Co.
Question. Are they manufacturers of gins?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How did it come about that a gin manufacturer has the ownership of an oil mill?
Answer. Well, they were formerly in the-manufactured cotton oil machinery, and when this mill was formerly built in 1919–20 they furnished the machinery, and the mill went into bankruptcy; it didn't operate more than a year; I don't think, and just when the deflation came in, and the mill went into bankruptcy, and the banks who were the creditors and the Murray Co. took over the mill in order to protect their interests.
Question. Has the mill been operated every season since that?
Answer. No, sir; the mill was dormant, it was closed down, it was sold by order of the courts I think in 1921 or 1922, I don't know when, but it was reorganized in 1924.
Question. And has it been reorganized ever since?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What was the approximate crush there last season?
Answer. Pardon me, I want to tell you about the stock. The stock has recently been acquired by myself and some other parties.
Answer. I started to say that we had recently acquired this stock from the Murray Co. in the last two or three months.
Question. The transactions have not been completed?
Answer. Well, they have been completed in a way. It is rather a long technical detail.
Question. Well, I don't think we need to go into that. Did you state what the approximate crush of the mill was last season? I don't think you did.
Answer. About 4,800 tons.
Question. How did that compare with the crush for preceding seasons?
Answer. Well, it was a little more than it was for the two seasons previous.

Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How many?
Answer. We have three ginneries.

Answer. Two in Greenwood and one at Troy.

Answer. Well, I would say about probably 35 per cent, or 40.
Question. And that comes to you as wagon seed?
Answer. Yes, sir; wagon and gin seed.

Answer. Through commission and by spot seed.
Question. Now, can you separate those two classes?
Answer. Can I separate them?
Question. Yes.

Question. About how many commission buyers do you have?
Answer. How many do I have?
Question. Yes.
Answer. I have three.
Question. And how many approximately spot shippers or independent shippers do you deal with?
Answer. Well, it is a pretty hard question to say right offhand.
I probably have dealings with 10 or 15 different concerns during the season. I may buy one car of seed from them.
Question. Are they mostly ginners?
Answer. Yes, sir; most of them are ginners.
Question. Some of them are seed merchants, you might say?
Answer. Well, sometimes I buy direct from the farmer.

Question. In car lots?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What is the territory from which you draw seed, the size of it, I mean, and the extent of it?
Answer. Well, I have bought seed at $3 at probably 70 miles, but it is very seldom we do it. The most of my territory that I buy seed from is in a radius of 40 or 50 miles.
Question. And on the seed that you transport by rail what is your average freight?
Answer. You mean on the seed that are shipped in?
Question. Yes.
Answer. I would say that my average freight is $1.25 for my carseed purchases.
Question. Do you make hauling allowance on the purchase of any seed?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. Have you ever done that?
Answer. No, sir; never have.
Answer. Yes, sir; I have had some who happened to buy seed for me but they never did buy any or very few.
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Did you ever have any question raised regarding the eligibility of any of them?
Answer. I don't recall that I did.
Question. What other mills are your chief competitors in buying seed in your territory?
Answer. Well, in the territory in which I operate I would say that practically all of them do some business, some of the larger mills, the Southern and the Buckeye, Swift, Kershaw interests.
Question. You would not put one ahead of the other particularly as an important competitor in your locality?
Answer. Well, just now as to seed that is bought in the particular territory in which I operate I would say that the Southern probably buys more seed in that territory. They have several ginneries and mills.
Question. Do you have some limited territory adjacent to your mill where you think you get most of the seed?
Answer. I don't know that I understand your question.
Question. Well, is there a territory immediately adjacent to your mill where you think you get most of the seed out of it?
Answer. Well, yes; I get the portion of the vicinity right around the mill.
Question. Well, what is the size of that territory?
Answer. Probably 7 or 8 miles.
Question. Seven or 8 miles?
Answer. Yes, sir; we probably draw seed in from about 7 to 10 miles.
Answer. No, sir; I have never bought but very few seed in that way.

Question. Have any of your independent ginner customers gone to other mills on account of gin loans being made to them?

Answer. Probably so; yes, sir.

Answer. Well, that would be my personal views. I would rather have $8 if I can't get $10, of course.

Answer. Let me see that a minute. [Examines letter.] Question. In the last paragraph.
Answer. I believe that word "the" should have been "a," not speaking of any particular high market.
Question. Has your Columbia mill or did it last season or at the time this letter was written, which was June 20, 1930, have a market for wagon seed that was higher than the wagon-seed market at other points in this State?
Answer. At the time that this letter was written there was practically no seed being marketed at all according to my recollection.
Question. It would be very late. At any time last season did your Columbia mill have a wagon market that was higher than that existing generally at other mills?
Answer. We have wagon markets at several points throughout the State I would say that are higher ordinarily.
Question. What are they?
Answer. I would say North, Elloree, Springfield, Johnston, and numerous other points.
Question. What causes them to be higher at those points, the wagon seed, than at other points?
Answer. That is a hard thing to say.
Question. Is it independent buyer competition?
Answer. I believe it can be brought about by many things.
Question. Is that one of them?
Answer. It can be brought about by independent competition, it can be brought about by a lien merchant who naturally wants to see a high market in his locality so that he can pay his debts.
Question. He may be an independent buyer?
Answer. He may be an independent buyer or he may be a buyer for a mill. There are lots of things about these local markets that we don't know ourselves.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. I suppose there are different causes entering into conditions at different points?
Answer. I would say so; yes, sir.
Question. You can not attribute any one condition to every one of those points?
Answer. Generally speaking I believe you can always attribute it to some strong-headed man.
Question. Well, you mean a strong-willed man among the independent buyers?
Answer. Among the local buyers. He may be a commission man, he may be an independent man.
Question. Well, doesn't the mill have control of its commission.
man as to what price he should pay?
Answer. Yes, sir; they are supposed to.
Question. Does he sometimes set up his will against that of his principal?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. I would think with disastrous results to the commission man.
Answer. Sometimes.
Question. They don't have to continue him unless they want to Answer. No, sir.
Question. As a commission man?
Answer. No, sir.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. Those discounts are published in a paper, and in quoting our commission men we show the discount or premium, as the case may be.
Question. If a seller of seed were informed that the discount for the week of January 10 was 8.40, and held his seed for another week and brought it in subject to the discount of 16.42, of course that would not represent any real change in the quality of his particular lot of seed in a week's time, would it?
Answer. It might and it might not.
Question. But you would not expect it to ordinarily, would you?
Answer. Seed that have begun a free acid germination would deteriorate very rapidly.
Question. Deteriorate to twice the extent in a week's time that they had already gone?
Answer. It would depend somewhat on the seed. I would not be surprised. Of course that is a pretty short time, I will admit.
Question. If a lot of wagon seed were brought in which you could tell from examination were likely to run off in quality even below the discount for the district, would you pay the average of the grade price for them notwithstanding?
Answer. Not if I thought they were particularly damaged; no, sir.
It would be suicide to do that.
Question. And if the particular lot of seed, wagon seed, looked to be prime, you would still follow the average of the grade?
Answer. Yes, sir. However, you could not tell a lot by the looks of them except if they were extremely badly damaged; and I don't think that would be a fair comparison to say that you would not give a premium when you propose to take a larger discount for exceedingly bad seed.
Question. Were you acquainted with the action of the executive committee of the South Carolina division on that point as to whether seed that was running prime by analysis should nevertheless be discounted according to the average of the grade?
Answer. No, sir; I am not acquainted with that.
Question. Of the action of the executive committee on that point?
Answer. No, sir; not that I remember.

Answer. He didn't want me to haul any seed. He wanted me to ship them. The freight would have been higher than the cost of hauling them.

Answer. I think so.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Well, I thought the objection to hauling was that it increased the cost of seed. In your case it had the opposite effect?
Answer. Yes, sir; you could haul them cheaper than you could ship them. They had to come over three railroads to be shipped.
Question. Did Mr. Taylor tell you that the mills in South Carolina generally didn't make hauling allowances?
Answer. I think maybe he did. He claimed that I was paying more than the other people because I took them right from the gin and they would have to move them about a hundred yards to put them on a car.
Question. Was it a fact that you were paying more than other people?
Answer. Well, all of the objections I know of was moving the seed.
We moved them probably-their gin was about 50 or a hundred yards from the sidetrack.
Question. The only difference was in your hauling?
Answer. Well, if they had shipped them to anybody else they would have had to load them in a car, and I loaded them in a truck right from their gin, which was 50 or a hundred yards from the sidetrack.
Question. Did you ascertain from Mr. Taylor what his interest was in your paying more than other mills were paying?
Answer. Question. How much difference did that amount to in price?
Answer. Well, some people would count it a different way. I was talking to a man the other day about buying-swapping some meal for seed, and he said he could load them for 10 cents a ton. He didn't count anything for his mules and wagon and his men that cost him a dollar a day, and he said he could load 10 cents a ton.
Question. I am interested in knowing about how much difference that amounted to at the time that Mr. Taylor took it up with you.
Answer. It would be the same thing then as now. One man might load them at 10 cents a ton and it might cost another man more.

Answer. Through brokers, entirely.
Question. Have you ever sold direct?
Answer. Not that I can remember.
Question. Do you prefer to sell through brokers, or would you prefer to sell direct?
Answer. Well, it is about as broad as it is long.
Question. You save the brokerage, at any rate, by selling direct?
Answer. Yes; but you can't get any more for it.
Question. What is the advantage of selling through brokers to you?
Answer. Well, it would give you market information that you would not ordinarily get from the refiner direct; inside information, in other words, market tips.
Question. Ordinarily, how much difference in price exists between refineries for the purchase of oil?
Answer. Usually, it is the same thing, but sometimes you catch one refiner who will pay a little premium over the prevailing price of the day for forward shipments.
Question. Well, isn't all your oil sold f. o. b. your plant?
Answer. Yes.
Question. You mean, by forward shipments, shipments later?
Answer. Yes; December or January shipments.
Question. Then, so far as the current price of oil is concerned, that is, for immediate shipment, you haven't noted any particular difference in price?
Answer. Sometimes one will have an eighth of a cent less than the other, two or three, some variations at times.
Question. Still, your general statement holds, that, usually, it is the same?
Answer. The same.
Question. Are there any refineries that will buy oil direct without brokerage, without brokers?
Answer. Really, we have never approached them to try to sell direct in recent years.
Question. How do you sell your meal?
Answer. We sell the bulk of it direct.
Question. In local territory?
Answer. No, sir; State of Virginia gets 75 per cent of our output.

Answer. Delivered and f. o. b. both.
Question. You figure your delivery cost in every case, from your own mill?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. So that your delivery price varies at different destinations?
Answer. Yes.
Question. When you buy seed, you buy it all f. o. b. shipper's point, do you not?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Why is it that you pay the same price for seed everywhere, regardless of distance from your mill, and sell your meal at different prices, depending on the distance from your mill?
Answer. Some buyers of meal want price delivered; others ask it f. o. b., either way they want it.
Question. Just take the cases where they are sold delivered, the delivered price varies according to the delivery points?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Why do you sell your meal on that basis and buy your seed on the opposite basis?
Answer. Because it is common practice with the mills to pay f. o. b.
prices has been for years.
Answer. It is the custom-meet the custom. Average freight is what counts, anyway.
Question. I don't think there is anything further I want to ask you, Mr. Johnston.

J. P. COMMANDER, being duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Will you state what your business is, Mr. Commander?
Answer. Well, coal and building material business, marble business, and I buy cottonseed.
Question. How long have you been engaged in the cottonseed business?
Answer. About 17 years.
Question. And what has been the nature of your operations in the cottonseed business?
Answer. Well, I bought for a salary at first up until about 1920, and I have been buying on brokerage ever since.
Question. For what companies did you buy on salary?
Answer. Buckeye, of Augusta, for seven years.
Question. Well, since 1920, then, you have been buying seed?
Answer. I buy on a commission.
Question. Do you own and operate a gin at your home?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Where is it located?
Answer. Sardinia, S. C.

Question. What proportion of them, of your seed business or the seed that you handled is seed that you buy at your own gin?
Answer. About 10 per cent.
Question. From whom, in general, have you purchased seed on commission?
Answer. You meanquestion. Of the owners or buyers?
Answer. I bought from the independent ginners in a radius of 20 miles around Sumter.
Question. As to the seed that you bought from gins, your own gin, I take it that that comes from the farmers?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. In wagon seed?
Answer. Wagon seed just as it is ginned.
Question. Now, those seed that you bought from independents, is that all car-lot seed?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. That is all car lot.
Question. Will you describe just how you have conducted that car-lot business, how you get the seed lined up, if that is a proper expression, and how you handle it all of the way through?
Answer. Well, it is a little hard to explain that at different times.
I keep in touch with the independent ginners. I telephone them probably-every change of the market I notify them and give them a chance to sell if the market goes up or down.
Question. Has the business with those independent ginners been handled in your own name or in the name of the mill to whom the seed are sold?
Answer. Generally they are handled in my name.
Question. You do your own financing?
Answer. Well, draft on the mill.
Question. Approximately how many independent buyers or independent ginneries have you dealt with over an average season?
Answer. Well, they get fewer and fewer every year.
Question. Well, take-give us the range, high and low, over a period of years.
Answer. Well, I suppose from 10 to 25. It used to be lots more during the good times, the war times, than there are now.
Question. Ten to 25 is the present number?
Answer. No; not now. There used to be 25 I used to buy from. I don't suppose there is over 10 or 12 I can buy from-that is, in my territory.
Question. Only some 10 now?
Answer. Ten or 12 who sold every year. I find ones that can not finance themselves and have to make a connection with an oil mill, and I can not buy from them.
Question. I was going to ask you what condition you have observed that is responsible for decrease in the number of independent ginners that you can buy from.
Answer. Well, since the boll weevil has got here there are not near as many gins operated. Some of them have burned up and not replaced and a good many that used to be independent can not finance themselves. They have to buy for an oil mill in order to be financed.
Question. Have there been independent ginners within your knowledge and experience who have gone over to buying on commission for a mill?
Answer. Oh, yes, sir.
Question. Has that been accompanied, as far as you know, by what are known as gin loans?
Answer. Yes, sir; I think the most of it is gin loans.
Question. Well, what has been the effect on your ability to get business from independent ginners when they take over-when they obtain a loan from a mill?
Answer. Well, you can not buy any seed from them, practically not; you may buy a car or two, but you are not supposed to get any at all.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Have you had independent ginners tell you that the reason they could no longer deal with you was because they had these loans from the mills?
Answer. Oh, yes, sir; yes, sir.
Question. Was there a time when you bought seed as a broker representing a number of mills?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. And how long ago?
Answer. Oh, I buy for two now.
Question. Beg pardon?
Answer. I buy for two mills now.
Question. But there was a time when you bought foranswer. Several of them-any that would pay a brokerage.
Question. Any number?
Answer. It was understood that any of them would give you a brokerage.
Question. How far back did that method of buying go in your experience?
Answer. Well, I bought independent for a-I mean on salary for the first seven years. I think that was probably from 1920 to 1925.
Question. Am I correct in understanding, then, for the entire period, say, of 1920 to 1925, that that was the period that you bought for various mills indiscriminately and received a commission on your purchasesanswer. Yes, sir.
Question. From the mill?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. And that commission was how much?
Answer. Fifty cents a ton.
Question. During that period did you ever hear any mill man raise objections to your method of doing business?
Answer. No, sir. They would just phone me and want to know if I could ship them, and give me a brokerage. It would not be my so much soliciting the mill as the mill soliciting me to get seed from me.
Question. Was there a time during that period when the broker's commission was in excess of 50 cents a ton?
Answer. No, sir; I don't think there was.
Question. Did you during those days share any of your commission with the seller of the seed?
Answer. Well, sometimes some other fellow would offer to do it, and I would do it to meet him.
Question. Some other broker, you mean?
Answer. Yes, sir; some other broker.
Question. Did you ever know the mills to raise any objection to that sort of thing?
Answer. No; I don't know whether they knew it or not, but I don't think they would raise an objection if they knew it.
Question. Did you attempt, as a broker, to get the best possible price for the seller of the seed?
Answer. No, sir; I always go by the mills, get the mills' quotations, and when I paid for them I never exceeded that or tried to get the mills to pay them any more.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Well, did you shop around among the mills to ascertain which mills were paying the best price?
Answer. Well, I would not shop around. You could find that out.
If I phoned a man and wanted to buy his seed and made him an offer and he had a dollar more bid by some other mill I would mighty quick find it out.
Question. You say you would quit finding it out?
Answer. I say I would mightly quick find it out.
Question. Well, then, would you go back to the other mills that were trying to buy seed?
Answer. No; I never tell one mill what the other mill is paying at all. I phone the mill that is paying the highest price. I never tell one mill what another is paying at all.
Question. Now, there came a time, did there not, when you were no longer buying from-buying for a number of mills indiscriminately?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Can you say when that time was?
Answer. That has been four or five years.

Answer. No, sir. The broker would not pay me a commission to handle the seed.
Question. That is, the seller?
Answer. Yes, sir.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Mr. DINKINS. Mr. Examiner, am I to understand by Mr. Wooden's questions about whether or not the commission has approved grading that he means to infer that the commission has not given its formal approval to the general question of grading of cottonseed?
Mr. WOODEN. No; I am fully aware that there is a rule among the Memphis rules, which we have quoted frequently, in which it is declared to be unfair competition and against public policy to buy and settle for seed, except on the basis of quality, cleanliness, and moisture content; and declaring that sound, clean, dry seed are worth more than damaged or trashy seed, and so forth. But I also call attention to the fact that that is one of the Group II rules, which the commission did not approve but accepted merely as an expression of the industry.
Examiner SHEPPARD. Does the Group II rules have anything to say about grading?
Mr. WOODEN. I have just read it.
Mr. DINKINS. One of my reasons for asking that question is because of the commission's former investigation of this industry, and in its report to Congress of March, 1928, it said that the commission also concludes that, as a result of this inquiry, that one of the main causes of dissatisfaction to both the producer of cottonseed and those engaged in its purchase and manufacture is the lack of a uniform system of grading. "Standards should be established for cottonseed as have been established for cotton and other products, so that those dealing in seed may arrive at a fair value, and which should, in some measure, at least, be reflected indirectly in the price paid the producer." And I don't quite understand why-in view of the commission's report to Congress in March, 1928, and this rule that Mr. Wooden has previously referred to, why there should be any doubt about the commission's attitude toward the general question of grading—if there was such doubt-and I was merely asking that question for my own personal information.
Mr. WOODEN. I don't think there was any doubt on the general proposition of grading as indicated by the 1928 report, but it is, nevertheless, a fact that the subsequent action of the commission on the Memphis rules placed the grading rule in Group II, which the commission did not approve.
Mr. DINKINS. I thought I understood you, in Raleigh, to say, Mr.
Wooden, that you did not know whether the commission had approved Group II rules or not.
Mr. WOODEN. No; I didn't say any such thing. I merely-you raised the question whether accepting a rule as an expression of the industry was not tantamount to approval, and I told you I did not know whether it was or not; but nevertheless the fact remains that Group II consists of rules that were received only as expression of the industry, and Group I contains rules that were approved. You can't link them.
Mr. DINKINS. Still, you wouldn't say that Group II rules were disapproved by the commission, would you?
Mr. WOODEN. No; I do not say that; I never did say they were disapproved.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY M. S. STACKHOUSE, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Will you state your business, Mr. Stackhouse?
Answer. I am a grain miller, mixer of feeds, cotton ginner, and cottonseed broker, at Dillon, S. C.
Question. Will you describe how your cottonseed business in both of those aspects has been conducted?
Answer. Why, up until this year, 1930-31 season, we have been independent ginners. We have operated a gin in connection with our grain mill at Dillon; have operated under the name of the Carolina.
Milling Co.
Question. For how many years past did you operate on that basis?
Answer. Why, we have operated as independent ginners since 1918.
Question. And this season your basis is changed?
Answer. This season we have signed a commission contract with the Buckeye Cotton Oil Co., and in that connection I might add that this season we leased a gin 3 miles out from Dillon, from the Palmetto Oil Co., at Bishopville, and of course that particular gin we signed a commission contract with the Palmetto Oil Co.
Question. Well, now, tell us about the seed brokerage business that you refer to. How has that been conducted?
Answer. Well, up until the last two or three years we have had quite a few independent ginners in Dillon County. We have a number of large farmers that operate their own gins, and they would accumulate from one to five cars of seed, and toward the last of the season we would buy these seed from those farmers, usually Question. Buy them outright?
Answer. Usually we would buy them outright from the farmers, and resell them to some mill.
Question. That wasn't brokerage business-that part of it, was it?
Answer. We would sell them to the high dollar.
Question. But, in buying them outright and reselling them, you were not acting as brokers?
Answer. In some instances we bought on a 50 cents a ton, but in a great majority of instances we would buy them outright.
Question. Will you explain a little further what you mean by selling them for the high dollar?
Answer. We would get in touch with a dozen different mills, and the mill that offered the most money we usually sold them the seed.
Question. How long did you operate on that basis?
Answer. Why, we operated on that basis ever since we have been in the cottonseed business, from 1918 up until, say, through 1926.
Question. Die there come about a change in your method of handling your brokerage business? If so, state what the change consisted of and when it occurred.
Answer. Well, I think the change came about in 1927. It partly came about in 1927, not so pronounced until 1928, and, of course, the present season.
Question. What was the change in your brokerage business?
Answer. We found that no competition existed, so to speak, any more. That is, we would call one mill; for instance, say we would call Buckeye Cotton Oil Co. in Augusta, and we would ask their INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY price for seed, and it was say $27 in carlots. Maybe we would call a dozen other mills, and they all had the same price, $27. Therefore, there was no competition, from our standpoint.
Question. In other words, would you say there was no further field for your selling seed for the high dollar?
Answer. That is correct.
Question. Did you ever read or learn of the provision of the Memphis resolutions relating to brokerage?
Answer. No; I don't know that I have.
Question. Well, there is a rule that reads, "Brokerage, if any, should be paid by the seller." If that rule were applied to your brokerage business, what effect would it have had?
Answer. Well, I don't think the seller would sell any cottonseed through us. I think he would most certainly sell them direct to the mill.
Question. Because he could get as much as through you?
Answer. Yes; he could get just as much as through us; and therefore he is not going to pay us 50 cents a ton to sell seed for him.
Question. How many different mills did you sell seed to in those days when you sold to a number of them?
Answer. Possibly 8 or 10 different mills. I don't recall the exact amount.
Question. Well, has there come about a condition under which you have since represented only one mill?
Answer. Why, at the present time we are buying, as I told you, on a commission for the Buckeye Cotton Oil Co. and the Palmetto Oil Co. at Bishopville.
Question. I am speaking of your car-lot purchases?
Answer. On car-lot purchases, so far as that is concerned, too, of course, we give them the preference on car-lot purchases.

Answer. No; I don't recall that we did.
Answer. Not that I recall.

Question. Even in the days when you also did a brokerage business?
Answer. That is right.
Question. What were the reasons which, if any, in addition to what you have already said, led you to take a commission contract rather than continue as an independent?
Answer. Last season, 1928-29, we bought seed through our gin and virtually at car price, on account of local competition that existedquestion. Competition from what source?
Answer. From Southern Cotton Oil Co., through their local gin plant.
Question. Well, who initiated that practice of paying-did you say paying a car-lot price for wagon seed?
Answer. Car-lot price; yes.
Question. Who initiated that?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. Mr. Caldwell, who is the lessee of the Dillon Oil Mill Ginnery. It is owned by the Southern Cotton Oil Co.
Question. You did not initiate it yourself?
Answer. No, sir; we did not.
Question. Was that the first season that had been done?
Answer. No, sir; that has practically been going on for the last 8 or 10 years.
Question. Who initiated it back that far?
Answer. It was initiated by them?
Question. Do I understand, then, that for a period of eight years or thereabouts you had been required to pay the car-lot prices for wagon seed?
Answer. Yes, sir; that is correct.
Question. Did you sell your seed last season, subject to grade?
Answer. Sold them subject to grade; yes.
Question. In general, what was the result in the way of deductions?
Answer. We lost from $2 to $4 a ton on them.
Question. In seasons prior to the inauguration of grading, were you able to come out whole on the season's operations, even though you paid the car price for wagon seed?
Answer. We made money prior to the grade rules, because there was quite a bit of margin in there, as a rule. It was good speculation.
As a rule, seed would open up low at the beginning of the season, and toward the last of the season they would advance $5 or $10 a ton over the opening price, which left a good margin of profit in there.
Question. How many years would you say that that condition existed, to your knowledge?
Answer. Why, since I have been in the seed business, since 1918; certainly up through 1926. In 1926 I made as high as $17 a ton on some seed.
Question. That was some particular lot?
Answer. About 2,000 tons.
Question. And all that time you were paying as much for seed as the mill buyers in the locality?
Answer. Paying car prices.
Question. Well, if you were getting that profit, what did the mills make? You were paying the same prices they were.
Answer. I can't tell you what happened to the oil mills around.
Question. How long, ordinarily, in those days, did you hold seed before selling?
or Answer. From two to five months.
Question. Last season, did you hold it a similar length of time, Answer. My recollection is we sold the bulk of our seed last year in January. We were holding on, of course, hoping the price was going to advance and let us out.
Question. Of course, under a commission contract, you are selling promptly as you accumulate it?
Answer. We sell it the day we gin it.
Question. How much difference was there last season in your locality between the car price and the wagon price of seed?
Answer. Why, I think the average was about $3 a ton, sir.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Do you know what grading district your locality is in?
Answer. I don't recall the district just now.
Question. Do you know what I mean when I refer to the "grading district"?
Answer. I understand the State of South Carolina is divided into districts, and they draw various samples of seed and send it in to a chemist, and if our district is running high in free fatty acid and moisture, our price will be maybe from $1 to $2 a ton lower than some other district that is running a better grade. I am familiar with the grading system, all right.
Question. Well, under its operation did you understand that the wagon seed was an average of the grade for the entire district?
Question. Do you know how the average was arrived at?
Question. You don't know whether or not the quality of the seed represented by particular samples had any bearing upon the average arrived at?
Answer. No; I really do not. I am not familiar enough with the grading to tell you that, to answer that question.
Question. Well, how did the purchase of wagon seed in your district last year under this grading system operate or affect your business?
Answer. Why, you know, this is the first year that the zoning system has been in effect. I think that is correct.
Question. Last year?
Answer. 1928? I didn't hear of the zoning system, if it was in effect. So far as I know, it was the uniform price of the territory.
1930-31, this year, is the first year that the zoning system has been in effect in South Carolina.
Question. I think you are mistaken. It was last year.
Answer. Last year we were not governed by the zoning system.
This is the first year we have been governed by it.
Question. Yet you are paying the car price?
Answer. No; we are not paying the car price. This is the first year we have not paid the car price.
Question. Isn't there any other independent in that locality whose competition would result in the wagon price being run up to the car price, or somewhere near it?
Answer. We have no independent seed buyers on the Dillon market, and the only ginners there are ours, and Caldwell, who is the lessee of the Southern Cotton Oil Co., and the Palmetto Oil Co.'s plant, which is 3 miles out, and so far as I know this season the price paid has been regular. It has stuck to the wagon price.
Question. The first season in eight years?
Answer. About eight years; yes.
Question. Do you think that is a mere coincidence, that this is the first season you have not operated as an independent?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. I feel like our connection with these other mills has been a great help to us this season.
Question. Well, the grading system last year, then, in your locality didn't really affect you?
Answer. Didn't amount to anything, so far as the ginneries were concerned.
Question. Well, so far as car-lot seed, what has been your experience with the grading system?
Answer. The two lots of seed that I refer to last year that we sold in January were two lots, one for Marion Cotton Oil Co. at Marion and the other for Maxton Cotton Oil Co. We sold those two mills about equal tonnages of seed. When we shipped those seed out we shipped one car to one and one car to the other. We gave one car to Marion and one car to Maxton, and we finally got returns. Marion Cotton Oil Co. had sent their samples of seed to one chemist, and the Maxton mill had sent their samples to another chemist. This represented a lot of seed of about 800 tons. Marion sent their samples to C. W. Rice; Maxton sent their samples to Law Co., and in the final wind-up we found that the Marion analysis was from $1 to $2.50 a ton better than the Maxton analysis.
Question. How do you know, or do you know, that the samples sent to that the cars sent to the two different mills and the samples taken from those cars represented the same quality of seed?
Answer. We don't know it, except for the fact that the mills told us so that they drew the samples. The samples were drawn after arrival of the seed at the mills. After that happened we registered a complaint with Maxton that their analysis was not satisfactory, and they agreed that they would send their samples (they kept duplicate samples) to Mr. Rice, and on the reanalysis we came out from $1 to $2.50 better on the Maxton. In other words, they came up to the Marion analysis.
Question. Was that without any knowledge on Rice Co.'s part of what the Law Co. analysis was?
Answer. So far as I know. It was handled entirely by the two mills.
Question. In your opinion, is it possible for an independent ginner to operate on a margin, gross margin, of $3 a ton?
Answer. No, sir; I don't think so, under present conditions, that an independent ginner can live at all. I believe that the independent ginner is bound to sign a commission contract to-day in order to stay in business over the average year. Of course, I heard Mr. Commander's testimony a few minutes ago. As he says, this has been an extraordinary season, and this has been one year that the independent has really fared better than the man on a commission contract, because the seed this year has brought a decided premium.
Question. This is the first year that a premium has been paid?
Answer. This is the first year a premium has been paid, of course.
Question. Of course, I take it that your own action in shifting from an independent to a commission basis is the best evidence of the reality of your convictions on that subject?
Answer. That is correct. We realized we couldn't live as an independent, and therefore we signed a commission contract.
Question. Have you been in touch with any other independents as to their experience on a similar subject?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. Well, in my particular county, I don't know but one or two small gins that are operating to-day on an independent basis.
Most of them are affiliated with cotton-oil mills.
Question. On what do you base your statement that most of them are affiliated with cotton-oil mills?
Answer. Well, I am acquainted with most of the ginners in Dillon County. Some are connected with the Southern; some with Buckeye; some with Marion Cotton Oil Co.; different mills in the territory. And the farmers very largely quit operating their own gins, largely, on account of the decline in cotton products.
Question. How far back does your knowledge of this reduction in the number of independent ginners in your county go?
Answer. Well, it has been steadily on the decrease, I would say, since 1920.
Question. Has that shown any unusual amount of decrease in the last several years?
Answer. Well, I would say this past year several independents in my county have signed a commission contract.
Question. How many independents are still left in your county?
Answer. That would be hard for me to state just offhand. I don't think there is any ginner of any consequence, but one or two, that are operating as independents.
Question. How many gins are there in the county operating?
Answer. I am not able to answer that question.
Question. Approximately?
Answer. I would say approximately 12 of the major gins that gin the principal part of the crop.
Question. I understand that you get 50 cents commission on seed that you buy under your present contract, that you buy in car lots from other ginneries?
Answer. That is correct.
Question. Do you buy some seed from independents who are not ginners?
Answer. Well, all the seed that we buy are bought either from ginneries—that is, on the commission basis, or from large farmers that operate their own gins-so in one sense of the word they are ginners; while they don't operate gins for the public, they don't operate them only for themselves.
Question. Under your contract have you gotten more than 50 cents per ton on car seed, or any more than $3 on wagon seed?
Answer. Not except where we reported them in advance, on a declining market.
Question. Well, explain that; I don't quite get it.
Answer. Well, for instance, if seed were $28 and the mill called us up and told us the price was going to decline on seed, and wanted to know if we wanted to report any seed, we might report 500 tons ahead, 200 tons, 300 tons.
Question. Before you bought it?
Answer. Yes; that is correct; go short on the market.
Question. Have you in the past years, particularly last season, had mill representatives inform you in advance of declines that were coming?
Answer. We might have a millman to call us up and tell us a decline was coming, but wouldn't necessarily specify the amount of the INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY decline, whether it was going to be $2 or $3 a ton. In former years seed usually declined around $3 a ton at a clip, but that is not true any more. We might be notified of a decline and we would think a decline was coming, yet we wouldn't know how much it was going to be.
Question. Well, you have spoken of the identity of price between different mills at different times. Has that been just as noticeable on declines as on advances in price?
Answer. I think it has. It has been less true this year than in former years. I find there is less coordination or cooperation between different mills this year than there has been in other years.
Question. Well, you spoke something of the period during which your company offered seed, sold it for the high-dollar. When did that period pass out?' Answer. About 1926 was the last good year that we had.
Question. There has been no particular change from year to year since that time?
Question. Lack of grading was a way out from the uniformity of price, as viewed from your standpoint?
Answer. That is correct; from our standpoint.
Question. Then, last season, did you find any mills that didn't grade?
Answer. Up until October 1, I think, there were several mills that didn't grade.
Question. After October 1?
Answer. After October 1, I think, all mills graded.
Question. Do you know any other points in the State last season where a car-lot price was being paid for wagon seed?
Answer. I understand, over Tatum, S. C., they are paying carload price for wagon seed.
Question. Last season or this season?
Answer. Both last season and this season. I don't know that to be a fact, of course; it is hearsay on my part.
Question. How about seasons prior to last season in Tatum?
Answer. I am not in a position to say. I understand there has been quite a fight over there; but I don't know whether it was last season or this season.
Question. Do you know between whom the fight is?
Answer. I don't know; I understand the Southern operates a mill over there, but I understand there has been a fight between the Southern and a local ginnery.

On that particular lot of seed, if you will allow me to bring that in, we bought from a farmer friend of ours, who had about 80 tons of seed. He asked me to go to his place and sample the seed, which I did, and had samples sent to Sapona Mills. They were not buying on the particular samples; but he wanted to gain an idea of about what his seed were going to be worth, and we got returns on the samples and it showed that about half of the seed were graded off about 95 cents a ton, as well as I recollect, and the other half showed a deduction of about $4.10 a ton, and on the strength of the samples that we sent he sold me the seed, thinking that was all the deductions, and when the seed were shipped the seed that showed a deduction of $4, one car almost tallied exactly with the analysis of the sample that was sent on previously, but the other car showed a deduction of around $5 a ton under that.
Question. You mean the quality of the seed improved while it was being shipped?
Answer. No; it looked like the quality lessened; that is, the analyses on three cars were practically the same as the samples sent in advance, but the other was about $5 a ton less than the advance analysis.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. What is the approximate volume of business done in a season?
Answer. About 400 to 500 tons of seed.
Question. Do you operate your business on an independent basis?
Answer. We have almost entirely, up to this year.
Question. And what is the business this year?
Answer. This year for the first period-I don't know the exact dates-but for part of the year we bought on commission for one of the oil mills.
Question. What company was that?
Answer. Southern Cotton Oil mill, of Columbia.
Question. Was that at the outset of the season?
Answer. At the beginning of the season.
Question. And how long did that arrangement continue?
Answer. I would imagine about one month. I didn't bring any information with me, you know.
Question. Do I understand that since that arrangement was discontinued that you have gone back to operating on an independent basis?
Answer. We have.
Question. What competition have you met with in the purchase of seed at your gin?
Answer. Our competition-well, we have other gins, one 4 miles from us, and another 8 miles from us, and another probably 10 or 12 miles. In fact, the whole country is dotted about. Those are the closest gins to us.
Question. Do you know whether these gins operate on an independent basis?
Answer. Some do, and some buy on commission.
Question. How do you determine the price you pay for wagon seed at your gin?
Answer. When we are buying on commission, the price is instructed by our principals. When we are buying independently, we naturally must meet competition and pay the same price for seed that other gins in the neighborhood pay.
Question. Well, when you buy independently, do you ordinarily buy on a $3 differential below the car price?
Answer. Exactly.
Question. Did you sometimes pay higher than that?
Answer. On occasion.
Question. Buy them on your own initiative or because competition required it?
Answer. Because of competition; because of local conditions.
Question. Well, then, do I understand that you didn't initiate the payment of more than the regular wagon price yourself?
Answer. No; we didn't.
Question. Have there been any gins in your locality buying on commission that have paid more than the regular wagon price?
Answer. No.
Question. The competition you refer to, then, is evidently that from other independent gins?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How have you been accustomed to ascertain what the car price was on seed?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. Well, if I haven't got the information, I call one or two oil mills and get the price, or frequently I get wires from them quoting the price if there is any change.
Question. What oil mills were you accustomed to get quotations from when you were buying independent?
Answer. The Southern Cotton Oil Co. at Columbia, the same company at Savannah, the International Vegetable Oil Co. at Savannah, Swift Co. Oil Mill at Augusta, Kershaw Oil Mill at Kershaw.
There are some other minor ones that I do not recall now that we didn't do business with but we frequently got quotations from.
Question. Well, take last season for the time being. What condition did you find among mills that you were in touch with with reference to the degree of uniformity of their prices at one given time?
Answer. The price was always the same all of the time.
Question. How long after a change in the market occurred was it before all of the mills again had the same price?
Answer. Why, we would frequently get three or four wires on the same telephone call, and I think in almost every case we would hear within one or two hours from all of the mills we were in touch with when the change came.
Question. Did you find that those changes were followed by all of the mills in case of decline in price as well as in advances?
Answer. I did.
Question. Did you ever have any advance information given you by mill representativesanswer. No.
Question. That a decline was coming?
Answer. No.
Question. And I suppose the same thing applies to an advance or forecast?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Have you found it the practice among mills to protect you on a decline, that is, by allowing you to sell seed at the old price?
Answer. Well, not after the price had been published.
Question. Well, then, that was an arrangement made in advance?
Answer. Well, it was possibly a report of some seed that we hadn't bought; in other words, sell short; but I can not say I have ever been given any information that such was going to be the case.
I was just using my own judgment.
Question. Were you able to sell any of your seed aside from that at a price above its general marketanswer. Never.
Question. That you have described?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. Now, we were talking about conditions last season.
Answer. They are practically the same.
Question. Well, when you say practically, I take it that there was some difference?
Answer. No; I would say actually the same. I do not know of any differences. The same procedure was in effect then.
Question. Well, compare those two seasons with seasons preceding for several years.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. Well, as far as I can remember, since I have been connected with the cottonseed business there has never been any difference in the prices published or offered by any of the mills that we were in touch with.
Question. Isn't it true that prior to the 1928 season, for instance, that you could occasionally get a little higher price from some mill than its bid price?
Answer. Well, I do not recall having been able to do so.
Question. Mr. Linthicum, who interviewed you, states you as stating that, beginning with the 1928-29 season, for some reason conditions in the seed market began to tighten up. Do you recall that?
Answer. In 1928-29?
Question. Yes.
Answer. You mean in respect to grading policy?
Question. I take it that this relates to the matter of price. He further reports in that same connection that you found it increasingly difficult to find some mill that would give any better price than what all of the mills quote.
Answer. Well, that is true.
Question. Well, then there was some difference between the 1928-29 season and the preceding season?
Answer. Well, of course, you know, I didn't look up any record, I didn't know just what you gentlemen were going to ask me. When Mr. Linthicum interviewed me I was in the office. And that is, as I say, a general thing. I do not remember very much in the matter of competitive prices for the last several years, I do not remember the dates or anything like that. It seems to me that for the last four or five years conditions have been just about the same as they are now.
Question. Now, coming down to this season, what condition do you find as to price uniformity this season?
Answer. Well, every mill seems to have the same price at identically the same time, and whenever an advance or decline comes they all go together.
Question. No difference between the present season and last season?
Answer. Not that I can see.
Question. Have you followed the prices as published in the newspapers published here in Columbia?
Answer. Yes; I do.
Question. Have you noticed any difference in the prices reported there in one section of the State from another?
Answer. I have noticed some; yes.
Question. Well, do you consider that a difference from the preceding seasons?
Answer. Well, I do not recall. In fact, I do not remember that price publication ever being in effect before this year. at least I didn't notice that it was.
Question. I understand it began last winter some time, but you did not notice it?

Answer. No, sir.
Question. In your vicinity are there any markets where the wagon price is on a basis other than the regular $3 differential below the car price?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. None that I know of.
Question. How do the prices published in the newspapers this year correspond to the prices in your locality?
Answer. Practically the same.
Question. Well, aren't these prices published in the paper this season, don't they show different prices paid on the same day by different mills?
Answer. In different sections? The only thing that I ever pay any attention to and the only thing that seems to concerns us as independent buyers is the basis seed price. I notice sometimes they may quote a different price in a different part of the State, but it is not of any interest to us because our price is always fixed at $3 under the basis seed price.
Question. How wide a territory is your knowledge confined to?
Answer. Well, I would say to the county in which we operate, Colleton County.
Question. Did you sell your seed last season when you were operating independently subject to grade?
Answer. No, we did not.
Question. Through what mill or mills did you sell much last season?
Answer. We didn't sell any seed last year. We exchanged it for cottonseed meal.
Question. Your entireanswer. In volume all that season.
Question. Are you selling your seed this season subject to grade?
Answer. Yes.
Question. In selling or exchanging, rather, your seed for meal last year did you find any difference among the mills as to the conditions of exchange?
Answer. The basis of exchange was the same in every case.
Question. How many mills did you get in touch with to find out that that was true?
Answer. We did all of our trading with three mills.
Question. And they were what?
Answer. International Vegetable Oil Co. in Savannah; Southern Cotton Oil Co., of Columbia; Swift Co. oil mill, of Augusta.
Question. What was the extent of your knowledge and familiarity with the grading system as established in your territory last year?
Answer. Why, I didn't pay any attention to it last year, not being interested, having exchanged seed for meal. It is my recollection, however, that the grading system didn't go into effect at the beginning of the season but took place some time later in the season.
Question. October 15, I think.
Answer. And as we were practically through ginning at that time we were not very much interested.
Question. Did you sell your seed subject to grade during the season of 1928-29?
Answer. Let's see. This would be termed the season of 1930?
Question. Yes.
Answer. That, in other words, is two years back?
Question. Season before last.
Answer. We sold some that wasn't subject to grade. I believe the same condition prevailed then, that the first part of the season the INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY mills didn't grade, but some time during the season they put the grading policy into effect.
Question. You rather strongly objected to the operation of the grading season that year, didn't you?
Answer. I did.
Question. What was your objection based on?
Answer. It was based upon what I considered a very unfair practice inasmuch as the mills didn't grade the seed that was bought by their commission men but did grade the seed that was sold to them by independents, yet the independents have to meet the competition of the commission men.
Question. They had to pay as much for seed as the commission men?
Answer. Exactly.
Question. And did they know how much they were going to get for it when they bought it?
Answer. Had no idea at all.
Question. Or even when they sold it did they know?
Answer. Didn't know until 10 days or two weeks afterwards.
Question. Do you know to what extent independent seed was unloaded at the mill before the independent knew what he was going to get for it?
Answer. I didn't get that, sir.
(The reporter reads the question.) Question. I am just speaking of your general knowledge.
Answer. On my general knowledge I think that is true generally, that they do not know, none of the independents know, what they are going to get for it until it is unloaded and graded.
Question. If the independent were inclined to question the mills on the grading or analyzing, how would he get his seed back?
Answer. He could not get them back.
Question. He would just have to make the best settlement he could with the millanswer. Exactly.
Question. Knowing that he could not get his seed back?

Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Is there anything further or any other point in connection with that matter of grading independent seed to which you took exception or made objection?
Answer. I object to the policy; you mean-pardon me, you are referring to some correspondence I had on some matter I took up at that time?
Question. I have some such correspondence, but I haven't anything definite in mind with regard to it. I just want to give you the opportunity of bringing out any other point or objection that you had to the grading system as it affected you.
Answer. Well, in general I objected to the grading system because there is no way in the world that a seed buyer can protect himself from it. While it is possible for the oil mills through their chemists to grade seed in carloads, it is not possible for the independent buyer to grade seed in wagon lots.
Question. Could he protect himself if he paid the same price for wagon seed that commission buyers did?
Answer. He could not.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Because he would not know what he was going to get for it; is that the answer?
Answer. That is the answer. I think it is very significant right here. In October-November 20, 1928, the basis prime seed was $45. It was necessary for us in order to meet the competition to pay $42 a ton for the seed. When this seed was shipped and received at the mill after.it was analyzed and graded we received $27.82.
Examiner SHEPPARD. You mean you received $27.82 a ton for what you have given $42 for?
The WITNESS. Exactly.

Question. What has been your experience this year with selling seed subject to grade?
Answer. Seed that we sold subject to grade this year as a rule have been off in grade from 47 cents per ton to $4 or $4.50 per ton.

Question. Were the seed in your locality during the 1928-29 season generally of poor quality?
Answer. Why, not to my knowledge.

Answer. Oh, you are referring to the 1928-29?
Question. 1928-29.
Answer. That was season before last. I think the seed were bad that year to the best of my recollection.
Question. But I presume that your seed were no worse than those being bought by commission buyers for the mills?
Answer. Exactly.
Question. What factors led you at the beginning of this season to decide to operate on a commission basis instead of continuing on an independent basis?
Answer. Our experience during the past showed that if the grading was going to be in effect this year we would simply stand a loss, besides we wanted to make comparison, we wanted to see how we would be treated on a commission as compared to how we were treated when we were independents.
Question. Well, did you find by the comparison?
Answer. We found that the seed we shipped bought on a commission basis wasn't graded.
Question. Well, why did you go back to buying an independent basis after that?
Answer. Well, we felt that we might benefit by so doing in order to get the breaks in the market which we occasionally do and feeling that the seed was running pretty good we did not think that we would stand any loss on account of the grades this year.
Question. But you understood that premiums were being paid this year?
Answer. In some cases.
Question. Did that have something to do with your Answer. Exactly.
Question. Decision?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Was it possible during the season of 1928-29 to get the mills to sample your seed before it was shipped?
Answer. No.
Question. Was that true throughout the season or just a part of the season?
Answer. I never recall having been able to get them to sample seed before they were shipped. I think the universal practice is and always has been since the grading policy has been in effect that the seed have to be shipped to the mill before it is graded.
Question. Do you consider it feasible or practical for wagon seed to be bought on grade?
Answer. I do not.

Answer. It would.

Question. Will you agree that whatever benefits come through a system of grading should accrue to the benefit of the farmer?

Question. Have you seen or observed any benefits from the grading system already applied that resulted in benefits to the farmer?

Question. Have you seen any results that you thought tended in the other direction?
Answer. No; I can not say that I do, for this reason, that the independent buyer has been bearing the burden of the loss, and it has not yet been passed on to the farmer.

Answer. Exactly. He has got to meet the competitive price of the commission buyers.

The WITNESS. I merely state that I offer that comparison in order to show that my opinion is that the grading of seed by analysis is more or less a gamble.
By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Chemical analysis?
Answer. Chemical analysis is more or less a gamble. It depends on getting a fair average sample from each lot. For instance, one wagon lot of seed may have been picked and ginned from a swampy piece of land where the foliage is heavy and the sun can not get in there. Well, the sample may be taken from that particular lot of bad seed and not be a fair average of the car. On the other hand, the sample may be taken from a particular part of the car which is very good seed and would grade accordingly higher. I am not familiar with the methods of sampling, but I understand that they take it from several parts of the car. But that still, in my opinion, does not get a fair average of the contents of that car.
And it is my purpose in submitting these papers to bring out that point.

Answer. No, I have not.

A. B. BENNETT, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. What is your business, Mr. Bennett?

Question. Well, some idea.
Answer. Ten or 12 or 20 years, something like that.

Answer. Yes, sir. I have been buying them a good long time.

about 250 tons, something like that.

Answer. Well, even if they were not unloaded we would have to take the analysis anyway.

Answer. I guess so.
Question. But it would be expensive at best?
Answer. Oh, yes.

Answer. Oh, no.
Question. You sell it at a certain basis price?
Answer. Yes.

Answer. Yes.
Question. How do you determine the price you pay for seed when you buy it?
Answer. Well, I usually when I buy any, just buy it at the market price they are paying for seed. I buy very few.

Answer. Well, I think probably that I have.
