Question. Were you making objections, or registering any complaint against the grading system?
Answer. Yes; not only the grading, but the way of handling them.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. What do you mean by handling them?
Answer. The farmer produces the seed; the mills set the price, weigh the seed, grade the seed, and all the farmer has to do is produce it no say at all in the price.
Question. Wellanswer. In other words, as I look at it, it is a combination against the farmer who produces it, the producer.

One man may be willing to buy for a dollar, and he would cut his commission on it and sell it. We have always had a pretty good market for seed there; that is, up to the limit.
Question. Now, during what period of time has that condition obtained?
Answer. That is just on wagon seed, during the ginning season.
Question. Has it occurred every year?
Answer. Yes; every year, I would say, up to two or three years ago, the mills bought very few seed there up to late in the season.
They were all bought by the speculators.
Question. What caused the wagon price to be above the usual differential of $3 below the car price?
Answer. Well, what I have bought I have got in the warehouse now-haven't sold it expect it to go up-speculation.
Question. Do I understand that prior to this season, there have been other independent buyers at your point?
Answer. Not so many last season. For the last few years we have had very few independent buyers.
Question. Have you sold at any time through commission buyers, in order to avoid deductions on account of grade?
Answer. I have not.

Answer. Yes; sometimes get just as good a price.

Answer. That has been several years ago.

Dr. W. C. HAMRICK, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Where do you live, Doctor Hamrick?
Answer. Gaffney, S. C.
Question. And what is your business?
Answer. Cotton manufacturing.
Question. What do you have to do with the cottonseed business?
Answer. I run a cotton ginnery.
Question. Do you buy seed at the ginnery from farmers?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Are you a farmer yourself-do you have farming interests yourself?
Answer. Not directly.
Question. Well, do you have some indirect farming interests?
Answer. Tenants on some property that I own-land that I own.
Question. How long have you been in the cottonseed business?
Answer. I have been running a ginnery this is four years; I began in 1927.
Question. How did you come to go into the business of buying cottonseed?
Answer. Well, I bought a ginnery more for the benefit that accrued to the mills that I operate in buying cotton direct.
Question. Are you interested in cotton mills?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. This cottonseed business then I take it is a minor operation.
Answer. Yes.
Question. Of the entire business?
Answer. Yes.
Question. What has been the average amount of the seed bought at the gin per season?
Answer. Well, it has varied some. I would say that it has averaged something around 800 to 1,000 tons per season.
Question. Has not varied over that in the entire four seasons that you have been operating?
Answer. Well, I would not be positive. That is about my average, I would say.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Is it your experience that the farmer ordinarily sells his seed at the time his cotton is ginned?
Answer. Well, this year they have been selling probably 60 to 65 per cent anywhere from 50 to 65 per cent at the time cotton was ginned.

Answer. Not quite so much.

Answer. Seed are running very much better this year.
Question. Were you able last year to find any mill that would not that did not agree?
Answer. No, sir. Well, now, I sold some seeds to the Victor Oil Mill last year. He got a sample from the seed house and had it analyzed and he bought the bulk, perhaps two or three hundred tons, I don't recollect just what, he bought the bulk on the basis of the analysis of the seeds that he had gotten out of the seed house.
Question. And you knew exactly what net price you were going to get before you shipped them?
Answer. Yes. On that basis he made me a bid on so many hundred tons in the warehouse; and I didn't sell any seeds except subject to analysis.
Question. Well, were those seed sold on the basis of a deduction below the basis price?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. And what have you to say with reference to the practice of analyzing and grading your seed only after it is shipped to and arrives at the mill?
Answer. Well, I could not question the chemist. They are presumed to be high-toned gentlemen. I could not question them.
Question. Well, you would prefer to have your seed analyzed before it left your possession?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Do you know whether or not your seed is unloaded at the mill before you get the chemist's report on it?
Answer. I do not.
Question. Did you ever have any experience with variations in reports of chemists on the same lot of seed?
Answer. Well, I might ship one or two or even three cars of seeds out of the seed house in the same week, and it is hardly likely that the analyses of the chemist would be identically the same in all.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Well, what I had reference to was any experience upon the identical lot of seed or a split sample of the same lot of seed being analyzed by more than one chemist?
Answer. No.
Question. Have you ever considered taking a commission contract?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. Do you know any ginners who have taken commission contracts on account of this grading?
Answer. I have only heard of them.
Question. Have you talked to any of them?
Answer. Not to any extent.
Question. If you didn't have the cotton mill business as the principal part of your business and if your ginnery and seed business was the principal, would you continue to operate on an independent basis?
Answer. Well, that would depend on my circumstances. If I had the capital to operate it and buy seeds and take chances on an advancing market I might do it.
Question. Notwithstanding this deduction on offgrade seed applied against independent seed and not against commission seed?
Answer. Well, I think it would be a hazardous business.
Question. Whatever speculative risk there has been in it in the past would not be a circumstance to the speculative risk in the future?
Answer. Well, for me to make money on cottonseeds it is purely a matter of trading. If I can buy the cottonseed and believe that we are going to have a better market later on and seek those seeds and hold for a better market, if I get a better market I make money; if I misjudge the situation and get less for the seeds I lose money.
Question. A good deal would depend on the quality of the crop during the season?
Answer. Yes. Of course, some seasons when the seeds have a good percentage of moisture it is impossible to keep them very long to hold for any probable advance.
Question. Were you familiar with the method used last season and I think also this season with reference to buying wagon seed according to the average of the grade in a particular district?
Answer. I understand that the zoning system went into effect this year. Now, I don't know much about the methods, I am not on the inside of anything that the crushers do. It is only what I see in the papers.
Question. Well, of course we know the general method of buying wagon seed on the average of the zone or district. You don't know anything about that last season in your locality?
Answer. As to the zoning it is only what I see in the papers.
Question. And I understood you to say that last season the ordinary $3 differential obtained in your territory between the car and wagon price?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Does that mean that you observed no time last season when the differential was greater than $3 in your territory?
Answer. Not to my knowledge.

Answer. I don't know that I have anything to say.

Question. Yes.
Answer. Well, I don't see that it would have any effect on him.

Answer. Yes; if the average of the district showed a deduction the farmer with the prime lot of seeds would suffer the deduction.
Question. I suppose that is really so apparent that we should not ask you about it. Have you been in touch with farmers sufficiently in your locality to know what their reaction is to the conditions in the seed market?

Question. Include that; yes. Take that up first.

Question. Their only reaction is to the price then?

Question. As to whether it is high or low in their opinion. Does the farmer in your locality know anything about the method of grading seed?
Answer. The more intelligent farmer knows that seeds are graded.
But when he sells them in wagon lots he is never faced with the fact that your seeds will be graded and we will have to deduct from the price we are paying him if these seeds are off.
Question. Well, does the independent buyer have to absorb that grading situation there?
Answer. Yes. There seems to be one price, observing that differential of $3. We buy a load of wagon seed this morning and we pay him $1.35 per hundred-I mean a dollar per hundred, $20 a tonsay, and that is what the oil mill pays, a dollar, but when we go to sell the oil mill the identical seeds that we bought and paid a dollar for, the seeds not analyzing up to prime seed, we have to absorb the independent ginnery has to absorb that loss.
Question. And there is no way that you can pass it back to the farmer?
Answer. No, sir; because we don't know whether his seeds are prime or not.
Question. Is there any way that you can pass back to the farmer that you are getting this year?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. We don't know whose seeds they are.

Answer. There is no way that we could.

The WITNESS. No. It is between the independent buyer and the crusher.
Examiner SHEPPARD. That is my understanding.
The WITNESS. Well, we observed last year a $3 differential when the seeds graded below prime just as we are this year when we get a small premium above prime.
By Mr. WOODEN : Question. You can not lower your price to take care of expected deductions because the competition of mill buyers will not permit you to lower it?
Answer. Well, we have no way of anticipating lower price, we have no hand in the making of the price and we can only operate on the price that is handed us. We are buying seeds to-day at a basis price, we may get a card in the morning that they are up or down. We don't know.

Answer. The only way that I see that you could do is to analyze every load, and where the farmer has better than prime seeds give him the benefit of it.
Question. Do you think that is practical?
Answer. No.

Answer. No, sir.

Answer. Well, I would say for 1928, 1929, and 1930.

Answer. I haven't for the past two years, probably the past three.
I am not sure as to that. I certainly have not for the past two.

Answer. No, if I understand it, now-I have never practiced the commission business-but, as I understand the commission, the buyer gets so much per ton as a commission regardless of the price or anything else.
Question. Yes.
Answer. Well?
Question. But I am talking about this exchange feature of meal and seed. Is the independent in any different position on that than the commission ginner?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. Well, I think so because he is directly affected and as I see it, the commission buyer is only looking for his $3 or whatever he gets for buying the seed and I am a trader in exchanging meal; in that I have to sell that meal and compete with the oil mill's price.
Question. Is there any reason why seed should be exchanged on an even basis for meal, if their cash value is different?
Answer. Well, I don't know that I could answer that question, because that is in the business of the cottonseed crushers to work that out, and I am not prepared to say.
Question. But you made the point that you had found the basis of exchange among the different mills the same, just as their prices were the same.
Answer. Yes.
Question. Have the different seasons in which you have operated shown any marked differences in the character and extent of price fluctuation?
Answer. Yes, my recollection is.
Question. What has been the character and extent of it?
Answer. You mean variation in price?
Question. From time to time throughout the season?
Answer. Well, for instance, from the opening of the season until December 31, why, I would say yes. My recollection is that in 1927 and 1928 the fluctuations were considerably greater than they were in 1929 and 1930.
Question. Can you give us some idea of the amount of difference?
Answer. Well, in 1927, I am not positive what the prices that season opened with, but as I remember it was somewhere around $26 or $27 a ton early in the season with us and it went as high as $50.
Question. You are speaking of car prices in both cases?
Answer. Car prices, yes. It went as high as $50 about the end of the year. I sold as high as $50.
Question. All right. Now, try and compare that with other seasons.
Answer. Well, last year the market opened in our territory, the best I recollect, at about, oh, somewhere around $25, $26, $27. I don't recollect just offhand, but, of course, it would vary every few days, but somewhere around that neighborhood the prices opened and I don't think they went as high as they did the year before. That is my recollection.
Question. Speaking of last year now?
Answer. Yes; this year the price in our territory opened, oh, it was about, I'd say, $23 or $24.
Question. This car seed?
Answer. Yes; and it has been as low as $21 and is now $27. That is the two extremes this season so far in car prices.
Question. How long has it been since that $27 price went into effect?
Answer. About 10 days ago, I think, somewhere along that.
Question. Did it jump from $21 to $27?
Answer. No.

WESLEY JOHNSON, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Where do you live, Mr. Johnson?

Answer. Well, the seed from about 400 bales, 350 or 400 bales.

Answer. Well, it would be varying, somewhere about 60 or 75 tons, I guess.

Answer. Since 1910.

Answer. Yes, sir.

Answer. Yes, not a great many, though, there. We gin mostly for large farmers and they haul the seed back home, and then sell them in car lots later in the season. We just buy for late ginning, something like that.
Question. About how many seed in the course of a season have you been accustomed to buying?
Answer. Oh, anywhere from 7 to 20 cars, about 20 tons to the car, something like that, varies in the season, though.
Question. Have you operated your ginning business as an independent, buying for your own account, or as a commission buyer for the mills?
Answer. Both ways.
Question. Will you distinguish between the times and the ways you operate ?
Answer. We bought on a commission basis until the last few years, when seed went so low, and then we bought independently.
We bought on a commission until I would say, maybe, 1927.

Answer. Up to now, yes.

Answer. Yes.

Answer. Buckeye Cotton Oil Co.; for the International Vegetable Oil Co., and for, I believe, maybe the Planters-those other two mainly, the first two mainly.
Question. What commission did you receive?
Answer. $3 a ton in wagon lots, 50 cents a ton when we bought in car lots.
Question. Have you been accustomed, as an independent, to hold your seed and sell it later in the season, or dispose of it?
Answer. We have tried that, yes.

Answer. We bought independently last season.

As an independent citizen and also as an oil-mill operator, I want to enter a protest at this point against the admission into evidence here of the wild, sweeping statements made by witnesses on the stand, which they don't themselves support with any facts. I submit this is manifestly unfair and uninvestigation OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY just, and I ask you hereafter to rule out any such testimony before this tribunal.
Mr. WOODEN. I asked him the name of every mill he had dealt with or been in touch with, to develop to the fullest possible extent his information. The record shows the extent and the foundation for his knowledge. It seems utterly absurd for me to go ahead and ask him about this mill and that mill and every other mill outside of those he has named, because he clearly said the ones he named were all he had. Why should I ask him about the others in detail? Of course, the witness's testimony, any witness's testimony, is to be taken and interpreted according to the extent and basis of his knowledge, and the witness's testimony about the uniformity of price is necessarily limited by the extent of his knowledge; and I think the record is clear that the extent, the exact extent, of the character of it is shown, limited to his territory.
Examiner SHEPPARD. Just to make a long story short and to cut out this argument and talk, hereafter I am going to accept the witness's statement as to his locality, his local condition, and the mills with which he has come in direct contact. It is manifestly impossible that in a State of the size of South Carolina, where, the testimony shows, there are 40 or maybe more mills, that these witnesses haven't come in contact with, that they should be required to testify for the whole State. I am going to take their evidence as applying to the district or locality in which they are located and which they personally know about.
Mr. WOODEN. Answer. Without grading?

Now, as far as the farmers-any farmer in our territory can get carload prices, of course, for seed if he has got as much as a carload of seed, he gets as much as I would or anybody else, of course.
Question. Well, do you-is the matter of storage involved in that situation?
Answer. Just what do you mean?
Question. Well, stored at the mill by the farmer, is that involved in it?
Answer. Well, I don't mean by the mill, I mean they ship them in carload lots. For instance, I do myself; I have got farmers' seed now that I pay-left them at my place and sell them and give them carload prices for them. And I think that is the general custom, not only the mills but seed buyers and all, if they have a carload of seed.
Question. Well, then, are such seed sold, then, subject to grade or not?
Answer. Now it is; but that grading didn't start until late last season, and I have had-I haven't had much experience with the grading so far up until this year.

Answer. From the oil mills?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. How has the matter of not knowing what you were going to get for the seed until after chemical analysis made after arrival at the mill affected your ability to borrow money on the seed?
Answer. Well, I will tell you the money I borrowed on the seed, the way I worked it was a personal game for a personal reason; the banks charge 8 per cent in this territory, and it has been customary for them for years-I say for years, a good many yearsto lend money at 6 per cent on cotton receipts and seeds. Well, the only money I ever borrowed from the banks I have done it for those loans to save 2 per cent, of course. I didn't have to give them any grade. I just did that for personal account of 2 per cent. I didn't have to give them any grade or anything like that.
Question. Well, then, the selling of seed on grade and your not knowing what you are going to get for them until after they have arrived at the mill has not affected your borrowing money?
Answer. The way you ask the question is a little misleading, because, as I said, I do not recall borrowing money. I will explain to you how I work it. For instance, if I owe the bank, which I did in this particular case, some money, and pay 8 per cent on it, I will go in and say, "I want to change this," and maybe I would not have any security from 8 per cent to 6 per cent on seed, you see. So far as the bank was concerned that did not make any difference to them. In other words, if my seed didn't bring as much as I was borrowing from them I would have to pay it, anyhow. I never borrow money on seed in that way. In other words, I put my seed in there to reduce my interest from 8 per cent to 6 per cent. That is the motive-that is the reason I did it.
Question. Well, now, in that connection, Mr. Linthicum, who interviewed you, reports you as stating that the refusal of the mills to quote a grade price to the independent shipper, except a price that is based upon the quality at the mill, because it amounts to the sale of a commodity that the seller has no idea of what it is worth when he sells it, also has an additional disadvantage to the seller because when he has seed in his warehouse which he has not yet sold, he has a commodity which has a monetary value at which it is impossible to arrive, and for this reason it is very difficult, if not impossible, for the independent shipper to borrow money on his cottonseed, whereas, in former years he could very readily do so.

Answer. Well, that is true.

Answer. I didn't intend to tell him that I was borrowing money.
Of course I didn't go into its particulars like I am now, because that is the only way I have ever borrowed any money on any seed. Of course I was just speaking from general knowledge. The banks, if a man goes in a bank to-day and to borrow money on seed and he wasn't worth anything but this seed he was borrowing the money on, that would be the difficulty he would have to confront.
Question. Have you known of any such difficulties?
Answer. No; I have not.
Question. Well, are there someanswer. In fact, I do not know of any banks that loan money on seed, I do not know of any other thar ry case, and I do not say they do or do not because I don't know.

Question. In case it ran below, did you buy it on the average of the grade for the district?
Answer. Well, I don't know whether we did or not, but we used our judgment lots of times about buying seed all the time. If we think it is best to buy them, we buy them; if we don't we don't.
Question. If you knew the seed were poorer than the average of the grade for the district, you wouldn't pay the average of the grade price for them, would you?
Answer. Well, that depended a whole lot.
Question. Well, depended on what?
Answer. Competition, for one thing.
Question. In other words, if competition forced you, you would pay the average of the grade for seed that was poorer than the average of the grade?
Answer. Well, we-I don't know particularly about that, but we might have sometime, and sometimes we probably didn't.
Question. In case the particular lots of wagon seed ran higher than the average of the grade, did you buy them on the average of the grade, or pay a premium above the average?
Answer. How was that question, again?
(Reporter, thereupon, read the question, commencing, "In case the particular lots," concluding with, "or pay a premium above the average?") We use our judgment about that, depends on what happened.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. How did you use your judgment?
Answer. For instance, if we could make any money on them, we'd buy them; if we couldn't, we'd pass them up.
Question. Did you discount on wagon seed that was running prime?
Answer. Well, it is hard-It might have been, a fellow came along with 50 pounds of prime seed and we would buy them less than the basis price. Of course, that 50 pounds or 20 pounds, or whatever it happened to be, would be discounted.
Question. According to the average of the grade for the district?
Answer. You can take a wagonload of seed out here and get a handful out of this corner and a handful out of that corner, and get Mr. Rice to analyze them, and they'd run different.

ROBERT B. DAWKINS, previously having been sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Did you hear the testimony of Mr. Kendrick a few moments ago on the interview between you and him, with reference to the deduction made on seed and the deductions made on various products from seed?
Answer. I did.
Question. Will you state what occurred between you and Mr.
Kendrick at the time and what figures you got from him on those points?
Answer. I asked Mr. Kendrick at the time I was in his office to, if he could, estimate for me the average deduction per ton on meal which his company suffered during the 1929-30 season, because of off grade, and Mr. Kendrick, after some figuring, gave me an estimate that it amounted to 5.2 cents per ton on seed crushed. I asked also for an estimate of the deduction which his company suffered during the same season on linters, because of off grade, and he estimated that figure for me at 11.6 per ton of seed crushed.
Question. Did he do that after figuring or reference to any records?
Answer. Yes; he used some records and did some figuring, but I can not state from memory just what particular records they were.
I do recall, however, that he did some considerable figuring in arriving at these figures, and I might say that, in connection with all these figures, about which I am testifying, that we went over them together and at the time we were both familiar with the methods used in arriving at the particular figures. He gave me also an estimate of $1.18 per ton of seed crushed as the amount of deductions which his company suffered during the same season on oil sold. The total deductions add up to the figure of $1.348 per ton of seed crushed as being the deductions because of off grade on all products. We then took the reports of analyses of seed which he had in the office from Law Co., ascertained the percentage of deductions on each analysis report, and averaged those discounts, arriving at a figure 5.06 per cent, as being the average discount on seed as shown by the analysis. Mr. Kendrick told me that he believed that the analysis reports used were fairly representative of the quality of the seed handled by the mill that season. We then applied the percentage of discount on seed as shown by the average of the analysis to the average cost per ton of seed for his company during that season, and arrived at a figure of $1.49 per ton, which was representative of the discount on seed, if the mill had discounted all the seed according to grade.
Question. Did you have the figure that showed the average cost of the seed for the season?
Answer. Yes. Mr. Kendrick got that from some reports which he had in the office.
Mr. WOODEN. Mr. Kendrick, I understand that is one of the things you have no objection to showing, the average cost of seed for the season?
Mr. KENDRICK. No; I don't object to that.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Can you refresh your recollection from any papers that you may have that shows what the average cost of the seed for the season was?
Answer. This paper which Mr. Kendrick supplied, at my request, shows the average cost of seed to his mill over several seasons and for the season 1929-30 the figure given is $29.45 per ton.

CHARLES W. RICE, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Where do you live, Mr. Rice?
Answer. I live in Columbia.
Question. And your business is what?
Answer. Chemist.
Question. What is the name under which that business is carried on?
Answer. Charles W. Rice Co.
Question. Are you the controlling factor in the business?
Answer. No, sir; I am half owner of it.
Question. Half owner?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Who is the other half owner?
Answer. Mr. Simpson, R. E. Simpson.
Question. Both of you chemists?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How long have you been operating the business?
Answer. I started the laboratory in 1915. Mr. Simpson came with me in 1919 or 1920. I don't know which; 1919, I think.
Question. What is the extent of yours and Mr. Simpson's training as chemists?
Answer. Well, I graduated from Clemson College in 1908, had a bachelor's degree. Mr. Simpson graduated in 1910. He has a bachelor's degree, bachelor of science.
Question. Have you any degree in chemistry as such, or is that included in the master of science degree?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. I have forgotten-the diploma, I think, usually says that you have finished the prescribed course and are given the bachelor of science degree.
Question. Did you major in chemistry?
Answer. Yes, sir. Then I did a little work at Purdue University two years after I graduated.
Question. Will you describe generally, Mr. Rice, what the character of your business as chemist has been, what products you have worked with?
Answer. Our particular work has been with fertilizers and cottonseed products.
Question. Will you state approximately what proportion is cottonseed products and what proportion is fertilizer?
Answer. Well, in the last two years the cottonseed products has been, I guess, 60 or 70 per cent of our business. Before that time it was about half and half probably.
Question. Now, when you say cottonseed products do you include cottonseed as well?
Answer. Yes, sir.

Question. You are basing that on the income to yourself?
Answer. Not just now. Approximately how many samples of seed we had last year.

Answer. The division, you mean, in the number of samples?
Question. Yes. You took that as a basis in estimating 60 or 65 per cent had been seed?
Answer. About 60 per cent.
Question. Now, in amount in income to your firm would the division be approximately similar?
Answer. Would be approximately similar; yes.
Question. Now, as between the products themselves what has been the bulk of your chemistry work, analytical work?
Answer. Meal and hulls and oil.
Question. Would oil be the predominant one among those?
Answer. No; we had more meal and hull samples than we have oil.
Question. To what extent have you analyzed and tested oil?
Answer. Well, we have been testing oil for the last 10 years, I guess. For a long time I didn't attempt the oil analysis at all because I didn't have the equipment for it, and then we didn't have but very little call for it.
Question. Have you tested oil as the representative of the crude oil mill or refiner or how?
Answer. Both.

Question. Have you been a member of any committee of the National Cottonseed Products Association?

Answer. No, sir. No; it meant that you could handle samples on a settlement basis, either as referee or as an original chemist who was doing the original work.

That was your opinion too?
Answer. It would depend on the amount of free fatty acid. I think on a sample that is very high, say 7, 8 or 10 per cent free fatty acid, a variation of 1 per cent between laboratories is fair. On lower percentages it ought to check closely.
Question. Haven't you been able as yet in your investigations to ascertain any factor that would tend to account for variations?
Answer. My experience is that the nature of the seed, I think, have a good deal to do with it. Sometimes we find that we have no difficulty in getting perfect checks on some samples; other samples we find that we can not check so well. So I would think that sometimes the very nature of the seed makes it that way.
Question. Have any steps been taken toward standardizing among different chemists the equipment and the methods of analysis?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How far have those steps gone?
Answer. Well, I think in all of the laboratories that are doing this seed grading, either the chemical laboratories or the mill laboratories, the chemists committee of the National Association has a certain set of plans for equipment that these laboratories have to have before they are approved by the chemists committee as being properly equipped to do the work.
Question. To what extent have those plans been carried out?
Answer. I think most of the laboratories have been inspected.
Question. When was the inspection made, this season?

Answer. Well, any laboratory is supposed to have chemically pure chemicals. I don't know that that is mentioned. But they are supposed to have that.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Is there a certain strength of solution that is specified?
Answer. I don't know that it is specified. You mean for the free fatty acid?
Question. Yes.
Answer. I think it is suggested. I don't know that it is specified.
Question. Well, what is the effect of using different strengths of solution in the testing for free fatty acid?
Answer. Well, if you have a low free fatty acid, you want to use a very weak solution in making that test. If you have a high percentage of fatty acids, you want to use a strong solution, because you get a better reaction.
Question. Suppose you used a weak solution with seed that were high in free fatty acid, what result would you get?
Answer. You ought not really get any different result except that the operator in the managing of those solutions can tell better about the reaction that has taken place with a strong solution if he has a high fatty acid.
Question. You mean that the net result in the amount of free fatty acids will not differ according to the strength of the solution used?
Answer. It should not; no, sir; except on very low fatty acid.
For instance, if you have a seed that is only 0.4 or 0.6 free fatty acid on it, you would not want to use the strength of solution in that, as that had 10 per cent, for the reason that one drop of that solution that you are using in the low fatty acid might give you a reaction all at once; just one drop of it.
Question. Well, can you get a larger amount of free fatty acid by using a strong solution?
Answer. No; not if you do your work correctly you can not, but you would not use a strong solution with a low fatty acid.
Question. Well, of course, you can not tell before you use it whether it is low fatty acid or not, can you?
Answer. Well, you can have a pretty good idea.
Question. Based just on general appearance?
Answer. General appearance and odor of the oil.
Question. Well, is it a matter, I might say judgment of the chemist how strong his solution should be then?
Answer. Matter of experience and judgment; yes, sir.
Question. Well, those factors then ought to be sufficient to account for some variation between different chemists, ought not they?
Answer. Well, they would; yes. And chemistry in itself is not exact, because of the variation in the-I mean mathematically exact-because there is variation in the equipment, in the glassware and stuff that you have to use.

Question. Would it be possible in your opinion if the chemist were interested in showing a fatty acid content that was lower than the actual to make his solution such or his methods analysis such that would show it lower than it actually was?
Answer. I don't think the solutions have as much to do with it as some other factors.

Answer. Well, one factor is in the preparation of the sample.
Another factor is probably in the amount and quality of oil which he used.
Question. Well, then would it be possible by differences in the oil and the other things you mentioned to show free fatty acid lower than the actual amount?
Answer. It is probable; yes.
Question. Would it not also be possible to show a free fatty acid higher than the actual amount by reversing the process?
Answer. I don't know about that. I don't believe you could get it any higher than it actually is.
Question. Well, I thought if it was possible one way why won't it be possible the other?
Answer. For instance, the more perfect extraction of the oil that you get, the more representative of the oil, the more representative the sample is of that particular lot of seed, and the more oil you get, of course the more nearly representative is going to be the oil and the free acid in there.
Question. Well, why would that be positive in one direction and not so likely in the other, not so possible in the other?
Answer. Because you can not-if you don't get enough oil out of the seed you would not get all of the fatty acid out; if you get all of the oil out of the seed you would get all of the fatty acid out.
Question. I see. I think I do anyway. Do you have in mind there the length of time during which they run this petrolic ether through the sample?
Answer. That has something to do with it.

Answer. I attended that but I don't recall anything about the discussion.
Question. Were you aware that there was any opinion among chemists to the effect that free fatty acid in oil was not the determining factor in whether the oil was off grade or not?
Answer. I don't think they have ever taken the free fatty acids into consideration.
Question. Well, hasn't oil been graded and analyzed on the basis of free fatty acid basis?
Answer. Not on the basis of free fatty acid. I never have done it that way. We base the analysis on the free fatty acid condition but the value of the oil has never been based on the free fatty acid contents.
Question. Well, what does this controversy shown here in the Cotton Oil Press covering the 1927 convention mean with reference to whether or not free fatty acid was the proper method of determining quality of the oil?

Answer. Well, there is plenty of free fatty acid in bad oil.
Question. But is it also present in good oil?
Answer. A small quantity.
Question. Mr. Johnson says here that the free fatty acid of the oil is precipitated in refining, and you allowed a discount for the free fatty acid in the increased loss which free fatty acid makes. Answer. What other discount was he talking about?

Answer. I think that is the way it is; yes. That is on the refined oil?
Question. Yes.
Answer. If it is off-color and off-odor, off-flavor.

Answer. I don't see it.
Question. You say there was never any discount made for free fatty acid in oil as such?
Answer. Not that I recall, not since I have been analyzing oil I don't think there has been any.
Question. Well, whether they call it that or not hasn't there been a discount for free fatty acid under some other name than free fatty acid?
Answer. The only discounts that I recall that I know anything about have been discounts for excessive refining loss, bad flavor, or high color.
Question. Well, isn't the refining loss, excessive refining loss, just another way of saying free fatty acid?
Answer. Well, in some cases it is; not in all cases.
Question. Wasn't there a rather long-continued controversy between the refiners and the crude-oil mills over the deductions on crude oil?
Answer. I don't know anything about it.

Question. He makes the statement there that the Gossypol titrating method gives an erroneous result and free fatty acids determined in the usual way are frequently not free fatty acids at all. What have you to say about that last statement there, that free fatty acids determined in the usual way are not free fatty acids at all.
Answer. I don't know what he bases that statement on.
Question. Well, whether you know or not do you agree or disagree with it.
Answer. I disagree with him. I think the usual method that we use certainly takes care of the acid in the oil. Whether it is free fatty acid or not is a question I don't know.
Question. He makes the further statement that the free fatty acid test may show an acidity due to other causes than free fatty acid. Do you agree with that?
Answer. Well, I don't like to disagree with Doctor Wesson, but I do not see how it is possible if it is pure oil.
Question. Notwithstanding you don't like to disagree you do disagree with him on that?
Answer. Well, it is certainly an acid reaction in the oil, but whether it is free fatty acid or not I am not able to say.
Question. The oil itself is a fatty acid?
Answer. Yes; it is a glyceride.

R. B. CALDWELL, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. What is your business?
Answer. My principal business is banking. I am president of the Commercial Bank in Chester. I also practice law and do some farming on the side.
Question. What is the extent of your farming interests?
Answer. I own about 1,500 acres of land that I farm.
Question. You raise cotton on it?
Answer. Beg pardon.

Answer. Yes, sir. I manage about 3,500 acres of clients' farms.

Answer. Probably 1,500 bushels.

Answer. Sir?

Answer. Well, that is about, let's see, we measure cottonseed by bushels. About 25 to 30 tons of my own.

Answer. Well, let's see; I get about 150 bales of cotton. That is 30 bushels to the bale. 4,500 bushels. It would be somewhere around 40 to 50 tons.

Answer. I do on one farm; yes, sir.

Answer. Yes, sir; gin for the neighborhood.

Answer. Yes, sir.

Answer. Possibly a couple of cars. Two or three cars a season.
Question. Have you been managing the gin at that place?
Answer. Well, I have a superintendent that runs the gin under my general management; yes, sir.

And three years ago, I believe it was, we dropped to 15,000, but we are back up now. Last year we made 22,000, and this year we will probably make twenty-five or twenty-six thousand.

Question. Is it your experience that the average small farmer sells his seed at the time the cotton is ginned?
Answer. I would say up there in my trade territory that 90 per cent at least sell their seed at the gin.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. And what are the conditions which cause such a high percentage to be sold at that time?
Answer. Well, it is because of the financial condition of the farmer. The average farmer has borrowed money to make his crop, and the man from whom he borrowed the money expects him to deliver the cotton to him. It is a general practice to allow the farmer or tenant to have the cottonseed. They sell the cottonseed at the gin and pay for the bagging and ties and they get the balance to live on.
Question. Within your experience how important is the amount received for cottonseed in the farmer's living, meeting the farmer's living expenses?
Answer. Well, it is practically the only available cash that the cotton farmer has in the fall of the year. The supply merchant or banker will supply money usually until July or August until the cultivation of the crop is completed, and in the fall of the year the cotton grower has to live on the proceeds of his seed.

Question. Well, are they ginners, these buyers, some of them?
Answer. Yes, sir; gins and-most of them gins, some few buyers at the other little towns also. Most of them are gins, though.

Answer. Well, most of them-well, most of them get their money from the Southern Cotton Oil Co., and my understanding is that they have the privilege of selling to somebody else if they get a better trade than the Southern Cotton Oil Co. gives them, but as a practical thing the seed goes to the Southern Cotton Oil Co.

We are advocating that all of the time for our customers. Of course our district is low. A man in the district that has good seed does not get any advantage at all if he sells by the wagon load.

Answer. Well, of course, if the cotton grade is low it would indicate that the cotton before it was ginned had not been properly cared for; and while I don't know, I judge that that would affect the grade of the seed to some extent.
Question. I suppose it follows as a matter of course, Mr. Caldwell, that if you had seed to sell that was poorer than the average of the grade in your district you would profit by it?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. It has been suggested to me, Mr. Caldwell, that there is not any relation between the quality of lint cotton and the quality of the seed. What have you to say on that?

Question. Yes. In other words, you may have a very good quality of lint cotton and a poor grade of seed out of it.
Answer. Well, as I said a while ago, I have never examined that question, but just as a matter of practical experience in handling cotton, selecting seed for planting and things of that sort, if you have got a good quality of cotton, showing a good grade of cotton, showing good color, a quality that shows that it has been taken care, you get good seed. On the other hand, if you have cotton that has been damaged by the weather or anything of that sort, I think the seed would be damaged along with the lint. I certainly would not use those seed for planting. I don't know how the chemical analysis would show up. As a practical matter I know it would be risky to plant that kind of seed.

J. H. HARDIN, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Where do you live, Mr. Hardin?
Answer. Chester.
Question. What is your business?
Answer. Farming.
Question. What is the amount of cotton that you raise per season?
Answer. In 1920 I raised 82 bales; this year I raised 20.
Question. Last year how much?
Answer. About 18 or 19.
Question. How do you sell the seed that you raise on your farm?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. Well, we pick the cotton, carry it to the gin house, and put a bale on a wagon and carry it to the gin, have it ginned and sell your seed, after they take out the ginning, bagging, and ties.
Question. Do you sell your seed at the same time the cotton is ginned?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Have you always done that?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Why is it that you sell it then, instead of waiting?
Answer. Well, I haven't been able to-need the money.
Question. Do you get any cash out of your cotton?
Answer. No, sir; I have been borrowing money to raise cotton.
Of course, give a crop mortgage, and when the cotton is ginned, why, we just turn the money over to-the bank.
Question. Have you been accustomed to get cash out of the sale of your seed?
Answer. Get the cash?
Question. Yes.
Answer. Yes.
Question. Do you sell your seed in wagon lots?
Answer. Wagon lots, altogether.
Question. How many wagon lots would you have during the course of a season?
Answer. Well, this year there would be 20 wagon lots, 1 wagon lot for each bale.
Question. Where do you sell your wagon seed?
Answer. Have some at different places; sell some at the gin, Southern Cotton Oil Co., at Chester; some at Rawley's gin, about 3 miles out, 4 miles west from Chester, and some about a mile below Chester, at the Mcallelly gin.
Question. Well, what are those gins that you named, besides the Southern Cotton Oil Co.? Are they independent ginners?
Answer. Yes; Mcallelly Bros. operate that gin at Evans Station, a mile below Chester, and Mr. Rawley operates the other gin which I told you about.
Question. Have you found any different price being paid for your wagon seed by one buyer than another?
Answer. No; they all seem to have the same price; doesn't seem to make any difference which gin you carry it to; you get the same price; you would be paid the same price per bushel.
Question. What has been your wagon price this season?
Answer. Started around 30 or above, but the bulk of the seed was sold at 2512 cents a bushel.
Question. Do you know how much that figured a ton?
Answer. That figured around $17.
Question. Did you sell your seed for cash this year?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Did you ever exchange seed for meal or any other products?
Answer. No, sir. When seed was selling at 252 cents a bushel, I got to thinking that possibly maybe I could in some other way help myself a little, so I tried to make an exchange.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. What did you do?
Answer. Why, I went to the Southern Cotton Oil Co. at Chester and asked them how they would trade me meal for seed, and I was told that they had no authority to make the exchange.
Question. Who told you?
Answer. Mr. Quinton, who was in charge. There was a Mr.
Ancrum that left Chester. Then I asked him what he wanted for meal in ton lots. He said $37, and I asked him how much he then wanted for hulls in ton lots. He said $11.
Question. Did you have seed with you that you were offering to exchange?
Answer. No; I didn't have some, but if I thought I could make a trade with them for a ton or two I could gin and deliver the seed, which I believe I did that way a year or two ago.
Question. Did you tell them that you were figuring on an exchange?
Answer. I asked him if he would make an exchange with me.
Question. Did you get a quotation for your seed on that basis?
Answer. They were paying 2512 cents at that time. I knew what he was paying that day.
Question. That was $17 a ton?
Answer. Around $17; yes.
Question. Did you tell him how much seed you had and how much meal you wanted?
Answer. No; I asked him if he would make the exchange and when he told me he had no authority to make the exchange, why, we didn't go into the details.
Question. Well, what do you mean when you say that he had no authority to make the exchange?
Answer. I mean thisquestion. Yes?
Answer. I guess he got authority from Columbia, here.
Question. Well, I know; but you don't get my meaning. Did you ever make an exchange on an even-swap basis?
Answer. I guess I meant he had no instructions.
Question. Did you ever make an exchange on an even-swap basis?
Answer. I made a little better than that. I have swapped myself on an even-swap basis, and through a friend of mine who operates big farming interests, and I suppose raises 500 or 600 bales of cotton.
One year I ginned at his gin, left my seed there, and he made an exchange of 2,200 pounds of meal for a ton of seed.
Question. When was that?
Answer. I don't remember whether that was three or four years ago. It was either three or four years ago.
Question. Well, I don't quite understand what you mean by this man of the Southern's saying he had no authority or instructions to make an exchange, and yet quoting youanswer. I asked him for the prices. I just wanted to see what they were getting for meal and hulls at that time.
Question. Well, you were trying to get an even swap then?
Answer. Why, I didn't know whether they would give me an even swap or around 1.800 pounds that would have paid to make an exchange on that basis.

Answer. He didn't make any offer to exchange at all.

Answer. He said he had no authority to make any exchange or swap in hulls and meal. I then asked himquestion. On any basis?
Answer. Yes, on any basis.
That is correct. So I then asked him the price for a ton of meal, which was $37, and a price for a ton of hulls, which was $11.

Answer. Why, I am satisfied that the seed were average seed. I have never heard of any farmer being deducted on account of inferior seed this season. If they have got a price, 25 or 30, or any other price, everybody that gins at that gin gets that price without any question as to quality of the seed. I haven't been asked this season as to the quality of seed.
Question. Well, so far as your seed goes, so far as you know, what was its quality?
Answer. I would say average quality.

D. M. LIPSCOMB, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. What is your business, Mr. Lipscomb?
Answer. I am assistant secretary of the South Carolina division, National Cottonseed Products Association.
Question. How long have you been acting as assistant secretary?

Question. Well, will you tell us the extent of the continuity of your employment since then?
Answer. Well, I was with them from October, 1928, until about the first of January, 1929, and then, from September, 1929, to the present time.

Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Was there a time between Mr. Acree's death and Mr.

Answer. I don't think so.
Question. How many of them were there that were, you might say, hesitant about it?
Answer. I don't remember.

J. G. BREAZEALE, being duly sworn, testifies as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Will you state your business, Mr. Breazeale?
Answer. In general-merchandise business, sell fertilizer, buy cot ton and cottonseed.
Question. Do you have any farming interests?
Answer. Yes, sir; I have some.
Question. What is the extent of your farming interests?
Answer. I farm about 300 or 400 acres of land.
Question. And you raise cotton and seed on your own farm?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How much seed do you have from your own farm?
Answer. Well, we range around 75 to 80 bales, and sometimes not so much, and sometimes a little more; depends on the year.
Question. Will you put that in terms of seed. How much seed does that make from your own farm?
Answer. I hadn't figured it. When we make that much, we get about 800 pounds to the bale of seed.
Question. Do you operate a gin?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. In connection with your general merchandise business, do you make any advances or carry any other farmers?
Answer. Yes, sir; we sell about sixty to seventy-five thousand dollars' worth on time.
Question. Do you have anything in the nature of a crop mort gage to protect you on such indebtedness?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Do you get your payment for it out of the cotton crop?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Well, how is it with regard to seed? Does your crop mortgage cover seed?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How long have you been buying cottonseed?
Answer. About 22 years.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. You have never owned or operated a gin during all that time?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. What has been the quantity of or volume of seed handled by you in the course of a season?
Answer. Well, that has ranged from 1,000 tons down, approximately.
Question. What was it last season ?
Answer. About 250 tons.
Question. And was it as much the season before that, or how much was it the season before?
Answer. I don't remember the year before, but our business has ranged from around 1,000 tons down to two or three hundred tons.
Question. Well, has it shown a steady decrease in volume?
Answer. It has for the last two or three years.
Question. What are the conditions that you attribute as causing the decrease in the volume of your business?
Answer. Since we have had no competition in sale of seed, me not running a gin, I can't pay an extra price. That is the way I have bought seed, is to pay a little bit more than the rule or the fixed price, as they call it, because farmers won't haul them out of the gin, you know, at the same price that the ginner pays.
Question. In other words, not having a gin, you were accustomed to pay more than the regular wagon price for seed?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How much more?
Answer. I'd pay all the way from $2 to $4 a ton.
Question. And over how long a period of years did you do business in that way?
Answer. About 18 or 20.
Question. Well, now, explain that a little further. You paid more than the regular wagon price in former years. Did you sell that at the car-lot price?
Answer. I didn't sell it at the fixed car-lot price.
Question. What car-lot price did you sell it at?
Answer. Well, I could find many mills, you know, some mills, that would pay more than the others and out of line with what they called the agreed price.
Question. Well, who called it an agreed price?
Answer. Well, that was general talk, you know, that the association, the Cottonseed Crushers Associationquestion. You said "they," and I wanted to know who you meant by "they." Answer. The cottonseed organization, that is who Iquestion. I know; but who referred to prices as being fixed in any way?
Answer. Well, I don't know that I could fix anybody that did that, but, way back yonder some years ago, the organization in this State, when Mr. Taylor used to be president of it, they had an agreed price.
Question. What do you know about that, what is the basis of your statement there?
Answer. I didn't get it from them.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. In other words, you are just stating an opinion?
Answer. General understanding, but I couldn't fix it onto any person becausequestion. Well, was it a matter of common talk?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How long has it been since you have been unable to get competitive bids on your seed?
Answer. Last season and this season.
Question. Prior to that time you could get competitive bids?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What mill buyers are represented in your locality?
Answer. Well, we have the Kershaw interests and the Buckeye and the Southern Cotton Oil Co. and others coming around there, too, from other mills.
Question. Have you been accustomed to sell your seed in car lots or wagon lots?
Answer. Car lots; won't sell them any other way.
Question. Have you made it a practice to ascertain from time to time during the season what the prices of those mills that you named were?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How would you get such information?
Answer. Well, the Kershaw interests and the Buckeye people have traveling men representing them that come there, and others, too, but they come there oftener than any other interests-that is, I see them oftener.
Question. You got your information as to their prices from representatives of the mills, then, did you?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. And is it the information obtained from those representatives that forms the basis for your statement that their prices were always the same this last season or two?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Did you have contact with any mills other than those three, so that you knew what the prices of any other mills were?
Answer. Yes, sir; sometimes the Southern Cotton Oil Co. would call me up and tell me what the prices were.
Question. You mentioned the Southern and the Buckeye and the Kershaw.
Answer. That is the only three this season, I believe.
Question. Were there any others last season?
Answer. Yes; there was some others, but I forget now what their names were; they are the only three I remember now.
Question. Was there a mill at Grenco that you had contact with?
Answer. At where?
Question. It is the Grenco Co. at Greenwood.
Answer. Yes, sir; yes, sir; I did last season.
talk with them this season.

Answer. Yes; the same thing.

Question. Well, how far have you had information in the last 30 days?
Answer. Well, I have heard from all three of them at different times, through their representatives. They all quoted me the same price at the same time, and changed their price at the same time.
Question. Well, I want to ask you about changes in price. When changes in price came about, how long was it before they were on the same price basis?
Answer. Well, when I would hear from them it would be on the same day.
Question. Well, how long after you heard from one would you hear from another?
Answer. Sometimes I'd hear from all of them on the same day;' sometimes it might be a day later from the Southern.
Question. Do you get telegraphic or mail information from the mills as to their prices?
Answer. Sometimes I would get it over the telephone and sometimes the representatives of the Kershaw and Buckeye would come around, and others, by telephone.
Question. Have you had any instances where buyers from more than one mill would predict a decline and the amount of the decline that was coming?
Answer. Yes.
Question. When?
Answer. Say when?
Question. Yes; when did you have such predictions?
Answer. I couldn't fix a date, but this fall I had Mr. White from the Buckeye at Anderson, and Mr. King at Anderson, with the Kershaw people, and they would want to know if we wanted to sell any cottonseed, said it was $23 to-day, but to-morrow it would be $21, and if we wanted any protection on it why to sell it. At different times we would have that.
Question. You say that the instance that you described in the fall is not unusual? You say that at different times you have had that happen?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. Yes, sir; for the last two years, last two seasons; season and last season is what I want to say.
this Question. Well, did the reduction predicted by those millmen, those mill buyers, come about as predicted?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Did you ever know it to fail?
Answer. No, sir; never have.
Question. You told us of the instance where the price was $23 and the prediction was that the next day it would be $21.
Answer. Yes.
Question. Do I understand that that sort of thing happened on other occasions, where the exact amount of the decline was predicted in advance?
Answer. Yes; they would say the exact amount. Make that statement with it.
Question. Did you ever know them to miss the exact amount?
Answer. No, sir; never did.
Question. You mentioned a Mr. King, of Anderson. Is that the Kershaw man?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Who was the Buckeye man?
Answer. Mr. White. I don't know his initials.
Question. What are they-traveling buyers?
Answer. That is what I would term them. They go around representing their companies, buying seed.
Question. I suppose advance notices of a decline coming is some advantage to you, isn't it?
Answer. It would be if I wanted to sell seed; yes, sir.
Question. You could sell short and accumulate seed against the decline, could you?
Answer. Yes, sir; they would let you sell and deliver later. I don't know that it would be unless you have got them, but if you have the seed, you can ship them along at your convenience.
Question. Well, that would give you the advantage in case of a decline, of having a larger spread in there too, wouldn't it?
Answer. Yes, sir; would be giving you the advantage if you had to sell, of getting a better price.
Question. Have you sold during the last season or two, this season and last season, I will say, ordinarily, on a margin of $3, or what has it been?
Answer. I haven't sold but one car of seed. I have all the seed I bought this season, except one car.
Question. Well, take last season. Did you sell your seed last year on the $3 differential between the car and wagon price?
Answer. I don't know, sir, because I kept my seed last year and sold them later; nearly all held them. I could have; you know it is all the time open between the wagon price and the car price.
Question. Have you exchanged seed for meal and hulls with dif ferent mills?
Answer. I have at times. I have some sold for exchange now to the Southern Cotton Oil Co., but haven't exchanged this season before. I haven't shipped but one car.
stion INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Have you made it your business to find out what basis of exchange the different mills would make?
Answer. Occasionally along; yes, sir.
Question. What did you find with reference to the basis of exchange of the different mills? Was it the same or different?
Answer. It was the same thing; up to right lately, I haven't tried it from different mills.
Question. How long have you noticed that condition?
Answer. Just this last season, and this season.
Question. Did it begin the same?
Answer. I haven't gone into that as particularly as I have about the price, because I haven't been wanted to make any exchange.
Question. Were you able last season to sell any of your seed above the general market?
Answer. No, sir; I wasn't.
Question. And how long did you hold it last year?
Answer. I sold them some time after Christmas. I don't remember what time.
Question. Did you sell them at a loss?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Had you paid above the general wagon market for them?
Answer. I did for some of them; yes, sir. Last season is the first time I have ever lost anything on cottonseed since I have been in the cottonseed business.
Question. Did you sell your seed last season on basis of grade to be determined at the mill?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Was that the first time you had ever done that?
Answer. Yes, sir; as to analysis.
Question. Well, that is what I mean, chemical analysis.
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Did you make any effort last season to locate a mill that would take your seed without chemical analysis?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What effort did you make?
Answer. Well, I don't remember the particular mill, but I talked with several and kept the seed longer. When they would inquire about buying seed, I stated to them that I wanted to sell them straight, without analysis, and nobody would buy them that way.
Question. That is what I wanted to find out, whether you would find a mill that would protect you; that would take them that way.
Answer. No, sir; I didn't find any mill that would do it.
Question. What has been the range of gross margin per ton that you have made in seasons past, buying seed and reselling them?
Answer. Well, I would have to estimate that, but I would range from $2 up to sometimes $5 or $6.
Question. And could you do that and still pay $2, as much as $2, more than the mill's buyers were paying for wagon seed?
Answer. Yes, sir; I have paid as high as $4 more than the wagon price, and sold them for that much profit.
Question. How recently have you done that?
Answer. That has been some years ago.

Answer. Yes, sir; but it was very satisfactory to me.
Question. How much of a deduction was it?
Answer. Why, it ranged down from 10 to 12, and maybe as high as 25 cents. We had a very wet season, and I sold them to Southern Cotton Oil Co., at Spartanburg, and I thought I got very fair treatment, just judging from looking and knowing what the seed were.
Question. Was the seed in your entire locality bad last season?
Answer. Yes, sir. Now, this year, I shipped a car of seed, and we never had any rain up there at all, to the Buckeye people, and they deducted 92 cents, and I looked over a record yesterday, where there had been quite a number of cars shipped by the Westminster Gin Co.
there, and 50 cents was the most they had taken off of any car.

Answer. That is a company that has gins around Westminster.
They have their seed analyzed by Law Co. in Atlanta, on their own account, and they got a premium on quite a number of cars of their seed this season, and 50 cents is the most that had been deducted on account of its not being the so-called prime seed, and the Buckeye people took off 92 cents on the analysis of the car I shipped them to Augusta.
Question. Have you got any premiums this year?
Answer. That is the only car I shipped.

Question. Well, how can you determine what price you can afford to pay for seed when you don't know what you are going to get for them until after the seed is shipped to the mill and analyzed chemically?
Answer. We have got no way of knowing whether we are paying too much for them or too little.
Question. Well, what is the only-or, what-is there only one safe thing for you to do, under those circumstances, and what is that?
Answer. Well, if we was figuring just from a strictly business standpoint, it would be to try to buy them cheap enough not to lose any money, if you was going to base them on that, because it is out of the question, you know, to have wagon seed analyzed and then come into town to sell them for the farmer; you know what that would be.

than the regular wagon price for seed?

O. R. BROWN, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN: Question. You live at Bennettsville, Mr. Brown?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What is your business?
Answer. We are in the fertilizer, feed, and seed business.
Question. What is the name of the business, under which it is conducted?
Answer. Jas. N. Drake (Inc.).
Question. What is the character of the cottonseed business done by that firm?
Answer. Well, for the past two years, our business has fallen off considerably.
Question. Well, I am not getting at the volume of the business.
What is the character of that cottonseed business?
Answer. Well, we buy and sell.
Question. You buy outright for your own account, and resell?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Do you operate in some respect similar to, or in any respect similar to the method followed by Mr. Breazeale, who just preceded you?
Answer. Yes; we sell fertilizer and supplies on credit, take crop mortgages and what personal property we can get, and pay back during the fall.
Question. What proportion of your present business is in seed!
Answer. Well, it is very small now, compared to our other business.
Question. How long have you been engaged in the seed business?
Answer. I have been with the firm since 1924.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. And the firm has been engaged in the seed business ever since then?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Did you ever operate on a brokerage basis?
Answer. Yes.
Question. In seed?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Will you state just how you operated as a broker in seed?
Question. From whom?
Answer. From the mill.
Question. Did you sell to more than one mill?
Answer. Yes; we used to sell about 10.
Question. How long since you have done any business as a broker?
Answer. We are doing a brokerage business now.
Question. Still do?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Well, how much of your seed business at the present time is a brokerage business?
Answer. Well, practically all of it is now.
Question. Are you now selling only to one mill?
Answer. No. We have sold to three this past season.
Question. Which ones?
Answer. The Cheraw Oil Mill and the Southern Cotton Oil Co., and the International Vegetable Oil Co., Savannah.
Question. Do you know anything about any rule or provision that a broker should represent one mill, exclusively?
Answer. I understood that was the rule.
Question. Where did you get your understanding?
Answer. Just from general conversations.
Question. With whom?
Answer. Well, I couldn't say exactly.
Question. Well, did you get it from any of your mill people?
Answer. Well, the mill would allow you to represent him, you were supposed to be his broker.
Question. Exclusively?
Answer. Yes.
Question. What mill or mills informed you to that effect?
Answer. Well, we had contract last year with the Southern.
Question. And you were supposed to represent only the Southern last year?
Answer. On a brokerage basis; yes.
Question. Did you represent only the Southern last year on a brokerage basis?
Answer. James N. Drake (Inc.) only represented them.
Question. Which condition did you prefer, to operate under as a broker, representing various mills, a number of them, or one exclusively?
Answer. We would rather be independent buyers.

Answer. Yes.
Question. And I am talking about that. Would you prefer to represent one mill exclusively as a broker or buy for various mills!
Answer. Well, I think it would be best to buy for various mills.
Question. Why?

Answer. Ten.

Answer. Well, different ones of us represented a certain mill, different members of the firm.

Answer. Around that, around four years ago.
Question. Well, was there a time during that experience as an independent, where that was not frue?
Answer. I couldn't say it wasn't true, but I know while I have been buying seed off and on for 20 years, that I haven't been able to make my own deal with a certain mill at a certain price.

Question. How far back is that?
Answer. I couldn't say correctly.
Question. How long a period was it that you say the prices were uniform?
Answer. Well, to tell it exactly like I feel it was, I think it was around 8 years, or 10 years, that they have been trying to get it all at one price, and as far as the prices that I could get it at.

Answer. Well, the best I can remember, I think we won one year and lost three years. Something like that.

Answer. I am pretty sure it was. In other words, they claim that seed was running so bad, they had to make the difference.
Question. Did you buy some seed on that $24 basis?
Answer. No, sir; I absolutely quit. I wouldn't buy any more; I didn't buy another seed.
Question. Even though you were a commission buyer?
Answer. That is right, sir; I absolutely quit.
Question. Why?
Answer. Well, I felt like it was too much difference, and there wasn't many seed to come in. The fact of the business is that when I spoke to the parties that had wagon seed, they said the difference was too great, and they weren't going to sell them. They carried them home.
Question. Would you say that farmers have become accustomed to getting a wagon price that is only $3 below the car price?
Answer. Become accustomed to it?
Question. Yes.
Answer. Well, if they think they are getting wagon seed-getting what the wagon seed is worth, they will accept that without much talk about it, but, as I tell you, whenever cotton is selling for a fairly good price, they don't think about then selling their seed at wagon prices. They carry them home and keep them. Of course, there is a certain amount of seed sold at wagon prices all the time, but the majority of them will hold it.
Question. Do the farmers in your locality know the car prices of seed?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Do you know what facility the farmers there have for ascertaining the car price of seed?
Answer. Well, they come to me-they can go to anybody that is interested in seed and they will tell them, and I think the mills keep them posted pretty well. They keep a man on the road to let them know what seed is worth.
Question. Well, the mills would buy direct through such buyers only in car lots, I presume?
Answer. Yes; that is the only way they could buy them, from the farmer. They would buy a car of seed from him.
Question. Did you ever hear of the so-called Memphis rules, or code of ethics adopted by the oil-mill industry?
Answer. Well, I heard of it in a general way, andinvestigation OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. When did you first hear of it?
Answer. I think I heard of it along about last year, first of this year.
Question. How did you first hear of it?
Answer. I think I got a letter about it. I really didn't pay much attention, because I didn't think much of it at the time, andquestion. A letter from whom?
Answer. I don't know who it was from; it might have been a circular. It might have been sent to me by the Southern, I don't know, but I glanced at it and I didn't think anything of it as a whole, and threw it away. I didn't go into it to learn anything from it very definite.
Question. Did you receive any brokerage or other compensation on the seed that was sold to the Sapona Mills?
Answer. No, sir; I didn't get a dime out of it-didn't want a dime. All I wanted to do was help those people sell those seed because the way things looked to me, it looked like it was mighty hard on them.
Question. When did you first learn, if you ever knew, that the Federal Trade Commission had approved any rules for the conduct of the industry?
Answer. Well, I don't know as I can say exactly when I first heard about it, but this gentleman (Mr. Linthicum) came to see me.
Of course, we discussed that then, and I told him I didn't think much of it; I didn't see where it was doing anybody any good; looked to me like a proposition where the mills just got together and said, "Well, we will do so-and-so, and we will go up there and get the Federal Trade Commission to approve.
"" Question. Did you ever discuss the Memphis rules or resolutions with any mill representatives?
Answer. I may have, in a general way, but I was not posted on it enough to go into any intelligent discussion of it, because I didn't care that much about it.
Question. Do you recall anything that any mill representative ever said to you about the Memphis rules, or the Federal Trade Commission in regard to them?
Answer. Oh, I think there has been several mentioned it to me and explained to me how it was, in a general way. In fact, I think Mr. James went over it at the time.
Question. Who is he?
Answer. He is the manager of the Southern Cotton Oil Co. at Darlington. I just didn't think anything of it. It just looked to me like a proposition where a man had a car of seed, if he wanted to sell them, all he had to do was ship them into the mill, and if the chemist said so-and-so, that was the end of it; and if he didn't want the price, why he could take them back. That is the way it appeared to me.
Question. Have you had any loans or advances from the Southern Cotton Oil Co. in connection with your commission buying?
Answer. Yes; we got a little money from them this fall, but as a general thing, we don't need the money.
Question. This fall is the first time you have had such advances?
Answer. No; I think we got two or three hundred dollars from them last fall, but the way we generally work that is this: We know INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY about what seed we are going to ship them, and when we get this money from them, it is generally applied against the commission.
In other words, we make our arrangement with the bank to handle our checks, see, and we deposit their seed tickets against these checks that we draw, and whenever we get money from them, sometimes we need a little bit to finance the seed with, and sometimes we don't, but it is generally applied against the commission, and at the end of the season we settle up.
Question. In buying on this commission arrangement with the Southern, was your seed ever docked for offgrade?
Answer. No, sir; because, as I said, they gave us a price to pay for wagon seed, and it worked along very satisfactorily in 1929, until they dropped from $31 to $24, see, then I quit; I didn't buy another seed, because I felt that was too hard.
Question. With that exception, you bought on $3 less than carseed price, did you?
Answer. Yes.
Question. How was the quality of seed in your locality last season?
Answer. Well, they were damaged to a certain extent, but I can't believe they were damaged as bad as some cars were docked from time to time. Of course, as far as we were concerned, the seed went right on in at less than $3 of the car price. Of course, if I had undertaken to have done anything with the car seed-I didn't buy a single car of seed to ship in 1929-the only way I could have bought them was to see the man and tell him to ship the seed into the mill, and they would be graded and they would send him whatever they figure out they were worth. Naturally, I didn't buy and couldn't buy any seed much because I didn't think it was a fair proposition.
Question. What did you think was not fair?
Answer. I just figured this way: If I had a car of seed and the mill come to me and says, "You ship the seed in and we will get some chemist to analyze the seed; then we will tell you what they are worth." If the price wasn't satisfactory to me, all I would have to do is ship the seed back to myself, pay the freight on it both ways, unload them, and put them back into the house; and I wouldn't certainly go out among my friends, from whom I buy seed, and recommend that they ship the seed into an oil mill and not be able to give them any satisfaction as to what they would receive for it.
If they would come to a man's pile of seed and take 100 samples of it, and then tell the man what he would receive for the seed, I would have no hesitancy in telling them to do it, because they could accept it or reject it.
Question. Were there independent buyers last season buying seed in competition with you there, as a commission buyer?

Question. Did they pay as much for seed as you did?
Answer. Sometimes they paid more.
Question. What have you to say as to not having your seed graded that you bought in competition with them, when theirs was graded?
I didn't see anything wrong with that if you wanted to take it, and if you didn't, don't.
Question. Did you find a number of mills that did that last season?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Last season?
Answer. There wasn't any but Sapona that would draw samples.
Question. Were you familiar with the method of buying wagon seed on grade last season?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. On the basis of the average of the grade for the district?
Answer. No, sir; I was not. I think I discussed that with this gentleman here-Mr. Linthicum. I am not familiar but I heard about it and didn't pay any attention to it. I think they have the State now divided up into districtsquestion. We understand that much. Have you been in any closer contact with it this season than last?
Answer. I haven't paid any attention to it at all, because if they wanted the seed, they'd give us the price. Things have been so bad we couldn't afford to take any chances.
Question. Did you ever, while operating as an independent, sell any of your seed through brokers?
Answer. No, sir.

Answer. Well, if they were, I knew nothing about it. I had no business with them. I generally try to do my business direct with the mill.
Question. The question is suggested that I ask you whether you have always followed exactly the wagon price furnished you by the manager of the Southern Cotton Oil Co. at Darlington?
