Question. Well, what percentage of cases haven't you?
Answer. Now, I couldn't determine that off-handed.
Question. Is it a minor percentage?
Answer. Yes, sir; a minor percentage, I'd say, a minor percentage.
Question. What conditions caused you to depart from it at times?
Answer. Well, I will tell you how that came about. If we heard about another buyer paying a different price, naturally, we want to stay in the market, see, and we get in touch with them and talk to them. Sometimes I do it on my own responsibility, and it is there in black and white for him to see, and if he has any kick coming, he can jump on me about it.

Question. Who?
Answer. The manager of the mill.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Has he jumped on you about it?
Answer. Sometimes he does.
Question. Do you suffer a loss of any part of your commission in such cases?
Answer. Before I'd let him get in any trouble about it I will be willing to take my medicine.
Question. Have you had to take any medicine on account of it?
Answer. I may have had to take a little bit.
Question. Has competition from independent buyers caused you sometimes to pay higher prices than the regular wagon prices?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Is that the principal cause?
Answer. I wouldn't say that it was the principal cause, because you see other mills are operating there too, don't you see, and therefore if he goes up, I wouldn't expect a man to sell me seed if he can get 50 cents or a dollar more than that somewhere else. All those things contribute to it, and, as a matter of fact, all the farmers are interested in is the high dollar out of his seed, and if he can get the independent in there, the independent will get the seed.
Question. But, as I understand it, there is no independent operatfing there this season?

W. H. ANDERSON, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Where do you live, Mr. Anderson?
Answer. Summerton, S. C.
Question. What is your business?
Answer. I am in the cotton business myself and farming, and run a gin, Mcclary Anderson; we have a gin up there, Mr. Mcclary and myself.
Question. How much cotton and cottonseed do you ordinarily raise on your own farm?
Answer. Oh, I don't-I have tenants and share croppers and things of that sort. I suppose we raise around 300 bales of cotton this year.
Question. Do you operate a gin?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How long have you been operating a gin?
Answer. Since 1914, that is the time I have been in it. Mcclary has been in it longer than that.
Question. Have you also had some banking interests in Summerton?
Answer. Yes.
Question. What?
Answer. I was vice president of the Bank of Santee there. Since the bank has been sold to the Peoples State Bank of South Caro lina, I am on the board now, the local board.
Question. You are a member of the board still?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. When were you vice president?
Answer. Well, about a year or such a matter, before they sold the bank. They sold it last spring.
Question. What volume of seed business have you done in an average season at your gin?
Answer. Well, we had been in recent years ginning around 1,500 to 2,000 bales of cotton. Of course, it varies very much since the boll weevil. We ginned lots more than that previously to that time, but in recent years, it has averaged-the last five years-it has averaged not over 1,800 bales.
Question. Can you put that into tons of seed?
Answer. Let's see, two bales run practically a ton, about 900 tons, wouldn't it be?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. On what basis have you operated your seed business?
Have you operated on an independent basis, or bought for mills on commission?
Answer. Always been independent.
Question. What method have you followed of disposing of your seed there at Summerton?
Answer. Why, we called up the different mills and sell to themsell them to the high dollar-that is all there was to it.
Question. Were you accustomed to hold your seed until late in the season, or sell it more or less currently as you accumulated it?
Answer. We sold practically everything as we accumulated it until last year. We held a few, I think, probably around 150 tons.
Question. How have you arrived at the price you pay for seed at your gin?
Answer. Why, they would tell us what they paid for wagon seed, and there was a difference of $3 on the car lot.

Answer. Always.
Question. You didn't pay more than the wagon price?
Answer. No.
Question. And you couldn't pay less? Not, and get any seed?
Answer. No.

But, when they commenced to grade it is the only time we had any trouble, because we really didn't know how to operate, because Swift Co., just across the railroad track from us, they all paid the same wagon price; if seed was $27, we had to pay $27 or got no seed, no ginning, and I always understood that representing Swift, they shipped their seed in and got their commission regardless of grade, and we had to grade, and that is the only time we ever had any trouble.
Question. When did you encounter that grading situation?

Answer. That is about the middle of our season, because we are very early down there we are over half through at thiat time-it is the tail end of the crop.
Question. Well, how did your deductions on seed run last season?

Answer. I would judge that the average was about $4, probably.

J. A. MCCOLLOUGH, being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Where do you live, Mr. Mccullough?
Answer. Lane, in Williamsburg County.
Question. What is your business?
Answer. Merchant.
Question. Are you also a ginner?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. You have any farming interests?
Answer. A little; yes, sir.
Question. How little is it?
Answer. Why, about 150 acres of cotton.
Question. The seed that you raise on your farm is rather small in amount, I take it?
Answer. Oh, it goes right through my gin. I operate a gin.
Question. How much is there?
Answer. I think I raised about 80 bales this year.
Question. How long have you been operating a gin?
Answer. I have been operating a gin since 1908.
Question. Have you operated your gin in the purchase of seed on an independent basis or on commission basis?
Answer. Independent.
Question. Always?
Answer. I believe I operated one year under the commission basis Question. How far back?
Answer. It must have been 15 years ago.
Question. With that exceptionanswer. Buckeye.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. With that exception always independent?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What has been the approximate amount of your seed business in the course of a season?
Answer. Well, it has varied a good deal with me. I used to operate three gins and I only operate one now.
Question. How long since you have had just the one?
Answer. About 10 years I have been operating one.
Question. Well, give us the approximate value of your seed business last season.
Answer. This season?
Question. No; last season.
Answer. Last year ?
Question. Last year.
Answer. It is about like this year. I handled about 10 cars of seed.
Question. Do you put them in wagon lots from farmers who gin their cotton with you?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How do you arrive at the price that you pay for seed that you buy in that way?
Answer. Well, it is by the mills. There is wagon and car price.
Question. You buy always on the basis of the wagon price of the mills?
Answer. Not always; no, sir.
Question. Well, in what proportion of the causes do you?
Answer. Well, sometimes I sell ahead; know that the market is going down. I give the farmers the benefit of that. For instance, I sell a car or two cars ahead-I give the farmers the benefit of it.
Maybe I am paying one or two dollars more than the market price at times.
Question. In what proportion of your purchases have you bought on a regular wagon price and what proportion would you say that you paid above the regular wagon price?
Answer. It is pretty hard for me to tell.
Question. Can you say which is the exception and which is the rule, if there is any difference?
Answer. Well, I suppose I bought more above the price, usually selling ahead.
Question. And are you speaking of a period of years when you say that?
Answer. No.
Question. Of some particular season?
Answer. The past season.
Question. Sir?
Answer. I am talking about the past season.
Question. Well, how has it been over a period of years, has the price that you paid for wagon seed been the same as the mill wagon price or above?
Answer. Well, it has been about the same, working about the same way.
Question. Was last season, what you said about last season, an exceptional season? That is what I am getting at.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. Well, I think it was. I think the price went up and down more than I have ever known. Sometimes they go up 3 and down 3 twice in a week.
Question. In your immediate locality last season, last year, what was the relation between the car and wagon price of seed?
Answer. $3 differential, I believe.
Question. Didn't it vary from that at any time during the season?
Answer. Not with the people I sold to.
Question. What other seed buyers are there at your place?
Answer. Well, there is no one except myself. Mr. Shirer buys car seed.
Question. Are there any mill buyers of seed there?
Answer. No, sir.
Question. No mill gins or commission gins?
Answer. None except one. Oh, there are several gins around, surrounded by gins, but none in the little town but one.
Question. How near?
Answer. There are 8 gins there in a radius of 10 miles.
Question. Are they competitors of yours in the purchase of seed?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Are those gins within that radius, some of them commission gins?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. And some independent?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Do you know which are which?
Answer. Let's see.
Shirer Bros. are commission. It is about 4 miles. Blakeley Bros. are commission.
Question. Do you know for what mills?
Answer. Shirer is the Planters, I think. I am not sure about that. He will be here.
Question. Yes.
Answer. Blakeley is with the Hartsville people.
Question. Now, any other commission gin buyers in your competitive territory?
Answer. No, sir; I think that is all of the commission seed buyers.
Mr. Brown is an independent. Salter, 5 miles; that is independent.
Examiner SHEPPARD. What county is Lane in?
The Witness. Williamsburg.
Examiner SHEPPARD. Williamsburg?
The WITNESS. Yes, sir.

Question. How have you been accustomed to dispose of your seed when you accumulated it, have you sold it direct to the mills or through some intermediary?
Answer. I sold direct to mills?
Question. What mills have you sold to in the last year or so Answer. To the Southern for the past three years.
Question. Entirely?
Answer. Entirely. I know for the past two. I am not sure about three, but I know for two.
Question. Do you-you had no contract with the Southern to buy seed for them, have you?
Answer. No, sir.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. How does it happen that you have sold entirely to them in the past couple of years?
Answer. Well, they are the nearest mill; and they are all the same price; it didn't make any difference where you sold.
Question. Well, now, when you say that they are all the same price I want to get the basis for your knowledge on that subject.
Answer. Well, it is my understanding that they are the same price. They all put out the same quotations.
Question. I want the basis for your understanding. Were you in contact-direct contact with other mills than the Southern to know what their prices were?
Answer. I had offers from other mills.
Question. Are you speaking now of last season?
Answer. Yes, sir.

Answer. Hartsville, too.
Question. You had offers from Hartsville?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Did you have any means of ascertaining the prices being paid by mills other than the ones you have named?
Answer. The basis of the price I bought on, you mean?
Question. No.
Answer. I knew what the prices were; yes, sir; the rest.
Question. How did you know about the rest?
Answer. Communication with the other ginners buying for the other mills and shipping to them.
Question. I see. How many times last season were you in touch with different mills so as to know what their prices were?
Answer. Well, it is pretty hard to tell.
Question. How frequently during the season?
Answer. I didn't ask them for their offers very much because I was shipping to the Southern and understood that the prices were the same.
Question. Well, can't you say whether or not you found out what the prices were once a week or once a month? That is what I am getting at. How often during the season did you check them?
Answer. If the price dropped, they notified us. If the price was going down, they would wire us or phone. If the price was going up we would get a circular letter.
Question. Well, I am still trying to ascertain how many times during the course of a season approximately were you in a position to know what the prices of the mills were?
Answer. Well, I didn't try very much to find out except the one I was with.
Question. Well, I know, but you have told us that you had quotations made to you by other Answer. Oh, yes.
Question. Than the one you sold to.
Answer. Yes.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. That is what I mean. How often in the course of a season did you have those quotations made to you?
Answer. Why, I got cards from different mills and quotations and circular letters from different mills.
Question. Can you say whether it was once a week or once a month?
Answer. Well, usually when the price changed they would notify you by cards or circular letters.
Question. Did you ever get that from-advance information from that the price was going to decline within the next day or two?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Did you ever get that from advance information from more than one mill at the same time?
Answer. I don't think so, sir. I don't remember-recall.
Question. Well, did the decline as predicted come about?
Answer. Every time; yes, sir.
Question. Or in case of a decline by one mill can you state how long it was after that before other mills were in line with it?
Answer. My understanding was it was all the same time.
Question. Well, what I am getting at is whether it was-you would not say the same instant, would you? But was it in the course of a short period of time? That is what I am getting at.
Answer. The way it was with me they would wire me that the price of seed would be down to-morrow, and I would usually sell a car ahead, or two, whatever I might have on hand. Sometimes I did not have any and I would sell a car.
Question. This information that you spoke of getting by phone was from the Southern?
Answer. Yes, sir; Southern.
Question. How does that condition that you have described with reference to the sameness of price between different mills last season compare with seasons prior to that?
Answer. Well, the same conditions for about three years.
Question. Well, you include the present seasonanswer. Yes, sir.
Question. When you say three years?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. And what conditions did you find prior to three years ago?
Answer. Oh, there was a great deal of competition in the seed business among the ginners and mills.
Question. Did you find different mills paying and offering to pay different prices for seed prior to three years ago?
Answer. Yes, sir. Yes, sir.
Question. And over what period of years did that condition exist?
Answer. Well, it existed from the time I started in business until about three years ago, with the exception of during the war when the Food Administration had control, you remember. I think there was one or two years at that time.
Question. I see. Have you noted any difference in that condition this season compared to last?
Answer. I haven't. It seems to be about the same as 1929.

Question. Will you describe the method that you have followed in conducting your brokerage seed business?
Answer. Well, I have had two methods. Up until 1928 I followed one method and after then I had to change my method.
Question. Describe this difference.
Answer. Well, up until 1928 I purchased seed and shipped to several mills. At times they would trade me meal, and I would take the meal and sell it at a profit and make an additional profit there as well as my commission on seed. And then at times there would be mills who were willingquestion. Who were what?
Answer. Who were willing to pay me a little more to turn them to them.
Question. More than what?
Answer. More than the prevailing carload price.
Question. You know that there is a-how many mills on an average would you sell seed to in the course of a season?
Answer. Well, with the Southern Cotton Oil Mill at Chester, Kershaw, and Lancaster a few cars; I never did do any extensive business with those fellows; they had a buyer that lives in Chester and travels out of there. And then the Buckeye people, Caldwell people, the Caldwell Co. at Spartanburg, and the Highland Park Manufacturing Co. of Rock Hill. I think that-well, yes, I made a few trades with the Union Cotton Oil Co. at Union. Whether it was operated under that name then or it was changed after their reorganization I have forgot, but anyway the same mill.
Question. What was your rate of compensation when you were operating buying for those mills?
Answer. Why, 50 cents a ton commission on the seed.
Question. Who paid it?
Answer. The mills that I bought for. And then when I traded meal for seed any additional profit that I made would be mine.
Question. Uh huh.
Answer. I would pay the shipper for the seed and let them draw a draft on me for the mill, and I sold the mill for what I could 121200 S. Doc. 209, 71-2, pt 6- -56 INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY get for it; if I made 50 cents or a dollar it was mine, and if I lost it was mine.
Question. On that exchange proposition in this basis were you able to get a better deal from some mills than others?
Answer. Yes, sir. It enabled me frequently when a man had a considerable lot of seed I could maneuver around and scalp the market and pay him a dollar over and make a dollar myself.
Question. How much difference did you find mills were willing to pay above the prevailing market for seed that you sold?
Answer. That difference didn't come in in the direct price as much as it would be a concession in price or commodities to get the seed.
Question. What commodities?
Answer. Hulls and meal.
Question. On the exchange?
Answer. Yes. Yes. Frequently I would say, "I have got a hundred tons of seed; what will you sell me hulls for?" Question. You didn't buy the seed outright when you operated as a broker?

Answer. I might say it got very active in the last two weeks.
Question. Active, in what way?
Answer. Well, they have been disregarding the prevailing carload price and buying seed on their own prices, and at their own ideas.
Question. Has there been any bidding up of the carload price, as a result?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. How much?
Answer. Well, if it wasn't for their activity, I don't think seed would be bringing over $25 to-day in car lots.

Answer. $27 and $28.
Question. How recently have you noticed this difference in policy, on the part of the Buckeye?
Answer. In the last two or three weeks.
Question. Didn't notice it earlier in the season?
Answer. No, sir; didn't notice it in the earlier part of the season.
Question. Well, what was its policy last season, by contrast with the present season?
Answer. They stayed in line.
Question. In line, with what?
Answer. With the prevailing carload price.
Question. How about seasons prior to last season-Buckeye's policy?
Answer. Well, I don't know. The year before last, they stayed in line very well, and then, back there, six, seven, years ago, occasionally they'd get pretty bullish on seed, drive them up. Now, last year, at one time, our market around Rock Hill and that section, maybe it applied to the whole State, I wouldn't say, was $32 on the carload price; in North Carolina, where they operate more extensively than they do in South Carolina, it was $30 on the car-lot price.
Well, North Carolina had the best seed, according to the chemists, in the Piedmont section, and I got instructions from Mr. Johnson to go to North Carolina on Saturday and put that market at $32, and buy some cottonseed.
Question. What did that have to do with Buckeye?
Answer. Well, it didn't have anything to do with Buckeye, but it had something to do with us, though, at Rock Hill-the fact that the market was $2 higher where we were operating extensively than it was where they were operating extensively.
Question. Are you familiar with the mill's method of figuring spreads between products prices and seed prices?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What is the basis of your familiarity?
Answer. Information given me by the mills.
Question. Have you ever worked out yourself figures on products values and seed prices?
Answer. Oh, yes; yes.
Question. Seed prices spreads?
Answer. Yes.
Question. What do you know, if anything, about the costs of crushing?
Answer. Only information that has been given me by the mills, the managers themselves.
Question. Did you state to Mr. Dawkins, who interviewed you, that last year seed were bought by the mills on too wide a spread!
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What is the basis of that statement?
Answer. Well, they bought last year on the basis of $10, $11, $12, and $13 a ton, and the cost of crush depends, of course, on the amount of seed that a mill crushes; the number of presses they have got will determine it to a certain extent, but $7 cost, as well as I can gather from the mills, based on a reasonable crush, would be reasonable. Of course, that $7 wouldn't allow them any profit, but INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY it would cover, according to my information, all overhead, taxes, insurance, depreciation, upkeep, etc., and anything in excess of that, would be profit.
Question. Well, do you know any mills whose costs, including overhead, are as low as $7?
Answer. Oh, yes.
Question. Can you name them?
Answer. Highland Park Manufacturing Co.
Question. Any others?
Answer. No; I don't know. Now, as I say, I know that because Mr. Johnson said that.
Question. Well, you are, you might say, a part of the Highland Park Co.'s business in a way?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Very closely allied with it.
Answer. Yes; I guess so.
Question. You are their principal buyer of seed, aren't you?
Answer. Yes, yes; I buy 80 per cent of what they crush.
Question. How much?
Answer. Eighty per cent.
Question. I think I have nothing else to ask you, Mr. Roper.

The WITNESS. Yes; higher quality.

Answer. Yes.

Answer. Yes.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY L. W. FAIREY, Orangeburg, S. C., being first duly sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN: Question. Will you tell us your business, Mr. Fairey?
Answer. I run a farm and a country store, country merchant and farmer.
Question. What is the amount of your cotton and cottonseed raised on your own farm?
Answer. Well, I suppose about 75 or 100 bales, sir.
Question. Can you put that in tons for seed?
Answer. Yes, sir; it would run around 30 to 40 tons.
Question. Do you operate a gin?
Answer. No, sir; my brother operates a gin.
Question. Have you ever operated a gin?
Answer. Yes, sir; I helped my father with it before I was married. After I was marriedquestion. Do you have a general store also?
Answer, Yes, sir.
Question. Have you bought seed from other farmers in your vicinity?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. To what extent, in what volume, say, last season?
Answer. Well, last season, I reckon 200 or 250 tons.
Question. That is in addition to what you raised yourself?
Answer. No, sir; I would take it altogether, that is about what I shipped.
Question. It includes what you raised?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Have you operated on an independent basis in the buying of seed, or on commission?
Answer. Until this present season, I did, sir.
Question. Independent?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. For how many years?
Answer. I started on a small scale 30 years ago, bought without a wagon scale the first year, and the next year, I bought a wagon scale, and have been in it ever since.
Question. Has the volume of your business varied much from the figures that you gave by going back some years?
Answer. Not a great deal, sir. Of course, it increased the last two years, but that was on account of putting in-my brother putting in improved gin machinery, giving him more ginning to do, giving him more seed.
Question. How have you operated your seed-buying business?
Have you operated it in connection with your brother's gin business, to any extent?
Answer. No, sir; I just bought independent myself-any seed that was for sale, I would buy it.
Question. How were you accustomed to figuring your price when you bought independently?
Answer. Just what the general market price was, sir.
Question. You mean, you bought on the wagon price?
Answer. Regular wagon basis; yes, sir.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Did you ever run above it in your purchases?
Answer. No, sir; I made a rule just to follow the wagon price, except when I was loading a car, possibly. If some farmers would haul it and put it into the car-I live a mile and a quarter from the railroad station-I would allow them $1 more per ton for hauling.
Question. For hauling?
Answer. Yes; and for putting it in the car.
Question. Did you sell your seed rather promptly as you accumulated it in car lots, or did you hold it?
Answer. Some years, in fact, the first of the season, I always had to, on account of green seed.
Question. Had to do what?
Answer. Had to sell it. It wouldn't do to hold green seed; it would damage on you; but later in the season I would hold some of them. I didn't have very much storage capacity, several cars, possibly; I would hold some for a rise in price.
Question. What was your experience with reference to whether an increase in price would come about in the latter part of the season?
Answer. Usually did after Christmas; yes.
Question. Well, when you say "usually," in what proportion of the many years that you have been in the business was it true?
Answer. Well, I suppose it has been three-fourths of the time, that there has been a better price, perhaps.
Question. Can you say ordinarily what proportion of your seed you held for the expected increase in price and what proportion you sold promptly?
Answer. Well, on account of my small storing, I don't suppose I have more than a fourth of them, hardly, because I couldn't hold more than three or four cars at a time.
Question. Ordinarily, you sold three-fourths of your seed currently as you accumulated it?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. What was the general quality of seed in your locality last year?
Answer. The last were somewhat off, and a year before they were a little worse, I believe.
Question. Why is it, after operating independently so many years, that you, this season, took a commission contract?
Answer. Because I was forced to do it, sir.
Question. Explain how and why.
Answer. Well, because if I shipped seed independently-I remember, three years ago in the fall I sold one car just before the grading went into effect, and the next car I shipped I received $11.30 and some-odd cut on my same seed.
Question. On what basis?
Answer. $40 a ton.
Question. All right, go ahead.
Answer. And, of course, later then, I had to take other losses.
I couldn't get any redress at all, you know. It was just-you had no come back, whatever, and so last year, the first of the season-they didn't put the grading rules into effect right at the beginning of the season-and I still continued to buy independent, and then when INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY they started to grade I found, I think, one car lost about $7 a ton I found, instead of making $3 commission, I was losing about $4.
Question. On commission? You were not buying on commission then, were you?
Answer. Not buying. I figured I would get the commission, and if they went up, why, more, and sometimes I had to sell them at a loss; and last year, then, after they put the grading rules in, why, I still didn't sign a buyer's contract, but I sold them through another buyer there that loaded them, and I stood the weights and he gave me practically all of his commission, but I found there was some complaint from other buyers in the same town, so I just signed a contract with a mill myself.
Question. What mill have you gone into a commission contract with?
Answer. Hartsville oil mill.
Question. What do you have, as a basis for your statement, that there was a complaint about your turning your seed last year through these commission buyers?
Answer. Well, they claimed he had no right to divide his commission, he being a commission buyer, to divide his commission with me.
Question. Who was that?
Answer. Mr. J. D. Fersner.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY B. F. TAYLOR, recalled, having been previously sworn, testified as follows: Gentlemen, I was asked by you to check over Exhibit 847 and advise whether or not that exhibit was correct. That is Dawkins's sheetquestion. Tabulation?

Now, I have written this letter to Major Sheppard, examiner: I was asked by you to check commission's Exhibit 847 and to advise as to the correctness of same. This exhibit purports to be a tabular statement of f. o. b. basis prime seed prices, telegraphically reported to and by the secretary South Carolina Division, National Cottonseed Products Association.
The statement includes a number of items "Reported by mail" and "Reported verbally," hence I conclude all reports should have been incorporated in the tabular statement. And as a matter of fact all should have been included to get the facts. I have therefore checked the tabular statement on that basis.
I find 105 reports from mills have been omitted, most of them telegraphic reports.
I find 26 secretary reports omitted from the tabular statement, 2 of which were circular reports, the rest wire reports.
I find 10 errors in tabulation in the statement.
I find 2 errors of price in the statement.
The report of wagon-seed prices is often more important than the report of car-seed prices, hence I have included these in my checking.
In my opinion the statement is so far from being correct that it would be worthless as an attempt to show the method of reporting or the price changes during the period.

Question. What are you doing with North Carolina samples?
Answer. Well, I got them because I want to make the comparison and show it wasn't confined to South Carolina but to North Carolina as well. As a matter of fact, I was well, that is by the way; Now, if you will figure the number of pounds of oil in a ton of seed from those analyses you will find that it amounts to 377 pounds.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY My experience covering a number of years in checking the results of mills against the chemical analyses is that there is about 65 pounds of oil left in the products and lost in manufacture; so if 65 pounds be deducted from 377, it would indicate that the mills in North Carolina should have obtained a yield of 312 pounds of oil.
Examiner SHEPPARD. Per ton of seed?
The WITNESS. Per ton of seed.
The Census Department report, which I have attached, shows that during the period there was crushed in North Carolina 86,961 tons of seed, producing 7,205,341 pounds of oil, or a yield of 312.8 pounds to the ton.
By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Is that all for North Carolina?
Answer. North Carolina, yes. Now, a similar comparison for South Carolina is as follows: Two thousand one hundred and fiftyseven samples of seed, showing an average analysis of 18.28 per cent of oil that would indicate after deducting the 65 pounds loss referred to above, a yield of 300.6 pounds of oil per ton. The census report shows that South Carolina crushed during the period 85,179 tons of seed, and produced 25,885,172 pounds of oil, or a yield of 303.8.
Now, you might think that that difference of 3 pounds in South Carolina was material. At 62 cents, which is about the present market for oil, it is 19 cents. I would consider that a most remarkable check of chemical analyses against actual results.

(Thereupon, said document was received in evidence marked "Commission's Exhibit No. 946, Witness Taylor.") By Mr. WOODEN : Question. May I ask a question there, Mr. Taylor? You spoke a while ago of the variations in chemists' analyses of free fatty acid being due to the conditions of the observance of the end reaction?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Will you amplify what you mean by that?
Answer. Well, in determining the amount of free fatty acid in the oil a certain given quantity of oil is placed in a bottle, and there are two methods used, one is alcohol solution and the other is salt solution. The indicator to show the end point is usually phenolthalin, which becomes a bright scarlet when the reaction of the solution is alkaline.
Question. In other words, is that the point at which the showing of free fatty acid is complete?
Answer. Is complete, but not only complete but in excess of complete. So in observing the end reaction the chemist must be very INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY careful not to put more caustic solution in to neutralize the free fatty acids. It is also a factquestion. Suppose he does that?
Answer. It will show more fatty acids than it ought to. Another question of skill in the analysis is the shaking of the sample so as to bring about an intimate contact of the caustic solution with the free fatty acids in the other solution. And if that shaking is not done violently and carefully and thoroughly you might not get the reaction complete. That is, that you might not have the free fatty acids entirely satisfied chemically by the caustic soda, and hence in that case would show a lower result.
Question. Would there be anyanswer. Now, this is accentuated in oils containing a great deal of free fatty acid, and where they run as high as 7 to 20 per cent it is seldom that chemists will agree without great care.
Question. If the shaking and mixing is most thoroughly and completely done, or just so assume that it is overdone, what effect does that have on the showing of free fatty acid?
Answer. That would have none.
Question. Well, there is a large element of personal skill and personal reaction of the individual chemist in handling those matters!
Answer. There is; and that is the reason the association has taken the stand that all of those chemists engaged in seed grading and oil analysis should be supervised and more or less licensed. I am not sure that they license them-yes, they do; they are not given a permit to operate for the association unless they are.
Question. There is no automatic way of regulating that factor in the situation?
Answer. No. I think it takes from two to three years of work in a laboratory under an efficient supervisor for a chemist to become expert in those lines.
Question. Is there any way to get rid of that human element or personal equation in that?
Answer. There is none in any chemical analysis.
Question. All right, what is the next?
Answer. The next thing is that since I have made the efforts at correcting the troubles at Cheraw I have obtained the results of six duplicate samples sent off from that mill. The average of Rice's indices is 100.15. The average of Law's indices is 101.1. Now, you might think that that one per cent is material. As a matter of fact, on $2.30 seed that 1 per cent would mean 30 cents, and the per cent value is much less. Now, in this series of analyses you will note what I have indicated, that the chemists might disagree, but on the average that with identical samples they will come out about the same.
Question. Were these samples that you have just been talking about samples made on purchases in the ordinary course of business!
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Were they drawn by the regular licensed samplers of the mills?
Answer. They were. The sample was provided after I left there.
And since then they have a regular sampler who attends to that matter.

Answer. Yes.

Thus the trade rules, which it is claimed, are designed for the protection of the farmer operates to his extreme detriment.

S. A. S., December 4, 1930.") B. F. TAYLOR, recalled, on his original subpoena, having previously been sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Will you explain, Mr. Taylor, how your method of reporting prices in the newspapers, how it came into existence?
Answer. It came into existence because the Memphis resolutions require that the prices shall be published by all available means to the public, and it was to get it to the public as far as I could see; the best was through the newspapers. It would be impractical to send it out in the form of circulars.
Question. So far as you know, had there been any newspaper publication of prices in this State prior to your beginning them last winter some time?
Answer. There had not.
Question. How do you account for the fact that there had been no such publication although the Memphis resolutions were adopted in 1928?
Answer. I can't account for it because I wasn't present and don't know what happened.
Question. Is it your opinion that the publication of prices in the newspapers is of value and interest to the general public?
Answer. It hasn't appeared so, in my experience.
Question. As a matter of fact, you have expressed yourself rather strongly to the effect that such publication is of no interest to the public, haven't you?
Answer. As far as I know.
Question. It was not then, I take it, your own individual desire and judgment that led to the inauguration of the publication?
Answer. It was solely my desire to conform to the Memphis resolutions.
Question. Well, who was it that suggested to you, if anyone did, that you inaugurate this publication in the newspapers?
Answer. I don't recall that anyone suggested it. I think the suggestion came from me.
Question. At that time did you have the opinion that it would not be of interest to the public?
Answer. I had that opinion at the time.
Question. Well, why did you inaugurate something that personally you thought was of no interest to the public?
Answer. Because the method that had been pursued up to the time I took charge of the office did not take the public into consideration, so far as the publication of prices was concerned.
Question. Have you found that the publication of prices in the newspapers has been of value and importance to the mills?
Answer. It has, to some extent.
Question. What do they get from that that they do not get through your price reporting system?
Answer. Usually a brainstorm on account of the publication of some higher prices than some mill wants to pay.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Examiner SHEPPARD. Mr. Taylor, your predecessor, Mr. Acree, did not use the newspapers ?
The WITNESS. No, sir.
By Mr. WOODEN : Question. You made some reference this afternoon, Mr. Taylor, to the importance of a tabulation showing wagon-seed prices?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Will you explain why the wagon-seed price is so important?
Answer. First, because it is usually the first price paid by a mill when a change is inaugurated; consequently, it would get the information to those interested quicker, of a change. In the second place, any change that comes by telegram, whether it be wagon or car prices, should be published in the same way.
Question. Have you not made the statement that this publication of prices in the newspapers was inaugurated simply to meet the assumed legal requirements of the situation?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. Comparing the reports you received from mills this season with those you have received last season, have you not received this season a much larger percentage of wagon-seed price reports than last?
Answer. Undoubtedly.
Question. How do you account for that?
Question. Well, do you know how the number or proportion of wagon-seed prices the early part of this season compared with the early part of last season?
Answer. I do not, except that from the records I know there were very few in Mr.- Question. Very few what?
Answer. Very few wagon-seed prices appearing in the records that were in the office when I went in there.
Question. Even for the some comparative part of the season?
Answer. Even for the same period. I also want to call attention to the fact that the executive committee late in the year 1929, I think it was, specifically provided for the reporting of wagon-seed prices.
Question. Aren't you quite convinced in your own mind that the present season-not nearly all the car prices paid have been reported!
Answer. They do not report every price of a carload or 100 tons, about, unless they have changed their price. That is, by telegram, Mr. Wooden; you understand that?
Question. Yes; during this early part of the season when the prices reported to you had been so predominantly wagon prices, have you published car prices by figuring a differential of $3 above the wagon price?
Answer. I have not.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. You have not done that, either in the newspapers or in your reports to members?
Answer. No, sir; in neither.
Question. When a wagon price is reported to your members would you not say that the mills would understand that that carried a $3 differential between the car and wagon price?
Answer. No, sir; there is no relation, real relation, between a longestablished custom and the price-reporting system. Since the Federal food administration days there has been a differential in South Carolina of about $3 between wagon seed and car seed, and that is generally understood by the shippers, mills, and anybody that is interested in the business, although that differential may vary at times for specific reasons.
Question. Would not, in your opinion, any mill receiving a report of a wagon-seed price of so much assume that the car price was $3 above that?
Answer. Naturally; I would if I were a millman.
Question. What method have you followed, Mr. Taylor, of figuring your wagon prices for newspaper publication, in view of the varying averages in different districts?
Answer. I have reported the high and the low, giving the range; where it could be specified I have done so. And I say that in reference to the newspapers not desiring to have the report take up too much space. For instance, I would say wagon seed at such and such a point, or at various points, so much. I could have specified the points but it would have taken too many; and I discussed the matter with different people several times to try and arrive at some accurate and satisfactory method of reporting, and I have not yet satisfied myself as to what ought to be done about it. Now, for instance, when a mill would report paying so and so at Cope to meet competition the objection was made that that might be interpreted to mean that there was no competition anywhere else, and consequently that I was calling attention to some particular case of competition that should be brought directly to the attention of the inills, which was not the fact.
Question. Well, you have not published such things in the newspapers, have you, that the price at any point was made to meet competition?
Answer. I have had those reports come to mequestion. I mean, as far as publication in the papers was concerned?
Answer. I don't think I have used those words, but I have used the words "disturbed conditions," which came nearer carrying the idea than the other.
Question. Well, have you attempted to confine your wagon-seed reports in the newspapers to publication of the daily reports that you get from your members?
Answer. Yes; and I want to say that in many instances I have considered them inaccurate, to this extent: That regardless of the fact that we have impressed upon the mills, as much as possible, that those reports should be made on basis-grade wagon seed, yet, when some of them have been paying a discount of $1, they would almost invariably put that down $22 wagon seed, when it should have INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY been put down as $23 basis wagon seed; and I, not having any method of knowing whether the man was really reporting the zone grade price or the basis price, have never considered that I had the right to interpret those reports and have, consequently, put them in the paper as they were received by me.
Question. You mean that you have or have not put them in the paper as basis prices?
Answer. I put them in the paper as received, and call them basis cottonseed.
Question. Although believing that some of them were not on the basisanswer. Believing that some of them were $1 below basis seed, say, but I didn't think I had the right to interpret a report.
Question. Does the newspaper report read "basis wagon seed"?
Answer. If he has placed it under the basis price $22, when it should have been $23, I report it to the newspaper as $22, just as he reports it to me.
Question. If a mill were paying a premium for wagon seed, a premium of $1 for wagon seed, what would you do in that case?
Answer. Same thing.
Question. You said something this afternoon, Mr. Taylor, off the record, in the hearing of a number of us here, to the effect that since we fellows had been here in the State, we had caused all sorts of disturbance, and things were slipping with regard to grading and price reporting. Do you recall that?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Will you state just what you meant by it?
Answer. Well, seed has been bought in this State in the last 10 days as is, and several of the mills have failed to report, and some one should have been jacking them up to make them report. I am furthermore satisfied that there are other practices taking place in the State that are contrary to our rules that should be checked up and straightened out.
Question. Will you specify what you have in mind there?
Answer. What-about being straightened out?
Question. Yes.
Answer. Well, for instance, there is a hauling charge up here in Union, S. C., put into effectquestion. By what mill?
Answer. By the Union mill. And that resulted in a $29 price at Jonesville, which was published in the newspapers.
Question. Johnston, you mean?
Answer. No; Jonesville.
Question. Well, a $29 price was published in the last few days at Johnston, wasn't it?
Answer. Yes, Johnston; yes; but that was a different occasionthose seed at Johnston being bought at $29, wagon seed, without grading.
Question. Has the result of those various things you mentioned been to increase the price paid for seed by the mills?
Answer. Well, I wouldn't say that. It has, in places, undoubtedly, Question. Do you attribute that to the fact that this inquiry and investigation has been on here in the last few weeks?

Question. In Exhibit 797, which are the minutes of executive committee meeting of September 23, 1929, there is a paragraph relating to meal exchange, and it was resolved that it was the sense of the committee that all exchanges of products for cottonseed should be expressed in pounds; that such exchange price should be made public and that they should bear a definite relation to the published f. o. b.
cash prices for cottonseed, and published delivery cash prices for products. Now, in Exhibit 795, which is a copy of the meeting of the South Carolina Association in August, 1928, a resolution was adopted along somewhat similar lines, but reading this way: "that exchange prices shall be f. o. b. stations for cottonseed and delivered price for cottonseed meal." I want you to explain about that delivered price for cottonseed meal, or, for products. Is that the basis on which you have been publishing exchange prices?
Answer. Yes, sir. Carload shipments of seed exchanged for meal are taken on some basis of poundage; at the present time the exchange for meal is 1900 pounds of meal for 1 ton of seed, in carload lots, in which case, the mill pays the freight from the mill to the delivery point and pays the freight on the seed from the shipping point to the mill.
Question. But I thought this exchange rate was on the f. o. b station price for cottonseed?
Answer. It is.
Question. And delivered for meal?
Answer. Yes.
Answer. Oh, certainly it means something.
Question. Well, the delivered price of meal varies according to delivery point, doesn't it?
Answer. Yes, but not so far as the prices are concerned at the basing points. The meal would be based on price at what the mill asked for the meal at the mill. The seed would be based on the price that the mill paid for seed f. o. b. cars at station.
Question. Well, as I understand that statement, it doesn't corre spond to the basis, as I understood it, from these exhibits-in other words, that the meal exchange basis was on a delivered basis.
Answer. It is, but the poundage is not, and the price is not. I will show you what I mean. I will do a little figuring. [Illustrates. Usually; yes.
Question. Then why add that 50 cents for freight on seed?
Question. I have seen a number of the reports and telegrams reporting exchange basis, but I have never seen one that referred to delivered price.
Answer. Because that is understood.
Question. Well, then, how can it be understood without some common delivery point to figure on?
Answer. Any point, just like seed-when you quote a price of seed you mean any point in South Carolina, regardless of the cost of the freight from that point to your mill.
Question. I may be dense, but I don't understand how you can figure an exchange on the published delivered price of meal without having someanswer. Difference, you meanquestion. Some common point to figure it on.
Answer. You don't have to have a common point at all.
Question. Well, will you say that your method of publishing exchange basis has been in accordance with what is set out in Exhibits 795 and 797, that I read to you?
Answer. No; I won't say that. I would say my method of publication has been the same as that of publishing the prices of seed; whatever exchange rates a mill reports to me, I report. They are not always the same.
Question. Isn't exchange ordinarily made right at the mill?
Answer. I imagine that the bulk of it is done on wagon seed.
Question. Well, then?
Answer. Or car seed delivered at the mill.
Question. Then why figure any delivered price on products for an exchange that is made without any delivery cost?
Answer. Just because the fool mills want to give away the freight, that is all.
Question. Do they give away the freight, regardless of how much it is?
Answer. It looks so. I don't say they all do that, because I know of an instance that happened this year where they exchanged on the basis of the buyer paying the freight. It is a question of what trade you can make with your shipper.
Question. Do I understand then that you have not followed that basis of publishing exchange that is specified in these Exhibits 795 and 797?

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. I have occasionally by telegram, by I haven't put them in the newspaper.
Question. And only occasionally by telegram? Ordinarily, you have published the exchange basis on the f. o. b. mill price for products?
Answer. Whenever a telegram comes to me quoting exchange, I quote the exchange in the telegram that goes out. If there is no exchange mentioned, I don't mention it.
Question. Did you ever see a telegram from your mills reporting their exchange basis and saying anything about delivered price on products?
Answer. I don't recall that I have.
Question. I have seen a number of such telegrams, and I don't recall it either. That is why I don't understand these references in the minutes to publishing exchange on the basis of delivered price of products.
Answer. Well, all I can say is that it has been the custom in this State ever since I have been in the oil-mill business to make exchanges.
of meal for seed, and it has always been customary, generally, to pay the freight on the meal and to pay the freight on the seed, and no price is mentioned to the farmer ton or 1,900 pounds for a ton exchange. Now, I will tell you this, that the farmer understands this thing perfectly. There is about 900 to 1,000 pounds of 7 per cent meal in a ton of seed; that is, 7 per cent meal.
Now, there is only 32 per cent ammonia in a ton of seed, and when a man wants meal for fertilizer and can exchange something that has 32 per cent of ammonia in it for something that has 7 per cent, thereby getting 100 per cent increase in the value of the fertilizer in the material, why he is going to do it, and that is the reason that price doesn't enter into the situation. It is what you are going to use that meal for.
Question. Do I understand, Mr. Taylor, that when a mill reports, for instance, that its exchange basis for meal is 1,900 pounds, that that exchange basis is the same 1,900 pounds whether the exchange is made right at the mill or whether it is made 50 or 100 miles from the mill?
Answer. Yes.
Question. And the mill pays the freight both ways?
Answer. The mill pays the freight both ways.
Question. All right. I am showing you exhibit marked "932." Mr. Kendrick, the other day, identified that as coming from his files, but was rather uncertain about the rest of it. Can you tell us the origin of that printed circular?
Answer. To the best of my knowledge and belief, it is a transcript of the rules prevailing at the time it was issued in the Interstate Cottonseed Crushers' Association, regarding the grading of cottonseed, and it was printed at Columbia and quite a number of these are now in my office.
Question. Do you know how long the rules quoted there were in effect?
Answer. I can't say just now, but I should think for 20 years, up to the time of the modified Meloy plan.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. Well, do you mean, then, that for that length of time the percentage of deductions for damaged and immature seed was figured on the basis of the delivered price?
Answer. I don't think that those rules were observed in South Carolina. As was indicated here the other day, or to-day-I forget which by one of the witnesses that appeared, when seed were received in a damaged condition at the mill, they just used their best judgment and made what settlement they could with the shipper, and they didn't regard those rules in this State.
Question. Do you mean there was a total disregard of them?
Answer. In that they didn't sit down and make a percentage grading in accordance with the rule. They would do the best they could and make a settlement with the man; if they were too badly damaged they would return them to him or sell them for his account to be used as fertilizer.
Question. Do you think it a fair basis of deduction to figure the deductions on the delivered price?
Answer. Yes, sir; because the mill pays the freight.
Question. Then the seller and shipper ought to have some of the deduction for damage taken off the freight as well?
Answer. Certainly; it has cost me that much money. That is what I have to pay when I ship meal that is off in quality. That is based on the freight plus the cost of the meal at the delivery point.
Question. Wasn't that basis of deduction changed just shortly after the modified Meloy plan went into effect?
Answer. Yes, sir.
Question. On what basis was it changed? Did you hear Mr.
Culvern speak of that?
Answer. No, sir; not changed. They still deduct for excess freight.
Question. You mean that the deductions for excess free fatty acid have been figured on the delivered price?
Answer. No; I had particular reference to foreign matter.
Question. Did you hear Mr. Culvern's testimony regarding the basis of figuring deductions?
Answer. I don't recall it.
Question. Well, as I recall it, he said that shortly after the modified Meloy plan went into effect in 1928, that the basis of deduction was shifted from the delivered price to the f. o. b. shipping point price.
Answer. Well, I am not surprised that I don't remember it because I wasn't operating in the oil mill game then.
Question. Well, he though that the deductions on the basis of the delivered price were not on the proper basis; and you don't agree with him on that?
Answer. I don't know.
Question. I didn't understand.
Answer. I don't know.
Question. I thought you said a few moments ago that you thought that was the proper basis?
Answer. No; I don't think it is the proper basis, not from quality.
Question. You want to change your testimony in that respect?

Question. Are licensed samplers provided for, always mill employes?
Answer. Usually they are, because it is impractical to get independent samplers, so to speak.
Question. Do you know any in this State that are not mill employees?
Answer. No; as a matter of fact, I don't know any except myself.
I am employed by the mills.

Answer. I said, I don't know any but myself. I have never had the pleasure of meeting a single one of them.
Question. Well, are you a licensed sampler?
Answer. I am.
Question. Didn't you come in contact with the licensed samplers at the Cheraw mill when you checked over their sampling?

When I make out my reports for the newspapers each day I haven't got those things, and I don't get them until a week after sometimes. Now, how in the world can I put them in? That is why I tell you these are not reported, because of this complication.

Question. I am informed that this compilation of telegrams represented by Exhibit 952 shows during a period of three months this season that the Southern Cotton Oil Co. sent 15 wires reporting wagon prices, and only one telegram reporting a car price. Is that in accord with your general understanding of the situation?
Answer. Well, I think that nearly represents the situation, for this reason: That this year, as I told you before the seed moved rapidly early in the season and wagon seed represented at least 50 per cent of the purchases made by the mills up to along about November 1, and consequently I would say that the wagon-seed prices would be more promptly and more often reported than the car-seed prices.
Question. Well, don't these daily reports show car purchases almost every day?
Answer. Yes; they do, but then you see, wagon seed purchased may be only a ton. Everybody will buy some wagon seed every day. Their car-seed purchases may amount to several hundred tons at a time, and they'd only report one price representing several hundred tons of car seed. That is the reason that car seed represents such a small proportion of the reports.
Question. I am also told that out of the total of telegrams received from all mills amounting to 120 during the last three months, that only 26 of them relate to car seed, the balance, wagon seed.
Answer. That may be true. I don't know.
Question. Is that in line with your general knowledge of the situation?
Answer. I think that would be about right.

By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Well, how do you account for their attracting attention in the last two weeks?

The mill at Union some time back in the season, made a hauling contract and took some seed from Jonesville and paid the shipper the freight, and at the same time he reported it and I told him he was making a mistake, that it was going to result in a price rise of cottonseed over what he wished to pay for it at that point on account of his action, if any of the mills ever undertook to buy any seed from that particular party. It resulted just as I had predicted. The Southern Cotton Oil Co. went there and found this hauling charge in existence, and paid that man the price they were then paying for cottonseed, $28 and a dollar added, and went right back to that plus one that worried North Carolina so badly. As soon as that was done, and published in the newspaper, Caldwell, who was only 9 miles away from Jonesville, who was trying to buy seed on the $28 basis, had his shippers to come into him and say, "We see in the Spartanburg Herald where seed brought $29 at Jonesville. Why can't you pay $29?" So Caldwell got very much exercised about the $29 price being published at Jonesville, and said it didn't represent the facts in the case, that it was impossible to explain to his seed shippers about it and they gave him a great deal of trouble. Union immediately called up and wanted to know why they had paid $29 at Jonesville.
Question. Called up whom?
Answer. Me. I told him I said, "You know perfectly well why.
I wrote you a month or six weeks ago that that was going to be the result of your hauling contract, and if you don't mind, it is going to result in a raise in the price of seed at Union itself because Union is a delivery point of those seed and any mill that wants to compete with you would offer at Union your carload price for seed, plus your hauling charge for seed delivered in a car." Question. Now, will you state why?
Answer. Well, if I was running a gin and buying on commission basis and buying bad seed and all kind of seed, why, if it went off there was no trouble; but if I step out here and buy a carload of seed from a farmer, then those seed have to be graded, and probably he would not get as much for his seed as if he had sold them in to me at wagon loads. I believe seed ought to be graded but I just feel like it is just not fair to everybody all of the way through just like it stands now.
Question. Do you think an independent man can continue to operate with the grading enforced against him?
Answer. Mighty hard; mighty hard for me to do it.

Question. Well, if other mills met your price you would not get any more seed than you had before, would you?

B. F. TAYLOR, recalled, having previously been sworn, testified as follows: By Mr. WOODEN : Question. Has it been your experience, Mr. Taylor, from a large number of years that ordinarily the normal price of cottonseed products advances in the spring?
Answer. I would think so ordinarily.
Question. The cost of carrying them and holding them would have something to do with that, wouldn't it?
Answer. Not that so much as the fact that there is a heavy demand for fertilizer meal in the spring when the farmers are planting their crops and the forage crops have mostly been consumed and that makes a greater demand for hulls until grass comes in in summer; and so far as oil and linters are concerned I do not think that you could say that either advance particularly in the spring or decline in the spring. Sometimes it is one way and sometimes it is another.
Question. But treating products from a ton as a whole would you say that it is normal for the product prices to advance in the spring!
Answer. It is normal for the product prices to advance.
Question. Referring to the matter of spread, is there any way that a mill can narrow or reduce its spread in spring without raising its price for seed?
Answer. Well, of course, it could sell its products for less money than they are worth or something like that.
Question. Which they would not do?
Answer. They would not do that. And if the spread is reduced it is largely due to the higher price paid for seed.
Question. Then when you issued circulars to your members advis ing them or urging them not to narrow or reduce their spread in the latter part of the season it was tantamount to advising them or urging them not to increase their price of seed, was it not?
Answer. You may take it that way; yes. But they might increase their price of seed, Mr. Wooden, or the prices of seed might be reduced and yet the spread widened. So the way you put the questionquestion. That would be naturally the case?
Answer. You might pay $20 for seed in the fall and only have an $8 spread in the price of products. When the spring comes you might be paying $50 for seed and have a spread of $14 or Don't you see what I mean?
Question. I appreciate that; yes.
$15.
Answer. In other words, it depends entirely on the price of seed and the price of products.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Question. In other words, it is possible to have a higher spread in the spring than a reduced spread?
Answer. Yes. So my circulars were not intended to affect the price of seed, but it was to warn them to look carefully as to the value of the products and to try to preserve more or less a uniform spread based upon the value of their products.
Question. It was your theory, was it not, that a narrowing of the spread in the latter part of the season amounted to a discrimination?
Answer. That is the way we looked at it. We thought that the farmer should be given the advantage of the spread rather than the independent buyer or some person who was speculating on the seed.
Question. Did you consider that a violation of the Memphis rule prohibiting discrimination price?
Answer. Well, I rather thought that might be inferred.
Question. Yes.
Answer. But I would not say that it is a fact.
Question. Well, if the prices of products as a whole tend to advance in the spring or compared to their price in the fall, wouldn't that by the same token constitute a discrimination?
Answer. No.
Question. Why not?
Answer. Because that is simply a question of market conditions over which neither the farmer or mills nor anybody else has any control.
Question. Isn't the same thing true in the purchase of seed?
Answer. It is in the purchase of seed so far as the price is concerned; but you are talking about a spread now.
Question. Yes; I am talking about a spread just now.
Answer. Wellquestion. I am talking about your proposition that it was discriminatory to narrow the spread in the latter part of the season.
Answer. That was my idea.
Question. Yes. Why isn't it clearly discriminatory to sell products at a different price in the latter part of the season?
Answer. Because, as I told you, the price of products to-day is dependent or should be upon the markets prevailing to-day, and that has nothing to do with what products may be selling at last spring.
Now, the spread part of the proposition would apply in either case if you were going to preserve a uniform spread and be fair to everybody, why your spread would be the same thing with products worth $40 a ton as worth $50 a ton, and the farmer or whoever had seed at that time would naturally gain by the speculation if it went up, if products went up.
Question. If products prices go up in the spring, as you said they ordinarily have and normally have, and the spread remains constant -no, strike that. If the products market prices go up in the spring, as you say they normally and ordinarily have, and the price of seed is not advanced, there is an increase in the spread then, is there?
Answer. Providing you have got the products; but the mills don't speculate on their products; they have to sell from day to day as far as they can, and they could not hold all of their products waiting for an advance in the spring; they are not speculators except in cases where they pay more for seed than the products market justify; INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY and, consequently, mills never profit from this advance that takes place in the spring. They are absolutely unable to hold meal and oil and hulls and have them to sell on the market when the increases come about. They try to make a profit on the day-to-day sales. It is not speculative to the extent that you think.
Question. Well, isn't the meal and hulls largely disposed of, as you said, I think, a while ago, in the springtime.
Answer. No; I did not say that. I said the prices were higher.
Question. Well, didn't you say something about some of the product going to the farmersanswer. Advancing price.

Answer. Fertilizer season.
Question. Well, those products that are used in the spring are accumulated throughout the season, aren't they?
Answer. As I am telling you they can not accumulate much.
They have to sell on the market as they go along. They haven't got the storehouse for them.
Question. But the proper market is later?
Answer. I could not say that. I think the general policy of the mills is to sell their products as fast as they can dispose of them on the market.
Question. There are exceptions to that, of course?
Answer. Well, there may be exceptions in this way, that a mill may speculate by disposing of their crude oil and buying refined oil on the board in New York; and that is a common way of a mill holding its oil, because they haven't got tank room to run more than a month at those mills, and when those tanks get full they are obliged to dispose of the oil on hand in order to keep running.

Mr. Wooden, I want to read this and offer some exhibits here that will illustrate what I was talking about: Last night you read into the record a great many price reports received in my office by mail and not published in the newspapers. My recollection is that most of these prices received, but not published, as read by you were prices higher than those that were published. In this connection I wish to state that in my opinion there were probably as many lower prices received and not published as there were higher ones. The record as it now stands obviously looks bad without an explanation, and I was able to properly explain this matter last night. After careful consideration, however, and after checking back over my records, I find that the omissions are perfectly excusable when all angles to the situation are considered.
To begin with, the practice of receiving price reports by mail and publishing them in the newspapers began on or about January 15, 1930. Like all other new projects, we have had a great deal of trouble in trying to perfect this method, and, although it has already been in force practically 11 months, it is still not perfect. There is another fact that I wish to call to your attention, and that is, that daily reports do not propose to be all of the reports received in this office, but they are reports which were received in this office as of some particular date. For instance, in the Columbia State of December 5, 1930, you will notice by the caption, which is the same as has always been furnished the newspaper, that it reads as follows: ..
'Daily prices paid for cottonseed and received for products in South Carolina as reported to the South Carolina Division of the National Cottonseed Products Association, as of December 3, follows:" (Italics mine.) To The chief fault with the system has been the failure on the part of the mills to send in these reports to my office daily. As a consequence of this failure, many times we have received several reports in one day's mail, these reports at times covering purchases and sales for an entire week.
give a concrete illustration of instances which have happened many times, to-day we received four daily reports from the Clover Cotton Oil Gin Co.
covering their purchases and sales for Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday of this week. Now, the way this situation has been handled in the past is that we have given to the newspapers their report for Thursday and have gone back on our files and checked the reception of daily reports covering purchases and sales for Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday. Analyzing this situation carefully you will see that Thursday's report was the only one that would properly be published in the newspapers, whereas if several months from now some of your investigators came into my office and again checked my records, they might think that I had received the reports for Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday promptly and should have published them, whereas the lack of their publication is perfectly justifiable, as set out above. In conclusion, I wish to state positively that to the best of my knowledge neither Mr.
Lipscomb nor I ever intentionally withheld from the newspapers any market report that could have been properly published. I realize, of course, that the INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY • above system has not been perfect, and we are now trying to arrive at some method by which the mills can be persuaded to send their reports in daily, and if they do this, then there should be no further trouble along these lines.
I also want to submit in connection with the Clover report that he has reported there a price for wagon seed that is $1 less than the current price that I know he is paying or offering for wagon seed, that is, with the grade off. If you notice there that grade is off $1.
Question. How do you know the current wagon-seed prices?

Answer. He has told me there what that was, and I know that he has taken that discount and I know that he was buying on the zone grade. I know that from having visited his place and know that that is the practice. Take this other report, here is the report for to-day, transcript of the report of to-day, which will show the reports of the mills which we had received up to the time we sent the reports to the newspaper. We received in the mail this morning reports from Bennettsville dated the 3d. And the newspaper report thereof you will see Bennettsville purchases of car-load seed at 28 and 27. These reports were not published in the newspaper because I had no means of publishing them, not knowing what the report was yesterday. Now, on December 4, which is this last sheet I have handed you, Bennettsville only reports $23 wagon seed. Now, that is an explanation of the reason I had to say, "I don't know" when you asked me why I didn't publish a certain report in the newspaper.

Question. As a mill operator would you prefer to have the price-reporting system conducted on the basis of paid or bid prices?
Answer. I would prefer bid prices.
Question. Why?
Answer. Because as a mill operator I would prefer to know what my competitor is bidding rather than what he has paid.
Question. When you publish a paid price do you pay that price in all transactions until a new price is reported except the transaction necessary to permit the publication of the new price?
Answer. No.
Question. What are the exceptions?
Answer. When I publish a paid price I am under no obligations whatsoever to maintain this price any length of time. I might change my price either up or down in the next 30 minutes according to market conditions. And, consequently, my price would not be my published price.
Question. As soon as a purchase was made at a different price from your last published price would you report the new price to the division?
Answer. Yes.
Question. Do your mills buy seed in any State other than South Carolina?
Answer. We buy a very small tonnage in North Carolina.
Question. Has it come to your attention that at times the general current price for seed in North Carolina varies from the general current price in South Carolina?
Answer. I have known that to be the case.
Question. When such a difference exists, does the line of difference generally follow the State boundary line?
Answer. As a general proposition I would say it probably does.
Question. Do you think that the difference generally follows the State boundary because of the method of making and publishing prices by States?
Answer. I don't know. My opinion is that it may have some bearing on it, but at the same time I would not say that it is due to this as I feel like there are other factors that may enter into it.

From your experience with this average of the grade would you say that an average for an agricultural district would quite likely be above or below the actual condition of seed in counties and localities within the district?
Anwer. We think that that is probably true. INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Answer. Mr. Jordan told me that the Hartsville mill during the 1929-30 season suffered deductions for off-grade oil to the amount of $40,037.76, and received premiums for oil to the amount of $165.71.
Question. Did you have data supplied by Mr. Jordan from which you figured out the per ton rate of oil deduction?
Answer. Mr. Jordan told me that the tonnage crushed during that season by the Hartsville mill amounted to 18,440.2 tons. And from the figures I have just stated I arrived at the average deduction for off-grade oil amounting to $2.15 per ton of seed crushed.
Question. Did you obtain from Mr. Jordan any information or record data with reference to the amount or average deduction on seed, off-grade seed?
Answer. Mr. Jordan gave me a file of analysis reports covering analyses made both by his company chemist and by public chemists on seed purchased by the Hartsville mill during that season. And from those I took the discount shown on each of 859 analysis reports, totaled them, divided the total by the number of analyses and arrived at an average percentage deduction on seed of 9.45 per cent.
In that connection there were times when his company chemist analyzed the same lot of seed which was analyzed by a public chemist, and in some instances it was difficult to tell whether or not one analysis report was a duplicate analysis or not. But it may be that in the 859 analyses that I have referred to there may be two analyses of the same lot of seed in a number of instances. In such a large number, however, it appears most likely that any errors would more or less average themselves out. And in this same connection I requested Mr. Jordan to furnish me a statement showing the percentage of deductions on all seed which were analyzed after eliminating duplicate analyses, which might result from having the same shipment of seed analyzed by his mill chemist and subsequently analyzed by public chemist. And he finally agreed to do this; but up to the present time I haven't received or seen any such statement.
Mr. Jordan also estimated for me that the deductions on off grade on meal sold amounted to about a dollar a ton, which reduced to the terms of seed would be approximately 45 cents per ton of seed. In reference to any losses which his company may have suffered on linters coming from damaged seed, Mr. Jordan said that he didn't feel that he could make an estimate of that kind because it was almost entirely a matter of guesswork to say how much of the lower grade might be due to damaged seed; and he didn't give me any estimate of loss on linters.
Question. Did you state the amount per ton that those deductions figured out?
Answer. No; I did not. I should state that Mr. Jordan gave me the average price paid for seed by his mill as $30.07 per ton. Apply ing the average percentage of discount arrived at on seed to the average price paid for seed would indicate an average deduction on seed if all seed had been bought according to grade and the deductions indicated enforced by the mill of $2.84 per ton of seed. The deductions which the mill suffered on oil and the estimated deductions on meal total $2.60 per ton of seed. This does not include any loss on linters.
