The general puropse of the corporation, and the nature of the business it proposes to do: Is to gather statistics on cotton, cottonseed products, seeds, beans, foodstuffs, grains, food products, and supplies of any kind that can be used or sold by oil mills or other manufacturing enterprises, and to disseminate the information obtained; to investigate the production of any kind of crop or the use of any kind of machinery that might be of use to the stockholders and members of this corporation or to any other parties not members; to investigate and examine the processes which are applicable, or which might be applicable to the manufacture of any articles above mentioned, and to furnish to the members and stockholders of this corporation and to outside other parties the information so obtained as well as the condition of the market for raw material or manufactured products, and to purchase for the benefit of the stockholders of this corporation collectively or individually such raw materials as may be desired; to advertise the products of the factories of the stockholders of this corporation and to act as their representative in all matters of general interest to them; to impart to its members as stockholders or to the public whatsoever information of interest is desired and to have the right at any time to make such charges on behalf of this corporation, either to the stockholders or to the public for the information so desired; and to do and perform all the other necessary things and acts, necessary in the furtherance of said business.
EXHIBIT NO. 793 NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION (INC.).
SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION, Columbia, S. C., July 14, 1930.
GENTLEMEN: The executive committee of the South Carolina division met in Columbia, S. C., Friday, July 11, and elected the following officers to serve for the season 1930-31: F. E. Culvern, chairman; J. N. Lipscomb, vice chairman; B. F. Taylor, secretary; D. M. Lipscomb, assistant secretary.
The matter of budget for the coming season was discussed and detailed expense accounts for last season were presented and studied. It was decided that 6 cents per ton on seed crushed should be assessed for this division, with the understanding that if that amount should not prove sufficient another cent per ton could be assessed later. Three cents per ton on seed crushed was assessed for the national association.

EXHIBIT NO. 794 DECEMBER 12, 1929.
Mr. J. J. LAWTON, Hartsville, S. C.
DEAR MR. LAWTON: Before holding any district meetings which I think are highly desirable, I would like to have your approval of that step. Apparently these district meetings in Georgia and North Carolina are proving very beneficial. It would be my idea to have one district in the northern part of the State including mills at Spartanburg, Union, Gaffney, York, Kershaw, Rock Hill, Lancaster, Clover, and the Southern interests. This meeting might very well be held at Charlotte at the same time that the North Carolina meeting is held there so that the mills may be brought in contact with the mills operating out of Charlotte and in North Carolina near the South Carolina line.
The next district I would propose meeting at Anderson and would include Greenville, Honea Path, Ware Shoals, Pendleton, Greenwood, Ninety Six, representatives of the Augusta mills, Elberton, and the Southern Cotton Oil Co. interests.
The third district, I would have meet at Columbia and would include your mills, Newberry, Prosperity, Leesville, the Augusta mills, Savannah mills, Marion or the Steven's interests, and the Southern Cotton Oil Co.
I would like to have a meeting next week at Anderson, and would, therefore, be glad if you would drop me a line at once in regard to this.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.
EXHIBIT NO. 795 MEETING SOUTH CAROLINA COTTONSEED CRUSHERS ASSOCIATION, JEFFERSON HOTEL, 11 A. M., AUGUST 29, 1928 President Allen being unable to be present, Mr. Russell Acree acted as chairman, and called the meeting to order at 11 o'clock a. m. standard time, with about 40 members in attendance, including representatives of the Buckeye, Swift, International Vegetable Oil, and Planters Cotton Oil Co.
Mr. Acree stated the object of the meeting, at the same time stressing the importance of proper cooperation and maintaining among the membership a spirit of confidence in each other.
The first matter which Mr. Acree brought to the attention of the members was on an interpretation of section 9 of the Memphis resolutions, which reads as follows: 'Brokerage, if any, should be paid by the seller." In this same connection Mr. Acree brought to the attention of the meeting section 6 of the Memphis resolutions, which reads: "The payment or allowance to sellers of seed or buyers of the products thereof of commissions, bonuses, rebates, or subsidies of any kind, confidential prices or the use of any device which does not include in the price paid or bid the entire consideration, is hereby declared an unfair method of competition in the form of commercial bribery. This section also applies to contracts for the exchange of manufactured products for cottonseed and no evasions or subterfuges can be practiced or included under such guise." Mr. Acree then requested the meeting to discuss and pass on the question of who is to be excluded from becoming a commission buyer under the resolution above set out.

$5904 INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Mr. Acree then called attention to paragraph 3 of section 11, of the Memphis resolutions, which reads: "That the payment of such commission to other than bona fide seed buyers who render a service, and/or in such manner that any part of it goes to the seller directly or indirectly through the medium of partners, influential friends, kinspeople, or under any other guise whatsoever is hereby declared to be against public policy and an unfair method of competition." Considerable discussion was had on the question of employment of inde pendent ginners, and sellers of seed who own stock in gins, as 50-cent commission or salaried buyers. Mr. Lawton called attention to the fact that there were several influential men in the State who owned gins and farms of their own, and who have heretofore been allowed this 50 cents, and if this were discontinued, the oil-mill industry might be subjected to some adverse legislation during the coming session of the legislature, and he felt that some special arrangement should be made in regard to these agencies. Mr. Maguire was of the opinion that where a man owned a small amount of stock in a gin it should not interfere with his receiving a commission on purchases of seed. Mr. Fishburne called attention to the fact that the North Carolina association took the position that a man who owns any interest whatsoever in a gin is absolutely ruled out.
On the question of drayage and hauling Mr. Fishburne, of the Southern Cotton Oil Co., reaffirmed the position of that company previously stated by Mr.
Reynolds, that his company was unalterably opposed to payment for drayage or hauling in South Carolina, but could not go on record as stating that they would never engage in the practice. It was his personal opinion that the practice was fraught with danger. If his company ever felt that they were forced to go into the practice, due notice would be given to all concerned.
It was the sense of the meeting that in the exchange of products for seed there should be no discrimination.
The meeting then adjourned for lunch to reconvene at 3.30 p. m.
The meeting was again called to order by Mr. Acree, acting as chairman, at 3.30 p. m.
After a full discussion the following resolution was passed unanimously: "It is the sense of this meeting that in making new salaried contracts for wagon and gin seed buyers, that said contracts shall not be out of line with $3 per ton on wagon or gin seed and $1 per ton on retail meal and hulls. In figuring salaried contracts the carload business in meal and hulls that the buyer does should be figured on basis of 50 cents per ton for meal and 25 cents per ton for hull. Exchange prices shall be f. o. b. stations for cottonseed and delivered price for cottonseed meal." There being no further business, on motion the meeting adjourned.

EXHIBIT NO. 797 NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION, SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION, Columbia, S. C., September 23, 1929.
MINUTES OF MEETING OF EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE Pursuant to the resolution passed at the general meeting held here on September 4 that the executive committee meet, subject to the call of the secretary, immediately after the meeting of the North Carolina division," the committee met at the Jefferson Hotel, Columbia, S. C. on September 16 and 17.
Upon the committee being called to order by its chairman, Mr. J. J. Lawton, it developed that all were present except Mr. J. O. Wilson, who was represented by his alternate, Mr. F. H. Jarrell, and Mr. J. B. Caldwell, who was represented by his brother, Mr. R. M. Caldwell.
The resolution passed at the general meeting on September 4, "That this meeting go on record as approving in principle the grading of cottonseed, and that the matter be referred to the executive committee for the working out of details was put before the committee for action.
"" After a full and detailed discussion of the matter of grading cottonseed, and upon motion duly seconded and passed, a committee, composed of Messrs.
Jarrell, Culvern, and Fishburne with Mr. Acree as its secretary, was appointed and given full authority to take final action on the matter. (The report of this special committee is inclosed herewith.) Assistant to secretary.-Upon motion duly made, seconded, and passed, the secretary was instructed to secure an assistant.
Statistical reports.-Upon motion duly made, seconded, and passed, the secretary was instructed to discontinue the usual weekly report on seed received and cotton ginned.
Secretary's salary.-Upon motion duly seconded and unanimously passed the secretary's (Mr. Acree) salary was made $7,000, effective September 1.
Future meetings of executive committee.-Upon motion duly seconded and passed, it was decided that until further notice the executive committee meet every other Tuesday at 11 a. m. at the Jefferson Hotel, Columbia, S. C.
Meal exchanges.-Upon motion duly seconded and passed, it was resolved that it was the sense of the committee that all exchanges of products for cottonseed should be expressed in pounds; that such exchange price should be made public and that they should bear a definite relation to the published f. o. b. cash prices for cottonseed and the published delivered cash prices for products.
There being no other business put before the meeting, the committee thereupon adjourned to meet again at 11 a. m., Tuesday, October 1, 1929.

.5906 INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY EXHIBIT NO. 798 Meeting of the executive committee Tuesday, January 28, 1930.
Present: Messrs, Lawton, Jordan, Culvern, Caldwell, Fishburne, Monsalvatge, Maguire, Taylor, and Lipscomb.
Mr. Dinkins reported to the committee the status of the house resolution calling for an investigation of the cottonseed-oil business in South Carolina.
The matter was referred to Mr. Benet with power to take such action as seemed best to him in the matter.
A letter was read from Mr. Benet, giving the status of the various investigations and matters pending before the Federal Farm Board and the Department of Agriculture.
It was decided that the present method of reporting prices paid should be continued and it was not necessary to send out daily circulars to the mills.
The executive committee expressed itself as considering it unethical for a mill to issue a quotation either raising or lowering the price on an article and then continuing to buy at the old price. It is not considered fair to the sellers and such practice would mean having two prices.
The question of seed grading was brought up and apparently the conditions in the State were fairly good. Nearly all mills are cooperating in the grading of seed.
It developed in the discussion that several of the members who have chemists connected with their companies had compared analyses by Mr. Rice's with their own and found that Mr. Rice apparently was consistently low in his report of free-fatty acids and the secretary was instructed to see Mr. Rice with reference to this and find out whether or not he was including all of the analyses in the averages of the different districts.
There being no further business the meeting adjourned.
Maguire, Albert Jordan, J. N. Lipscomb, H. E. Neal, Fred E. Culvern of the executive committee, and Doctor Hunter, Mr. Christie Benet, Mr. Wicker, Mr.
Dinkins, Mr. Jones, Mr. Lipscomb, assistant secretary, and Mr. Taylor, the secretary.
The question of holding district meetings was brought up and it was decided to arrange for such meetings at as early date as possible.
The secretary was instructed to communicate with Mr. Christie Benet with reference to the payment of dues to this division by mills located out of the State on such seed as they might garner in the State.
The question of prices paid at mill towns and gin points where they might vary from the general price paid by an operator was discussed and it was the opinion of the executive committee that all prices paid, of whatever nature, should be reported to the secretary and the information distributed by him to those interested. It was also decided that more frequent reports of prices paid should be sent in to the secretary by every mill whether there be any change in prices paid or not.
The question of statistical reports and checking up the various mills on their carload and wagon-seed purchases was discussed and it was decided that there was no useful purpose in compiling seed receipts at this time and it was not deemed advisable to pass any opinion on the matter of checking up the books of members. But where information was desired, the member might be asked for it and if he saw fit to give the information, proper use should be made of same.
The question of taking gin seed as received and making a settlement at some later date beyond 15 days from date of receipt at the gin was discussed and it was decided that such practice would be the same as storing seed under the South Carolina division rules.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY The request of the Community Chest, of Columbia, for contributions was read and it was decided that since the members of this association contributed in their respective towns to the charitable institutions located there, that it was not deemed proper that the money of this association should be appropriated for the use and benefit of the Community Chest in Columbia.
It was ordered that all checks issued by the secretary's office should be signed by the assistant secretary and the secretary; two signatures being required.
The secretary was further ordered to communicate this authority to the bank with which we do business. It was resolved that both the secretary and the assistant secretary should be put under $5,000 bonds, the premiums to be paid by this division.
The sale of the automobile to Mr. H. E. Sessions for $605 was authorized.
It was ordered that the secretary transmit to Mrs. Acree $750 immediately and advise her that a like amount would be paid as soon as the funds were available.
Mr. D. M. Lipscomb was elected assistant secretary of the division for the fiscal year ending August 1, at a salary of $200 per month. Mr. Lipscomb advised that he would give an answer as to his acceptance of the position in a day or two.
The question of 50-cent commission buyers was brought up and lists submitted. It was decided to refer this list to a committee of five, with request that they make report at the next meeting of the executive committee. The chairman appointed on this committee, Messrs. Monsalvatge, Fishburne, Culvern, Jordan, and Allen of Greenwood. The names of all new commission buyers not already on the list are to be submitted to the committee to determine their eligibility under the Memphis resolutions.
The file of letters which the Federal Trade Commission examiners copied was submitted and read by some of the members of the executive committee.
Mr. Benet addressed the meeting on a number of subjects of interest, particularly with reference to the investigation now in progress, and read several letters which he had written with the view of dissipating the erroneous impressions that the public seemed to have in regard to the oil-mill business.
There being no further business, the meeting adjourned.
EXHIBIT NO. 800 The meeting of the South Carolina division of the National Cottonseed Products Association was called to order at 10 a. m., June 6, Mr. J. J. Lawton, chairman, presiding.
A list of members present was taken and is attached hereto. The secretary read his report.
The new seed-grading rules were discussed, and Mr. Rice illustrated the method of allowing premiums and making discounts.
A committee consisting of Mr. C. C. Fishburne, Mr. Mikell, Mr. Jarrell, Mr.
Culvern, Mr. Jordan and Mr. Rice, was appointed to adopt a form of reporting deduction for foreign matter and allowances and the premiums, from chemist's report. The same committee was requested to handle the matter of appointment of independent, unbiased samplers of cottonseed.
The trading rules governing the buying and selling of cottonseed in South Carolina were read paragraph by paragraph. The latter part of rule No. 4.
was referred to the executive committee for such change as might become necessary. Rule 5 was amended by inserting after "of" and before cottonseed the word "basis". Rule 8 was amended to read as follows: "All seed shall be bought on the basis of sound, dry, and unadulterated seed, the grading rules of the National Cottonseed Products Association to form the basis of grading. Boards and grain doors are to be considered a part of the tare weight of the car." Rule 9 was referred to the executive committee for such changes as they might find it necessary to make. All of the other rules were adopted without dissent.
The matter of publication of prices paid was discussed, and it was decided that where mills fail to make daily reports of prices paid, the secretary could send collect telegrams to them asking for the necessary reports, and that such telegrams would be paid by the mills.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY The present method of reporting prices was considered satisfactory, with the exception that the secretary was requested to have the daily prices published in other papers in South Carolina.
The auditing committee consisting of Mr. Mikell and Mr. Craig reported that the books of the division were found correct and in order. Total receipts for the year from all sources were stated as $16,652.59, with expenditures of $14,314.45.

EXHIBIT NO. 801 SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION NATIONAL COTTON SEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATIONREPORT OF THE SECRETARY From the end of the crushing season of 1929 until late in August the conditions seemed so bad that it was not thought worth while to have a meeting of the association. But on September 4 a meeting of the mills operating in South Carolina was held and Mr. Christie Benet addressed them on the Mem phis resolutions and the grading of seed. It was decided to form a division of the National Association and to adopt the rules which had been approved by the Federal Trade Commission the previous October. Mr. J. J. Lawton as elected chairman and Mr. Russel Acree secretary of the division.
Mr. Acree immediately employed Mr. D. M. Lipscomb to assist him in getting the mills to subscribe to the rules and adopt the grading system for cottonseed. Also to become members of the national association. On October 11 another meeting was held and plans laid for the season. Unfortunately Mr. Acree died suddenly on the night of October 15. The duties of the sec retary were committed to Mr. Lipscomb and acceptably discharged, but it was found that two men were necessary to conduct the affairs of the division and on December 3 Mr. Taylor was elected secretary and Mr. Lipscomb assistant secretary.
The grading of cottonseed went into effect on October 15 and apparently occasioned no particular shock to the producers up to the 1st of December though the analyses of seed from districts 5, 6, and 7 showed from 10 to 20 per cent discount for offgrade. The independent buyers were complaining INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY D and doing everything possible to break down the grading system and in some instances effectually brought about conditions that nullified the rules so far as wagon seed was concerned. A few of the mills were induced for one reason or another to forget their obligations to grade in the case of carload shipments.
The publication of prices paid up to February 1 was by telegrams to the members of the division and other mills and individuals interested. After that date the prices were published in the two daily newspapers in Columbia.
According to advice from General Council Benet, the mills were required to report daily prices paid for seed and received for products. It has seemed difficult to get 100 per cent reporting, but while the mills were running the office could count on a substantial majority of mills reporting. It is desirable and probably imperative that all mills report daily.
We are giving reports of prices paid to the newspapers for the benefit of the public. In some States the telegraphic and circular letter service is supplied to any person desiring it for a small fee estimated to cover the cost.
It has been suggested that this division do this. It also occurs to us that it might be a good idea to supply the reports of the chemist showing the discounts applicable to wagon seed in each district.
Under Group I rules it is imperative that prices paid be published. Only three mills located in the State and members of the division have failed to publish promptly changes in prices paid for cottonseed and in each case the underlying reason seemed to be a desire to avoid a strict compliance with the grading rules and thereby reap some advantage over competitors. There is only one mill in the State that is not a member of the division, and that mill has not apparently attempted to grade seed.
The grading of cottonseed is covered under Group II rules. Seven mills have been found remiss in the matter of grading on occasions, but three of these cases were in a way unintentional. One mill came into line promptly when reported, two were guilty in only two or three cases, and the fourth persistent in any case involving a round lot of seed that was not very much off in grade. Judging by the attitude of those persons when faced with the charges they were ashamed of what they had done and I feel sure will be better observers of the rules another season.
The matter of buying seed at stations without grading or on analyses of samples taken at shipping point was indulged in by only two mills in the State who are members of the division, but three mills located in other States have on occasions bought seed in that way.
We have visited every operating mill in the division, except Darlington, Bennettsville, and Marion, one or more times during the season, and we have had several group meetings. In most cases we have had the books opened to us to check up on the grading of seed and have been given voluntarily valuable information as to yields and local conditions. We have had a number of charges of violations of grading rules filed with the office which upon investigation proved to be unfounded. We are advised by Mr. Dinkins, Mr. Benet's assistant, that complaints of this nature should be made in writing and kept in the files with a report of the investigation. We have not done this heretofore.
The field agents of the Federal Trade Commission visited this office and got a number of reports and letters but so far as we could judge these had reference mostly to prices. Inasmuch as your present secretary had only been employed by the division a short time before, the agents did not bother to ask him any questions. Our own examination of the files indicates that there was nothing questionable in the operation of the office by my predecessor.
As you know the House of Representatives instructed the Attorney General to investigate alleged unlawful practices of the oil mills in this State and to take such steps as he deemed necessary to put a stop to them and to prosecute any of them found to be committing unlawful acts. Mr. Benet, Mr.
Lawton, and your secretary called on the Attorney General and offered to supply him with any available information. We have not so far been called on for anything. Harmon of Mississippi, prepared a preliminary survey of the seedcrushing business of that State covering four years, which he intended to submit to the attorney general and legislature. It would be timely to prepare a similar survey for this State, separating from the statement the other lines of business which some of the mills have. I have asked the mills to advise me if they are willing to give this office such statements with the understanding that individual statements shall be held as confidential. Figures obtained from the tax commission do not reflect the true conditions because the results of ginning, fertilizer mixing, cotton milling, flour milling, ice manufacture, etc., are included in the reports.

EXHIBIT NO. 803 JANUARY 19, 1928.
AIREY STOUSE, New Orleans, La.
We hesitate, however, to officially advertise the New Orleans exchange, or, in other words, we do not see how we could indorse it without indorsing, at the same time, all other exchanges which have the same purpose.
We inclose herewith a list of the active oil mills in South Carolina this season and wonder if your purposes will not be accomplished by your mailing direct to them any facts about the advantages your exchange has to offer.
Personally, we believe that there are only a very few of the mills in this State which trade in the future market, but those who we think do are fully acquainted with the services you are prepared to render, therefore, we do not think anything we might say about the New Orleans exchange would change the situation in the least, while our officially undertaking to do something of the kind would violate our general principle that this office does not advertise the business of any of its regular or associate members.

Interpretation committee Report No. 2.
Question: Can a mill make a regular $3 per ton commission trade with a gin in one location and then make an additional trade in the same town or community with the owner, principal stockholder, or anyone else financia fly interested in the same gin, or interested through the medium of kinspeople, to buy seed for the mill on a salary even though separate seed house and scales are used?
Answer: No.
The interpretation committee then unanimously passed the following reso- lution: Resolved, That it is the sense of this committee that all trades or contracts in conflict with above interpretation should be changed immediately so that they will be on a salary basis only or on a commission, which salary or commission - must be in accord with resolution No. 11 of the Memphis resolutions.

EXHIBIT NO. 807 TRADING RULES GOVERNING THE BUYING AND SELLING OF COTTONSEED IN BOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION SEASON 1930-31 Rule 1. There are two classes of seed shippers, known respectively as class 1 and class 2.
Rule 2. Class 1 is a shipper who buys and ships cottonseed on his own account, furnishing the necessary capital and facilities.
Rule 3. Class 2 is a shipper who buys, under a written contract, requiring daily reports, and ships cottonseed to a mill for a fixed compensation, and who is furnished by the mill with the necessary funds, houses, and scales with which to carry on business, and who buys and sells under the direction of the mill.
Rule. 4. Compensation to be paid a class 2 shipper is a commission of $2 per ton of seed shipped, plus actual loading charges, said cost of loading not to exceed 50 cents per ton of seed and to be allowed only when seed are loaded from buyer's seed house at station, and in the event of loss in weight and allowance not exceeding 1 per cent of weight of seed as weighed into mill. Or in lieu thereof a total commission of $3 per ton, which shall include all cost of loading, hauling, allowance for loss in weight and all other expenses, or at a salary in keeping with the Memphis resolutions. Salaried buyers are to be allowed not exceeding 50 cents per ton loading charge, and then only when seed are loaded from buyer's seed house at station, nor more than 1 per cent loss in weight, if any. Nobody shall be paid a salary or commission unless there is a real and tangible service rendered therefor.
Rule 5. F. o. b. car seed is defined as being 10 tons or more. All cottonseed sold in less than 10-ton lots shall be paid for at $3 per ton less than the f. o. b. car price. Settlement for f. o. b. car seed shall be made on actual mill weights ascertained over the scales at the mill. In order for wagon seed to be paid for at the carload price a delivery of 10 tons or more must be made within a period of 15 days. All cottonseed bought in carload lots are to be loaded by the seller, shipped in the seller's name and remittance made direct to the seller by the mill on the basis of mill weights at destination.
Rule 6. In case a shipper of class 2 furnishes houses and scales, compensa tion for same shall be for houses not more per annum than 6 cents per square foot of floor space used, and for scales not more than $10 for each set of scales. This rule will also apply in case a mill rents houses and scales to shippers.
Rule 7. The commission for buying seed in car lots is 50 cents per ton of seed. Cottonseed bought in carload lots through such buyers are to be loaded by the seller, shipped in the seller's name and remittance made direct to the seller by the mill on basis of mill weights at destination, and in no case shall the commission be paid to the owner of the seed.
Rule 8. All seed shall be bought on the basis of sound, dry, and unadulterated seed. Grading rules of the National Cottonseed Products' Association to form basis of grading and deductions made in accordance therewith. Foriegn mat ter shall be ascertained by either separating the trash and sand from the seed.
or ascertaining the percentage from a fair average sample to be used as the basis of settlement. Boards and grain doors are to be considered a part of the tare weight of the car.
Rule 9. Loans and/or advances shall not be made to so-called f. o. b. contract shippers wherein it is agreed by the mill to furnish cash for the purchase of seed in consideration of the preference on such seed; nor shall any advances be made to f. o. b. shippers unless a definite contract of purchase is made covering the sale of enough seed then on hand to cover the advance. Mills may pay 75 per cent against B/L for seed, and all sales of merchandise to shippers should be on same terms as to other merchandise customers.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY C Rule 10. No mill shall engage in the storing of seed for customers at any point.
Rule 11. Seed shall not be bought at a stated price and later settled for at a higher price.
Rule 12. Options for future purchase or sale of seed for future delivery shall neither be taken nor given.
Rule 13. Seed shall not be purchased from any seller unless the seller has the seed on hand at the time of sale and for shipment within 15 days.
Rule 14. Contracts for the purchase of cottonseed, whether written or oral, shall be for a definite tonnage and time of shipment-a variation of 10 per cent permissible and any excess or shortage beyond 10 per cent shall be settled for at the market on date of shipment.
EXHIBIT NO. 808 NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION, SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION.
Columbia, S. C., September 25, 1929.
GENTLEMEN: Rule 11 (formerly resolution 9) and rule 12 (formerly resolution 11) of the code read as follows: Rule 11. Brokerage, if any, should be paid by the seller.
"Rule 12. Whereas excessive commissions have been paid to seed agents for the purchase of seed, which has resulted in such commissions being paid directly or indirectly to sellers of seed, the effect being the publication of fictitious prices for seed and the inability of the public to know at all times the actual market for cottonseed: Therefore be it "Resolved, That where the practice of buying seed through commission agents is in existence, the payment of any amount in excess of $3 per ton on wagon seed and gin seed, such payment to include storage, handling, loading, loss in weight, and all other charges of every kind, and the payment of any commission in excess of 50 cents per ton for buying carload seed, is against public policy and hereby declared to be an unfair method of competition.
"Resolved further, That the payment of such commission to other than bona fide seed buyers who render a service, and/or in such manner that any part of it goes to the seller directly or indirectly through the medium of partners, influential friends, kinspeople, or under any other guise whatsoever, is hereby declared to be against public policy and an unfair method of competition.
Yours very truly, Mr. W. H. HASTY, RUSSELL ACREE, Secretary.
EXHIBIT NO. 809 SEPTEMBER 30, 1929.
Manager Maxton Oil Fertilizer Co., Maxton, N. C.
Rule 11 (formerly resolution 9) reads "brokerage, if any, should be paid by the seller." The trade in discussing the interpretation of this resolution seemed to be of the opinion that a cottonseed broker is one who offers seed to any and all mills in an effort to get the very best price possible. There can be no critiinvestigation OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY cism of him for doing this but at the same time when he does it he is serving the seller, therefore the seller should pay him. From this conception of what a broker is, we arrive at the conclusion that if one is to be paid the 50-cent commission he must work for one mill exclusively.
Yours very truly, RUSSELL ACREE, Secretary.
MAXTON OIL FERTILIZER CO., Maxton, N. C., September 27, 1929.

JANUARY 17, 1930.

MAXTON OIL FERTILIZER CO., Maxton, N. C.
You will note in the rules adopted under the Memphis resolutions that the practice of buying seed through commission agents limits the amount of com mission to be paid to $3 on wagon and gin seed and the payment of 50 cents per ton for buying carload seed. In the latter case, the intent is that the seed bought in carload lots should be shipped in the name of the person from whom the seed are bought and not in the name of the commission buyer and where such seed are bought in that way the commission buyer would be entitled to get 50 cents for his services.
In the matter of Mr. Kirkwood at Bennettsville, it seems to us that it would depend entirely upon how he handled the purchases of seed. If he ships in his own name, he would be entitled to only $3 over the wagon-seed price as a commission buyer but if the cars are shipped direct to the mill by the owner, he would be entitled to 50 cents, therefore, the question of cancellation of your contract with Mr. Kirkwood would depend entirely upon his method of handling the carload purchases.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.

NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION (INC.), SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION, Columbia, S. C., July 14, 1930.
GENTLEMEN Rule 12 of trade-practice rules recites "That when the practice of buying seed through commission agents is in existence, the payment of any amount in excess of $3 per ton on wagon and gin seed, such payment to include storage, handling, loading, loss in weight, and all other charges of every kind, and the payment of any commission in excess of 50 cents per ton for buying carload seed is against public policy and hereby declared to be an unfair method of competition." "That the payment of such commission to other than bona fide seed buyers who render a service, and/or in such manner that any part of it goes to the seller directly or indirectly through the medium of partners, influential friends, kinspeople, or under any other guise whatsoever, is hereby declared to be against public policy and an unfair method of competition." "That the names of such 50-cent buyers be made available to the public." You are therefore requested to file with this office immediately a list of all 50-cent commission buyers with whom you have contracts and as contracts are made in the future you will give names and addresses of new buyers by letter.
The payment of 50 cents commission by a mill in such case should be reported in the price paid for seed.
It is well understood that you can pay any price for seed you please, but it must be reported promptly.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.
EXHIBIT NO. 813 NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION (INC.), Mr. J. N. LIPSCOMB, Victor Cotton Oil Co., Gaffney, S. C.
SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION, Columbia, S. C., February 13, 1930..
DEAR JUNE: I got Lipscomb to telephone you yesterday following our conversation of the day before about the purchase of seed at Grover. He tells me that you expressed yourself as being of the opinion that nobody was interested in the transaction. After I talked with you, I found that the rules adopted for the South Carolina division precluded any hauling of seed regardless of whether the mill owned trucks or not. Furthermore, that several of the mills, particularly, Ninety Six and Pendleton who both own trucks, had cut out hauling of any seed except from gins owned by the respective oil mills. In the case of Ninety-six, they lost some 300 tons of seed by reason of this abandonment of hauling.
You will remember last year that the Kershaw Oil Mill particularly, who owns no trucks, would raise the price of car seed at any point where hauling was engaged in so that they might be on what they thought was the same basis as their competitors. The result was a very disturbed and unsatisfactory seed market.
The hauling charge is in existence in North Carolina and what you did is in line with the North Carolina custom but entirely contrary to the rules for South Carolina. It is not a question of what you have a right to do or what you might think no one had any interest in but a question of policy to be pursued in order to keep your business and that of your competitors on a profitable basis and I would like to urge upon you the importance of observing the rules even in small cases. This transaction may not have involved more than a few cars of seed on which you would save by hauling something like $1.50 per ton. It might cost you several dollars a ton on several hundred tons of seed if it resulted in the abandonment of our rules.
I wanted you to call Mr. Pursley yourself and explain the matter to him and if possible and in line with the facts in the case, to tell him that it was a mistake on your part in view of the fact that the seed were located in North Carolina. Of course, Mr. Pursley, himself, may have done things that were not in line but we shall have to bear with a few irregularities on the part of every one if we expect to maintain a reasonable condition. The only way to do this is to call attention to those offending and endeavor to prevent a reoccurrence.
I wish to assure you that I am just as assiduous in calling such matters to the attention of your competitors as I am in this case. There is nothing personal about it. It is a plain matter for businesslike consideration and I am sure that you will take this letter in that spirit.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.

AUGUST 2, 1928.
Mr. C. M. ALLEN, Swift Co. Oil Mill, Macon, Ga.
I am reasonably well informed that the Buckeye takes about the following position: First, that they have lost considerable tonnage because others have been allowing it and they have not. Second, that they know nothing about itwhether it can be done economically or in what manner it best be done, if done at all. Therefore, they expect to conduct experiments in an effort to find out how they can best accommodate themselves to it, situated as they are, if it is to become a generally established practice in the trade. I further understand that they will not conduct such experiments in those States where it is not already being practiced. The Southern will not say that hauling is wrong in principle, but I am led to believe that they will not put it in where it does not already exist. We are, therefore, directing our efforts to try to keep the paying of hauling out of this State, and I am very hopeful that we will succeed for the present, no matter what the future may bring. Personally I am convinced that if and when use is made of a hauling charge to "turn seed," whatever efforts are made to control it, that it will mean a fight. I do not venture to predict the result of such a fight, but I hope the battle ground will not be in South Carolina.
The code says nothing about loans. Those present at Memphis were about equally divided on whether the code should contain a clause on it, but it was finally decided to accede to the judgment of those who thought best not to advertise to the world that the industry would lend money. We still hope in South Carolina to keep away from advancing money for the refusal of seed or to use such advances to get agents to sign a $3 commission contract by reason of such advances. Naturally I can not speak authoritatively on the conditons regarding loans and/or advances in Georgia. I suggest that you ask Mr. Hutchinson or Mr. Murphy for the information.
Resolution No. 9, dealing with the brokerage question, contemplates a distinction between a broker and a commission agent. The resolution is supposed to define a broker as one who gets in hand one car or many cars of seed and offers them for the high dollar, which means he is trying to get the highest price he can for the benefit of the seller, and therefore, the seller should pay him.
A mill's commission agent, on the other hand, is supposed to be working for his mill exclusively, trying to buy seed at his mill's prices, getting out of the INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY market when his mill takes him out, etc. Therefore, such an agent is working for his mill exclusively and should be paid by te mill. The idea is to get rid of the public broker, as you and I have understood him. Since the Buckeye would not give up their 50-cent men, who they say buy for them exclusively and who they say render a service, the balance of the industry has tried to reach the compromise as above outlined and thereby accept the Buckeye's view.
You understand the exclusive feature will not prevent a broker from offering seed to whom he pleases or to as many mills as he pleases, but he will have to get his pay from the seller, as the mill under the foregoing interpretation of Resolution No. 9 can not pay him a commission or brokerage unless he works for that mill exclusively. I repeat, it is supposed to do away with a mill's paying a brokerage or commission to what you and I have heretofore called a public broker, and forces him to get it from the one he has been serving, namely, the seller.
I have called a meeting of our crowd for the night of August 7, at which time we will undertake to come to some mutual understanding of what the resolutions mean as written and how we can reconcile any customs we have not expressly covered in the resolutions to the spirit of the resolutions. Some of these are hauling, rent for seed houses, and scales, salaries, loans and/or advances, and this exclusive 50-cent car buyer.
Will be glad to have you come to that meeting In the mean time, I presume to say that a strict compliance by all or by a substantial majority would certainly help the situation in your new field, if the conditions there have been anything like I have been told they were.
With personal regards, I remain, Yours very truly, RA: P.
Mr. F. M. HUNT, AUGUST 18, 1928.
Little Rock, Ark.
Secretary Arkansas Cotton Seed Crushers' Association, DEAR Mr. HUNT: This is to acknowledge receipt of your wire of to-day to which we replied as per copy inclosed.
I also inclose copy of the resolutions adopted at a meeting we held on August 7, as I do not find that I have sent it to you heretofore.
This question of hauling has so many angles I can not cover it in a letter.
I merely briefly state that if it is practiced it certainly should be regulated along the lines of the amount per mile to be paid and the places from and to which it should be allowed. Personally, I feel that paying hauling will mean an additional tax on the industry unless, of course, it can be passed on to the seed seller or to the products buyer. By this I mean that a good many seed are sold to small mills at this time on which they have been paying no freight.
I believe that if hauling is generally adopted and practiced that it will have to be paid on such seed. I believe that the terminal mill which is too far away to have seed hauled to it will have to have them hauled to some designated receiving point and then pay the freight.
The feature that concerns me most, however, is that certain strong interests in our State have insisted up to this present writing that they will not have a fleet of trucks of their own to do the hauling nor will they hire other trucks to do it, but that they will offer a cash consideration in lieu of hauling. There are other strong interests on the other side who say that they intend to haul with their own trucks and hire others also. This means a conflict which is certain to result in a raise of price for seed and a consequent narrowing of the spread.
Confidentially, it looks to me at the moment as if the question of hauling is the most serious that has confronted us since I have been in the industry.
I believe that if certain large interests go into hauling that it means that they will put receiving depots at every small mill town, the effect of which will be the same as if another mill were built in that town except they will not crush the seed there. This means a division of the local tonnage on both seed and products. In my humble judgment, therefore, a small local mill which 121200 S. Doc. 209, 71-2, pt 668 INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY thinks that a hauling charge is giving it a competitive advantage is going to find that it will be a boomerang and that it will lose far more than it gains.
I may be an old reactionary who is unwilling to keep up with the new economic developments in transportation brought about by good roads and trucks, but I am firmly convinced that the best thing to do with this hauling of cottonseed is to cut it out absolutely. I think it is loaded with both dynamite and TNT, not because of the economic question of whether it is cheaper to haul by truck or by rail but because of the competitive features it introduces in the buying of seed.
If there is any particular phase of it on which you would like to have my opinion I shall be delighted to give it to you for what it may be worth.
Yours very truly, RA: rm.

SOUTH CAROLINA COTTON SEED CRUSHERS' ASSOCIATION, Columbia, S. C., October 1, 1928.
GENTLEMEN: A general meeting of the South Carolina Cotton Seed Crushers' Association and others of the industry is hereby called for 8 p. m., October 3 (Wednesday night), Jefferson Hotel, Columbia, S. C.
The principal object of the meeting is to discuss the quality of the seed now being offered which grows out of the unprecedented amount of rainfall in this State since September 1.
It has been suggested that the seed should be sampled by a disinterested party, analyzed by responsible public chemist, and settlement be made on the basis of such chemist's grading in accordance with the rules of the Interstate Cotton Seed Crushers' Association.
We deem it highly important and necessary that some equitable and feasible plan be worked out to properly protect both the mills and the sellers of seed and urge your attendance at the meeting hereby called for that purpose.
We will be glad to make your hotel reservations, but suggest it will be better for you to make them direct.

EXHIBIT NO. 816 JULY 18, 1930.
Mr. CHRISTIE BENET, General Counsel, Columbia, S. C.
DEAR SIR: It was reported to me that the Greer Oil Mill Feed Co. of Greer, S. C. were violating rule 3 of Group I by giving bonuses to their commission buyers. I called on the manager, Mr. Kendrick, and president, Mr. Hughes.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY I in reference to the matter and found that bonuses had been paid for the last three seasons of 33, 30, 35 cents per ton at the end of each respective season.
Also that bonuses had been paid to all laborers and salaried men connected with the mill. The contracts made with the commission buyers do not provide for a bonus and the payment of same was entirely optional with the mill and is so understood by the commission buyers. I had a long talk with a Mr.
De Young, one of these buyers, who confirmed what the officers told me.
Mr. Hughes is a banker and has some very decided ideas about cooperation in business. He tells me he hopes eventually to do away with all commission buyers and pay each farmer a bonus on seed sold to the mill at the end of the season provided the operations showed a profit. He does not consider that he is violating rule 3, because he makes no agreement in advance of payment and the payments are optional with him and are not fixed in amount. He takes the stand that his commission buyers are as much employees of the mill as any other workmen, the only difference being the difference in the way they are compensated.
I have told Mr. Hughes that I would get your opinion on the matter. He has assured me that he would not pay a bonus at the end of next season until he had taken the matter up with the executive committee of this division.
Now, the other side of the picture is that the payment of the bonus makes it impossible for any other mill to get any of his men to buy for it. Actually it has taken a buyer from one mill who had no complaint of relations with it, and results in dissatisfaction of other buyers when they hear about it. If the system is continued, it will certainly mean that the $3 commission will certainly be raised by competitors.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.

INTERPRETATION COMMITTEE REPORT NO. 1 Question. Can a car seed buyer be employed in any other manner except for a compensation of 50 cents per ton, it being understood that such car buyer does not mean a regular traveling seed buyer employed exclusively by one company or mill on a salary?
Answer. A car seed buyer can only be employed for a compensation of 50 cents per ton commission for all car seed bought by him and received by the company or mill. The payment of compensation to a car buyer in any other manner or in any other way, is in the opinion of this committee, prohibited under the Memphis resolutions.

NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION, SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION, Columbia, S. C., February 26, 1930.
GENTLEMEN: Your attention is directed to the second paragraph of our circular letter dated February 11, 1930. We wish to advise that the figures mentioned in illustrating the matter of spread in buying cottonseed were entirely arbitrary, since it would be very unlikely that any two mills would have the same working cost, freight, cost of seed, or yields of products, hence the spread will vary with each mill. What we intended to convey was the unfairness to the producer of changing your basis toward the end of the season unless forced by competition to do so.
Mr. Benet's name was mentioned in connection with the statement because he has so often impressed upon us the moral obligation of giving the producer a fair deal. As you all know, no attempt has ever been made by Mr. Benet or any one else to fix a definite spread and such matters have always been left to the individual judgment of each mill operator.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.

EXHIBIT NO. 823 [From The State, February 26, 1930] TAYLOR PRESENTS FIGURES ON SEED-SECRETARY CRUSHERS' ASSOCIATION GIVES DATA TO HOUSE GROUP-MAKES STATEMENT IN CONNECTION WITH PROPOSED PRICE INVESTIGATION A statement compiled from the State tax commission records showing that the oil mills of South Carolina lost a total of $254,029.51 during the season of 1928-29 has been presented to the Committee on Agriculture of the House of Representatives by B. F. Taylor, secretary of the South Carolina Cottonseed Crushers' Association. These figures were submitted in connection with the consideration of a resolution in the House providing for the investigation by the attorney general of the State into the price of cottonseed.
The figures secured from the State tax commission's records showed that of the 27 oil mills which operated in the State during the season of 1928-29, 13 of them lost a total of $414,689.28, while 14 showed a total profit of $160,- 659.77, making the net loss for the industry in the State $254,029.51.
Concerning the 1929-30 season, Mr. Taylor said that on a crop of 845,000 bales of cotton, and on the same basis of marketing as last year, there should be available for crushing 240,000 tons of seed. Between August 1 and January 31 the mills received 150,463 tons, which left approximately 89,500 tons of seed yet to be marketed. He estimated that 15,000 tons of these seed were held by farmers and 74,500 by buyers and speculators.
OIL PER TON Analyses taken daily and weekly at eight points in the State representing the different sections show that the seed per ton this year have averaged 18.97 per cent of oil, Mr. Taylor said. There are 30 pounds of trash and sand to the ton. Deducting the 30 pounds of trash from 2,000 pounds of seed leaves 1,970 pounds, and 19 per cent of that gives 374 pounds of oil. The mills, he said, expect to produce this year 950 pounds of meal per ton, which will show 7 per cent of oil remaining in it, which would amount to 66 pounds which must INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY be deducted from the total amount of oil in the seed. This, he said, therefore leaves as a prospective yield 308 pounds of oil from each ton of seed.
Mr. Taylor presented figures for the 1929-30 season showing that the average profit from a ton of seed for the crushers was $2.40 and also that the yield and working costs set forth in the house resolutions were entirely erroneous.
Mr. Taylor expressed the belief that a large majority of the complaints concerning the present price of seed are coming from speculators, who from the beginning of the season accumulated seed which would not keep, with the result that the necessary deductions for off-grade at this time amount to from $5 to $10 a ton., "CHAS. It has been customary with some of the mills to send out quotations on the basis of grading, for instance, in the recent published price of $28 instructions have been sent to the commission buyers in one of our districts advising them to pay $25 for wagon seed, $3 being the discount in that particular district.

Mr. C. E. GARNER, Secretary Tennessee Division, DECEMBER 14, 1929.
National Cottonseed Products Association, Memphis, Tenn.
DEAR SIR: Replying to your letter of December 11 in regard to inspection and grading of cottonseed, will say that this office employs two men, one of whom is in the office at all times and the other making frequent trips to visit the mills and ascertain the market conditions prevailing. The mills have allowed inspection of their seed-return books, in which the quantity and value of seed is shown in making the remittance or giving credit to the shipper for the seed received. This necessarily gives the information with reference to the deduction made for off-grade of seed, if any. It is not compulsory by any means for the mills in this section to have any particular price. They should, however, publish any prices made by them, so that the information may be available to anyone interested. Should a mill receive seed that graded off and fail to make a deduction therefor, it would be the same thing as establishing a new price, and the information necessarily should be published. In this district both the Buckeye and the Southern Cotton Oil Co. have car-lot seed graded by the official chemist and settle on that grading.
We have before us at this time suggestions with reference to sampling seed 3 and retaining duplicate of sample, so that in case the seller should object to the grading he might have an opportunity to have the analysis checked by any chemist he might select. This is similar to the rules governing the sampling of crude cotton oil at destination. It seems to me that the fact that the Buckeye and the Southern in your district have their own chemist and grade the seed coming to their mills is similar to the matter of grading crude cottonseed oil. There should be no objection to their grading if the seller is satisfied. If there is a dispute, an official sample should be available to send to the official chemist or to one designated by the seller.
In my letter of December 9 I used some expressions that you might misconstrue. For instance, I said: "It is usual that if the wagon-seed price for prime seed is, say, $28, for the mill to make a deduction for grading and apply on all seed received until the next report comes in from the chemist." What I wanted to convey was this: That if the published price of the mill receiving the wagon seed is $28 that particular mill will make a deduction from their published price on all wagon seed received until the next report comes in and indicates some change in the discount.
121200 S. Doc. 209, 71-2, pt 6—70 INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY The mills over this side make their own prices for seed. The only thing that we consider it morally obligatory for them to do is to publish their price, whatever it may be, so that all parties interested may be advised.
The question of sampling seed for grading has become a matter of serious discussion in all of the Eastern States. In Georgia the commissioner of agriculture has designated official inspectors or samplers in that State whose duty it is to draw samples of car seed. These samplers are instructed to take samples in accordance with the grading system adopted by the Georgia division some time ago, one sample to be sent to the official chemist, one to be sent to the State department of agriculture, and the third to be retained at the mill, the samples sent to the agricultural department and retained at mills shall in addition to the certificate inside of sample carry exterior marks to permit identification.
In North Carolina it has been suggested that the North Carolina division itself appoint one or more official inspectors for the State at large and one for each mill, these to be sworn officers and are to observe the grading rules adopted by that division, and must issue certificates of inspection, transmitting to secretary copy of certificate and deposit with mill manager a copy and the original sample with the certificate to be sent to designated chemist without permitting sample to pass through hands of any interested party. In connection with the North Carolina suggestions it has been proposed that the sample must be drawn for seller and held for reanalysis or appeal for a reasonable length of time.
In Mr. Meloy's address in New Orleans last May, on page 4, he has considerable to say about the sampling of cottonseed. It will probably be neces sary to issue some instructions or rules concerning sampling to the parties who will perform this duty.
I believe that covers the inquiry that you have made.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.

Mr. C. E. GARNER, Tennessee Division National Cottonseed Products Association, Memphis, Tenn.
DEAR SIR: We have copy of your letter of December 18, and it appears to us that the same rules for grading and general trade practices should be adopted by the different divisions as nearly as they may apply to each division. There are some things that would be feasible in South Carolina that would not apply at all in Texas, and in some degree it would be difficult to apply some of the South Carolina rules to Georgia.
With reference to No. 1, it is impracticable to sample seed in cars. The only accurate method of sampling seed in cars is when they are being unloaded.
Any sample taken from the car should only be used as a preliminary test such as refiners make on crude cottonseed oil before unloading the tank, and be reported only as an indication of the character of the seed in the car so as to obtain permission from the shipper to unload, subject to official sample being drawn while the car is being unloaded.
No. 3, we think, would be rather impracticable except on car seed, and we have our doubts of the advisability of reporting such seed contracts to the secretary's office. It would entail a great deal of work. You may refer to the contract made with seed shippers; in that case all contracts should be uniform and there would be no objection to reporting them to the secretary's office.
We feel a need at this time of copies of laboratory reports on car seed received. The seed appears to be deteriorating very rapidly, and it is difficult to give average analyses and deductions to apply to wagon seed at gins, mills, and points where commission buyers are operating.
We can see no useful purpose in furnishing account sales to division secre taries except in cases where specific information is desired. It would be burdensome to the mills to send copies of account sales and it would furnish a mass of documents to the secretary's office that would be of no particular value.
Under the system adopted by the South Carolina division, the secretary may at any time ask for information about any transaction involving the grading of cottonseed at destination, and may ask for the account sales so as to see that the proper deduction is made.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.
C. C. Christie Benet, W. M. Hutchinson, W. F. Marsh.

It was decided that in order that the seed analyses might be representative, that each mill is to send two samples a week of wagon seed to Mr. Rice for analysis, and further, that all seed bought through commission buyers should be sampled when received, analyzed, and the results included in the wagon seed analyses for each district.

We want samples of seed from as many localities as possible. We have already indicated that if you are not willing to pay for these analyses yourself, that the association will undertake to bear the expense. It is the most important detail in the successful operation of the division. If seed grading breaks down, the whole structure will fail.

EXHIBIT NO. 831 Raleigh, N. O.
Mr. W. F. MARSH, JANUARY 8, 1930.
DEAR MR. MARSH: After some investigation, it appears to me that the different results obtained by public chemists from samples of seed drawn from the same stock is probably due to a slight variation in the methods of the chemist.
There is no use in going into technical details of the analysis used and the causes for these variations. The main point is to have the chemist absolutely uniform in every detail. When this is accomplished, I am satisfied more concordant results will be obtained. Mr. Rice has agreed to send check samples to several different official chemists so as to ascertain where the trouble lies and I believe will be able to correct the difficulty so far as the chemical work is concerned. Of course, we all know that it is very difficult to sample seed and get identical samples if the work is done at different times or by different men. But where a sample is carefully taken and immediately sealed and sent to chemist for analysis there should be no reason why there would be any material variation on account of difference in the samples.
I recall a good many years ago that we used to have the same trouble with analysis of oil but apparently the chemists check very closely now on free fatty acids, refining losses, color, and flavor of oil. There is no reason why we should not eventually get the same results in analyzing seed.
Yours very truly, C. C. C. W. Rice, C. C. Fishburne.
B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.

I also found that there was a small amount of storage being allowed to customers, but not to anyone that did not gin cotton at the mill gin. The management could not see where this could be called storage and also stated that some of the independent buyers at Anderson, about 15 miles away, were storing large lots of seed for customers.
At any rate, I am satisfied that with one or two more talks with the manage ment that most of these irregularities will be eliminated in time.
The Spartanburg situation, I think, is now in very good shape. I had talks with Messrs. Caldwell, Fitzsimons, and Lipscomb in respect to grading there and they now advise me that they will not give any further trouble in respect to this matter.

TAYLOR.
MAY 21, 1930.
DEAR HUTCH. If you will examine Group I rules you will be able to apply them to seed grading in the following ways: RULE 1, SECTION (a). It would be a discrimination in price to buy prime seed at the same price as offseed. The purchase of offseed at prime price would lessen competition.
SEC. (b). To pay the prime price for offseed and failure to state the grade or amount of discount applicable would be a failure to publish the correct price paid.
RULE 3. Purchasing offseed at the prime price is a confidential price and a form of commercial bribery and a device which does not include in the bid or price the entire consideration.
Under Group II, rule 8 and rule 10, the purchase of seed as is, declared unfair competition, would be conduct unbecoming a member.
the producers also and bring the association into disrepute.
It would be unfair to The procedure would be an investigation upon written complaint of another member or person; report of the evidence to the executive committee of the division with charges; a hearing at which the member complained of would be asked to appear; a verdict of guilt or acquittal; and if guilty, then an expression from the offending member of his intentions in the future; if he refuses to refrain in future from the violations, then the case would go to the president and board of directors of the national association for suspen sion until the next annual meeting or be reported to the Federal Trade Com mission.
In the latter case an examiner would be sent to see the party; and if be persisted in his course, and if that course was held by the commission to be wrong, the commission would apply to a Federal court for a restraining order.
If that order is granted after an opportunity to be heard, the injunction will be issued and a violation of that order would subject the party to fine or im prisonment.
Yours very truly, Mr. B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY EXHIBIT NO. 837 NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION (INC.), SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION, Columbia, S. C., June 14, 1930.
CHAIRMAN NATIONAL SEED GRADING COMMITTEE, ALL DIVISION SECRETARIES, CHAIRMAN (CHEMISTS COMMITTEE, MR. G. S. MELOY.
GENTLEMEN: The committee appointed by the South Carolina division to consider the form of chemist's reports and to suggest a manner of securing independent samplers of cottonseed in the matter of seed grading is of the opinion that these matters should be uniform in all districts, and, therefore, should be acted on as a general association problem. The committee also is of the opinion that such action should be had at as early a date as possible so as to be ready for the first movement of cottonseed. The committee suggests that representatives from the districts, from the seed-grading committee, from the chemists' committee, and Mr. Meloy meet during the second week in July at a point to be designated by the chairman of the national seed-grading committee.
This committee deems it advisable to have the chemist's reports of analyses of seed include the foreign matter as well as the value of the clean seed, so that a copy of said analyses shall show to the seller the complete and final value per ton of the seed represented in the analysis, also that the reports shall be as simple and free from technical details as possible.
As now provided in the rules, the trash and sand determination is to be made by the sampler at mill, which would bring about a divided responsibility for reports made as suggested in paragraph above. Hence the chemists who have had the matter presented to them say they would not be willing to make such a report unless they were also to make the sand and trash determination.
It would meet with the approval of this committee to have the chemists appoint the samplers of seed at mills, pay them, and be responsible for the correctness of their work. The mills would, of course, have to pay the chemists for this work.
There are a number of mills in this section that receive very few carloads of seed, most of their purchases being delivered by truck and wagon, and at such points the employment of a man for the sampling of seed would be very expensive, in some cases impractical. The committee believes that in such cases strict compliance with the rules could not be had, particularly as to drawing 50-pound samples and determination of sand and trash. At small mills the installation of a machine for the purpose would be expensive in relation to the amount of seed to be treated.
Attached hereto is a form of report desired by this committee with a hypothetical illustration. We think all reports should be uniform. The form is prepared on the assumption that the chemists will make all determinations.
Yours very truly, C. C. FISHBURNE, Chairman.
FRED E. CULVERN.
ALBERT JORDAN.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY EXHIBIT NO. 888 (Reprinted from the Journal of Oil Fat Industries, Vol. 3, No. 9, September, and No.
10, October, 1926)' CRUDE OIL ANALYSIS (By David Wesson) The discussions at the 1926 meeting of the American Oil Chemists Society have shown that the time is now ripe to discard the refining test, so long used in determining the value of crude vegetable oils, and resort to scientific methods of chemical analysis.
There was a time when ironmasters bought iron ore for their furnaces on what was known as the crucible assay. A known weight of ore, limestone and powdered charcoal or coke were heated in a Hessian crucible in a coke fire for several hours, after which the crucible was withdrawn, cooled, and broken, and a button of iron, separated from the slag and weighed. This was taken as the amount of iron present in the ore. Like our refining test, it was uncertain in results, depending a good deal on the skill of the operator and the character of the ore.
At the best, it was a rough test, and perhaps good enough for the primitive plants of its day.
With the advent of the chemist in the iron industry, it was found possible to determine exactly how much iron was contained in an ore, and the character of impurities which would influence the yield in the furnace, and the quality of the product. This information put a correct value on the ore.
logical reason why such methods should not apply to the valuation of crude cottonseed oil.
There is no In 1916 and 1917, the writer, working on the problem of improving refining methods, concluded that the first step was to find out how to analyze the oil so as to have some basis for getting at the efficiency of refining operations and the causes which influenced the losses.
With the assistance of Harold P. Gaylord, a method was worked out in the writer's laboratory. It was tested in other laboratories, and several years after was carefully checked up by Dr. Geo. P. Jamieson, of the United States Bureau of Chemistry. The method shows absolutely the amount of refined oil present in a given sample of crude oil and gives a standard by which a refining operation or method can be judged.
In applying it to commercial practice allowance would naturally have to be made for the efficiency of refining operations in the plant in getting at the value of the oil to the purchaser. If the refiner does not work to a high state of efficiency, that is his own misfortune, not the fault of the man who sells the crude oil. If the man who sells the crude oil pumps water and settlings into it, the result will be apparent in the sample when analyzed.
The following description of the test is given as written in 1917, and the numerous examples of its application bear tribute to its accuracy: ABSOLUTE METHOD FOR OIL ANALYSIS The object of this method is to determine the maximum amount of refined oil which can be produced from a given sample of crude or partly refined oil and at the same time to determine the amount of fat necessary to saponify and the amount of caustic soda necessarily absorbed in the refining of the oil.
It has been found as the result of careful experiment that when an oil is dissolved in gasoline the mixture of oil and gasoline can be shaken up with a large excess of caustic potash, which will combine with the coloring matter, free fatty acids, and break up the lipoid bodies in the cold inside of three minutes. By adding a considerable quantity of 50 per cent alcohol and water the excess caustic, together with the soap and products of decomposition of the organic matter, color, etc., settles out, leaving a clean gasoline solution of reifined oil which can be readily separated from the solution of soap stock.
After washing all oil out of the alcohol solution of soap stock there is no therein by following the regular procedure. It is also possible by this method, operating on a separate weight of oil, to determine the alkali absorbed, which INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY is done by titrating a blank representing the caustic potash started with and titrating the excess alkali in the alcohol soap solution, using phenolphthalein as an indicator.
