Table No. 2 shows the results of applying the method to refined oils. Samples marked "B were from different refinings at Bayonne. It will be noted in looking at this table that the sum of the free fatty acid and the moisture is a remarkably close check on the absolute loss as shown by the method. Results given on New Orleans Nos. 110 and 88 oil were made before it occurred to us to find out the reason for the absolute loss. The 88 oil in question came from Bayonne at a time when the plant was not running properly and unquestionably contained moisture and some free fatty acid, probably about .03 to .04 per cent. The New Orleans sample was taken from the refining kettle and doubtless would, if tested for moisture and free fatty acid, show up about the same as the Bayonne samples.
REPORTING OF RESULTS Table No. 3 gives analyses of composite samples sent from different refineries.
It also shows the way the results should be reported. The loss not fat as shown on this report is the difference between the fatty acids as soap and the absolute loss. In order to determine the organic matter in the loss not fat, the crude should be analyzed for moisture and the percentage of moisture subtracted. The Naoh absorbed shows the amount of caustic necessary theoretically to refine the oil. Below this is shown the Naoh necessary to combine with the free fatty acid. The difference between these two factors shows the actual excess of Naoh necessary to combine with the organic matter and form the fatty acids found as soap, which latter comes from the breaking down of complex glycerides. The free fatty acid is determined very carefully in the usual manner. The fatty acid-free fatty acid shows the amount of fatty acids saponified over and above the free fatty acid, and it is 'From March 22, 1917.
This has been determined by careful experiment. The last line shows whether the color drops slowly or quickly after shaking up with alcohol in the absolute oil test. We have found that when the color drops slowly an oily soap-stock or high free oil loss almost invariably happens.
Further tests showing accuracy of results are shown in Table No. 4. which gives checks on (12) Bayonne refinings, (8) New Orleans, and (8) Memphis refinings.
The application of analyses to actual refinings is shown in Table No. 5, which gives analyses and their application to refinings from different plants.
It is interesting to note, that with the prime crude worked, the average kettle efficiency was very close to 96.5 per cent. The tables show also that absolute oil and kettle efficiency are not entirely governed by free fatty acid Effect of settling of crude oil is shown very fully in Table No. 6, where the absolute oil is greatly increased by the settling of the crude-oil samples taken from different refinings.
Thorough settling on the three samples tested showed 1.45 to 1.83 per cent difference between the whole sample and the well-settled one. This is mostly due to the loss, not fat in the oil.
The analysis of cold pressed oil, given in Table No. 7, is interesting as showing an apparent free fatty acid of 1.48 per cent, whereas only 1.05 fatty acid would occur as soap. In other words, the gossypol titrating as free fatty acid gives an erroneous result, and free fatty acids determined in the usual way are frequently not free fatty acids at all.
SUMMARY It has been shown that it is easily possible to obtain the exact amount of refined oil in a given sample of crude by an accurate analytical method.
The refining efficiency in a well operated refinery is 96.5 per cent on prime crude oils.
That proper settling of crude oil results in an increase of the absolute oil of 1.5 per cent and upwards.
That the free fatty acid test may show acidity due to other causes than free fatty acids.
In the September issue an account was given of an accurate method for determining exactly the amount of refined oil in any given sample of crude.
The application of this method to factory control and the purchasing of crude oil was not mentioned.
Knowing the amount of refined oil in a given sample of crude and the efficiency of factory refining operation it is very evident that a factor can be used to show the maximum loss which should be expected.
The average absolute oil from the 40 refinings in the above tables was 973 per cent, which multiplied by the average efficiency gives us 93.7, the average results apply to prime oils only.
These This can be arrived at another way by adding the absolute loss to 100 Thus, the average efficiency being 96.3 per cent minus efficiency per cent.
we have efficiency loss of gives us a loss of 6.40, as against 6.30 as shown above.
When it is considered that the 40 refinings were all made at a very high efficiency, it would seem fair to add a factor of 4 to the absolute loss on all oil, assuming a refining efficiency of 95. This would give a factor of safety in buying oils, and at the same time be a nearer approximation to average kettle results than we obtain by the hard refining tests as now carried out.
The present refining test does not agree closely with the kettle results in most cases for the following reasons: First, the sample tested in the laboratory does not represent the oil in the kettle unless taken from a kettle during thorough agitation. Average tankcar samples taken from the tank cars are not accurately representative. This 1 Journal of Oil and Fat Industries, pp. 3, 9, 300-301.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY is proven by comparing the acidity of such samples with that of the same oil after thoroughly mixing in a refining kettle.
Second, the refining conditions in the laboratory differ greatly from those in the kettle, and very different results are frequently obtained.
With off oils, the stirring apparatus in both kettle and the laboratory is very inefficient, as can be proven by results. The efficiency can be determined exactly by means of the absolute oil test, and the correction of refining apparatus becomes a mechanical problem.
Referring to the previous communication, one or two points should be made clear. Any good 95 per cent alcohol or formula 30 can be used in making the test.
Caustic potash is used instead of caustic soda because it forms a liquid soap easily soluble in the alcohol-water mixture.
The quantity of caustic potash used is equal to 10 per cent of caustic soda on the weight of the oil. It is therefore sufficient to saponify 70 per cent fatty acid in the oil and is many times the amount ever used in practice.
In conclusion it is recommended that the value of crude oils be determined by determining the amount of absolute oil contained and estimation of the probable loss by adding a suitable factor to the absolute loss. Factors for off oils must be worked out.
In addition to the above test a laboratory refining should be made with a specified excess of caustic soda of sufficient strength to determine the color of refined oil which can be made from a given sample of crude.
MONTCLAIR, N. J., January 13, 1930.
Mr. B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary South Carolina Division, National Cottonseed Products Association (Inc.), Columbia, S. C.
DEAR MR. TAYLOR: I have yours of January 11 about heated seed, and it gives me great pleasure to tell you what little I know about it.
First, I wish to congratulate you, however, on your new position and for having gotten back into the fold of the cottonseed products manufacturers.
When cottonseed spoils it is due to either one of two causes. First, excess moisture while the seed is still in the field. This causes hydrolysis of oil with increase of fatty acids. Second, rapid heating due to germination, which happens when the seed is piled up in mass, as in a warehouse. The excessive heat from this cause will turn the seed brown and the oil almost black.
I have seen such oil from such seed which ran less than 2 per cent fatty acid and had a smell of putrefaction.
In the process of germination and heating under these conditions little or no hydrolysis takes place, and this accounts for the low fatty acid in the oil. In such cases it is quide evident that a rule based simply on free fatty acid and moisture will not cover the case. An addition to the present rule should read something as follows: "Prime seed must be sweet in odor and must show no darkening of the meats due to heating by germination or putrefaction." Now for the method of analysis: When a sample of seed shows darkened meats or bad odor, a sufficient quantity of the meats should be extracted with petroleum ether to yield at least 20 grams of oil. The petroleum ether extract should not be run to complete dryness unless in a vacuum and at a temperature low enough not to heat the residual oil.
A refining test should be made on the residual oil by means of the absolute method. This will show at a glance whether the seed will yield a good colored refined oil or not.
I would grade seed such as has been described above as very badly off. The color of the oil obtainable from such seed can be obtained by comparing the petroleum ether solution of the lot with the petroleum ether solution of the same quantity of prime oil. This obviously is a method which can be worked out.
If I can be of any further service in the matter, let me know.
With kind regards, I remain, Yours sincerely, DAVID WESSON.
P. S.-If this plan of procedure meets with your approval, I will be glad to dictate an analytical method along these lines which will be quite simple.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Dr. DAVID WESSON, Montclair, N. J.
JANUARY 15, 1930.
DEAR DOCTOR: I have your letter of January 13, also copy of crude oil analysis. I wish to thank you very much for your prompt attention to my inquiry.
The question of determining the damage to seed from heating, such as I have described, involves something besides the character of oil to be produced.
In the process of heating to produce such bad seed I believe that some portion of the nitrogen is oxidized or cooked out of the meats and the color of the meal obtained from such seed, as you know, is very dark and is fit only for fertilizer purposes. Even the lint and hulls are affected. So the analysis of the oil to determine the loss in refining only covers a part of the case.
Unfortunately our grading system is new and we are following instructions or methods laid down by the Department of Agriculture. We do not wish to criticize the methods until we have definitely gotten something practical to take their place.
Certainly I should be very glad to have you dictate analytical methods along the lines which you suggest, and I will get the chemist committee of the association to try them out and be ready for a report at the next meeting of the association.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.

Mr. B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary South Carolina Division, LAW Co. (INC.).
Atlanta, Ga., January 16, 1930.
National Cottonseed Products Association, Columbia, S. C.
There are several points that should be cleared up regarding the present method of grading seed. This plan is only partly that of the Department of Agriculture at Washington. It was agreed upon by collaboration with this department, the National Association, and the American Oil Chemists Society.
The deduction for free fatty acids content in oil was determined by taking averages of thousands of analyses of the past 10 years and figuring on the present method of oil claims as to what would be the proper figure. This will of course vary, depending upon the price of the products. The average color, loss, and flavor were all taken into consideration and an allowance made for the quality of other products, such as meal, linters, and hulls. The whole plan was worked out as scientifically as possible with the information in hand.
We are not claiming for the grading by moisture and free fatty acids, as at present conducted, that it is perfect, but anyone who is at all familiar with the situation must admit that it is far superior and much more accurate than the old cut and color grading. In our opinion by far the fairer method is the Meloy method of combining the meal and oil yields with the grading, or his so-called reciprocal index. This would take care of the situation in the valley and west where there are so many immature seed.
In reference to Doctor Wesson's criticism on the color of seed being frequently worse than the free fatty acids would indicate, our results and records on thousands of analyses this season show that this occurs only in isolated instances and is the exception and not the rule. It may be necessary to work out some plan of combining this color with the free fatty acids. Generally speaking, this would only appy to the meal as the flavor and loss on the oil are largely determined by the free fatty acids content and the color allowance comes from the general average. The loss allowance being twice that of the color on off oil makes the former of considerable more consequence.
It also must be taken into consideration that there is nothing like the heating of seed in storage now that existed some years ago. The large buyers are drying seed before placing them in storage, and all the mills are much better equipped to take care of seed than formerly. I would estimate that at least 75 per cent INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY of the damaged seed in Georgia this season came from field damage and not heating in storage. I agree with Doctor Wesson that occasionally we find a black seed that shows a low free fatty acid, but this invariably occurs when the seed has heated quickly, as when in transit and the car is delayed, and even then we find that the oil from these seed shows up much better than the appearance would indicate.
The grading of seed by the free fatty acids content is no longer a theory.
At the end of this season we will have a number of records of individual mills where we have analyzed every car of seed purchased and all the products sold.
At one mill last season records of this kind showed a check between the deductions on seed purchased and allowances on products sold checking within a few cents per ton of seed.
Very truly yours, LAW Co. (INC.).
THOS. C. LAW.
P. S.-Please understand that I am not wedded to this method, but it appears to be the most promising one that we have ever undertaken, and I feel sure that through collaboration it can be worked out.
C. C. Dr. David Wesson, Mr. Charles W. Rice, Mr. C. C. Fishburne.

Clemson persuaded one of our chief daily newspapers to offer $1,000 in prizes for the greatest production on five acres of cotton coming up to a certain length of staple and other requirements. To further the campaign of educating the farmers to grow a better staple, the college is stressing the importance of growing better varieties and of keeping planting seed pure. One important step in this is at the gin, and they are appealing to all ginners, oil-mill gins included, to assist the farmers in this most necessary part of the program to improve the planting seed.
I appreciate that your letter deserves a very much better thought out reply than this, and I apologize for so poor an attempt to offer suggestions, but I repeat I see no way to render the grower a real service except to assist in getting him a better price. I may take the liberty, some other time, of writing you further on this subject.

APRIL 24, 1928.
Chief Economist, Federal Trade Commission, Washington, D. C.
DEAR SIR: Replying to yours of the 19th, the price or sales information and statistical reports compiled by our association are sent to our members, to the secretaries of some State associations, to the editor of the Cotton Oil Press, and possibly at times to a few others. They are not sent to the newspapers nor to the public generally, and those receiving them are entirely at liberty to use such reports in any manner they see fit. We have no machinery for making the reports available to the general public, nor do we think the general public would be interested in the data carried in the reports.
As a matter of fact, the same statistics carried by our reports are made public once a month in a more reliable and widespread manner by the Bureau of the Census in its report on cottonseed and its products. As to price information, which is based on past and closed transactions or bids, it is always available to such of the general public as are interested and who want to be posted on conditions in the trade of which this association is a part. However, again we have no machinery to broadcast this information.
Our bulletins on better cultural methods for the production of the raw material and for the purpose of extending the uses of the manufactured products are sent to our members for distribution by them among their trade and the public generally where their judgment indicates such distribution will bring results.
In reply to that part of your letter in which you ask for a statement of the policy and views of our association, and of my own, on the question of making public trade-association statistics, the industry is now working on a plan, following the report of the Federal Trade Commission on the investigation of the cottonseed-oil industry which was filed with Congress March 5 past, to set up a code of business principles for the cottonseed-oil mills. In this effort the industry is in touch with the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Commission, and it is possible that out of this effort will come a plan whereby information as to the condition of the industry may be made public regularly and promptly. The Federal Trade Commission in its report specifically found that such information should be made available, and I personally feel that much good would come from the completion of such a program. I am not in position to say what the attitude of the association would be, as this has not been discussed.
Any reports and data sent out by this office or by the Census Bureau would be much more valuable if they could show commitments, which are not now included. Any statistics gathered by the Government would be much more valuable if they could be more frequently compiled and released more quickly and closer to the close of the period wh.ch they cover.
The outcome of such a situation might be that there would be no need for this association to attempt to duplicate the work which the Government is now doing. This association and others have cooperated with the Census Bureau in speeding up the comsumption report, and the gain in time which has come about there has already made the report more valuable. It is still rather late, however, to be of value to manufacturers who are actively engaged in buying and crushing cottonseed and selling the products thereof.
I hope this covers the points you have in mind, and if not please write me, as I will be happy to cooperate with you fully.
Sincerely yours, Secretary.
RA: P.

Secretary Oklahoma Cottonseed Crushers' Association, Oklahoma City, Okla.
I shall be very glad to DEAR MR. JOHNSTON: Thank you for yours of the fifth.
keep you advised of the current news in this State. It might be advisable for all secretaries to put each other on their permanent mailing lists.
The season is trying to get under way over here and, as you mentioned, we are having the usual starting pumps and hazards to contend with. I am impressed, however, that the most of the trade seem to recognize the fairness of the Memphis resolutions and I am hoping that under our prospective crop we will have a good season.
Carload seed are $30 per ton f. o. b., and what we call wagon and gin seed are from $27 to $30 per ton, the last price being paid by so-called speculators or dealers.
Please bear me in mind as I am always glad to hear from you.
Yours very truly, RA: D.

EXHIBIT NO. 845 NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION, SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION, Columbia, S. C., November 1, 1929.
To the members of the South Carolina Division: GENTLEMEN: You should have received through the mail copy of instructions for publication of prices for the State divisions of the National Cottonseed Products Association, sent you by General Counsel Benet. If you have not received your copy, or if you wish additional copies, please write me and I will forward one immediately. These instructions are very important, and I hope you will not alone read them carefully but have your employees read them.
Your special attention is called to paragraphs 2 and 5. The secretary's office can not be expected to know that you are paying any price, or to assume anything in reference to your prices. You should notify the secretary's office of your changed price promptly and fully. When any operator fails to do this it makes it impossible for the secretary to give authentic information to sellers or buyers as to what the true market condition is.
You may already have a bulletin or blackboard, but if not you are urged to provide one of convenient size at once. It should be placed where it may be easily seen by those who come to the mill to sell seed or buy products. As soon as you change your prices for cottonseed and products they should be posted on the bulletin board. After your prices are posted this office should be advised promptly.
If there are any questions in your mind about any of the above, please take it up with me.
Yours very truly, D. M. LIPSCOMB, Assistant Secretary.

EXHIBIT NO. 849 NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION, SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION, Columbia, S. C., December 26, 1929.
GENTLEMEN: At a meeting of the executive committee December 23 all mills were requested to send samples of seed for analyses at least twice a week. We find that the failure of mills to supply samples is causing the report of Mr. Rice to be practically worthless in some districts. It's hard to overestimate the value of these reports when properly made. We know that the deductions on seed for offgrade will amount to the difference between a small profit and a loss even in sections of the State where conditions are the best.
One of our members has sent in analyses of seed from gins at Easley, Six Mile, Anderson, and Norris. In all these instances the deductions under the rule would run $1 a ton and in two instances the deductions just missed the $2 bracket.
Mr. Christie Benet is advised that the Federal Trade Commission has mailed out to the members of our division two questionnaires. He urges that the members fill these out and send to Washington promptly. It will not be necessary to have copies of your replies sent to his office.
Mr. Benet also impressed upon those attending the executive committee meeting the necessity for frequent reports from all mills stating prices paid for cottonseed and the prices at which products have been sold. Unless these INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY reports come in frequently this office will be unable to give the necessary information to its members.
As to the daily reports which we requested you to make to this office, we understand fully that you are reporting to Mr. Marsh in North Carolina, but inasmuch as a part of your tonnage comes from South Carolina, we think it important that we should at least have reports from you on transactions in South Carolina. Of course, the compensating benefit is that we supply you regularly with reports on the South Carolina situation. If there are no transactions it is not necessary to send a report, and I would suggest your writing at the bottom of one of the blanks which we sent you that the following are the paid prices to-day, and unless there is some change that you would not make another report. In that way we could count you as reporting daily.
I talked with Mr. Mikell regarding your request that I should find out what their attitude is about buying and settling for seed with customers at Latta, and Mr. Mikell says if you will be more specific as to what you mean that he will be very glad to answer fully.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.

Mr. W. F. MARSH, Raleigh, N. C.
JANUARY 20, 1930.
DEAR MR. MARSH: Mr. Lipscomb tells me that you called up to find out why we were sending out a telegram on prices so soon after the previous one.
We consider it just as important that low prices should be published as high prices and that at this particular instance it was very desirable that all mills be given the range of prices in this State, particularly in vew of the fact that the yield of oil is very low in some sections and the quality of the seed getting worse every day.
We are publishing daily the range of prices in two newspapers at Columbia so that all mills in the State and anyone else interested will have available the information contained in the report for that day. There are a good many mills that do not get these papers, particularly those on the outside of the State, and for that reason it will be necessary occasionally to use the telegraphie method of distributing the information.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.

Mr. J. J. LAWTON, Chairman, Hartsville, S. C.
DEAR MR. LAWTON: I am sending notices of the joint meeting of North and South Carolina divisions by this afternoon mails. I inclose a suggested draft of program, which I ask you to look over and make suggestions concerning.
Marsh asked me to draw up a program and send to him, so I am sending this tentative one.
I can not find any rule in the papers in this office concerning the matter of hauling seed. That is an important matter for discussion and it is not covered by the trade practice conference rules. It must have been an executive committee rule, or else something that was done at a meeting a few days before Acree died. That meeting was never recorded, as far as I can find.
Another matter I should like to have your advice about is publication of prices. Only four or five mills are buying seed and reporting. The rest of them have stopped reporting and presumably dealing only in local sales of products.
I can see no use in sending telegrams of price changes to any that are not reporting, since the prices are published in the newspapers. With your approval I shall advise all mills that telegraphic advices of price changes will be discontinued except to such mills as send reports of prices paid to this office regularly.
Yours very truly, B. F. TAYLOR, Secretary.
EXHIBIT NO. 855 JOHNSTON In a memorandum sent to you on Tuesday, February 11, I stated that the Leesville Oil Mill had bought one car of seed from Bouknight at $30, basis prime, and that since that time two other cars had been shipped by Bouknight to Leesville. I made a more careful checking at Leesville and at Johnston in regard to this matter and found while the purchase from Bouknight was for one large car as Leesville had stated, that Bouknight elected to ship in two cars. The other two cars received at Leesville from Johnston were shipped by Mr. Clark, their regular salaried buyer at Johnston. Mr. Duncan issued instructions to Mr. Clark in my presence to continue as he had been doing in the market at Johnston at 402 cents, and not change that price under any consideration without instructions from Mr. Duncan. Further, he was instructed to give me all the information that he had in regard to the Johnston market upon my arrival at that point. This Mr. Clark cheerfully did, showing me his seed book, in which he has kept an accurate and regular account of every load of seed for which a seed ticket was issued. In only one instance during the whole season has Mr. Clark apparently paid more for seed than the prevailing market price at that point. This happened on February 8, last Saturday, when two loads of seed which had been sent to town to be delivered to Mr. Clark at 402 cents were met by Mr. Derrick, who buys for the Planters, who offered 42 cents for them. Mr. Clark at first refused to take the seed, then went to Mr. Derrick and asked him if he had made the offer, which Mr.
Derrick said he had, whereupon Mr. Clark took these seed.
I am prepared to say that Leesville has been more conservative in the Johnston market than either of the other buyers at that point. The only thing to be criticized at the moment in connection with this market is the fact that they are paying $27 for seed without making any deduction for the zone grade.
Under circumstances that have been prevailing there it seems that this is the best that can be done for the present.
In regard to Mr. Derrick, the buyer for the Planters, of Augusta, it seems that he is using a house which is rented by the Planters from Mr. Cassels, an old seed buyer, and Mr. Derrick is a comparatively new seed buyer, not yet having established much of a clientele. Mr. Cassels is much interested in having his warehouse rented. I understand he gets $300 for the season.
though that may be a mistake. He has stated that he told Mr. Derrick to raise the price of seed from 37½ to 40 cents on February 4 or 5. His object INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY was, of course, to help Derrick get a tonnage of seed that would justify the renewal of the rent lease for the coming year.
Now, on December 10, 1929, the market was quiet at 40% cents for wagon seed. Mr. Derrick put the market up to 45 cents and proceeded to buy a car of wagon seed. On January 25, he advanced the market price from 37% to 40 cents and bought a car of seed. On February 4 and 5 he advanced the market from 372 to 40 cents and bought a car of seed. All other buyers in this market agree on these facts, and Mr. Derrick does not deny them. It will be necessary for Mr. Derrick to be given absolute and positive instructions as to the price that he must pay at this point, and he should be allowed no leeway as to the making of prices there.
Mr. Kemp, who buys for Swift Co., Augusta mill, is a ginner, his gin being located several hundred yards from the depot. For such seed as are bought at the gin he is allowed a commission. He also buys seed on the street, on such seed he is allowed a salary. At the beginning of the season Mr. Kemp went to the Leesville Oil Mill office and stated that he wanted to cut out the storage of cottonseed at the gin, to which Leesville cheerfully agreed. He also went to Mr. Clark, the salaried buyer for Leesville, and told him that his intention was to cut out the storage of seed. Later, without giving any notice other ginners, he rented a warehouse and allowed a number of farmers, whose names were given to me, to store seed therein, and also proceeded to allow seed to be stored at the gin. He admitted these facts to Mr. Clark. He now has on hand at the two places of storage a considerable amount of seed estimated at two or three hundred tons. Mr. Kemp is paying 40 cents for wagon seed, but those who have stored seed with him have been demanding $30 for the seed ungraded, because the seed were put in his hands in good condition and are now not in good condition. Naturally, Mr. Kemp wishes to settle for these seed at as low a price as possible. It is natural to suppose that the storage seed at the gin that are closed out to him will be reported on his commission contract, and that the seed in the warehouse up town will be purchased under his salary contract. The mill is liable to get stuck for the offgrade, as in neither instance would the seed be graded. Mr. Kemp does not like the $30 as is price put in by Mr. Miller, the manager of the Trenton Fertilizer Co., and has a suspicion that this $30 price was put in in order to get these seed without having to pay any commission, that is, on the part of Swift Co.
Mr. Miller, of the Trenton Fertilizer Co., bought several lots of seed, most of which have been loaded. At least we understand that the last of these cars was being loaded yesterday, February 12, and the representative of Mr. Miller.
Mr. Marsh, said he did not know whether he was going to buy any more seed or not. When asked if they were going to grade seed, he said, "Oh, yes; we'll grade them by cutting them and also grade them at the mill." In connection with the seed purchased it appears that he had no one there to weigh the seed.
and he got Mr. Mccreight, who is the ginner for Bouknight, to weigh the seed for him. The sced were weighed on the scales of the Leesville Oil Mill by per mission. Hence the assumption that Bouknight was the party who was buying these seed at $30, as is. As a matter of fact, Bouknight has not bought any seed at $30, as is.
We are advised by Swift Co. that they purchased 150 tons of seed from the Trenton Fertilizer Co. at $28, basis prime, and that the seed was subject to grade. As far as I have been able to ascertain there has been no trade made by Miller with any of the farmers by which he would be able to regain the $2 difference in price and the offgrade deduction. Hence all buyers in that market do not believe that he is taking a loss on these seed.
The Trenton Fertilizer Co. is offering kainit and acid at $15, delivered.
Johnston, which is much lower than any other fertilizer concern has offered to sell. It would not appear, therefore, that they are able to gain back any of the loss on seed through the sales of fertilizer at this price.
You have already been advised that the International's activities in that market are limited to a trade with Holmes on car load of seed, which was in order and they will probably buy seed of Holmes Boatwright basis.

on the same My conclusion is that the Johnston market can be easily controlled and brought down to a basis with other points in the State if the necessary steps are taken to control the buyers of the Planters and Swift. The buyers for Leesville in that market is absolutely under control and is a man that appears to me to be conservative and of good business ability. In addition to his coninvestigation OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY tract with Leesville, he handles fertilizer for the Read Fertilizer Co., of Charleston, and sold last year 900 tous of fertilizer. He also sells meal and hulls.

JACKSON, MISS., September 10, 1929.
DEAR MR. ACREE: Agreeable to your request, I am attaching a copy of the minutes of a meeting of the executive committee of this State division of the national association, which includes the resolution outlining the method to be used in publishing price changes in this State.
While the plan is working fairly well, we still have to impress on the mem- bers that each mill should wire its price changes, whatever the reasons for changing, so the secretary may be informed as to what each mill is paying for seed. Heretofore most of the mills have assumed that the secretary would know they had met the price published. But it is important that each mill take individual action in wiring its change, so the secretary can answer any questions asked by interested persons as to what any individual mill is paying.
I hope that if you have any suggestions as to improvement of this plan or have a better plan you will write me, so I can put the matter before the committee. Our plan is doubtless subject to revision, but is patterned after the plan used by Mr. Haines in the refiners' division. It is going to be costly if there are frequent changes, but I believe it will be worth all it costs, and has already been beneficial.
With regards and best wishes, I am, Very truly yours, S. M. HARMON, Secretary.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY EXHIBIT NO. 857 OKLAHOMA COTTONSEED CRUSHERS' ASSOCIATION, Oklahoma City, Okla., September 5, 1929.
Mr. F. M. Hunt, secretary Arkansas Cottonseed Crushers' Association, Little Rock, Ark.; Mr. Walton Burgess, Louisiana Cottonseed Crushers' Association.
Shreveport, La.; Mr. S. M. Harmon, Jackson, Miss.; Mr. J. H. Dubose, secre tary Tennessee Cottonseed Crushers' Association, Memphis, Tenn.; Mr. T. R.
GENTLEMEN: The crushing season is about to open up in southern Oklahoma, and I understand that the following are the prices being paid for cottonseed, viz: Carload lots f. o. b., $32 per ton; less than carload at gins, $28 to $29 per ton On account of our unusually long drought in the State of Oklahoma, the seed now being received at the gins is of very poor quality, bolls opening prematurely on account of the lack of moisture, and seed being very deficient in oil. I doubt if it will produce more than 35 gallons per ton of seed, if that much. The product prices are about in line with the Dallas posted quotations, but there seems to be a very active demand for hulls on the part of livestock feeders, who are anticipating a scarcity of other roughage due to the long dry spell.
Our oil-mill men seem to be going into the season imbued with the idea that they are going to make an honest effort to live close to the trade-practice code and avoid the various tricks of the trade in which they have heretofore indulged I hope that the reformation may outlive the first 15 days of seed buying, which is the period usually testing the sincerity of the revival.
I hear from Messrs. Hutchinson and Harmon frequently, but I would also like to hear from the other gentlemen to whom this is addressed.
With best regards and good wishes, I remain, Yours sincerely, J. H. JOHNSTON.
OKLAHOMA COTTONSEED CRUSHERS' ASSOCIATION, Oklahoma City, Okla., September 21, 1929.

GENTLEMEN: I am pleased to announce that there seems to be a decided improvement in the State of Oklahoma in the matter of observance of the trade practice code, and I am inclined to think that many of the former subterfuges to create discrimination have been discontinued.
The most trouble we seem to have at the present time is trucking, loading, and unloading charges, upon which we have not yet obtained such definite information as to place all buyers and sellers upon an exact equality, but we are working on it and hope to get it ironed out before a great while.
So far as I have been able to discover, the Oklahoma seed price is still $2 f. o. b. car, which is perhaps a little more than seed is worth, due to the fact that up to this time all the seed received was that which prematurely opened due to the very long drought, and in no case has the average analysis shown over 31 gallons of oil.
In the extreme southeastern portion of the State, where the seed is a little better so far as the oil content is concerned, I understand the price is $34 in line with the Texas price across the Red River.

Sincerely yours, J. HOHNSTO INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY OKLAHOMA COTTONSEED CRUSHERS' ASSOCIATION, Oklahoma City, Okla., September 28, 1929.

OKLAHOMA COTTONSEED CRUSHERS' ASSOCIATION, Oklahoma City, Okla., October 14, 1929.
Mr. T. R. Cain, Secretary Alabama Cottonseed Crushers' Association, Montgomery, Ala.; Mr. F. M. Hunt, Secretary Arkansas Cottonseed Crushers' Association, Little Rock, Ark.; Mr. W. M. Hutchinson, Secretary Georgia Cottonseed Crushers Association, Atlanta, Ga.; Mr. Walton Burgess, Secretary, Louisiana Cottonseed Crushers' Association, Shreveport, La.; Mr. S. M. Harmon, Secretary Mississippi Cottonseed Crushers' Association, Jackson, Miss.; Mr. H. A. White, Secretary North Carolina Cottonseed Crushers' Association, Greenville, N. O.; Mr. Russell Acree, Secretary South Carolina Cottonseed Crushers' Association, Columbia, S. C.; Mr. C. E. Garner, Secretary Tennessee Cottonseed Crushers' Association, Memphis, Tenn.
GENTLEMEN: I have advice from practically all mills in Oklahoma that the price of cottonseed has been reduced to $33 on account of the decline in the price of cottonseed oil, and the higher moisture content in seed caused by the recent rains.
Oklahoma seed is coming in rather slowly, and the farmers seem to be taking back an unusual amount, being somewhat resentful account of the great difference between the price of seed and the price of cake and meal, and, it seems right difficult to get them to understand that the decline in price of oil is responsible for the lower price for seed.
We have had abundant rains in this State in the last few days, and there will undoubtedly be some damage to cotton which has been beaten out of the boll into the dirt, but a few days sunshine will undoubtedly start picking with renewed vigor.
Sincerely yours, J. H. JOHNSTON.
EXHIBIT NO. 858 SOUTH CAROLINA COTTON SEED CRUSHERS' ASSOCIATION, Columbia, S. O., August 9, 1928.
DEAR SIR: A Conference of the oil-mill industry of South Carolina, and others interested, was held here on Tuesday night, August 8, at which practically every interest doing such business in this State was represented, and at which INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY the Memphis resolutions were discussed and their principles and purposes enthusiastically indorsed.
The resolutions were read and adopted both separately and as a whole without amendment, and it was agreed that they are to become effective immediately.
The following resolutions were introduced from the floor and adopted: Resolved, That it is the sense of this meeting that in making new salaried contracts for wagon buyers that they shall not be out of line with a compensation of $3 per ton commission for the purchase of seed, and the proper compensation for sale of products.
Resolved, That it is the sense of this meeting that a commission buyer is one who acts for one principal exclusively.
Resolved, That it is the sense of this meeting that the rules governing the buying and selling of cottonseed in South Carolina be readopted (with certain changes you will note in the text per copy attached) as interpretative of the Memphis resolutions and to define and govern other trade practices prevalent in South Carolina but not specifically mentioned in the Memphis resolutions.
Resolved, That an interpretative committee be appointed by the president, to interpret the various questions arising under the actual operation of the code, the committee to consist of at least seven members, of which at least five shall constitute a quorum.
The meeting then went on record as opposed to the practice generally known as allowing drayage and/or hauling.
The meeting went on record as understanding that the exchange prices for seed were to be made public and announced, just as are the cash prices.
The South Carolina rules were then read and adopted separately and as a whole.
Yours very truly, RUSSELL ACREE, Secretary.
SOUTH CAROLINA COTTON SEED CRUSHERS' ASSOCIATION, Columbia, S. C., August 10, 1928.
In the above connection we wish to advise that the authority for the decision reached to make the resolutions effective immediately was the permission granted by Judge Mcculloch, of the Federal Trade Commission, at the Memphis conference, as outlined in a letter dated August 4, 1928, from General Counsel Bent to the State secretaries, which was read at the meeting on the 7th, from which letter we quote as follows: "Judge Mcculloch specifically stated that pending action on the report by the entire commission, the mills in the various States would be allowed to operate under the provision of the resolutions." This office understands, therefore, that since a substantial majority of the mills buying cottonseed and selling products in this State were represented here at the meeting on Tuesday, August 8, 1928, and voted to adopt the Memphis resolutions, that they are now operating under them.
We also remind you that an interpretation committee will be appointed which will interpret the various questions arising under the operation of the code.
Yours very truly, RUSSELL ACREE, Secretary.

-1 MINUTES OF MEETING OF EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE Pursuant to the resolution passed at the general meeting held here on September 4 "that the executive committee meet, subject to the call of the secretary, immediately after the meeting of the North Carolina division," the committee met at the Jefferson Hotel, Columbia, S. C., on September 16 and 17.
Upon the committee being called to order by its chairman, Mr. J. J. Lawton, it developed that all were present except Mr. J. O. Wilson, who was represented by his alternate, Mr. F. H. Jarrell, and Mr. J. B. Caldwell, who was represented by his brother, Mr. R. M. Caldwell.
The resolution passed at the general meeting on September 4, "that this meeting go on record as approving in principle the grading of cottonseed, and that the matter be referred to the executive committee for the working out of details," was put before the committee for action.
After a full and detailed discussion of the matter of grading cottonseed, and upon motion duly seconded and passed, a committee composed of Messrs. Jarrell, Culvern, and Fishburn, with Mr. Acree as its secretary, was appointed and given full authority to take final action on the matter. (The report of this special committee is inclosed herewith.) Assistant to secretary: Upon motion duly made, seconded, and passed, the secretary was instructed to secure an assistant.
Statistical reports: Upon motion duly made, seconded, and passed, the secretary was instructed to discontinue the usual weekly report on seed received and cotton ginned.
Secretary's salary: Upon motion duly seconded and unanimously passed, the secretary's (Mr. Acree) salary was made $7,000, effective September 1.
Future meetings of executive committee: Upon motion duly seconded and passed, it was decided that until further notice the executive committee meet every other Tuesday at 11 a. m. at the Jefferson Hotel, Columbia, S. C.
Meal exchanges: Upon motion duly seconded and passed, it was resolved that it was the sense of the committee that all exchanges of products for cottonseed should be expressed in pounds, that such exchange price should be made public, and that they should bear a definite relation to the published f. o. b. cash prices for cottonseed and the published delivered cash prices for products.
I will be glad to go into this matter further with you when the time comes.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY D. N. BAKER Olanta, S. C.
SEPTEMBER 4, 1928.
J. E. FELDER, Cope Supply Co., Cope, S. C.
H. H. KEARSE, Olar, S. O.
C. L. PEEPLES, Estill, S. C.
DEAR SIRS: With reference to the seed business for the coming season, you have, no doubt, heard of the code worked out between the oil mills and the Federal Trade Commission and Interstate Commerce Commission of the Federal Government.
Under this code no mill is allowed to pay any more or any less to a seller for cottonseed, as that is determined a discrimination. This means that we would be unable to pay you the 50-cent brokerage on any seed shipped us, you being in any way interested in the seed shipped or interested in the price that the seed brings. We are not permitted to employ on a salary or a brokerage basis any independent ginner or seed merchant.
We could make a straight reporting $3 per ton commission contract with independent ginners or seed merchants and in this contract to allow a brokerage of 50 cents per ton any outside car lots of seed which the party might purchase on our quotation, where he is in no wise interested in the seed or the prices of the seed. In this case these outside car lots of seed would be shipped in the owner's name, settlement be made with the owner on mill weights, and the 50-cent brokerage credited or remitted to our buyer.
Just as early as possible we expect to have a representative see you, and if there is anything further that you do not understand will endeavor to explain it to you fully.
It is our desire, of course, to continue handling your business and we can do so on equal basis with our competitors. We assure you that we have always appreciated your business and will continue to do so; and we will also look very carefully after any shipments made us; and it will be our pleasure t keep you fully informed and to have you call us over telephone at any tin Yours truly, fec-t.
Vice Presider.

THE NORTH CAROLINA COTTON SEED CRUSHERS ASSOCIATION, Greenville, N. O., November 9, 1928.
Mr. FRED E. CULVERN, Vice President, Kershaw Oil Mill, Kershaw, 8. C.
Re Mr. J. L. Mckay, Wagram, N. C.
DEAR SIR: Your letter of October 29 received, and I have been delayed in handling this matter awaiting certain information I was seeking from other parties at interest.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY T Paragraph 3 of rule 12, group 11 of the code reads as follows: "Resolved further, That the payment of such commission to other than bona fide seed buyers who render a service, and/or in such manner that any part of it goes to the seller directly or indirectly through the medium of partners, influential friends, kinspeople, or under any other guise whatsoever is hereby declared to be against public policy and an unfair method of competition." Under application of this section of the code Mr. E. Hervey Evans, president of the Maxton Oil Fertilizer Co., contends that Mr. Mckay is thoroughly qualified to become a 50-cent car-lot buyer because he does render a service, and that no part of his commission goes to the seller, and he further says that if anyone can produce evidence to the contrary he will immediately cancel the contract.
The North Carolina interpretation of rule 12 reads as follows: "The purpose of this resolution is to prevent the payment of commissions directly or indirectly to sellers of seed, and it would therefore be considered unfair practice for mills to employ as a car-lot commission buyer or salaried agent a person, firm, or corporation engaged in the business of independent seed dealer or independent ginner." Mr. Evans says that Mr. Mckay represents his company as an exclusive carlot buyer and is neither an independent seed dealer or ginner and that he is therefore qualified to act in this capacity under the North Carolina interpretations.
Yours very sincerely, H. A. WHITE, Secretary-Treasurer.

SEPTEMBER 14, 1929.
Mr. JOHN T. STEVENS, Asheville, N. C.
DEAR MR. STEVENS: I this morning talked to Tom Whisnant, Swift Co., Augusta, about Williston and other high points. He stated most positively that he had canceled their contract with Mr. Green, who runs two large gins there, and is paying 52 cents per bushel for seed. He also stated that they were not furnishing Mr. Green any money; and that they had only received three cars of seed from him this season. I told him that our representative, Mr.
Blaine, was there; and that he was told by several of the other buyers there that the seed were going to him at Augusta; he denied this. He said that he was informed that he was holding his seed. He also said that he understood both the Southern's buyer and the Buckeye's buyer of the Augusta mills were meeting Green's price; and that he was working on the situation there with the others interested.
I also told him that we had good information that his buyer, Mr. Wiggins, Holly Hill, was storing seed; he stated that he had given him positive instructions it; and that the buyer for Swift Co., Columbia, is also doing it, as are, I think, some of the independent seed buyers. We have not been able to buy any street seed there, although we have a buyer.
A good many of the markets, like North, Neeses, Swansea, etc., are $30 or higher.
Most of this disturbance is in the territory where this occurs every year.
Whisnant said he was willing to do anything that he possibly could, and would do it, to correct conditions.
Rain was quite general yesterday afternoon and last night, both in the Piedmont, Marion, Hartsville, and the lower part of the State; so that it will hold back the ginning to some extent.
The car-lot market for 7 per cent meal seems to be about $36 to $36.50 Augusta, $37 Charlotte, advanced from $36 yesterday. Loose hulls, $9 to $9.50 Augusta. Swift and the Southern have been selling a little lower at Columbia.
We are not trying to sell anything and are only quoting customers in car lots at the present.
121200 S. Doc. 209, 71-2, pt 6- -74 INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY I sold this morning two tanks oil first half October through Harris, Charlotte, to Simonin, Philadelphia, at 74 cents. This covers our seed. They would not buy for any earlier shipment and would not buy any more. All of the others are paying 7% cents. Offered it to Swift at 74 cents; they declined it, claiming that they were buying what they wanted at five-eighths. Procter Gamble bid five-eighths.
Yours truly, fec-t.
SEPTEMBER 17, 1929.
Mr. JOHN T. STEVENS, The Manor, Asheville, N. O.
DEAR SIR: I have just returned from the executive committee meeting in Columbia. Each member was present except you. They all inquired about you.
It was decided that we would each control our buyers on the local markets or cancel our contracts and would take steps to do this immediately. All seem determined that we should run the business instead of the buyers.
We approved the Georgia plan, which is somewhat similar to the one we had in effect last season.
I was appointed, with Fishburne and Jarrill, of the Buckeye, to meet the North Carolina executive committee to-morrow at noon in Raleigh and help them get their grading plans started so they can notify all the mills, and then Acress will immediately seed the small mills in this State who were not represented. He has engaged D. M. Lipscomb to assist him.
We are running here on one shift; and, on account of the rains, it will probably be several days before we can start on both shifts.
Lancaster has started on one shift and possibly can go ahead that way this week.
Marion is running on both shifts.
I sold Swift direct two tanks oil to-day at 74. We are keeping the oil moved out as made and purchases covered.
I spoke to Mr. Lawton about buying the West Union and Rock Hill mills, but he said he did not think he would be interested at the present, unless he was sure that business was going to be better. He thought the Rock Hill lease might not be so bad, if we could get it at $10,000 and the taxes.
The option at West Union expires the 24th. What do you think we had better do about this? If you should decide to buy it, I think I should first go there and see the two gins from which we have arranged to handle the seed on commission and from which Mr. Darby has been buying for several years, as we would want some assurance, at least, that we would continue to get that business.
I am inclosing letters from Matheny regarding the exchange. I have talked to Evans, Buckeye, Charlotte, and he stated that while he had let Mr. Robins have some money on his gin, that he was an independent buyer; but that he would do what he could to keep him from storing seed or offering even exchange.
I sent Joe in that section and told him to see Lattimore Oil Mill, particularly, and the independent gins, and explain to them the trouble that might come from the storage and the excessive exchange.
I think that Matheny may be a little unduly excited; and I believe if we will wait a little while we can get the matter straightened out.
Regarding Matheny's brother helping him at Forest City, you will doubtless want to see and talk to him, so I am not replying to this letter. I believe, however, that we should get some one there who will do the work, keep up with it, at less expense than Mr. Newman; and then, too, it seems to take Newman entirely too long to do anything and to get us the information we should have.
Yours very truly, fec-t.
Vice President.
KINGSTREE, S. C., September 28, 1929.
KERSHAW OIL MILLS, Kershaw, S. C.
GENTLEMEN: The reason that I have been unable to buy any more seed is that Mr. J. L. Brockington is paying $32 per ton for wagon seed. He is buying independently and accepting seed from farmers, storing same, and will ex INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY I change with his customers when they get ready to settle at whatever the market price is.
The gins are buying seed for $30 per ton, and unless the street buyers can I pay more, the farmers will sell to the gin.
I hate not to get business; but if you will advance me, say $30 per ton, I will buy the seed, paying the difference myself, and store and insure until the market advances. I think one of the companies is furnishing Mr. Brockington. If your representative is in this territory will be glad if he calls to see me.
E. C. BURGESS.

Mr. W. F. MARSH, EXHIBIT NO. 875 OCTOBER 10, 1929.
Secretary, North Carolina Cottonseed Crushers' Association, Raleigh, N. C.
DEAR SIR: You will remember while we were in Charlotte, considerable discussion and complaint by Mr. Hamrick, of the Lattimore Oil Mill, Lattimore, N. C., regarding an even exchange that a Mr. Crowder, who operates a gin very near Lattimore, was giving. You will remember these seed were going to the Southern Cotton Oil Co., Shelby, and the meal coming from them. Mr. Hamrick was not satisfied, as you noted, with Mr. Jenkins's statement of this. I think it will be well, just as soon as you can spare Eugene, to let him go straight to Lattimore; see Mr. Hamrick, and see if he can not get this matter straightened out.
I sent one of our men up there, but have not as yet received his full report on this.
If this is not stopped in some way, it will affect that entire territory. Lattimore and Mooresboro are very close together, Crowder's gin being only a very short distance from Mooresboro. If it spreads to Mooresboro, it will probably spread to the Forest City territory; so we are anxious, if possible, to get this straightened out.
With kind regards, I am Yours truly, fec-t.
Vice President.
Montgomery, Ala., July 18, 1929.
Mr. FRED E. CULVERN, Vice President, Kershaw, S. C.
I have been absent from Montgomery most of the time recently, in connection with gin financing for the Montgomery mill. We have taken on quite a number of gins, and it has been a job to get property titles straightened up to the satisfaction of attorneys.
Most of this work has now been completed and we are looking for a big increase in our crush. If the crop does not deteriorate too much we hope to crush 30,000 tons at Montgomery.
Yours very truly, E. T. ALLEN, Treasurer.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY DECEMBER 28, 1929.
Mr. R. W. YOUNG, Manager Alabama Cotton Oil Co., Huntsville, Ala.
DEAR SIR: On yesterday I wrote you regarding the claims to be made on cottonseed, since which time I have been giving careful thought to this ques tion, and I find from inquiry that our competitors are having exactly the sam experience.
Therefore, I find that we will have to return to the old rule basis for deductions for quality, and if we can not buy cottonseed on this basis, it will be best not to buy them; though it is my impression that all the mills will return to the old basis through necessity.
I have figured as closely as I could the probable actual losses we will sustain on the seed represented by the 46 samples, and I have reached the conclusion that we will have claims for quality, and for low oil yield, equal to $5.50 per ton. The Meloy claim would have allowed us $2.48 per ton.
Therefore, please adopt the old rule, and if it is not entirely clear to you exactly how to handle the old rule, please advise me. I think, however, that you understand it.
I should be very glad to hear from you as to whether you will have any difficulty in handling this matter as suggested.
Yours very truly, ETA: AB.
Copy to Mr. Fred E. Culvern, Kershaw, S. C.
Treasurer.
DECEMBER 31, 1929.
Mr. E. T. ALLEN, Montgomery, Ala.
DEAR SIR: We are in receipt of your favor of the 28th instant, with reference to claims on cottonseed that we are receiving at our mill, and for your information we have for several days before receiving your letter been using the old rule, as we felt confident that it would ruin us to figure by the new rule. Of course, we have some kicks with reference to the claim; however, we believe we satisfy the customer before leaving our office.
We believe that we can use the old rule on all seed and keep our seed shippers satisfied.
Yours very truly, y-s.
Copy to Mr. Fred E. Culvern, Kershaw, S. C.
ALABAMA COTTON OIL Co., Manager.
JANUARY 15, 1930.
Mr. E. T. ALLEN, Treasurer, Montgomery, Ala.
DEAR SIR: With reference to the off meal about which you are writing Mr.
Young, is it not possible to sell it to the local fertilizer people to a better advantage than to ship it off. We have found generally around our mills that the local fertilizer people, or the big farmers, will use this meal at $1, $1.50, or at most $2 off of the price of prime meal. No doubt a good many of the big farmers will be using meal in their fertilizers more than usual on account of its being cheap.
Regarding the second cuts on hands there, make an extra effort to dispose of these. You have made a light cut of seconds, and it looks like some of the mattress people would be interested in them at a reasonable price.
The first cut market is dull, and we have not offered ours in this section at less than 5 cents, although on firm offer we might sell at 52 cents. We have declined 5 cents.
Recently Mr. Young advised that he had a great deal of old stock, flues.
motes, etc., stored from last season. This is expensive, so I hope it can soon be moved, together with the lint.
Yours truly, fec-t.
Copy to Mr. R. W. Young, manager, Huntsville, Ala.
Vice President.

This agreement, made and entered into this 17th day of June, in the year 1926, between the Lancaster Cotton Oil Co., of Lancaster, S. C., party of the first part, and J. H. Mills Son, of Inman, rural free delivery No. 3, South Carolina, party of the second part, witnesseth: First. That this agreement is to apply to transaction in the shipping of cottonseed from the date hereof until canceled as per clause 9.
Second. The Lancaster Cotton Oil Co., party of the first part, is to issue, from time to time, quotations fixing the price of seed, and the latest quotation issued is to remain of force until it is withdrawn or another quotation is issued changing the price.
Fourth. The party of the second part agrees to report every day to the Lan caster Cotton Oil Co., party of the first part, the total amount of seed on hand purchased for the account of the party of the first part, which seed are to be considered from the date of such report as the property of the Lancaster Cotton Oil Co., party of the first part, at the price then ruling as per their quotation.
The seed to be shipped in as soon as a carload is obtained and empty cars can be had in which to ship.
Fifth. All seed are to be shipped in carload lots of 10 tons or more and must be sound and dry.
Sixth. All seed are to be carefully weighed on the track scale of the Lancaster Cotton Oil Co., party of the first part, and be paid for according to their weights; provided, however, the railroad company's weights may be obtained at the instance of the party of the second part and settlement made as per such weights, a comparison of the gross weights of the Lancaster Cotton Oil Co., party of the first part, and those of the railroad company being the basis of settlement.
Seventh. In case the Lancaster Cotton Oil. Co., party of the first part, sees fit to make advances in money to the party of the second part, such funds are to remain the property of the Lancaster Cotton Oil Co., party of the first part, until they have been expended for seed, and are to be considered as trust money to be used exclusively in the purchasing of seed and for no other purpose what soever. In no case are the funds of the Lancaster Cotton Oil Co., party of the first part, to be advanced by the party of the second part for seed for future delivery, but are to be paid out only upon the delivery of the seed to the party of the second part. Any products or supplies shipped open to the party of the second part by the party of the first part shall be regarded the same as trust money.
Eighth. It is expressly understood that there is to exist no verbal understanding between the parties of this agreement affecting advances, prices, and the like. Any agreement to be made not covered by this instrument or the regular quotation of the Lancaster Cotton Oil Co. are to be evidenced by an instrument in writing duly executed. Commission to be $3 per ton on all local wagon or gin seed bought on quotations of the Lancaster Cotton Oil Co. and shipped them.
Ninth. Either party to this agreement may terminate same by giving notice in writing of a desire so to do, provided the accounts between the parties to this agreement have been settled in full as per terms thereof.
This contract covers buying seed at gin at Holly Spring and at gin in county now building near Campobello, S. C.
In witness whereof the said parties above named have duly signed and sealed these presents, in duplicate, on the day and year first above written.
LANCASTER COTTON OIL CO., By W. G. TAYLOR, Treasurer and Manager.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY COTTONSEED SHIPPERS AGREEMENT WITH KERSHAW OIL MILL, KERSHAW, 8. C.
This agreement, made and entered into this in the year nineteen hundred and of Kershaw, S. C., party of the first part, and of day of between the Kershaw Oil Mill, of the second part.
party Witnesseth, first. That this agreement is to apply to transaction in the shipping of cottonseed from the date hereof until canceled as per clause 8.
Second. The Kershaw Oil Mill, party of the first part, is to issue, from time to time, quotations fixing the price of seed, and the latest quotation issued is to remain of force until it is withdrawn or another quotation is issued, changing the price.
Third. The party of the second part agrees to report every day to the Kershaw Oil Mill, party of the first part, the total amount of seed on hand purchased for the account of the party of the first part, which seed are to be considered from the date of such report as the property of the Kershaw Oil Mill, party of the first part, at the price then ruling as per their quotation.
The seed are to be shipped in as soon as a carload is obtained and empty cars can be had in which to ship.
Fourth. All seed are to be shipped in carload lots, of 10 tons or more, and must be sound and dry.
Fifth. All seed are to be carefully weighed on the track scales of the Kershaw Oil Mill, party of the first part, and he paid for according to their weights; provided, however, the railroad company's weights may be obtained at the instance of the party of the second part and settlement made as per such weights-a comparison of the gross weights of the Kershaw Oil Mill, party of the first part, and those of the railroad company being the basis of settlement.
Sixth. In case the Kershaw Oil Mill, party of the first part, sees fit to make advances in money to the party of the second part, such funds are to remain the property of the Kershaw Oil Mill, party of the first part, until they have been expended for seed, and are to be considered as trust money to be used exclusively in the purchasing of seed and for no other purpose whatsoever.
In no case are the funds of the Kershaw Oil Mill, party of the first part, to be advanced by the party of the second part for seed for future delivery but are to be paid out only upon the delivery of the seed to the party of the second part. Any products or supplies shipped open to the party of the second part by the party of the first part shall be regarded the same as trust money.
Seventh. It is expressly understood that there is to exist no verbal understanding between the parties of this agreement affecting advances, prices, and the like. Any agreement to be made not covered by this instrument or the regular quotation of the Kershaw Oil Mill are to be evidenced by an instrument in writing duly executed. Commission to be per ton on all local wagon or gin seed bought on quotations of the Kershaw Oil Mill, and shipped them.
Eighth. Either party to this agreement may terminate same by giving notice in writing of a desire so to do; provided the accounts between the parties to this agreement have been settled in full as per terms thereof.
In witness whereof the said parties above named have duly signed and sealed these presents, in triplicate, on the day and year first above written.
By KERSHAW OIL MILL, (L. &.) WITNESS: Approved by Date Manager.
Whereas the laws of South Carolina prohibit all arrangements, contracts, agreements, trusts, or combinations tending to lessen full and free competition and tending to control and depress prices and declare such combinations, arrangements, and trusts to be against public policy, unlawful, and void; and Whereas there is widespread notorious evidence of flagrant violations of these laws by persons and corporations engaged in crushing cottonseed and in the cottonseed oil mill industries, causing enormous losses and hardships to farmers of the State; and Whereas it is the duty of the attorney general, upon complaint being made to him, to begin actions against such persons, combinations, trusts, or corporations violating these provisions: Therefore be it Resolved by the House of Representatives of the General Assembly of the State of South Carolina, That complaint is hereby made to the attorney general that the provisions of article 14 and other sections of the code of laws prohibiting combinations, trusts, or corporations in restraint of trade are ap parently being notoriously violated in that the price of cottonseed has been and is being arbitrarily fixed so as to destroy the influence of competition; be it further Resolved, That the attorney general is hereby instructed to immediately investigate and ascertain whether or not there is any violation of any of the antitrust and antimonopoly laws of this State and to continue such investigation throughout the next cotton-ginning season, and to take the necessary legal steps to prevent and punish all violations of these laws, and to invoke the aid of the courts to protect the people of the State against all conspiracies in restraint of trade; be it further Resolved, That the attorney general is further instructed to report to the house of representatives on the first day of the next session of the general assembly the result of his investigations and the steps taken in pursuance thereof.
J. WILSON GIBBES, Clerk of the House.

This agreement, entered into this day of 19-, between Hartsville Oil Mill, Hartsville, S. C., hereinafter referred to as the Oil Company, party of first part, and of the county of party of the second part, hereinafter State of referred to as the second party: Witnesseth: That the parties hereto have contracted and agreed as follows: First. The Oil Company hereby employs the second party, and the second party accepts such employment, to purchase sound cottonseed for the Oil Company, at during the season beginning 192, and this contract shall continue season to season in full force, but may be rescinded or terminated at any time by either party, by notice to the other party.
Second. The second party shall receive as compensation a commission of dollars $- per ton of cottonseed bought in less than carload lots and shipped to the Oil Company under this agreement. It being understood and agreed that second party is to pay all loading charges, and all other expenses connected with handling the seed.
Third. The Oil Company will give the second party quotations and instruc tions with reference to purchasing sound cottonseed, and the second party will give his diligent efforts to purchasing such seed for his employer within these quotations and under these instructions, and will make daily written reports of all seed purchased, stating actual quantities and cost of each load purchased in such manner and on such forms as may be required by the Ol Company, and if at any time he succeeds in purchasing seed at prices below the existing quotations, the Oil Company shall receive the benefit of the lower price.
Fourth. The second party shall not report as received any seed unless it has actually been delivered and has been deposited in the storage place controlled by the Oil Company. The second party agrees not to purchase any seed for future delivery unless specifically authorized to do so by the Oil Company, in which event the quantity so purchased, price, and time of delivery must be immediately reported to the Oil Company.
Fifth. If the Oil Company can make satisfactory arrangements whereby cash seed tickets can be cashed in the town where the seed is purchased, the Oil Company may, at its option, require the second party to use such seed purchase tickets in settlement with the sellers of seed, but if this local cashing of seed tickets can not be satisfactorily arranged to the Oil Company, then in that event the Oil Company will advance such sums of money as it deems proper to the second party, and it is mutually understood and agreed and the second party hereby contracts, that such funds so advanced, whether in money or payment of seed tickets herein referred to are trust funds to be held, used, and accounted for under the direction and control of the Oil Company and are to be used only in the purchase of sound cottonseed, as herein provided, for the account of the Oil Company. All shipments of cottonseed products made by the Oil Company to the second party are to be considered the same as an advance of money, and all moneys received from the sale of said products and all cottonseed purchased with the same, belong to and are held in trust for the Oil Company by the second party and subject to the order of the Oil Company.
Sixth. The Oil Company provides a house or other appropriate place, with locks, for the storing of seed when purchased by the second party, and scales for weighing such seed purchases, which the second party hereby agrees are suitable for the purpose for which provided, and are now in good order. And INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY all seed shipped into the Oil Company shall be weighed at such point as the Oil Company may designate. The second party hereby guarantees his weights.
Seventh. It is understood and agreed by both parties to this contract, that where the second party furnishes the warehouse for the storage of said cottonseed, the Oil Company will pay to said second party a rental at the rate of 6 cents per annum for square foot of floor space used, and where the second party furnishes scales, the Oil Company will pay to said party a rental of $10 per annum for the use of said scales.
Eighth. The second party agrees to keep the seed purchased and on hand at all times under lock and key, and shall see that the scales are kept in good order and are frequently balanced.
Ninth. The second party further agrees to ship seed as directed by the Oil Company and upon notice, to complete shipment immediately of all seed reported purchased and received in storage, thereby entirely emptying seed storage house of seed and effecting a clean-up.
Tenth. On seed bought in car lots a brokerage of 50 cents per ton will be paid, it being understood and agreed that such shipments will be subject to mill inspection and mill weights.
Eleventh. The second party agrees that, during the existence of this contract, he will not purchase or sell cottonseed for or on account of any other person, firm, or corporation, or on his own account, unless authorized by the Oil Company.
Twelfth. It is distinctly understood that this contract does not become finally binding until ratified by the president of the Hartsville Oil Mill, Hartsville, S. C.
In witness whereof this contract has been signed in duplicate this day of 19-.

Eleventh. The second party agrees that, during the existence of this contract, he will not purchase or sell cottonseed for or on account of any other person, firm, or corporation, or on his own account, unless authorized by the Oil Company.
Twelfth. It is distinctly understood that this contract does not become finally binding until ratified by the president and treasurer of the Greenville Cotton Oil Mill (Inc.).
In witness whereof this contract has been signed in triplicate this day of 19.
