EXHIBIT NO. 881 INTERSTATE COTTONSEED CRUSHERS ASSOCIATION, Columbia, S. C., July 4, 1928.
To the members of the executive committee.
GENTLEMEN: In compliance with second paragraph of my letter to you of July 3, in re hauling." Upon my return from Asheville I found that some of the outstanding crude-mill operators in this State were convinced that the action taken by the committee would open the door to an extremely bad practice which is not present in South Carolina except in very isolated instances. Certain of these operators have been to see me, and without attempting to set out in detail their position, some of the outstanding points they make can be stated as follows: 1. That the question of allowing hauling or drayage is nothing new. It was generally paid here twenty-odd years ago, and then proved such an irritant to the oil mills and to a majority of their customers, to whom its operation could not be explained, that it was considered such a prolific source of trouble that it was cut out and has not been followed since.
2. That in its last analysis it means a delivered price for seed, and some contend not the same delivered price to every individual in the same mill town, which, if true, necessarily prevents the publication of a uniform f. o. b.
price, etc., which is one of the main objects of the code.
3. These gentlemen point out that in certain sections the mills were opposed to any statement as to commission for wagon or gin buyers, and that in deference to that opinion all reference thereto was omitted from the code.
They feel that a similar situation exists in South Carolina as to hauling and drayage, and feel that any statement of it in the code would open a door which could not be closed by any fiat of the executive committee.
4. In any event, they ask for an opportunity to present their position fully to the executive committee before any statement is given out.
The men who came here to see me were practical operators who are strongly in favor of the code but feel that the hauling allowance is a pernicious practice and would make the practical working of the other provisions of the code almost impossible. I was so much impressed with their position that I felt it wise to omit any statement on hauling or drayage in letter sent the industry, pending further consideration by the committee.
Trusting this meets your approval, I am, Yours sincerely, C. B.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Mr. J. J. LAWTON, EXHIBIT NO. 882 MEMPHIS, TENN., December 2, 1927.
In care of Hartsville Oil Mill, Hartsville, S. C.
I am still of the opinion that both cotton and cotton oil will sell higher later on, though I will admit that the evidence is against me right at the present time.
I have no doubt that there is a concerted action on the part of the spinning world to get cheap cotton, and they are harping every kind of propaganda to bring about this result. They are claiming that there will be a big increase in acreage, that the mills are not doing any business, that manufactured goods are piling up on them, etc., but this is all to effect cheaper cotton prices, in my opinion.
So far as oil is concerned, the refiners know exactly what they are doing; they know that none of their number is going out and bid higher prices than the agreed price, and they feel content to sit back, knowing that the oil mills in the South are all holding oil on account of the high price of seed. This can go on for a while, but consumption is still going on and it is only a question of time before they will have to come in and bid for oil, and when they do, in my opinion, the market will advance very rapidly.
As to the size of the crop, I agree with you; it will surprise me if the final ginning totals 12,600,000. During the last day or two the market has been very weak, and at one time 82 cents was the best bid price in the valley, but, so far as we know of, no oil was sold at that figure. To-day we are bid 84 cents for immediate or December oil and can sell February oil at 9 cents.
With kind regards, I am, Yours very truly, W. P. BATTLE.
NOVEMBER 29, 1927.
Mr. W. P. BATTLE, Memphis, Tenn.
I note what you have to say about the price of cotton. I do not believe the crop will go above 12,500,000 bales, and under ordinary conditions that should mean high-priced cotton. There is a tremendous bear propaganda that has been put on by the cotton mills that is having its effect upon the market. They are contending that goods are being banked up in their warehouses and can not be sold at a profitable price. My answer is that you can hardly expect to bull the goods and bear the product out of which the goods is made, but that is what the cotton-mill people are doing.
As to the price of oil, one trouble seems to me is the tremendous amount of oil that is held in the valley and in the West in the shape of crude. These refiners know how many tanks each one of us has and how much oil there is in them, and it seems to me they are just waiting to see if they can not squeeze out this oil at their price.
With kind regards and best wishes, I am, Yours truly, INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Mr. J. J. LAWTON, Hartsville, S. C.
EXHIBIT NO. 883 FARMERS GINNERS COTTON OIL Co., Birmingham, Ala., May 21, 1929.
MY DEAR MR. LAWTON: It was in my mind before reaching New Orleans to pick out six or eight of the prominent independent mill people in Alabama, Georgia, North and South Carolina, to discuss with them the future outlook of the independent cotton-oil companies, afterwards deciding to wait until after convention to approach the subject.
The independents are rapidly falling by the wayside. What can be done, if anything, to help them to survive during what looks like a reconstructive period?
The Federal free trade practice act may or may not help them.
Some may think it best to fight it out and let the weak fall and the strong grow stronger. I shall be willing only to take this viewpoint after having been convinced by the more important ones in the independent industry that this course is fair and right. I believe there is a place for the independent mill operator, that he is a distinct asset to the country in general. I do not believe that he can and will survive the next two years unless he completely changes his methods of operation. Some must become seed agencies-others stronger must improve their basis of operation.
Including all cost, a ton of seed must be done for $6 per ton, and what I mean by this is to include stamps, tags, brokerage, sacks, bagging, ties, and all other costs chargeable to a ton of seed.
I have been making a careful study of how to do this cost when seed are scarce on a 12-hour day operation. We have put through 25 tons of seed per press this season, a total working cost to April 1 of $5.65. I have asked a number of independent mills their cost to April 1, and where the same basis of calculation is used their expense runs about $9 per ton. Those in the business who have kindred industry, which can be used in supporting their mills may, over the next two years at least, figure no greater difference than $6 per ton, unless the Federal Trade Commission intervenes.
Consider the effect also of an independent organization. They might be able to make an impressive stand in the minds of other interests.
Would it be well to get together all of the independents in the sections named and undertake to work out each others' problems, or will it be best to let them perish or survive as may be the case?
I am writing several for their views and hold myself in readiness to aid if possible. On our basis of operation to April 1 we had an earning of $1.92 per ton. I think we can pass through this construction period referred to, but I am wondering if it is possible to attempt it single handed or to try to work collectively with my independent mill friends.
I shall thank you for your careful and considerate reply.
Yours very truly, T. J. KIDD, General Manager.

CAROLINA COTTON LINTER CORPORATION, Charlotte, N. C., August 30, 1929.
DEAR MR. LAWTON: Last season you stated to me very frankly that you would not trade with me on account of my not being a member of the Interstate Association and because William Fraser, jr. (Inc.), had failed to abide by an award of an arbitration committee, which was afterwards settled. I am writing to ask if this same position will be continued by you the coming season. I hope not.
I want to preface my statement by stating that I appreciate your friendship in the past. I have been accused of many things, but never to my knowledge for lack of loyalty and courage.
I want to talk frankly about my position and the manner of imposition imposed upon me by the association and some members. If the membership of the association knew the position I have been placed into they would not stand for it, I don't believe; therefore I have to let them know it.
William Fraser, jr. (Inc.), is a distinct entity in law.
William Fraser, jr., is an individual.
William Fraser, jr. (Inc.), has never had but one award against them by any arbitration committee. This award was settled by compromise and every nickel paid. This was the Consumers Cotton Oil Co. case. William Fraser, jr. (Inc.), had many arbitrations brought by them against oil mills, and William Fraser, jr. (Inc.), can prove in any court of law that they were right in two of these cases.
When I called upon Mr. Benet to get him to lay my case before the executive committee he did as requested, and the committee refused to act. Do you know why? I will tell you. Because Mr. Stevenson, of the Consumers Cotton Oil Mill, told the executive committee that the award had been settled satisfac tory and paid, but it was not satisfactory to the Consumers Co. for me to be reinstated. What do you think of this kind of man? Would you call him straightforward?
There is a letter in a certain chain oil-mills offices advised them not to trade with me. This is boycott. Restraint of trade. No other conclusion can be reached. The association is and has crushed me personally financially for the deeds of William Fraser, jr. (Inc.), when in fact William Fraser, jr. (Inc.), has been right in their actions.
I have never nor has William Fraser, jr. (Inc.), brought a lawsuit against any oil mill. William Fraser, jr. (Inc.), had two lawsuits instituted against them. One case, a directed verdict, was given in favor of William Fraser, jr.
(Inc.); the other case was decided by the judge in a court of equity and William Fraser, jr. (Inc.), given a verdict on every point.
Few linter dealers are members of the association. You trade with many that are not members, still you won't trade with me because I am not a member INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY My greatest offense has been my honesty of purpose-courage of my convictions. Because of these principles I am a party unfit-unclean-to deal with.
What must I do? Fold my arms across my breast and bow and scrape myself in a subservient manner to these people, who are lying to themselves when they pose as my superior? I am not lying to myself. I shall not attempt it.
What shall I do-defend myself as long as life lasts, to the bitter end. I have sought out every means except law to get the matter right. Now for the first time I go to law. The case has been given to attorneys and I shall now see what my rights are.
The main purpose of this letter is to give you the facts as they are and not take any unfair advantage of you because of your position in the matter.
With kindest regards to both you and Mr. Jordan, I am, Yours very truly, WM. FRASER, Jr.

NEW YORK CITY, March 27, 1928.
DEAR MAGUIRE: Hutch wired me about attending a meeting in Atlanta Friday, to which I replied that I could not be there on that date, but if the meeting were held Monday or Tuesday I could make it. Of course, if he has called the meeting for Friday he can not change the date, nor would I expect him to do so for my convenience, but I was not sure whether the date was fixed or tentative, so I wired him as I did.
If you want to attend, go ahead. Be sure, however, not to let any proposition pass which may be objectional or against our interest. These big meetings do not always express the real sentiment, as one or two ringleaders often can put something over, as the rank and file very seldom have clear cut enough convictions to express them intelligently, for one thing, and things are sometimes resoluted because there is lack of courage on the part of anyone to start opposition.
Another point I am rather positive of is that there should not be one kind of sauce for the goose and another for the gander. Whatever is done should apply to all alike or apply to none. I feel sure you have my sentiments in mind, and you can therefore assume whatever attitude seems best for our interests.
Yours truly, W. H. JASSPON.

Mr. J. E. CROWDER, Strother, S. C.
Several mills in this State have busted with stored seed. It is not like storing cotton, as the cotton can be delivered back in the same bales as stored and set aside, while seed are in bulk, liable to heat and not easily handled, and have more loss in handling than cotton. You would have no bonded warehouse receipt for seed as you would cotton.
I talked with a mill manager this afternoon that has stored some seed and he advises that he has required seller to call at least 30 days ahead of time he shut down and reserved the right to deliver the seed, in which event shipper would have to pay freight to his plant if seed are sold elsewhere at a higher price than he wanted to pay.
We would like to help you, but believe we will stay better friends longer to keep our trades clear where no misunderstandings may arise, and from what we have heard of mills that stored seed it has not been satisfactory.
We will give you at all times the very best trade for your seed possible; we have gone back to $1.40 per 100 pounds for wagon and gin seed and $31 per ton for prime car seed to-day and will exchange meal for seed at $34.44 per tou delivered your station; if you want any hulls, we will be glad to quote you our best price on either bulk or sacked either for exchange or straight purchase.
There is no better meal we know of than ours; it will please both your customers and yourself.
Believe you will have a better market for your seed to keep them there where, if you do not get what you want from one mill, you can try others; you will not find other mills so keen to buy seed stored with some mills when they know it and you would have to tell both the mill you have it stored with and the buying mill would know it, too.

AUGUST 31, 1928.
Hon. CHRISTIE BENET, Columbia, S. C.
DEAR SENATOR BENET: I am inclosing a copy of a letter to Acree. He wrote me that several had come to him and expressed themselves as what I said was to the point on Wednesday, and asked that I write him my views fully, and I have gotten a good deal out of my system in this letter, whether it is worth anything or not. It covers the troubles and other evils as I see them.
I want to see the code practices adopted as made and think this referring them back to States was a mistake. We can not operate successfully with every State trying to interpretate the code to suit themselves, and I favor everything coming under the interstate and having an interstate interpretating committee.
You have given yourself over to this and have had the help of the best talent in the business, and I think we should take it up and handle it just as if it was required by Federal Trade Commission until they approve or disapprove any part or all of it. If we waver we will not get anywhere. Any weakening will be taken advantage of and cause more trouble than if we had not tried anything.
I am writing and sending you this in confidence, not to be divulged but as information for your work.
Yours very truly, Mr. J. B. CALDWELL, SOUTH CAROLINA COTTONSEED CRUSHERS' ASSOCIATION, Spartanburg, S. O.
Columbia, S. C., September 3, 1928.
Personally, I am in hearty accord with your position, and I understand that Mr. Procter is taking somewhat your position on having one interpretation committee. It is my understanding that Senator Benet is to be home Wednesday and that the executive committee of the interstate will have a meeting on the 10th. I do not suppose that the executive committee will act as the interstate interpretation committee, but that it will advise the appointing of such a committee composed of several crude millers from each State. It is also my understanding that the nationalization of the interstate association contemplates that the State associations will be branches of the interstate. The attorneys are now trying to investigate the laws of the different States to see if there is any legal obstacle in the way of such a plan.
You will note, however, that the interstate interpretation committee and the nationalization scheme are to be completed some time in the future, while the season is now upon us and it appears that somebody will have to interpret the Memphis resolutions now rather than to put it off to some indefinite time.
I agree that the declaration in the Memphis resolutions to the effect that we will pay a fair price for seed and labor and sell our products at a fair price must be lived up to or the code will certainly be unworkable. The opinion of most mills, however, who are buying seed at the present prices is that they are losing money. Fishburne had 11 analyses on his desk the other day which showed an average moisture content of 19.75 per cent, oil 17.10 per cent, ammonia 3.05 per cent, which he says means 262 pounds of oil available and only 870 pounds of $7 meal. Fishburne figures there is only $42.95 gross value in a ton of seed which yields no more meal and hulls than above stated and, as you see, certainly leaves no profit and most likely a loss. Naturally you are not bothered with such a situation at this time because you are not buying, but those who are think the market price $3 or more too high.
You will be appointed on the South Carolina interpretation committee, and I am trying to arrange for a meeting of it on Thursday or Friday of this week.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Please hold yourself in readiness to attend. Some of the level-headed ones think we would lose more than we gain in getting rid of brokerage with all of its past evils, if it in its stead the industry pays excessive salaries. It is this particular feature that will be discussed at this meeting I am trying to arrange, and I hope also by that time to have a list of the exclusive 50-cent buyers, for which I have asked, and it may be that some contracts for such buyers will have to be canceled.
Please be thinking about these matters and come to the meeting prepared to offer your usual constructive suggestions.
Yours very truly, RUSSELL AOREE, Secretary.
EXHIBIT NO. 893 AUGUST 31, 1928.
Mr. RUSSELL ACREE Columbia, S. C...
It is my opinion that if we would stick to the code of ethics as worked out and thrashed out in Memphis, with the help of and opinions of Judge Mcculloch and Senator Benet, and have a uniform set of trade practices, that we would eliminate a lot of questions that are bound to come up if each State continues to try to interpretate the different clauses of the code to suit their individual members. What we are doing is like building a house and tearing it down and building it over after we have had an architect and builder to build it just because we find some little things that every time we tamper with it, it will stand better if uniform than if each State undertake to change the different items, besides it has cost too much and there has been too much time and thought given it to keep monkeying with it.
The Food Administration's rules were uniform and everybody knew the Government was behind them, now it was generally understood that our code was to be fair to producers, mills, consumers, and labor, and our prices would be fair to all, giving the mills a fair profit; and when I do this I don't care what any particular seller of seed though it be in large lots can do or say and if the Federal Trade Commission sanctions what we have proposed then we are justified in sticking to it uniformly and the sellers will work better when they find we are stabilized than if we wabble around. Furthermore, if this could be done, it would stop the hauling charge in North Carolina.
I favor Interstate Crushers Association being the head organization with the State associations as divisions of same and eliminating these differences of rules or practices in each State, and instead of each having an interpretation committee that we have one committee, the interstate; this will take out the petty differences in each.
It is my opinion that trying to unravel questions that arise may afford those inclined some reason for making question trades. We should start the season right and under the code, and even if they have not been approved by Federal Trade Commission; we should stick to and use them just as promulgated unless they make some changes.
As stated yesterday, I was glad to see seed price raised to $30. I think it is important if we begin to work under the code that we do not make the seller feel that we are going to try to buy his seed too cheap, and a fair price now is most important-that is a part of the code-$27 would have caused a lot of kicking after seed sold at $50 last of season and would have encouraged speculation and criticism by the larger sellers.
The main thing in my opinion that causes more trouble is the anxiety of some of the larger crushers to tie up and control all the seed, and it seems evident to me that they want them all, that keeps all on their tiptoes to get tonnage and try to give every advantage they can to secure seed; if we were fair to each other as we should be the flow of seed would be more satisfactory and the industry move smoother; no man in the business that is alive is willing for a large competitor to romp all over him and those dominating the business by any large interest or interests is going to be expensive to the industry.
We have not the tonnage at our mills we once had, there are fewer mills, there are six gone out of business in this county, the tonnage has gone to the larger interests, now with our investment, taxes, and smaller tonnages with others INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY increasing theirs, but we had rather work a smaller tonnage on a fair margin if others would than to go after the larger tonnage regardless of how we get it.
We all have some sportsmanship and pride in us and don't want to be just figureheads in the business and I feel that these matters are of importance, and the vital points effecting our business and the rules should be fair to both small and large interests with no special privileges to anyone and if sanctioned by Federal Trade Commission we should not try to change them or interpret them to suit any interest or interests whether that be a large influential seed seller, a large crusher, or any other interest; nor do I believe the Federal Trade Commission should permit any interest to operate its mills at a loss and make it up on other items it might manufacture. How can this be at all fair to the crushing industry?
I am with you for cooperation if others cooperate and will ask no special privileges not granted others, but if hauling charges go on in North Carolina I shall feel we will be at liberty to allow our North Carolina buyers the same thing paid for hauling in North Carolina; that, as you can see, is where the importance of uniform code comes in.
Very truly yours, Mr. J. T. STODDARD, Owings, S. C.

APRIL 17, 1929.
DEAR SENATOR SMITH: We understand that the tariff revision will have to do with foreign vegetable oils and seeds and nuts producing oils and fats as well as meal.
If you have observed the crude oil mill industry in South Carolina for past 10 years you have noticed that numerous small mills that were built by home capital have had to go out of business all over the State and that new so-called independent mills are operating to-day, on the other hand, large interests like the Procter Gamble Co., Southern Cotton Oil Co., Swift Co., and others have refineries and soap plants, are expanding and getting control of this business, beginning with the financing by taking mortgages on gins in existence or financing new gins, getting control of seed at source.
We have only four buyers of our cottonseed oil and it is generally customary when the price of seed goes up quickly, as it frequently does, the price of oil goes down just about the time the crude mill has to sell oil to pay for seed, the refiners usually hedge their seed and oil purchases by sales of oil on New York or New Orleans exchanges, manipulating the markets in such way as to take in their hedges, just as they are now doing, so that their purchases average the lowest prices of the season.
The Procter Gamble Co. have been acquiring additional soap plants.
having bought the Globe Soap Co., Cincinnati, last fall or summer, arranging to build a big plant in Baltimore. Now, we understand, they have told the Federal Trade Commission that they have not made any money in crude mills for some years, but their net earnings each year mount up larger and larger. The soap concerns of the country are getting to be enormous concerns, the Palm Olive Co. merged with Peet and later Colgate and now under name of Colgate-Palm Olive Peet Co.
Southern Cotton Oil Co. bought Empire Cotton Oil Co. in Georgia, mills in Birmingham, refinery at New Orleans, and paid 100 per cent stock dividend and retired preferred stock. Swift bought several mills and refineries.
We understand that some of these are opposing the tariff on vegetable oils and claiming it will increase the cost of soaps, fats, etc., to the consumer, INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY they have for some years had the size of all cakes of soap reduced about 35 per cent from what they formerly were when they had more small soap makers and no doubt be a similar change in prices of other products, as well as the prices paid the producers for seed.
There should be, we think, a tariff on imports from the Philippines. We understand that coconut production and the manufacture of oil and cake there is controlled by the large interests of this country; they have us with our backs to the wall and fighting for our existence; of course, it is going to take time to eliminate some of the better entrenched, but it's being done, a few each season.
You know more about the protection our industry should and would have from tariff than I do, but ours is a southern industry and it should be so that home capital would have some protection from the large concerns with all kinds of ramifications.
Pardon the length of this letter, but I hope it will put our trouble in line for proper improvement or investigation.
Thanking you for anything you can do, I remain, Yours very truly, APRIL 19, 1929.
Hon. COLE L. BLEASE, United States Senate, Washington, D. C.
DEAR SENATOR BLEASE: We are both sides of the tariff question when it comes to cottonseed and oil business, we need that business protection on foreign oils, especially from Philippines, as that business has grown rapidly while ours has gone the other way as rapidly. The larger interests like Procter Gamble Co.
that make oils in soaps and lard compounds naturally want to keep the tariff off. We have heard that on recent investigation by Federal Trade Commission that they admitted losses for a number of years in the crude cotton oil mill end of their business, but their statements show large earning each year and they continue to buy soap plants and are now planning to build an enormous plant in Baltimore.
Competition in our business as manufacturers of cottonseed products has been very keen for past eight years, and it looks as if the larger interests are so manipulating the oil end as to put the crude mills out of business. There are now in South Carolina over 50 dormant mills that were built by. home capital.
The seed that these mills formerly crushed is going largely to large companies, as they are in position to finance gins and get their seed at the source, and when the seed price advances the refiners usually manage to get the oil market down about the time the crude mills have to sell to pay for seed. Most of the products the mills have on hand now were made from $50 seed, but prices have dropped so for past 30 days that there is no profit on $40 seed, probably buying in their hedges on oil market, which is reducing their cost price of their oil and contracts in, and want to show that in the face of anything favorable to the producer of seed or crude oil that they can buck the situation, as is the case of any legislation to help the producer of cotton.
We do business with only about four large refiners, and their interests and ours are opposite most of the time.
When it comes to tariff on jute or the use of cotton bagging we think it is against the farmers' interest, and we agree with the position as taken by Carolina Bagging Co.-a letter of whom we are inclosing-while they are interested in protecting their own business, still, it seems foolish to try to do something sentimental when it will cost the farmer money, and there is a lot of good sound sense in this letter even if it has been gotten out by a bagging concern that is interested.
Mr. Woodall, of Fort Worth, Tex., had an article out some months ago when this matter was first mentioned, calling attention to some of the facts stated in this letter and, too, that when Texas used cotton bagging some years ago on round bales and other cotton that it was found that the Germans used the cotton bagging by shredding it up in place of low-grade cotton and that out cotton, if it was practical and linters could be used for bagging it might be to our interest, but we hardly think that would be practical, as we have other markets for linters.
" It, therefore, appears to us that we are both sides of these questions. We would like to have a tariff on oils and nuts and foreign-oil bearing seeds for INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY our protection against these that hold our prices down, which are being produced. We understand, by concerns affiliated with some of the larger interests that are our competitors, and on the other hand we do not think a tariff on jute good for our farmers, as they would be the buyers of their own cotton, and can buy jute bagging so much cheaper and make some profit on selling it on their cotton.
These are questions we are very deeply interested in, and we think should not be passed up too lightly, as it means so much to us all in the South.
Pardon this lengthy letter. I thought when I started out I could set it out in a few words, but its really hard to find a stopping place. With kindest regards, I remain, Yours very truly, Pt.
Hon. CHRISTIE BENET, Columbia, S. C.
MAY 23, 1929.

Mr. RUSSELL ACREE, Memphis, Tenn.
June asked me to advise him in my letter as we talked Saturday night, and his stenographer had left, and as I always have mine with me I wrote him.
As to the code, I think there is more trouble with the industry craving tonnage than there is with the code. It seems to me that if we could get all States on a uniform basis, or at least the Southeast, it would be better.
My idea is that we started off too low and with too tight trading rules, including grading rules, and have wound up too high with the relaxation at the worst time. It would be better if we could have worked into some of the changes more gradual and held to what we undertook.
I am in favor of seed grading where seed are off a sufficient amount to dock but think a few cents per ton unsatisfactory, but there should be some unl versal method, using the difference nearest a dollar, and there should be some way of advising the seller as to the value before seed is shipped, as this seems to be what sellers demand, and since we have conceded this late in the season it is going to be a hard proposition to do otherwise until we get a more satisfactory basis.
I hope you will have a good meeting; only wish I was in position to attend, as I expect it to be very interesting, and no doubt the experience of past season has taught us all that the code is worth while when we get to working as we should.
If you have any time here on your return between trains, call me and I will meet you at station.
Yours very truly, Mr. RUSSELL ACREE, Columbia, S. C.

OCTOBER 20, 1928.
Mr. D. L. STEVENSON, Winnsboro, S. C.
DEAR Mr. STEVENSON: Yours of 18th inclosing letter of Mr. H. G. Strange to you received. We talked over phone since these were written, as explained it would be impossible for us to send Mr. Mcculloch to inspect each car of seed shipped us, and besides that would not be in accordance with our trade practice as grading is based on samples drawn at destination by disinterested party selected by the mill and county demonstration agent jointly who is to be fair in his sampling to all parties, the sample to be sent to disinterested chemist and he to figure the value based on prime seed at price delivered mill.
We think we have a reputation for fairness and believe your friends will fare as well in our hands as any mill they could ship, in fact if seed are prime there will be nothing to it except that grading has been approved by the United States Department of Agriculture and the majority of mills have voted in favor of it. We do not want to fight the proposition and it has not worked bad on any of our shippers to this time; of course, if seed are damaged, they are not worth as much as prime seed, and no seed are as good as they have been in former season and some are very bad.
The market is now $45 for prime seed. If Mr. Strange wants to ship us a car we will be glad to have you advise us and we will send you a contract covering same.
We have been a little slow to take any drastic steps as we realize that we have to regard our customers' interests, but it seems that practically all the mills are buying under these rules. Do not think Mr. Strange need be too apprehensive, and suggest that you reason with him to try us with one car; he can tell as well as our man could how the seed look, but nothing but a chemical analysis will reveal the actual value of the seed. Now, as to hauling to local buyer there, if he ships or sells in car lots to get the carload price, his seed, though sold through the party there, will be subject to grading just the same at the mill he ships to as they would to us.
If you get the car please wire us collect so that we can book the car in the event there is any market change. The oil market is weak and we do not expect seed to keep on advancing always; in fact there is no profit to-day in seed at present price, and we think all the mills are getting seed freely.
We are anxious to build up our business and don't want to do anything that is unfair, but it is important that we cooperate in a general way with the general trade practices of our business. Thanking you for writing us and hoping this makes it clear to you and Mr. Strange. Hoping to hear from you, CALDWELL Co.

ing promptly that you may trace same and forward to proper mill, as we do not mark our samples in this manner.
Referring to your analysis No. 505869, we had a wire from the refinery we shipped this tank of oil this p. m. that their analysis shows free fatty acid 2.5, loss 10, color 7.5, flavor prime, entitling them to an allowance of 0.0712 per hundredweight. If you will check this with your analysis, you will find considerable difference; of course, it is in our favor this time, but it makes big differences in settlements now since sellers' samples are not considered; in fact, we wonder sometimes what's the use keeping on sending oil samples to you under present rules; there is so much difference in results on samples drawn from same tank that it does not look like same oil; we can't understand it.
At our different meetings I have heard other mill managers commenting on the same thing, and there is considerable dissatisfaction expressed about this matter of differences in analysis since it is used as a basis of settlement. We like to know about how our oil is running so that when we get refinery analyses we will have some better idea, but if we bring in the analysis of our shipping sample it's hard to get any consideration; they question method of drawing, deterioration in transit, etc.
We have been told that on off oil its better to ship it quick as free fatty acid increases and claims will be heavier; that above tank was made in November from some heated seed, and we shipped it last week.
We had Rice and Tom samples made of same mixed lot of a car of seed last week. Rice figured it off 75 cents per ton; Tom figured it $2.01. We wrote Rice and sent him the analysis of Tom's, but how about our settlement with our customer? If the seed shippers find these wide differences on analysis used for settlement purpose, they will be quitting one mill for another and raising more sand still. I felt like writing you this.
You may feel I want to complain, but I want to help to get on a better basis.
Yours very truly, FEBRUARY 28, 1930.

NEW YORK CITY, September 4, 1929.
Mr. A. J. MAGUIRE, Augusta, Ga.
You apparently have a mistaken notion about the working of the rules. The gold rules never had anything to do with the rank and file of the trade outside of the oil mill business, and the new rules are nothing more than the old rules so applied that a large percentage of the people engaged in the industry will have to trade under them. You see a very large part of the tonnage located in Texas and Oklahoma never came into the Interstate when they raised their dues three or four years ago, and by tying up the rules so no one but members trading with members could use the arbitration privileges, it was hoped, and it has proved out, that most of the mills would come in.
In a way I feel as you do that there is not much to be gained by belonging to the association, as I think our standing individually and as a business is such that most everyone would accept our contract, though it might be that some would not, if they felt they did not have the advantage of the rules in case of trouble. Of course, I believe that we can not afford to do other than follow the crowd, and if the large interests join unanimously, we should also, as I do not think this is the time when we can afford to stand on the outside and be pointed to as being outside the pale.
The rules were never intended to apply to consuming customers, and after all, the great bulk of the products of cottonseed are handled through intermediates.
Yours truly, W. H. JASSPON.

Mr. W. H. JASSPON, New York.
Paragraph No. 1 means that, where a mill has their facilities, they can allow their representative to use the facility, but they are not allowed to build, buy, or rent facilities they do not now own. The thought is that all mills would like very much to dispose of their seed houses and scales and if no more are erected in the course of a few years, they will not own any.
Paragraph No. 5 means that a commission or salary buyer can not store seed for his account or for the account of his principal in the same building that he stores seed he buys for his principal.
Mr. Cain made an exception, stating that he did not think it would be possible for the mills to control a seed shipper as to the storing of cottonseed, he was to furnish his own storing facilities separate and distinct from the storage he uses for his principal. I do not agree with Cain as I believe we can handle 95 per cent of the shippers by simply giving them instructions.
Yours truly, AJM-MC.
EXHIBIT NO. 898 NEW YORK CITY, July 30, 1928.
Mr. A. J. MAGUIRE, Augusta, Ga.
DEAR MAGUIRE: I presume you have heard from Acree, or others, of the discussion which took place in Memphis, particularly on the hauling proposition.
I sided with Stevens and Lawton, because, while my position may be disadvantageous to our Montezuma mill in one way, yet the principle of allowing hauling charges will work against us at Augusta or any terminal mill.
We went through this hauling episode 25 years ago, and it took us many years to get rid of it. Of course, the situation is even more complicated in this day, with good roads and trucks. I appreciate, of course, that the hauling of cottonseed by trucks is a problem that has to be met, but my principal opposition was to accept the hauling principle for the country as a whole, in view of the fact that in certain sections like South Carolina we can handle the business on a basis more favorable to the oil mills if they pull together, and 1, therefore, aided in the movement to eliminate hauling from the code and INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY relegate the subject to each State, to be hauled as conditions in that State demand.
I wish you would please give this matter considerable attention and assume whatever position in the respective States is best suited for our interests.
I came away from the meeting very much impressed with Acree's judgment and ability, and I told him so. I also told him I was willing to spend more time in the southeast this season, because I could see from what was said and presumed that the situation is going to be a difficult one to handle.
The Buckeye are very much put out, I understand, over the North Carolina attitude on the hauling and expect to take steps to combat the situation in that State. It is my own idea that they do not contemplate losing any tonnage, and will do whatever is necessary to maintain their position. This is bound to complicate things, though there is not much use in anticipating the future too much, as sometimes our anticipated troubles are much greater than the actual Occurrence.
I believe the Southern are very much inclined to increase their business and to maintain their local situation by whatever methods are necessary. You have no doubt gotten some reflection of reaction on the seed situation in the two States, and I should like to have you write me what you know.
Yours truly, W. H. JASSPON.
AUGUST 2, 1928.
Mr. W. H. JASSPON, New York.
I have heard very little from the Memphis meeting, and do not know exactly what took place, but I was glad to see that the hauling was left out of the code. I have opposed hauling in any form at every time it has been mentioned. I think it is to our interest, regardless of Montezuma, to oppose hauling from a nonrailroad point in the country to either a mill town or a railroad station. I see no way to overcome the hauling from a railroad station to a mill town and believe this to be a handicap we will always have when competing with a local mill, but it is to our interest to object strongly to a hauling charge to be paid by a local mill from a strictly country point I have been unable to figure how they arrived at the conclusion that it is to their advantage to pay a hauling charge on business that will come to them without the additional cost.
As regards the Buckeye and the hauling charge. I think we are all right as regards the competition in Georgia and South Carolina. I feel sure they will continue to fortify themselves in all States so they can control the business at the source.
In North Carolina, I understand, they bought the Statesville and Mooresville mills as feeders and figured on buying the Forrest City mills, but for some reason the trade did not go through and Stevens bought this mill to get control of the ginnery.
The Southern in South Carolina may give more trouble than anyone else, Reynolds is feeling "his oats," and it is going to be hard for him to handle the business in South Carolina in one way and North Carolina another.
Yours truly, AJM-MC.
Mr. A. J. MAGUIRE, Augusta, Ga.
NEW YORK CITY, August 6, 1928.
DEAR MR. MAGUIRE: I telegraphed you this morning that I would be unable I will be the balance of the week, with possibly a few days in Dallas, and then to attend the Columbia meeting, because I was leaving for Memphis, where 1 to Atlanta, and probably Augusta. In the meantime please keep me advised of any developments which are of interest, either with reference to crop, markets, or seed situation.
You will notice that in the code a provision was inserted dealing with that legally the commission probably had no authority to enforce these proinvestigation OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY C visions of the code which the industry among themselves offered as measures which would right some of the situations which have existed, but the commission felt that they might have authority to exercise control of clandestine violations on the theory that if the industry accepts a code of practice and individuals secretly violate such a code, such individuals are really guilty of fraud on their competitors and the public and may therefore be subject to censure or other measures of control, the distinction being that where an individual openly announces that he will not live up to a certain provision of the code this was within his rights, and, as everyone was aware of his action, he would not be subject to any legal disability if such could be enforced.
I am writing you in detail about this feature, because I think it is of considerable importance.
I am naturally pleased that your views on hauling coincide entirely with the opinions I expressed on the subject at Memphis. It is beyond my conception of good business how a mill would be willing or anxious to pay for hauling seed to railroad points when such points are natural loading places, and the ginner must consider such hauling as part of the cost of his business operations. I feel that each State could handle this problem, and that where certain local conditions made hauling situation advisable and not against the interest of the industry in such a State exceptions might be worked out but the broad principle still applying.
I am of John Stevens's opinion that the way to bring pressure to bear against those who favor hauling is to openly announce that such situations will be met by advancing the car price to such an extent that competitive disability will be eliminated. You understand, of course, that I will stand right behind any positive position you assume, because I know in advance that such a position will be based on sound practice in its relation to our operations.
I am glad to feel that you do not look upon this hauling principle as one that will be detrimental to Montezuma. Of coure, wherever a local situation demands special consideration, whether it be ourselves or a competitor, I am in favor of such a situation being handled specifically, and not governed by a general principle which will not stand the test of actual trading.
Very truly yours, AUGUST 8, 1928.
Mr. W. H. JASSPON, Memphis, Tenn.
DEAR JASSPON: I attended the session in Columbia last night and we certainly had a long, hot meeting; started in about 8.30, and ended up about 3.30 this morning.
They found more to talk about than I thought it was possible to find in the few little paragraphs that go to make up the code. They tried to explain the various paragraphs of the code as they went along, giving their interpretation of the meaning.
I did object, however, to paragraph 8, which reads: "It is unfair competition to buy cottonseed in carload quantities except on weights and quality at mill destination." The interpretation of this clause meant that where you are buying seed in a local mill town the local mill can buy car lots of seed to be delivered to them by wagons and weigh up the wagonloads and settle for it, but the outside mill buyer is at a disadvantage, that he can not meet this competition; consequently, the outside mill buyers can not handle any car-lot seed in the local mill town.
We are not much interested in this, with the exception that we buy in a considerable number of towns in which Southern Cotton Oil Co. have dormant mills, and they have always claimed the rights to consider these as mill points and operate accordingly. Then, again, we expect to be in Bennettsville this year, and we may have to do some of this year's business at Bennettsville.
There was considerable discussion on the storing of cottonseed, which seemed agreeable to everyone with the exception of Johnson, of Rock Hill; he objected to this paragraph and put everyone on notice that he would not abide by it. He had always done this for his customers and would continue to do it.
Duncan, representing the Leesville mill, objected to everything; he claimed he was not in position to bind his company on the code.
Hauling came in for a lengthy discussion. I did not participate, as the others did enough discussing and handled it according to our views.
Reynolds, for the Southern Cotton Oil Co., made the statement that on account of instructions from his superior officers he could not do or say anything against hauling, and did not vote on the provisions which were construed to affect hauling. He made the statement that he was very much opposed to hauling in any form and that he would not allow any of the mills under his jurisdiction to haul seed. He further stated that his mills would not haul seed, but that if it should reach the point where he was forced into it, either by his company or competition, that he would put everyone on notice before he went into it.
The position of the Buckeye is that they will not haul seed in South Carolina unless they are forced to do it by competition, though Evans, from Charlotte, made the statement that Mr. Proctor has authorized the Charlotte mill to go into it thoroughly and protect themselves by buying as many trucks as they felt necessary to handle the business and protect their interest; if it took 100 trucks, they had authority to buy them. I think it is Mr. Proctor's idea to go into it as heavy as he can, and to make the hauling of seed so unprofitable to the mills they will stop it of their own accord. From what I can understand, the Buckeye pretty well broke up the storing of cottonseed last season by mak ing it unprofitable to everybody.
The only thing that I do not like is the attitude of Stevens. He was not at the meeting last night, but it is his present plan to not haul seed, but to pay the equivalent of his hauling to the carload price.
This hauling in North Carolina has certainly made a mess of the seed business in that State. It is too long to go into details or results from it, but it is proving very unsatis factory to a great many of the mills, and I am sure the smaller mills in the State have started something which is going to prove very unprofitable to them before they get through with it. As one instance, there is a gin about 3 miles from Clayton, N. C.; the seed should go to Clayton. There are four mills within a short radius of Clayton, with freight rates ranging from about 70 cents to $1.82 per ton; the hauling distance is practically the same to them all. For the Clayton mill to get this seed, which is right in their back door, they must pay this $1.82.
I do not think any other provisions in the code will affect us seriously; it will cause some inconvenience, but I think the benefits will exceed any inconvenience it may cause.
Yours truly, AJM-MC.

EXHIBIT NO. 904 APRIL 16, 1930.

DEAR SIR: I have your wire and wired you that Mr. Steinek would leave here Sunday night, which would put him in Memphis Monday morning. How long do you expect to run at Memphis?
The only reason for not wanting Mr. Steinek to leave here is for the reason that we are paying such a price for seed that it is essential that we get everything out of it that it is possible to get. In the meantime, I do not think there is any hope for the mills to reduce the limit they are paying for seed, for I understand the International Vegetable Oil, Savannah, has already charged out all its overhead expense for the year; they are working on the theory that any seed they can crush and get from it more than actual current working cost will be a profit to them. They claim they have made a small profit during the month of March, but I do not see how they could make it and also take care of the overhead.
With the present condition of the various markets, it would be better for us to go along as we are now going, buy what seed we can, and as much as we can through the summer and as long as we have our working cost, but I do not think we should buy seed to crush unless we have the full working cost.
The present outlook is for an increased acreage throughout our territory.
Was talking to a paint salesman, he travels all over the Carolinas, and he told me he noticed a lot of stubble land being broken. The fertilizer manufacturers have shot the cash price of fertilizer all to pieces and a great many of them have gone back to the credit business in which there is a big profit.
Yours truly, AJM-MC.
EXHIBIT NO. 905 NEW YORK CITY, April 16, 1928.
Mr. A. J. MAGUIRE, Augusta, Ga.
I think it is materially to our interest to work with the Buckeye and Swift on these trade-practice provisions, as our interests are more alike, and when the three of you agree on anything which should be done, it is quite likely to be done that way.
The terminal mills undoubtedly make the Georgia market, and I think that it is for the good of the industry that this be recognized. If the little mills could be made to understand that they can not get by with any sniping practices it would tend materially toward a more stabilized and uniform price of cottonseed in the territory.
The South Carolina plan is the best program. Of course, it may work out badly at times in certain localities, but at least you know what the market is, and half of our price troubles come about by reason of the fact that the mills INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY do not know what the market is, and without a uniform price on the seed there will always be trouble. I think this principle is recognized in Washington, and the theory of a trade-practice code is to make an open price so that everyone will know what the market is.
Yours truly, W. H. JASSPON.

Yours truly, EXHIBIT NO. 909 SOUTH CAROLINA COTTONSEED CRUSHERS' ASSOCIATION, Columbia, S. C., April 4, 1928.
DEAR SIR: Group meetings of the crude mills are now being held in the various sections of the belt, under the auspices of the interstate association, for the purpose of working out a code of business principles or fair-trade practices to be submitted to the Federal Government for its approval and permission to adopt.
Such a meeting from the four southeastern States was recently held in Atlanta at which a tentative draft was agreed upon, a copy of which is inclosed herewith. Please understand that it is tentative and subject to change. Nobody is or will be bound by it until the Government approves and a substantial majority of the crude mills adopt it. The writer thinks that the deductions for off-quality seed will be set out in detail and the maximum commissions to be paid wagon and gin seed buyers will also be specified. It may be that such deductions and commissions will vary in different sections of the belt, but they will very probably be specified for each section.
It is suggested, therefore, that, until further notified, no wagon or gin seed contracts be made or renewed which allow more than $3 per ton commission, which commission shall include all cost of loading, hauling, allowance for loss in weight, and all other expenses; and that on account of paragraph 7 of the tentative code, until further notified, no contracts of any description be made or renewed which allow a brokerage or commission for buying car seed.
It is expected at this writing that a meeting of this association will be held in Columbia Thursday, April 26, for the purpose of discussing the proposed code. We will advise you definitely later, but in the meantime please hold this date open.
Reports from all sections of the belt indicate a widespread interest in the code, and a belief that its adoption will work to the great good of all concerned.
Yours very truly, RUSSELL ACREE, Secretary.
NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION, SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION, Columbia, S. C., January 2, 1930.
GENTLEMEN: Please be advised that according to court decisions this office is not permitted to send out prices on products except where the trades have actually been concluded. In order to intelligently advise you of the current prices at which products are sold, this office must have reports from the mills.
It is also necessary that a majority of the mills at least report the prices at which they have sold products. It is just as important that you should know the current prices for products as it is to know the current prices for cottonseed; otherwise, you would be working in the dark in determining what price you should pay for the raw material.
The success of the association depends upon cooperation in the matter of reporting more than upon the maintenance of an office and secretary of the association. It will only cost you 2 cents to drop a line to this office at least twice a week naming the prices at which you have sold products and the price that you have paid for seed. If you will do this, we are sure that you would find the association much more valuable than it is at present.
I quote prices at which products have actually been sold in the last few days.

EXHIBIT NO. 910 NOVEMBER 17, 1928.
Mr. J. E. ROBERTSON.
SEED CONDITIONS You have already been advised our general car market is $46 per ton, which is supposed to be f. o. b. cars. We learn this morning the mills who are trucking seed are paying $40 at the ginhouse and that Sanford and the Kershaw interests are paying $46, plus $1 to load the seed. The exchange basis is supposed to be 2,150 pounds meal delivered, but mills are making a cash price delivered on meal that will give 2,200 pounds exchange on the $46 seed price.
We realize these prices for seed are entirely too high and are following your request that we buy seed from customers from whom we feel we should buy to maintain our relationship with them. As you know, we have pursued this policy now since October 14; and while our purchases since that time have been reasonable, at the same time they, of course, would have been considerably heavier if we had been in position to have felt we should try to buy seed instead of feeling that each time we bought a car of seed we were adding to our losses. Considerable seed have gone to other mills that we had expected to add to our tonnage; and while we still hope to get a reasonable tonnage, we do not see much prospects of getting the tonnage you told Mr. Ward you expected us to crush.
As regards our branches at Statesville and Jonesboro, where we have salary men on the job, we have been marking time at both of these branches for over a month on account of the cost of the seed being exorbitant. Seed at the Jonesboro branch to-day would cost us $46, plus a minimum hauling of 90 cents, plus $1 for buying costs, plus $1.92 freight, or virtually $50 delivered at Charlotte, giving us a loss of current costs of over $3 per ton on seed that could be bought for cash. On seed that is being bought on exchange, naturally the cost would be more. Under the conditions, we have discontinued weighing in there for the time being and will continue to do so unless you think it advisable to resume the practice from a policy standpoint. If you wish this changed, you can advise.
The same thing is virtually true at Statesville, although we are doing some weighing in at this point where we have much cheaper freight rates.
REE-b.

SEPTEMBER 22, 1928.
Mr. J. E. ROBERTSON.
Referring to conversation we had while you were here about Southern's competition.
G. W. Ratliffe, about 10 miles from Wadesboro, has been buying for us a number of years at $3.25 per ton commission delivered to our Morven agency, which is about 8 miles from his gin. On account of the trucking problem being somewhat unsettled, we told Mr. Ratliffe all along that we would haul his seed INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY this coming season, but was not in position to make him a definite proposition; that we would do so as soon as the basis for hauling was established. At the meeting the North Carolina mills had in Raleigh, which I did not attend, they agreed to give the same price for seed trucked as loaded on cars, and to allow hauling charges based on the railroad mileage. I was on the road when this took place. The Southern's manager at Wadesboro immediately got in touch with Mr. Ratliffe and told him he would give him $3 f. o. b. his gin house; and while Mr. Ratliffe would not trade with him, he insisted that Mr. Ratliffe tell him that if he did not get a better offer he would trade with him. When we got to Mr. Ratliffe he told us he did not want to quit, but that he had promised Hardison, and unless we could do a little better he would have to trade with him. We had no way of increasing the $3 and lost the customer after we had shipped him a set of scales. Our scale has not been installed, and the Southern replaced it when they got the trade. Mr. Ratliffe stated this proposition looked so good to him he was afraid to turn it down completely. Mr. Hardison had repeatedly told me that he did not expect to make any effort to take Mr. Ratliffe or any of our customers away from us. Our Mr. Little and also Mr.
Simpson feel sure, however, that Mr. Hardison worked on Mr. Ratliffe very hard, and it looks this way to me.
Mr. Sullivan at Wadesboro, who operates three or four gins in that im mediate section, has been buying for the Southern for a number of years on $3.50 per ton commission, 1 per cent loss in weight, plus a certain allowance for loading. We had told Mr. Hardison we were not trying to trade with Mr.
Sullivan, and in talking with him about the Ratliffe matter, he claimed that our men had been trying to trade with Mr. Sullivan, which our men deny.
At Monroe, the latter part of last season, Lee Winchester, who had bor rowed $8,000 from us to build their gin, came to me and stated they were going to get the money from a bank and pay us up. It later developed that the superintendent of the Southern mill at Monroe had bought an interest in this gin, and the Southern had furnished them the money.
The Southern's manager told these gentlemen if they would buy for them independently they would guarantee them $3 profit and give them the advantage of the rise in the market on any seed they had on hand when the market went up.
We have another trade with a ginner 3 miles from Monroe to whom we let have some money last season. He told me the Monroe mill had told him that if he would buy independently he would take care of him in a way so he could make more than $3 per ton.
In talking with another ginner about 7 miles from Monroe a few days ago, he stated he did not have a regular commission contract with the Southern, but the Southern gave him $3 profit on all of his seed and gave him advantage of the rise, allowing him to make $5 per ton on some of his seed.
Last season we had the promise from a man building a gin at Stanfield that if we would loan him some money to help him build his gin he would buy for us, we telling him we would give him the prevailing commission which we suppose would be $3 per ton. The Southern's traveling man out of Charlotte saw him and told him he would give him $3.50 per ton commission, furnish the money, and a large scale. This man was under the impression our commission did not exceed $3 and traded with the Southern's traveling man. As you know, the trades last season were not supposed to exceed $3 commission.
Yours truly, REE-R.

A. G. M.
NOVEMBER 2, 1928.
Mr. J. E. ROBERTSON.
Mr. Ward and I have gotten up a proposed plan for regulating trucking which he will deliver to you and discuss.
As I see this matter, it is going to be absolutely necessary for a differential to be made in seed loaded on car and ginhouse seed. Our plan is based on this differential being 50 cents per ton less at ginhouse than loaded on car.
I feel 50 cents will come nearer solving this trouble than any other arbitrary difference, since about 75 per cent of the seed can be loaded on cars for 50 cents per ton or less. Consequently, if a shipper sells at say $40 per ton loaded on cars and pays 50 cents to get the seed loaded from the ginhouse on the car, he gets net $39.50 at the ginhouse for the seed. If the differential is $1 and the shipper was offered $40 loaded on the car, or $39 at the ginhouse, he would in the majority of cases load the seed on the car to get the additional $1 per ton, thereby making a profit of about 50 cents, since it would cost him around 50 cents to load the seed. This would bring about a condition where most of seed would be put on cars and it would be an ideal situation for us, but since the small mills realize the advantage they have by receiving seed on trucks, they would not, in my opinion, permit this seed to be loaded on cars, giving the terminal mills the same chance at the seed they would have. Therefore, I do not believe the small mills would let $1 per ton differential work. They might agree to it under present conditions, but as soon as a profit got in the seed and they saw ginners were having to load seed on box cars to get the full price, and found these seed were being shipped to terminal mills instead of trucked to them as formerly, they would not continue quoting $1 less at the ginhouse than loaded on cars.
If we made our basis price at the ginhouse instead of loaded on cars and add 50 cents to load on car instead of deducting 50 cents from the loaded car price, the psychological effect would be better, as naturally if the seller feels he is getting the car price when hauled, he would be better satisfied than to think he was being penalized when seed were hauled and 50 cents taken off the basis price. At the same time, if we made basis at gin instead of loading, this would interfere with our $3 loaded on car commission basis, as the plus 50 cents to load would make the commission contract $3.50 loaded instead of $3 loaded. For instance, $40 at gin for car seed, plus 50 cents to load, $40.50; on commission basis $37 wagon seed and $3 commission loaded, $40; making commission seed cost loaded $40 and independent seed cost loaded $40.50.
When you consider our Federal trade rule has already fixed commission at $3 loaded, and also consider that the basis price is considered by the industry to be loaded on cars, also consider the bulk of the seed bought, particularly by terminal mills, is loaded on car, we feel that the basis should be loaded on cars.
If you feel the basis should be at ginhouse and add 50 cents for loading at other than mill towns and 50 cents for loading at mill towns, where seed are not hauled over 3 miles, 90 cents where hauled 70 miles to car in mill town, or mill direct, we suppose we could interpret our Federal commission rule to read loaded on truck, instead of loaded on car, as the rule, when it says $3 loaded, does not specify loaded on car or truck. This would necessitate our INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY commission being $3.50 loaded on car, or $3 loaded on trucks. Could not this additional expense be taken care of by having uniform $1 less price? For example, if to-day's market was $37 and $3 loaded and we went to 50 cents plus basis, make the wagon seed $36 and $3.50, car seed $39 plus 50 cents loaded, this would give us our extra 50 cents collected from the farmer and an additional 50 cents to help cover cost of over 50 cents where trucked into oil-mill towns.
My motion in Raleigh was basis ginhouse, or plus 50 cents basis, since Mr.
Borden had made the definite statement he was going to pay the basis price at the ginhouse.
I hope some fair regulation can be arrived at, but frankly, I do not believe it worth while to regulate it on $1 per ton differential, as, of course, there is no need of regulating it on a basis that the little mills will not allow to stand.
As I have already stated, the $1 per ton differential would certainly be fine for a terminal mill, as, in my opinion, it would have a tendency to virtually kill trucking, which I do not believe will ever be done in this State.
As regards your suggestion yesterday of allowing the price of the seed to take care of all hauling. I do not feel this could be done. I do not feel that an arbitrary price for hauling, regardless of distance, would be possible to put over. It seems to me under our plan, the terminal mills could buy seed at all towns, except oil-mill towns, at the basis loaded car price. If they expect to buy seed that are in the immediate vicinity of an oil-mill town, part of which seed is loaded and part of which seed is trucked to the mill, they could pay the price loaded on the cars, which would be the basis car loaded price, and if the seed were trucked into the town and loaded on the car in the mill town, and the mileage was over 3 miles, they could soon get a list of the dis tances from these gins that haul to the oil-mill towns and know how to quote based on the mileage to the oil-mill town. Stevens Lawton's view on this is say at Stony Point, 10 miles out of Statesville, gin at Stony Point would haul to the Statesville mill to get the mileage for hauling. Under my plan, the South Carolina mills would offer this shipper say $40 loaded on the car at Stony Point. If the Statesville mill bought the seed to be trucked to the Statesville mill, the shipper would get $39.50 at the ginhouse, plus 90 cents, making $40.40 delivered Statesville, or only 40 cents per ton more for trucking the seed 10 miles. In my opinion, he would load at Stony Point, which is his natural loading point, unless, of course, he wanted to get meal from the mill.
There are some advantages the little mills have which terminal mills will never take away from them, except by opening up concentration points in their mill towns and then the local sentiment usually is in favor of the small mill.
So far as putting a terminal mill on equal buying basis with the small mill, I do not feel it is possible to do it any other way.
REE-b.
CC: Mr. B. A local oil mill receiving such seed benefits in price (50 cents) compared to the cost an outside mill must pay for seed on cars in the same town.
ت (d) Seed from country gins delivered to oil mills.-Such seed should not cost the mills more than seed from town gins, so it is logical that the price paid at the mill for such seed should be the same as that paid for town gin seed, regardless of the distance such seed have to be hauled. The price paid at the point of origin should take care of this expense.
(e) Seed at country gins (over 4 miles from towns).-There is an expense attached to putting this country seed on the same market basis as town seed.
ESTABLISHMENT OF THE ABOVE PLAN It seems that the above is fair to all mills, terminal and local alike, and, further, it is fair to all seed sellers also. Then only one factor could cause its rejection as the basis for trading: Willingness of mills to give up their location advantages as to price of seed in order to control tonnage, or, expressed another way, unwillingness of mills to allow seed to move from their respective immediate territories to other mills on the same market basis.
Unless this arrangement is put into effect by all mills, there can be no certain market-price basis for seed. Seed at the same place under the same conditions will bring different prices. Misunderstanding, leading to price wars, unwarranted price increases, will occur. Satisfactory market conditions, in which everyone interested could have confidence, can not be realized without this understanding.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY SUGGESTED REGULATIONS FOR COTTONSEED TRADING IN NORTH CAROLINA Can not allow commission ginners a hauling charge according to our arrangement.
Ginners about 10 miles from town will probably pay the same price at their gins that the other country gins are paying. As long as the price will allow them $1 for hauling to town, some will do so. When the spread falls below $1 they will let the mills come get the seed. Such a ginner can pay $1 of the differential to the producer and still make $3.50 profit to cover hauling cost and profit, but only $1.50 profit if the mills send for the seed.
Two dollars for hauling is sufficient inducement to cause these ginners to haul their own seed and none of them would agree to buying seed on a commission basis with no hauling allowance.
From this discussion it is apparent that pressure from producer on country ginners and competition between ginners themselves will not let a differential between town and country seed of $2 or even of $1 stand. In addition, there are 53 oil mills in North Carolina, 44 in South Carolina, and gins in these States are so located with respect to these mills that a $1 higher price in oil-mill towns than in other railroad towns would attract great volumes of the seed, the ginners using the differential for business-getting purposes.
Why should seed in oil-mill towns be worth more than seed in other railroad towns? The Proctor Gamble Co. does not pay more for crude oil produced at mills in Macon than it does for oil produced at other points in Georgia.
RECOMMENDATION For reasons given above in the discussion of Plan I, I recommend the use of this plan with a differential of 50 cents only between railroad town and country seed, with no hauling allowances whatever.
J. E. ROBERTSON.

DECEMBER 31, 1929.
Mr. J. E. ROBERTSON, G. M.
We feel the marketing of seed by the farmer, through commission buyers representing reliable mills, the safet method to be used by the farmer. He is assured, under this method of marketing his seed, the prevailing market price, and, furthermore, he is assured of getting pay for his seed. The commission in effect is about as narrow a margin on which a man can afford to handle the business. We have known of any number of cases where seed were left with independent operators by farmers to be sold at a later date. The independent operator would sell the seed, dispose of the money, requiring the farmers to get settlement as best they could. In many cases, of course, the independent operator buys the seed at varying prices-usually as cheaply as possible. We have had independent operators request us this season to not wire our commission buyers increase in seed, but let them buy two or three days at the old price 1 before giving the farmer the advantage of the rise.
Yours truly, REE-b.

Mr. C. C. FISHBURNE, District Manager, Columbia, S. C.
DEAR SIR: Referring to your circular of June 20 and also our conversation this morning in regard to commission contracts. Beg to advise that I think the Buckeye has for some time made a rather liberal commission contract.
It is my understanding that they give the buyer the privilege of buying on his own account or either buy for them under the commission of $3 per ton.
In this way the buyer can elect when he is ready to ship whether or not he will ship the seed at cost plus a commission of $3 or whether he will ship them on a spot car seed basis. Sometimes, of course, when the market advances, It will be to the buyer's advantage to ship on a spot basis.
On the other hand, the Buckeye have somewhat of a hold on these seed, because the buyer generally feels inclined to give them the refusal of the car seed when he is ready to ship, and they have in this way not been forced to stay in the high market for local wagon seed.
Yours truly, THE SOUTHERN COTTON OIL CO., By C. FITZSIMONS, Jr., Manager.

DEAR SIRS: It is essential that we put in a new battery of four cotton gins with necessary equipment at the oil mill during the summer, replacing an old outfit installed in 1909. The approximate cost of the new gins, equipments, plus cost of bringing the two hydraulic cotton presses up to date, will be $5,300.
This price is subject to a 5 per cent discount for cash on completion of installation.
We are having keen competition for ginning with three near-by plants, all of which have new installations of the latest type. Quite a number of our old customers left us last season on account of the new outfits near by. We do not get the seed from these three plants, but they go to Buckeye, Southern, and an independent mill because these mills financed the installations.
We believe this will be money well spent, and shall be glad to have you consider the matter and advise us.

ROCK HILL, S. C., March 19, 1930.
Here is just what we are up against on the condition of seed. The free fatty-acid content decides positively the amount of excessive refining loss in the oil, and for every point over 9 per cent we are docked 1 per cent of the contract price, and in addition 12 per cent of the contract price for offcolor and flavor. On a tank of oil produced from cottonseed of the quality contained in the above car, we would have to pay a claim of $600, or approximately $3 per ton on the amount of seed required to yield a full tank. Besides, seed of this kind produces a meal graded off in color, which we have to sell at a big discount from prime meal. The Government has declared that we must not pay as much for seed of off quality as we do for prime seed, and for your information will state that right at this time the Government have representatives in the field checking our books and records to determine whether we have complied with their rulings in this respect and we can not I afford to attempt to hide any information that they might ask for, and the analyses on various shipments of cottonseed is the one thing they are sure to inquire for in their audit.
Understand, they do not attempt to regulate the price for seed for anyone, but do positively say that the mills can not discriminate in their purchases and the question of quality largely determines whether this has been done or not.
The condition which you state existed at Sardinia is something over which the Government has no control, but is a matter left entirely to those interested, and one must decide for himself whether it is good business to follow a speculator or not. This time, experience has proven a sad tale for those that did participate.
The prices paid this season by the mills generally provided for a reason- able spread and a small legitimate profit, except when the off quality seed I began to move to the market, and the results remain problematical thus far, with serious doubt in our mind as to whether or not we haven't worked them at a net loss.
If we were to reimburse you for any portion of the stated loss on the car in question, we would be assuming in all probability additional loss to what we already have, and we are sure you are business man enough to know that a business-like managed concern would be reluctant for standing for anything of the kind.
Our principals are located at Charlotte, and we must not only report to them but undergo an audit for the purpose of determining how we have conducted the business entrusted to us, and after 25 years at the game we would feel mighty bad to have to be called on the "mat." The writer is personally responsible for the conduct of the business, and feel sure you see our position and realize the situation we are placed in when confronted with a matter of this kind.
Let us suggest that you hold this matter open until the close of the season and if we can work a way whereby we can at least help you to some extent, rest assured we will do so; but in the meantime, realize what the situation is not only with us but with you, also.
Yours truly, HIGHLAND PARK MANUFACTURING CO.
SUMTER, S. C., March 21, 1930.
