The seed which were in the above car came out of the same house that three more cars were loaded out of and which were all right, and even at the price I got for them I had substantial loss. I realize fully that this is no funeral of yours, but as we have been doing business very pleasantly for a number of years, and if you could help me out any on this car without any actual loss to yourself, I would appreciate it very much.
This has been an unusually queer season, I have worked pretty hard and have practically made nothing at all out of the seed business this season, and when this season is over I am going to try and forget it and look forward to a better season this fall.
I will certainly be glad when seed get in a condition through this section so they will be bought on the old way and not on grade.
It is almost impossible to buy wagon seed, we will say at $21 or $22 when the farmer knows the car price is $28. They have always been used to getting $3 under the car price for their wagon seed and it certainly goes against the grain with them to take any less. If a man intends to stay in the seed business he certainly has to stand in with his seed shippers as well as the ones he buys wagon seed from, and I suppose the same applies to a certain extent with the mills.
Yours very truly, J. P. COMMANDER.

ROCK HILL, S. C., October 7, 1927.
We are inclined to wait until after the census report to-morrow to buy further lots of cottonseed for it is our belief that the market will decline.
On the present basis there is no money to be made in cottonseed. We are really glad we did not get more than five cars some time ago at $45. We are sure the mills are going to stop protecting the buyers as they have been doing in the past year or so by taking their seed on a declining market at I the higher price. This practice causes a tight market, with the mills the losers always and a very poor business method on the part of the mills.
When we are again in the market we will wire you.
Yours truly, HIGHLAND PARK MANUFACTURING CO.
ROCK HILL, S. C., October 31, 1927.
MENDENHALL JAMES, Greer, S. C.
We have taken more seed on storage this season than for a number of years, because we are inclined to believe that we will see lower prices. The oil market has been a weak feature of the products, brought about by competing oils from abroad, cheaper grains, and a large hog crop in the West.
We have been operating our mill for 25 years, and this is the first year in our experience that the mills have consistently paid several dollars a ton more for seed than has been possible to work out of them. This condition can't last, hence our opinion that a lower raw-material market must eventually come about.
Yours truly, HIGHLAND PARK MANUFACTURING Co.
ROCK HILL, S. C., April 1, 1929.
Mr. J. L. SPENCER, Treasurer, Charlotte, N. C.
DEAR SIR: Profits of the oil mill to close May 1 will approximate $3,000.
The season has been a very poor one, due to persistent advances in the price of cottonseed by the larger interests. At no time during the season could we figure any profit from day-to-day purchases of car lots of cottonseed, and in several instances on a declining oil market we would get an advance in the price of cottonseed.
We will close the books on May 1 and send you a full statement of the results of the season's operation.
Yours truly, HIGHLAND PARK MANUFACTURING CO. No. 2.

INTERNATIONAL VEGETABLE OIL CO., (Attention Mr. Suhr.) Savanah, Ga.
In regards to the deduction of $14.60, I sent a sample of these seed to another mill, and I am offered exactly $5.10 per ton more than you offered on the same sample.
Both samples were drawn this way: I had my man go to the seed house and get a handful from the various parts of the seed; they were brought to the office and thoroughly mixed. Some were put in one can and sent you and some in another and sent elsewhere. I don't see how there could be such a variation in the analysis.

Dillon, INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY You can readily see what this loss of $17 per ton means to the producer in this section. Further comparing the two seasons: In February, 1928, cottonseed sold as high as $52 per ton. On December 28, 1929, the cotton-oil mills in this section reduced the price of cottonseed to $25 per ton (the prevailing price at this writing). The cotton farmer in this section is only getting $22 per ton for his seed while he is paying the mills $34 per ton for cottonseed meal.
In other words, by means of a combination of the oil mills, seed to-day are bringing only half the price they brought one year ago.
With the knowledge and consent of the Federal Trade Commission the big oil mills employed smart auditors who considered actual, theoretical, and invisible costs of manufacturing cottonseed. They added to this a very liberal profit and on this basis every mill in the Southeast arrived at the same price to pay for cottonseed. Somehow the combination is ironclad, and every mill to-day has a uniform price.
If the Federal Trade Commission could reverse the process and have good auditors estimate every cost of growing cotton and cottonseed-and if the growers could come together like the oil mills, cotton would bring 25 cents a pound and cottonseed $50 a ton. The Federal Trade Commission knows that our 2,000,000 cotton farmers can not get together. It seems unfair to allow a few big cotton-oil mills to get together and at the height of the season buy the bulk of the cottonseed at prices far below the cost of production.
It is up to every southern Senator and Congressman to get busy and do his bit to break up the existing Oil-Mill Trust. Senator Harris, of Georgia, and Representative Patman, of Texas, are taking the lead in an investigation now being conducted.
This is to urge that you assist in every way possible in breaking up the Oil-Mill Trust and aid the farmer in getting a better price for his seed.

EXHIBIT NO. 934 SOUTH CAROLINA COTTONSEED CRUSHERS ASSOCIATION, Columbia, S. C., October 5, 1928.
GENTLEMEN: A general meeting of the South Carolina Cottonseed Crushers Association and others of the industry was held at the Jefferson Hotel, Columbia, S. C., at 8 p. m. October 3, at which a very full discussion was had of the variable quality of cottonseed now being offered for sale in this State. It was self-evident that cottonseed will have to be graded if the interest of the mills and the public are to be protected and discrimination avoided.
The following system of grading was then adopted with the understanding.
that it is to become effective immediately: Grading system: All seed received from independent shippers shall be sampled by a disinterested party, analyzed by public chemist, and settlement shall be made on the basis of such chemist's grading in accordance with the rules of the Interstate Cottonseed Crushers' Association.
It was further decided that since the system above outlined is more or less an innovation, that it is due the independent shippers of cottonseed that they be forewarned that all seed shipped by them are to be graded in accordance with the interstate rules, therefore, it is expected that all mills will at once send to each independent shipper of their acquaintance the following letter in which must be included a copy of the sheet setting forth the deductions to be made under the rules, a copy of which sheet is inclosed herewith and a supply of which we are sending you under separate cover: The bad weather conditions, which have been so harmful in your section, have caused the quality of cottonseed in many cases to be extremely low. The quantity and quality of products produced from these seed are seriously affected, and the cost of working them is much greater than if the seed were prime. Of course, we will continue to pay full price for prime seed, and we hope that the percentage of prime seed will increase very shortly. We want to do all we can to aid the farmers by buying these offquality seed as they are offered, but we are forced, if we are to stay in business, to deduct from the prime price of seed an amount per ton, which will fairly represent the depreciation and offquality.
In order to do this accurately and fairly we have arranged to have sworn samples forwarded to and analyzed by a public chemist. You will receive a copy of the chemist's report, and we will settle for the seed on the basis shown therein.
This method will, we feel sure, appeal to you as fair and right and will give you correct information on which to base your purchases.
The system also makes it mandatory that the mills shall stamp (a rubber stamp for that purpose is being sent you under separate cover) on all contract and all confirmations covering the purchase of independent seed the following: "It is agreed that settlement for the seed shipped on this contract shall be under the trade rules applicable to cottonseed based on analysis by a public chemist of a sworn sample drawn at destination." While this plan provides only for the analysis of seed received from independent shippers it is contemplated that the quality of wagon and/or gin seed from different sections will be determined and the value of seed marketed through commission and/or salaried buyers will be established and adjusted to the end that seed bought by both independent and commission buyers will be on a parity and discrimination obviated.
It is understood that the county demonstration agent in the county in which the mill is located and the mill will jointly select the disinterested party to do the sampling of the seed.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY It is further understood that when the mill forwards the sample of the seed to the independent chemist for analysis the mill will furnish the chemist the number and initial of the car, the name of the place from which the seed were shipped, and the per ton delivered cost ofthe seed, and that the mill will attach a copy of the chemist report to the returns on each car.
In connection with the foregoing we remind you of No. 5 of the Memphis resolutions which reads as follows: "It is unfair competition and against public policy to buy and settle for cottonseed except on a basis of quality, cleanliness, and moisture content. Sound, clean, dry seed are worth more than damaged or trashy seed or seed containing an excess of moisture.
Your loyal and enthusiastic cooperation in this system, which we believe to be equitable to all parties concerned, is earnestly requested.
Yours very truly, RUSSELL ACREE, Secretary.

The plan for grading cottonseed evolved by the Department of Agriculture's Mr. Meloy has been adopted by the National Cottonseed Products Association and has been officially incorporated in its trading rules. The oil mills will hereafter base their quotations on basis cottonseed and will pay premiums for quality cottonseed containing combined quantities of oil and protein (meal) above the basis standard. Likewise off quality product will bring less than basis cottonseed.
The plan is designed to benefit all interests in the industry, including of course the producers of the seed; and to be successful and effective it should have the cooperation of producers, shippers, ginners, and the oil mills.
This is a progressive step of great economic importance in the agricultural and industrial life of the South.
It must and will succeed.
W. A. SHERMAN, President, National Cottonseed Products Association.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY DEVELOPMENT OF STANDARD METHODS FOR GRADING AND EVALUATING COTTONSEED (By G. S. Meloy) It was about 1913 I think that the old Bureau of Markets of the Department of Agriculture undertook a study of cottonseed with a view to establishing a grading plan. Those studies disclosed some of the variables in cottonseed, with which you are doubtless familiar. There is a great variance in the percentage of kernels in seed due to different conditions; the thickness of the hulls, the fullness and development of the kernels themselves; in other words, due to the variation of conditions undergone by the plants during the growing season.
The oil is contained in the kernel as is, also the protein: The oil content varies from something like 25 per cent in the kernels to 42 per cent or 43 per cent.
The protein varies also in equally as wide percentages.
As a result of these studies of 1913, 1914, and 1915 there is a report on file in Washington showing that because of the great variety of their contents no plan was devised by which cottonseed could be graded. It was not until 1925 that at the request of the Interstate Cottonseed Crushers' Association, a new study was taken up by the Department of Agriculture.
We also found these same variables in the seed. Our first effort was to try to find a way to correlate these variables so as to set up a basis grade. Now it so happens that the oil and protein represent in combination approximately 90 per cent of the value of the seed. We therefore confined our attention to the correlation of these two products.
One of the interesting things that we first discovered was that there is an almost constant inverse ratio between the percentage of oil and the percentage of protein in the seed, and that usually when the oil is high the protein is low, and conversely when the oil is low the protein is high. That inverse ratio is not positive. If it were positive and uniform you would have but one grade of seed; but it is not and therefore, you have different grades of seed.
In searching for a method of correlating these two products, we began to study the ratio of value of units of protein and units of oil, taking a pound of oil as a unit and a pound of a definite quality of cake as a unit. We settled on 8 per cent (41.13 per cent protein) cake because it is about an average and would form a good basis for calculation. We found that the ratio of value was very constant. There was a fluctuation sometimes of 4 to 1, some times 5 to 1 and sometimes 6 to 1. However, 5 is the average relation and we have agreed to use this constant figure. Cottonseed oil competes in the mar kets of the world with animal oils and fats. When there is a surplus of animal oils and fats down goes the price of cottonseed oil. The same is true of the protein, which also competes with animal oils and fats because when we have a surplus of animal oils and fats the producers stop feeding cattle and down goes the price of protein.
So as I have said, we settled on the ratio of 5 to 1. The fact that 5 pounds of 8 per cent ammonia (41.13 per cent protein) cake was equal in value to 1 pound of oil gave us the method of converting oil and protein into similar terms or into a common denominator in terms of oil. So we take the pounds of 8 per cent cake and divide it by 5 and add that figure to the pounds of indicated oil. This gives us what we call an oil-cake reciprocal. We call it a "reciprocal" because it is the resultant of two or more interchangeable variables.
After the study of the analyses from a great many carloads of seed, we found the average analysis to be 19 per cent oil, 3.5 per cent ammonia and we set up that description of seed as a quantitative analysis of seed that could be taken as a basis grade.
Now having done that, we can use any analysis in the same way, first re ducing its protein content to terms of oil. Then by dividing the reciprocal that we get for any analysis by the reciprocal found from the basis description, we get an index relation to that basis description. It is simply a percentage relation. In other words seed grading 101 contains 101 per cent of the com bined products as compared with your basis description. On the contrary, seed grading 98 contains 98 per cent of the combined products of oil and protein as compared with the basis cottonseed representing 100 per cent.
Qualitative values.-We next took up the study of deterioration in cottonseed.
The grades are quantitative. They tell you the quantity of the combined oil and proein in seed in relation to basis cottonseed. But seed may spoil. They do spoil. They deteriorate in quality. The old so-called grading Rule 140 of the National Cottonseed Products Association was not a grading rule at all INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY It was a 66 discount rule." It assumed that all cottonseed was equal in quantitative value and that the only thing that could happen was that the seed would spoil, and generally they spoiled.
Somebody suggested some years ago that the color of the kernel was a measure of that spoilage or deterioration. But we at Washington could see no scientific basis for that, so we undertook to find a method by which we I might measure deterioration.
Oils are composed of fatty acids. We might say in common parlance, that these fatty acids are saturated, that is bound up, but when oils deteriorate or I spoil there is a breaking down of this combination and some of the acids are set free. We call them free fatty acids.
We drew curves representing increases of free fatty acids and increases of I deterioration in all of the products. The curve of the free fatty acids was the composite of the curves of deterioration or discounts on all products. Therefore it was suggested that the free fatty acids content might be used as a measure of deterioration in the seed.
Now we found that there was some free fatty acids more or less in practically all seed and that a certain quantity of these free fatty acids did not result in deterioration in the product. That percentage is 1.8 per cent and the industry has adopted that figure as the tolerance of free fatty acids in the basis cottonseed. This therefore forms a basis of grading seed. It forms a basis of grading the quantity of the products that may be obtained out of the seed, and it also forms a basis of measuring the amount of deterioration that has taken place in the seed.
The National Cottonseed Products Association has adopted as a basis grade description the following: "Basis cottonseed shall analyze 19 per cent oil, 3.5 per cent ammonia, not to exceed 1 per cent foreign matter, and not to exceed 1.8 per cent free fatty acids in the oil at time of delivery." This gives us a definite quantitative and qualitative basis on which cottonseed can be graded. It is a basis for quotations so that when the seed are bought and sold one may know exactly the quantity and the quality of the products. Knowing this and knowing the milling efficiency; knowing the cost of crushing, knowing all of the factors that enter into this question of price, the oil mills can arrive at the figure they are willing to bid for basis cottonseed.
Under this plan the oil mills purchase, grade, and pay for the seed in relation to that quotation. The price they will hereafter pay for any seed is the price of the basis seed plus the premium, if they are premium seed, or less the discount, if they are below the basis grade of 100.
"" The rule of the National Cottonseed Products Association says, "It shall comply with this description or its equivalent." The words," of its equivalent' are significant because under the grading plan, a deficiency in oil may be made up by an excess of protein and a surplus of oil may be reduced by a deficiency in protein. There are a great many combinations of oil and protein which will meet with the basis description.
Under the new rule, the mill will buy seed and will not buy dirt and trash in excess of 1 per cent. We have found from a good many studies that we can not expect seed to be cleaner than 1 per cent foreign matter. The rules further state that the seed shall be analyzed for foreign matter and the net weight of the seed determined, and then the grade of the net weight of seed must be found and the net weight of the seed shall be paid for on its grade.
Section 4 of rule 40 tells how to go about ascertaining the grade of any seed. It provides that you take the indicated pounds of oil and add to it a figure found by dividing the indicated pounds of 8 per cent (41.13 per cent protein) cake by 5. At 19 per cent 2,000 pounds of seed will contain 380 pounds of oil. Since 3.5 per cent is ammonia that will make 70 pounds of ammonia.
Now we are going to make 8 per cent cake. If 8 per cent is 70 pounds, 1 per cent is 8.75 pounds, 100 per cent is 875 pounds of 8 per cent cake. Five pounds of that cake is equal in value to 1 pound of oil, so we divide the amount of cake by 5, which gives us 175. We add this to the 380 and get 555 (the reciprocal of basis cottonseed). We do this same thing with any lot of seed.
Then we divide by 555. Of course, any lot of seed that works out 555 is 100 per cent or basis cottonseed. If it works out more than 555 it is a premium seed; if less it is a discount seed.
The next problem that we had was the sampling of seed.
We found that you can not go into a carload of seed and get less than 50 pounds of seed and have it represent all of the variables in that car, and it INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY was therefore recommended, as the rules of the National Cottonseed Products Association now provide, that the sample shall be not less than 50 pounds.
They first provide for taking the samples before unloading the car. We are not yet satisfied with the method of taking the sample before unloading, but it is an improvement over the old way. The rule says that the samples shall be taken in both ends and the middle of the car at 8 or 10 different points, not less than 50 pounds in all. As representative samples as possible shall be obtained by digging well down into the body of the seed, preferably not less than 30 inches, with a short-handled 8-tined fork. Do not put that sample in a gunny sack and put it out on the side of the railroad. It must be put in a metallic container and covered up. The rule also provides for getting a sample from a car during the time it is being unloaded. The new rules will furnish as nearly accurate a sample as it is possible to obtain.
Oil mills should furnish their samplers (who should be intelligent, competent men) with proper tools for taking samples. It is suggested that an 8 by 5 by 5 elevator bucket on the end of a pole or handle is a suitable sample-drawing instrument. The sampler must present that receptacle in the center of the unloading seed chute in a level position at regular intervals. Such an elevator bucket will hold about 2 pounds, so that in order to secure the 50pound sample he will have to present it not less than twenty-five times.
If a row of cars is being unloaded the men can pass from one car to the other and obtain the portions placing them in their proper receptacles.
Such a machine has been devised. It is a small shaker-cleaner with a hopper that will hold between 50 and 100 pounds of seed. The hopper has an automatic feed so that the seed will be distributed evenly over the screens. The end of the screen on which the cleaned seed ride is extended by a piece of sheet metal with openings through which a cross section of the entire sample may escape. The size of these openings is adjustable.
The gross sample is to be weighed accurately, and the cleaned seed sample is also to be weighed accurately. The difference in weight is the loss due to foreign matter, dust, dirt, or moisture lost in cleaning. The sampler is to make a complete record of weights and identifications and inclose a copy with the portion sent to the chemist. The portion sent to the chemist should weigh 24 pounds and must be sealed up in a friction-top can or Mason jar.
We also went into the chemical laboratories and found very few of them equipped with similar apparatus for making chemical analysis. We found very few of the laboratories proceeding to make these analyses in a similar manner. This question was out of my special field and we took up the matter with the Bureau of Chemistry and Soils. The expert in oils and fats, the expert on proteins, the assistant chief of the bureau, and one or two others, with myself as their humble chairman, were designated a committee.
This committee has outlined specific, accurate, and definite procedure for analyzing cottonseed in a chemical laboratory, which we believe will give you accurate and consistent results. The Oil Chemists Society has adopted these recommendations in their rules, and the National Cottonseed Products Associa tion has also adopted them.
So you see we have correlated this whole procedure of grading cottonseed.
The grading depends on the representativeness of the sample; the analysis depends on the representativeness of the sample of seed to the laboratory and on the procedure in the laboratory.
Thus far I have discussed the grading primarily from the angle of large shipments. We at the department are peculiarly interested in how this thing shall benefit and be reflected back to the producer. This is a problem and we have the same problem in grading the small lots of every other agricultural commodity. It is hard to draw samples of small lots of any agricultural commodity, whether it be corn, potatoes, or cottonseed.
The plans provide that each State be divided into districts by selecting counties in which similar cultural practices, similar varieties and what is correlated with that-similar peoples living under similar conditions obtainand then on certain days of the week (the days suggested were Monday and Wednesday, but these may not fit in all communities because in some places seed may not be sold on Mondays) samples of not less than 50 per cent of the seed delivered shall be submitted to designated commercial chemists. "Desiginvestigation OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY I I nated chemist means that such chemist has complied in both his physical equipment in his laboratory and in his mental equipment with the prescribed rules for analyzing seed.
Then on Friday of each week the average grade and quality of the seed in each of these districts shall be published; published for the benefit of the mills, for the benefit of the ginners and for the benefit of the producers, so that during the following week that report may be used as a basis for calculating the price of the small lots of seed.
Now the rules of the National Cottonseed Products Association go further. It appears that Alabama, Mississippi, and, I think North Carolina, have already taken steps to exercise some supervision over the graders of seed. Georgia last year made available its State chemist's office for the appeal work. Alabama will probably provide the same thing this year. Anyone may appeal to the State chemist. Doubtless other States have facilities that they can put into operation.
Many States have facilities for and should see the value and importance of broadcasting to the public information as to prices of cottonseed and cottonseed products, and I think they will also be glad to broadcast on Fridays the average grade and quality of the seed in the various districts so that everybody may have all of this important information.
(The above address was delivered July 10, 1930, at Dallas, Tex., before a group of oil-mill men and Texas agricultural officials. It is typical of the explanations Mr. Meloy has been making of the grading plan at conferences with State agricultural commissioners and their associates, and before groups of producers, cotton ginners, and oil millers throughout the Cotton Belt.) RULES OF THE NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION RELATING TO THE SAMPLING AND GRADING OF COTTONSEED BASIS COTTONSEED (Rule 40) SECTION 1.--Each sampler shall be provided with suitable scales and a shaker cleaner which shall be provided with adjustable vents through which a cross-section of 1,000 grams (24 pounds) of the original sample may escape during the cleaning.
MARKET INFORMATION The following resolution was adopted at the trade practice conference of the cottonseed oil industry, and approved by the Federal Trade Commission: "Each mill shall, by all available means, publish immediately to the selling public the prices paid for cottonseed and to the buying public the prices reinvestigation OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY ceived for the products thereof, and the reporting of any false or fictitious price, or the failure to report the exact price paid for cottonseed or received for the products thereof, is hereby declared an unfair method of competition.
The prices paid for cottonseed or charged for the products thereof is a matter of individual judgment to be determined by each unit concerned. No unit is or should be under obligation to change or maintain its prices to meet the wishes or views of any other unit or group of units." The association, through its State divisions, is undertaking to collect and disseminate information showing for the different markets the prices paid for basis cottonseed and received for cottonseed products. Its rules and regu lations governing the publication of price information provide that all such information shall be made available to all interested parties, including producers of cottonseed, agricultural agencies, buyers and sellers of cottonseed and cottonseed products, and otherwise made public.
ALL COTTONSEED SAMPLERS MUST BE LICENSED In order to provide that samples shall be drawn and handled in strict accord with prescribed methods (rule 240), and to insure impartial and efficient serv ice in this important part of the grading plan, the executive committee has authorized and instructed the executive secretary to license and, with the cooperation of the State divisions, to supervise all cotttonseed samplers employed under the plan. The committee, furthermore, resolved that samples shall be taken only by samplers licensed by the association or by those who may be licensed by a State or the Federal Government.

 EXHIBIT NO. 949A RULES ADOPTED AT A TRADE PRACTICE CONFERENCE OF THE COTTONSEED OIL INDUSTRY, HELD BY THE FEDERAL TRADE COMMISSION AT MEMPHIS, TENN., JULY 24, 1928 (Approved and accepted by the Federal Trade Commission, October 8, 1928) GROUP I Rule 1.-Whereas there has been discrimination in the prices paid for cottonseed and in the prices charged for the products thereof; and Whereas the Congress of the United States in passing the Clayton Act, and many States by enacting statutes, have condemned price discrimination; and Whereas in order that the market value of cottonseed and its products may be known at all times by all who are interested, and to the end that discrimination in prices may be prevented: (a) Resolved, That it is hereby declared unfair competition either directly or indirectly to discriminate in the prices paid to different sellers of cottonseed or the prices charged for the products thereof, when the effect of such discrimination may be to substantially lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly: Provided, That nothing herein contained shall prevent discrimination in the prices paid to different producers of such commodities on account of difference in the grade, quality, or quantity of the commodity purchased, or that makes only due allowance for difference in the cost of purchasing or transportation, or discrimination in the price in the same or different communities made in good faith to meet competition.
(b) Resolved further, That each mill shall, by all available means, publish immediately to the selling public the prices paid for cottonseed, and to the buying public the prices received for the products thereof, and the reporting of any false or fictitious price, or the failure to report the exact price paid for cottonseed, or price received for the products thereof, is hereby declared an unfair method of competition.
Rule 2. The price paid for cottonseed or charged for the products thereof is a matter of individual judgment to be determined by each unit concerned.
No unit is or should be under obligation to change or maintain its prices to meet the wishes or views of any other unit or group of units.
Rule 3. The payment or allowance to sellers of seed or buyers of the products thereof, of commissions, bonuses, rebates, or subsidies of any kind, confidential prices or the use of any device which does not include in the price paid or bid the entire consideration, is hereby declared an unfair method of competition in the form of commercial bribery. This section also applies to contracts for the exchange of manufactured products for cottonseed, and no evasions or subterfuges can be practiced or included under such guise.
Rule 5.-The strict observance in good faith of all these resolutions being to the best interests alike of the buyers and of the sellers of cottonseed and of the products of the mills: Therefore be it Resolved, That the clandestine violation of any of said resolutions, those accepted by the Federal Trade Commission merely as expressions of the industry as well as those approved by said commission, shall be deemed to be unfair methods of competition. (This rule was approved by the Federal Trade Commission, but on May 29, 1929, was rescinded and is therefore no longer effective.) INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY GROUP II Rule 6.-All contracts for the purchase of cottonseed should be for a specified tonnage at a specified price, and for the sale of products for a specified quantity at a specified price, entered into in good faith between buyer and seller and subject to no cancellation save for legal cause. The violation of the provisions of this rule is hereby declared to be an unfair method of competition.

To that extent and with that interpretation the rule is accepted by the commission as an expression of the industry.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY Mr. W. C. WOLFE, Manager, Ware Shoals Oil Mill, Ware Shoals, S. C.
CLINTON, S. C., October 18, 1930 DEAR MR. WOLFE: Relative to conditions in my territory regarding seed I wish to say, as has been reported before, that practically all ginneries are buying on commission contracts or on money loaned by oil mills which gives them preference on this business. There are a few independent buyers at scattered points who are slowly accumulating some seed and in some instances they are even having to offer some market inducement in order to get them from the gins. Consequently they are asking a higher price than the quoted markets for their holdings.
Due to the low price of seed, and also to their condition being good for keeping, many people are hauling back home and holding for better prices.
These seed probably will not be offered until sometime before Christmas.
However, there is quite a big tonnage of seed that I believe will move at $25 and up, and it's possible that if the market does not improve that some of this tonnage will move at a less figure than $25, sometime soon. I am keeping in touch with this trade and when ready to sell I see no reason why we can't get our share of it on equal basis.
Except for shipments of seed on commission contracts the sale of car-lot seed has been very light. Individual sellers of car seed are not disposed to turn loose at the present prices, but since they have obligations to meet soon perhaps some of this business will move. Dealers also report a slow sale for meal and are awaiting a more favorable exchange basis to put in stocks of it.
There has been more inquiries the last week regarding exchange though and this business should pick up soon. I have several cars of seed that I will be able to buy as soon as they have enough for car shipments, and have two or three cars in sight for exchange which I hope to close shortly.
Trusting that I will get some shipments moving at an early date, and with best regards, I am Yours very truly, M. R. HUNTER.

Mr. FRED E. CULVERN, Vice President Kershaw Oil Mill, Kershaw, S. C.
DEAR Mr. CULVERN: I just had a telephone conversation with Carl Stellings of the Southern Cotton Oil Co., Augusta, who said he had received two cars of seed, one of which cut 50 per cent damaged and the other 60 per cent and that he was making deductions of 11.35 per ton and $14 per ton, respectively.
He raised this very interesting question that whereas he had some protection in making deductions on seed bought from so-called independent or spot shippers that he had no protection on the wagon seed he was buying through his commission buyer if the difference between wagon and car seed remains only $3 and the seed marketed are of any such quality as above indicated.
Mr. Stellings stated that the two cars he received were ginned before the very heavy rains of this week and that he expects the seed that will be ginned next week to be just as bad or worse.
If you have any plan by which you expect to protect yourself from such conditions on the seed you buy from your wagon buyers, I will appreciate your advising me.
Yours very truly, Copy to Mr. Albert Jordan, Hartsville, S. C.

CHARLES W. RICE Co.
Columbia, S. C., November 2, 1928.

We were glad to check this sample for you; and, for your information, I want to say that the check is one of the best we have had. We haven't found it easy to get close checks on high percentage fatty acid seed. That fact caused me a great deal of worry for a week or more. I have talked with several chemists, one over long distance phone, who has had a great dealt of experience with seed analyses (that is the fatty acid tests) and the fact just mentioned seems the general experience. The explanation is the character of the seed. It is as easy to check by this method as it is by the cutting of the seed. I wanted you to have this information for you might request me to check another sample and I would not have you think that it is possible to get so concordant results on all samples.
With kind regards, I am, Yours very truly, CHAS. W. RICE, Mr. A. S. SMOKE, St. Matthews, S. C.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY MAY 3, 1930.
Mr. HARRY HODGSON, President National Cottonseed Products Association, Athens, Ga.
DEAR SIR: The seed grading committee reports that after a number of conferences with Mr. G. S. Meloy of the Department of Agriculture has, with his valuable assistance and counsel, formulated drafts of new rules covering the grading and sampling of cottonseed to submit for the consideration of the members of the association at the next annual convention in New Orleans.
Several drafts of the new rules have been made by both Mr. Meloy and the committee but not until yesterday was final agreement reached as to the proper wording of the rules. After several conferences at Hot Springs, Ark., during last month between Mr. Meloy and the committee, the committee drew up tentative drafts of the new rules which were submitted to Mr. Meloy in Washington, but these drafts were not exactly in accord with Mr. Meloy's wishes and thoughts so he kindly consented to meet in Memphis yesterday with those members of the committee located in and near Memphis. At that conference slight changes were made in Mr. Meloy's drafts of the rules with his approval and this committee is submitting for the consideration of the association, the rules as worked out yesterday with Mr. Meloy.
I wish to say that Mr. Meloy so well covered the questions in his drafts of the rules that the committee has adopted his exact wording with the two or three changes which were made yesterday.
I inclose to you herewith copies of these new rules and am also sending a copy of the rules, and a copy of this letter, to Mr. Sherman, chairman of the rules committee, and to other officials of the association.
Unfortunately, the committee was not able to finish the draft of these rules in time for them to be published in the May issue of the Cotton Oil Press, but I am mailing to-day to each State or division secretary a sufficient number of copies of each of the new rules to be distributed by them to the interested parties in their States or divisions.
While to some these new methods may appear to be somewhat complicated I am sure with a little study they can be easily understood and the benefit to the sellers and the buyers of cottonseed fully realized.
Respectfully submitted.
Members of Seed Grading Committee: E. E. CLARKE, Chairman.
THE SOUTHERN COTTON OIL CO..
Memphis, Tenn., July 11, 1930.
GENTLEMEN: I wish to advise that since the last meeting of the committee discussions regarding the new seed grading rules have continued and quite a bit of progress has been made along the lines of explaining the rules and the methods of application of them.
One important change will probably be made which should clarify rule 40 very much. Section 2 of rule 40 as originally written made reference to 11 per cent tare. Several members of the committee thought that it was not necessary to make any reference to 11 per cent tare because the percentage of moisture had no place whatever in the calculations, but, of course, the percentage of moisture did have a bearing upon the percentage of oil and ammonia which would be found in the seed by the chemists. Making reference to 11 per cent tare in this rule has confused a great many people who have given some thought to this rule, and I am glad to say that last week in Biloxi, Miss., Mr. Meloy, when the matter was brought to his attention, very readily agreed to the elimination of any reference to 11 per cent tare in the rule.
Prior to taking the matter up with Mr. Meloy again it had been submitted to the executive committee, who, as I understand it, decided that contingent upon Mr. Meloy's approval the executive committee would authorize the changing of this section to read as follows: "Rule 40, section 2. Basis cottonseed shall analyze 19 per cent oil, 3.5 per cent ammonia, 1 per cent foreign matter, and not to exceed 1.8 per cent free fatty acids in the oil, in the seed at time of delivery." Having gotten Mr. Meloy's approval I expect that the executive committee will immediately render its decision formally on the changing of the rule; however, it may be too late to get the changed wording printed in the new rule book.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY It has been thought that benefit would result if Mr. Meloy would permit the use of the name of the United States Department of Agriculture on the chemist's report. This matter was submitted to him at Biloxi last week and I am glad to advise that he gave his consent to the use of the department's name on the chemist's report in connection with the sampling and analyzing of the seed. He was unwilling for the name of his department to be used in such a way that it might appear that the department had approved any method of calculating the value of the seed, but he does unofficially approve the applying of discounts based upon the excess free fatty acids found in the seed by the analytical methods which have been proposed or approved by the officials of the department's laboratory. This, it is thought, will give the new method of grading the seed a background which could not otherwise be obtained.
It appears now that a very large majority of the members of the association are heartily in accord on the new method of grading seed and will adopt these methods the coming season.
It has been suggested that it would be well to get out a pamphlet in which would be printed the new grading rules and a full and frank discussion and explanation of the rules, this pamphlet to be distributed to all interested parties, including farmers, ginners, mills and, in fact, anyone who might dare to have a copy. Quite a while ago Mr. Meloy stated he would endeavor to write something along this line, but so far he has not had time to do so, but if something is not issued by him from Washington the executive secretary of the association plans to get out such a pamphlet in the very near future.
Assistance from the various members of the committee in the preparation of this pamphlet is solicited and will be appreciated, and it is urgent that whatever is going to be put out should be prepared without delay.
I do not know just when another meeting of the committee will be called, but possibly it will be necessary for the committee to get together again before very long. Should such a meeting become necessary I would like to know in advance in what city it would be most convenient for a majority of the committee to meet.
Very truly yours, E. E. CLARKE, Chairman Seed Grading Committee.
C. C. Mr. W. A. Sherman, president National Cottonseed Products Association, Houston, Tex.; Hon. Christie Benet, Columbia, S. C.; Mr. Earl S. Haines, executive secretary, Memphis, Tenn.
Mr. L. K. WIGGINS, Southern Cotton Oil Co., New Orleans, La.
MAY 27, 1930.
DEAR MR. WIGGINS: I have your favor of May 24 asking for suggestions as to how best to sell the seed-grading plan to the farmers.
It seems that the plan can be sold very easily if we compare former practices with present plans.
For instance, heretofore, cottonseed have been purchased at their average value, or below, when they have been of prime quality. They have been discounted, oftentimes erroneously and excessively, on the basis of the color of the kernels, when the color of the kernels has little or nothing to do with their actual quality.
In the future, as in the past, the oil mills will not buy or pay freight or handling charges on dirt. Only the net weight of the seed will be paid for.
But these clean seed will be graded, first, just as if they were absolutely sound. Seed will be quoted on the average or basis grade, just like middling cotton, but the basis grade of cottonseed will be known as grade 100 or index 100. This grade or index 100 means that such seed contain 100 per cent of the combined products, oil and ammonia (or protein or nitrogen, whichever term the local farmers are most familiar with).
Next, whenever cottonseed are found to contain more than 100 per cent of combined oil and ammonia they will bring premiums, just as strict_middling and good middling cotton bring premiums. If, on the other hand, the seed are found to contain less than 100 per cent of the combined oil and ammonia they will not bring the full quotation price, just as strict low middling and low middling cotton do not bring the price of middling cotton.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY And lastly, let the farmer know that a great mistake has been made and that generally he has been the loser when seed were discounted for quality on the basis of the percentage of dark or discolored kernels, but that a scientific basis for determining deterioration has been found. It is called free fatty acids.
I think that most farmers will understand that both butter and lard spoil, and that there are factories where butter and lard are renovated. Also they will understand that if the butter is only slightly spoiled it will take less work to renovate it, then if it is badly spoiled. So with cottonseed, the percentage of free fatty acids is a measure of how badly the seed have spoiled, and it is also a measure of the expenses and losses incurred when the oil from spoiled seed is renovated or refined. But a little of these free fatty acids do little harm, so that no discount will be made when the seed do not contain more than 1.8 per cent of these acids. However, more than 1.8 per cent of these acids increase the losses and expenses of refining rapidly, so that the discounts will be based on each one-tenth of 1 per cent of these acids above the 1.8 per cent that is allowed. In fact, these acids increase the losses and expenses of refining so much that if these are more than 11.8 per cent of fatty acids in the oil in any lot of cottonseed, the oil is not worth more than soap fat, and the meal is good only for fertilizer.
Just as a bushel and a peck of corn containing a few nubbins may be worth as much or more than 1 bushel of corn without any nubbins, so cottonseed containing 105 per cent of combined oil and ammonia-that is, grade 105even though the seed have slightly spoiled, as shown by the fact that they also contain excesses of free fatty acids, may be worth as much or more than cottonseed of grade 100 without any excesses of these bad acids; so the dis counts hereafter will be applied to the grade value and not always to the base or quotation price. For instance, a lot of cottonseed is graded 103 and contains 2.4 per cent of free fatty acids; it will still be worth the base price, because the 3 per cent extra quantity of products, that can be got out of those seed, will offset the 3 per cent discount that would be due on account of the excesses of the free fatty acids.
Some farmers may want to know how we find the grade. Just tell them that we analyze the seed in a chemical laboratory and the chemist reports that the seed contain such a percentage of oils and such a percentage of ammonia and that in the oil there is such a percentage of free fatty acids. Every ton of seed is 2,000 pounds. From the percentage of oil we find the number of pounds of oil in the ton of seed. From the percentage of ammonia we find the number of pounds of ammonia in the ton of seed.
Knowing the number of pounds of ammonia, we can figure just how many pounds of cake or meal with 8 per cent ammonia (or 41.13 per cent protein) can be made out of a ton of the seed. Since a pound of cottonseed oil is usually worth 5 pounds of 8 per cent ammonia cake, we divide the number of pounds of cake that can be made by 5 and add the result to the number of pounds of oil, and then we divide that figure by 355, which is the figure for grade 100. This gives us the grade or index of any lot of cottonseed.
Do not hesitate to write me at any time you may have a question.
Very truly yours, G. S. MELOY.
Senior Marketing Specialist.
THE SOUTHERN COTTON OIL CO..
Memphis, Tenn., April 26, 1930.
SEED GRADING COMMITTEE, National Cottonseed Products Association, GENTLEMEN: I regret that I have not been able to send you the drafts of the new seed grading rules and am really not in position to do so at this time.
Immediately after returning from Hot Springs four members of the committee, located in and near Memphis, got together and prepared drafts of new rules to take the place of present rules 40 and 140 and at the request of Mr.
Meloy these were sent to him in Washington for his consideration. He requested that no publicity be given to the new rules until after he had an opportunity of looking them over and giving his criticisms.
These new rules were written in line with what was discussed and decided on at Hot Springs, but Mr. Meloy does not entirely approve of the way in INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY which these rules were written and he has submitted his own ideas as to the way the two rules should be written, but in the opinion of local members of the committee his wording does not cover the situation; so we are really not in position to send out the committee's drafts of the rules nor Mr. Meloy's either at this time.
Mr. Meloy is going to attend the Texas meeting at Corpus Christi beginning on Monday, the 28th, and has agreed to stop in Memphis on his way back to Washington and at that time we hope to be able to draft these rules in such a way as to satisfy him and cover the situation fully from the standpoint of the mills and just as soon as that can be done I will send each member of the committee a copy of the rules for their consideration, and will also endeavor to send each State secretary a sufficient number of copies of the rules for distribution among all of the mills.
We had hoped to be able to get the wording of these rules decided on in time for the rules to be published in the May issue of the Cotton Oil Press, but as the editor of the Cotton Oil Press states that he will have to have all of his copy ready not later than Monday, the 28th, it is not going to be possible to have the rules published in the May issue, but it is planned to have something in that issue about the rules.
There is no conflict of opinion between the committee and Mr. Meloy as to the basis of fundamentals of the rules. We are in accord on the basis grade.
which will be 19 per cent of oil, 3.5 per cent of ammonia, not to exceed 1.8 per cent of free fatty acid, and not to exceed 1 per cent of foreign matter.
Premiums will be allowed for oil and/or ammonia in excess of the basis and deductions will be made for quantity of oil and ammonia under the basis, and a quality deduction will be provided for where the free fatty acid is in excess of 1.8 per cent. The rate of discount will be 5 to 1. All foreign matter in excess of 1 per cent is to be deducted for and it is thought best that the foreign-matter deduction should come off of the net weight of the shipment.
Sincerely hope to be able to get something more definite in your hands before the end of next week.
Very truly yours, E. E. CLARKE, Chairman.

ELBERTON, GA, October 10, 1927.
ELBERTON OIL MILLS, Atlanta, Ga.
DEAR SIRS: We beg to advise our local trade has been very quiet to-day, ginning rather small, as usual on Monday. Ginning will naturally fall off this week considerably on account of the heavy rains Saturday and Saturday night.
We advise the following purchases of car seed at near-by points: Stevens-Martin Co., Carlton, four cars at $48.50 f. o. b. Carlton; L. W. Hendrick, Bowman, one car $49 f. o. b. Bowman; Farmers Cottonseed Oil Mill, Martin, one car $48.50 f. o. b. Martin; E. P. Burton, Canon, one car $58.50 f. o. b. Canon.
We also advise the following South Carolina purchases: Drakes Ginnery, Pelzer, S. C., one car $47 f. o. b. Pelzer; Williamston Mills, Williamston, S. C., one car $47; J. H. Nance, Cross Hill, S. C., two cars $47.
The price of seed by South Carolina mills is supposed to be $47 per ton.
However, no seed are being bought at this price. The Buckeye Cotton Oil Co., of Atlanta, and the International Vegetable Oil Co., of Augusta, have been responsible for the $48.50 price of seed in our territory. Both of these mills buy large quantities of seed in South Carolina and they did not go beyond the Savannah River with their sky-high prices. We thought it good business to pick up a few cars of seed in South Carolina around the same price they saw fit to pay for seed in Georgia. By doing this we feel that we may be able to get some of the pressure relieved in our market.
We know it is a poor time to raise the price of seed. At the same time, it is necessary that we change our local price from $40 to $42 in the morning.
This is because there is so much difference between the wagon price and the car seed price that it is creating a great deal of dissatisfaction among our customers, both farmers, merchants, and seed dealers. The ginners who are buying seed for us on a commission at $40 are only getting $43 to $44 per ton, and they could sell them in carload lots from $47 to $48 per ton.
Moreover, the markets in our near-by territory, such as Bowman, Royston, and Carlton are $45 on the streets, or $2.25 per hundred. This change to $42 per ton is merely a compromise price and unless these high car prices are withdrawn from our territory we will, no doubt, have to raise our local price even higher than $2.10 the next few days.
Mr. Mickel is making a short trip to South Carolina and will probably pick up a few cars of seed over there at price around the figures above mentioned.
Yours very truly, JTD.
NEG.
ELBERTON OIL MILLS, -, Manager.
ELBERTON, GA., October 13, 1927.
I don't know of anything very unusual to write you. I am inclosing copy of letter I have written the Atlanta office to-day, which will give you some information as to ginning. Up to last Monday morning we had purchased 3,556 tons of seed at a cost of around $41.75 delivered in the mill. On last Monday morning we bought about 400 tons of seed, which will cost around $50 delivered in the mill. We found it necessary to take some of this highprice stuff in order to protect our near-by markets and retain our old customers.
Some of the border mills, particularly the International Vegetable Oil Co.
at Augusta, have given us a great deal of trouble recently, and they made a practice of paying $48.50 to $49 per ton for seed in our near-by markets. This has caused a good deal of dissatisfaction amoung our gin commission customers, on account of the vast difference in the wagon seed price and the car seed price. On last Monday we bought some 8 or 10 cars of seed in South Carolina around $47 per ton. The recognized price in that State being $45. We put the South Carolina mills on notice, through Acree, that we did not see why seed in South Carolina were not worth as much as Georgia seed. Our idea in doing this was to relieve some of the pressure in our local markets from the Buckeye, International, Swift, and others. I think this has already had a salutary effect.
We have received up to date, 4,000 tons of seed, and have 500 or 600 tons outstanding. We are getting our share as we go along and think, considering conditions we have worked under, that we have done fairly well as to the average cost of same.
Meal and hulls are moving freely and we have no stocks of products on hand of anything to amount to anything, outside of our paper oil.
I trust this finds you greatly improved, and will be glad if you will drop me at least a card and let me know how you are getting along, as I shall be anxious to hear. With personal good wishes, I beg to remain, Very sincerely yours, J. T. DENNIS, Jr.

Mr. J. T. DENNIS, Jr., Manager, Elberton Oil Mills, HENDERSON, N. C., November 18, 1927.
Elberton, Ga.
DEAR SIR: Your letter to hand this afternoon in regard to price prevailing in this section, and while $41 per ton is the published price at this time the prevailing price is right hard to ascertain.
All last week seed were sold at $46 per ton (including an additional $1 per ton commission to me). When the market broke quite a few seed were booked at $45 per ton, and the price of $45 was carried over into the current week by some of the mills, until the price of $41 was determined by the association.
Up until last night some of the mills were still trying to buy seed at $43, but in that most of the seed which were anywhere ready for movement had already been booked ahead at $45; I know of only a few cars which moved at $43. No seed have been sold at $41.
I have never seen the mills as short on seed, and very few seed have moved from this section under $45 per ton this season. There were several large ginners through here holding quite a quantity of seed expecting $50 per ton after the first of the year, which, with the present oil market does not seem probable.
I know of some 40 or 50 cars being held on this basis, though, of course, not all in this immediate section. It will be probably a week before the most of my trade have completed their $46 and $45 contracts, but in the meantime I shall be glad to hear from you as to what I may pay for your account in event anything turns up.
While mill storage has taken some of the seed, I have advanced money to quite a few through this section to get them to hold seed in their own storage, so will no doubt get a fair tonnage when they are moved. With best wishes, I am, Yours truly, D. BOYD KIMBALL SOUTH CAROLINA COTTONSEED CRUSHERS' ASSOCIATION, Columbia, 8. O., December 19, 1927.

ATLANTA, GA, January 27, 1928.
ELBERTON OIL MILLS, Elberton, Ga.
We are glad to note your estimated figures showing a slight over run, and not a shortage. We also note you think you have some additional hulls above the figures shown on your reports, and I don't doubt this because your invisible loss is, of course, too high in your clean-up figures.

INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY The oil yield shown is certainly very fine. On the other hand, your cake yield is 163 pounds less than the average mill figures, and likewise your lint yield is considerably lower than the average mill is figuring.
In this connection, I learned on yesterday that the Buckeye figures that they can get $56 out of a ton of products, just how they figure this much yield I certainly can't tell you, but judging from the price they are paying for seed they evidently must figure on some unreasonable figure on yield above what we can obtain.
I have just figured out your yield of oil at 8 cents, which is to-day's market and weak at that, meal at $38 which is to-day's market, and weak at that, lint at 4 cents and 10 cents, and hulls at $9, and I seem to arrive at a figure a little less than $51.50 for products. Regardless of what the other fellow can make out of a ton of seed, we can only base our calculations out of what we can get out of a ton of seed, and under the circumstances I think it will cost us a great deal less to shut down than it will to run if we have to pay practically as much for seed delivered in the mill as we get for products, without considering any working cost; so under these conditions I see nothing to do but stay out of the market and simply acknowledge that our competitors are able to pay more for seed than we can do. Right on this point, the Buckeye claims to be getting better milling results than they have ever made since they have been in business, but certainly so far as we are concerned, if they can pay the price they are paying for seed they deserve the business, and we and all others who can't get better results than we are getting, deserve to go out of business.
This is the goal at which Mr. Proctor is striking, if he is actually obtaining the results that he thinks he is doing he is no doubt happy in the assurance that he has succeeded in putting all his competitors out of business, for undoubtedly he has done so if he can make a profit at the price he is paying and has been paying for seed, but inasmuch as we are still from Missouri, and have seen this kind of price conditions before, I think we can afford to sit on the side lines and watch that gentleman spend some of his money.
Of course, it must be conceded that in doing that he undoubtedly gains a good bit of prestige with the shippers for future consideration, and it may be that he can afford to pay that price for prestige, we certainly can not.
Yours very truly, ELBERTON OIL MILLS, P. D. MCCARLEY, President.

NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION, (INC.), SOUTH CAROLINA DIVISION, Columbia, S. C. September 9, 1930.
GENTLEMEN: There seems to be some misunderstanding about figuring the pounds of products from a ton of basis seed. To begin with, basis seed is supposed to have 380 pounds of oil and 70 pounds of ammonia or any amounts of the two ingredients which when converted to the oil value in pounds that will give the reciprocal of 555. For instance, Pounds 19 per cent oil equals 0.19 by 2,000 pounds-- 3.5 per cent ammonia equals 875 pounds 8 per cent meal which divided by 5 (5 pounds of meal equaling 1 pound of oil in value) Reciprocal_-- 19.8 per cent oil equals 19.8 by 2,000 3.18 per cent ammonia equals 795 pounds 8 per cent meal which divided by 5 You will note from the examples above that there can be many combinations of oil and ammonia in seed that can give the reciprocal of 555 and consequently a difference in the yields of oil and meal from the seed of different analysis.
Nor is it possible to get all the meal and oil as yields which the analyses show the seed to contain. About 55 pounds of oil is left in the cake and about 3 pounds goes out in the hulls. There is also an invisible loss of several pounds of oil, so it would be safe to say that whatever the amount of oil in the seed about 65 pounds should be deducted to get the approximate yield from a ton of seed.
Similarly, all of the ammonia shown by analysis will not be available in the yield of 8 per cent meal. Some of the meats and some uncut seed invariably escape the separators and go out with the hulls. R. Lamar occupied the chair.
The following resolution was adopted: Resolved, That this division, at this time, favors calculation for discounts for excess free fatty acids on basis of 0.3 per cent of the index value for each 121200 S. Doc. 209, 71-2, pt 685 INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY 0.1 per cent in excess of the tolerance of 1.8 per cent, and that if, in the future, the quality of cottonseed warrants an increase in the percentage deduction, the executive committee of the national body shall be requested to authorize a legitimate increase.
The matter of change in the present districts of the State of Georgia was discussed, and the secretary was directed to circularize the mill membership for written expressions of opinions on the subject.
Grading and price publication were discussed, and the sentiment prevailed that the rules covering these features should be rigidly observed. They certainly can not show a profit at present prices of products.
Yours very truly, P. D. MCCARLEY, President.
NATIONAL COTTONSEED PRODUCTS ASSOCIATION (INC.), GEORGIA DIVISION, Atlanta, Ga., November 13, 1930.
GENTLEMEN: Amendment to grading rules.-The following has been adopted as amendment to section 4, rule 40, grading rules: Whenever the oil in seed is less than 17 per cent a. new basis reciprocal is to be used, which is calculated as follows: Subtract percentage of oil from 19 per cent and multiply the result by two. From this result subtract five times the ammonia in excess of 3.75 per cent. The figure thus obtained is to be the percentage by which the basis reciprocal 555 is to be increased. The reciprocal thus obtained is to be divided into reciprocal of the seed as shown by analysis and multiplied by 100 to obtain the index of the seed." Economic survey of the industry.-You have doubtless received circular, under date of the 6th, from Executive Secretary Earl S. Haines, together with the form referred to therein. This procedure has been unanimously approved by the executive committee, and I doubt not you will be glad to cooperate in the movement, as the information will certainly be very illuminating and should have a beneficial effect.
Prices of products.-On account of differences in price of products for future shipment, and the fact that the price reporting plan contemplates current movement of products, I suggest that in future where products are sold for delivery beyond 15 days a notation be entered under Remarks, explaining time of delivery.
Statistical figures.-Form No. 5 is inclosed. Let me urge you to send this report not later than Saturday.

Yours very truly, W. M. HUTCHINSON, Secretary.
ELBERTON OIL MILLS, Atlanta, Ga., November 17, 1930.
ELBERTON OIL MILLS, Elberton, Ga.
I have asked Mr. Law on the telephone this morning to average these four seed analyses and to figure against same as a basis on the mill work you are doing as indicated in the above-mentioned meal analysis. He called me back to state that the basis for standard of 0.80 indicates a deduction of 65 pounds of oil for the total content of seed. He told me, however, that taking our meal analysis mentioned, showing standard of 0.68, would indicate a deduction of only 57½ pounds of oil from the total oil content of seed; and that this in turn based on mill work shows production of oil 292 pounds and 897 pounds of 7.90 per cent cake. After this statement he then branched off into a conversation of " why and wherefore with regard to the original basis for "" INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY figuring analysis reports as started out at the beginning of the season. He then changed to different ones which have already been made in the figuration, and that it would be his idea that we really ought to be making 297½ pounds of oil from the seed as represented by these four analysis reports.
All of which I believe you will agree means nothing, so far as we are concerned, and which to my mind confirms our basis for action this year of handling our business of disregarding the rules as applied to grading cottonseed.
Mr. Law volunteered the further statement that whereas at the beginning of the season practically all seed showed a premium, but that now when they have changed the methods of calculation a deficiency. I asked him in turn what about the fellow who paid the premium at the beginning of the season and his answer was, that, of course, he figured the thing in accordance with the rules and that if the mills adopted a wrong basis for calculation the only way to correct it would be in the price they paid for seed. This, as you know, is largely "bunk." To my mind the facts in the case are that the mills have finally realized they were paying a premium for something they were not getting; as for instance, Mr. Law suggested the basis for figuring this year's business based on the average for the last 10 years. The oil content this year and the ammonia content this year, of course, makes the basis used entirely erroneous. Mr. Law, himself, told me that based on this year's yield the index basis should be 105.
You can draw your own conclusions from that. Of course you understand the seriousness of the situation is that while the ammonia content in these chemical analyses brings up the index and therefore the price at the expense of the low oil content; the oil content in seed is worth in price five or six times as much as ammonia content, and therein lies the trouble.
Yours very truly, P. D. MCCARLEY, President.
P. S.-I also call your attention to the weekly report of chemical analyses, as sent out by Hutchinson under date of November 14, from which you will note that your district shows 99.7 index-this would mean a deficiency of threetenths of 1 per cent-whereas judging by the analysis reports of seed above mentioned in this letter the actual yield is far below that figure in dollars and cents; and that is what the mill is interested in, for, of course, these theoretical figures may be all pretty on paper, but when they mean red figures in dollars and cents to the oil mills its a different story.-P., December 1, 1930.

Mr. C. C. FISHBURNE, District Manager, Columbia, S. C.
DEAR SIR: The wagon seed market in this section is very irregular. The discount from the price for prime wagon seed, according to the public chemist's last report, should be $2. Some mills seem to be applying this discount regularly without taking into consideration the fact that the seed in this section generally are of much poorer quality than is indicated by the chemist's report.
At Rowesville the Hartsville Mill's buyer is reported as paying $25 to wagons and one man who has about 25 tons told me that he was offered $26.50 per ton at Rowesville. I gathered that this was the Hartsville Mill's buyer and that he was splitting his commission with the seller.
Our buyer at Harleyville, in Dorchester County, District No. 7, has just called me on the telephone and asked for a price on a car of about 12 to 15 tons. He stated that the owner had been offered $25 per ton by W. T. Brown of St. George. Brown has been buying independently all season but told me that he had a commission contract with Kershaw and that at the time (when the basis price for car seed was $28) he could get $25 for a large quantity of seed that he has on hand, this being $22 per ton and $3 per ton commission.
I was told to-day that W. P. Kiser, buying for Hartsville at Holly Hill.
was paying $25 per ton and the party stated that buyer for Swift at Augusta had offered him $26 per ton in car lots, no grading, settlement to be made on mill weights. This also appeared to be a commission-split proposition.
The $25 price was for wagon seed.
The average of 12 samples sent to the public chemist in January from this county shows a discount of 17.78, or $5 off of a basis price of $27 per ton for prime seed. We are now paying $21 here and $25 at St. Matthews which we think about right for the average quality of seed at these points.
Yours very truly, WM. C. COOPER, Manager.
MARCH 18, 1930.
Mr. C. C. FISHBURNE, District Manager, Columbia, 8. C.

Williamson Bro. had on hand around 300 tons of seed. They wanted us to take a sample of this seed and either buy the seed on basis of the analysis of that sample or to advise them what they might expect for the seed if sold basis prime.
We advised them that we were not buying seed in that manner and that the only way we knew for them to get an accurate idea as to what the dockage INVESTIGATION OF COTTONSEED INDUSTRY on their seed might average would be to load a carload out of the house and sell it on basis of prime seed. We also agreed to take a car from them at $30 basis prime and to take the balance of their lot at $30 per ton, basis prime, settlement to be made separately on each car, if they wished to dispose of them on this basis after receiving returns on the first car.
We received only one car of seed and the discount on it was $4.86 per ton.
This, however, did not have a great deal to do with our not receiving the balance of them, as I think you know. I understand that this trade wound up by Swift's taking the seed as wagon seed, through a commission buyer, at $24 per ton notwithstanding the fact that the average discount applicable in this district called for a much lower price, and that this buyer paid to Williamson Bro. $2.50 per ton of his commission, netting Williamson Bro. $26.50 per ton for the seed as is.
Yours very truly, SOUTHERN COTTON OIL Co., By WM. C. COOPER, Manager.
EXHIBIT NO. 963 THE SOUTHERN COTTON OIL CO., To all managers trading posts.
Columbia, S. C., November 23, 1929.
GENTLEMEN: I talked to all of you to-day over the telephone about wagon markets. We want you to see to it that contract buyers buying seed for you under your direction adhere strictly to the prices quoted them by you.
We think that prices we are quoting for cottonseed in wagon lots and in car lots are high enough based on the present markets for products. Competitors may think otherwise, and you may find that in some places competitors are paying more than you are for wagon seed.
Regardless of that, we want you to instruct your buyers to pay prices named by you and no more. Of course if you find a competitor is taking seed away from you at points where you have buyers, I want you to notify me by telephone and I will tell you whether or not we care to meet the competition.
In South Carolina for the coming week unless there should be further changes in the market you are to quote for wagon your wagon buyers as follows: In districts 1, 2, and 3, $26 per ton.
District No. 4, the chemists' reports shows that seed is subject to a discount of 6.42 per cent, which means $2 per ton off the market for prime seed, or $26.
District No. 4 embraces the counties of Abbeville, Aiken, Edgefield, Greenwood, Mccormick, Newberry, and Saluda.
In district No. 5 the discount is 15.24 per cent, which means $4 per ton off prime prices of $24 per ton for wagon seed. This district embraces counties of Calhoun, Clarendon, Richland, Lee, Lexington, and Sumter.
In district No. 7 the discount is 17.81 per cent, or $5 per ton off the prime price, which means $23 per ton for wagon seed. This district embraces the counties of Allendale, Bamberg, Barnwell, Beaufort, Berkeley, Charleston, Colleton, Dorchester, and Jasper.
The discount in districts Nos. 1, 2, and 3, are not sufficient to justify any deduction from the prime price and you may, therefore, quote $28 per ton for wagon seed in these districts.
In case there should be any change in the products markets warranting changes in wagon prices we are offering for cottonseed during the coming week, the above discounts will still apply to the basis prime price for wagon seed.
Seed in carloads or carlots received, no matter where bought, is to be settled for on the actual analysis that that particular carload or carlots, upon receipt of report from the public chemist, shows to be the analysis of the carload or carlot in question.
There were no samples received by the public chemist from district No. 6 which includes Georgetown and Williamsburg Counties only. These counties are in the lower Eastern part of the State and no doubt the seed are badly off and if you have any wagon buyers in these two points you will please discount the prime price by at least $5 per ton.
Yours very truly, C. C. FISHBURNE.
P. S. I have no copy of the public chemist's report for North Carolina, but no doubt you have received report by this time and know what discounts apply to that territory in which you operate. Apply discounts shown by the chemist's report in North Carolina just as I have outlined for South Carolina.-C.C.F.

C. C. FISHBURNE THE SOUTHERN COTTON OIL CO., Columbia, 8. O., January 1, 1930.
Mr. C. H. STELLING, Manager, Augusta, Ga.
DEAR SIR: We are buying wagon seed in Orangeburg County based on the public chemist's report December 27, which figured $3 off prime, or $19.
I have an analysis before me this morning of Orangeburg's receipts for December 30, showing moisture, 13; oil, 184; ammonia, 3.73; free fatty acid, 10.5. On basis of the fatty acid as shown by this analysis the deduction should be about 252 per cent, or $6 per ton off prime price for wagon seed, and instead of paying $19 in Orangeburg County, it looks as if we ought to be paying $18.
You have a buyer at Bowman, Swift (Augusta) has one in Orangeburg; so has Buckeye, and Planters, I think, also buy in Orangeburg County.
I do not see any reason why we should not tell our competitors just what our information is as regards the quality of seed down there, and ask them to check up and see how their reports compare with ours.
So far as we are concerned, I don't see how we can continue to pay as much as $19 per ton for this kind of seed.
I will be glad to hear from you.
Yours very truly, Mr. C. H. STELLING, Manager, Augusta, Ga.
